verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The Mountain All Nations Climb
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A second superscription opens a new unit, and the vision is the widest in the book so far. In the latter days the mountain of the LORD's house is established as the highest, and the nations flow to it — uphill, of their own accord, asking to be taught (vv. 2-3). Verse 4 has God arbitrating between nations until weapons are beaten into farm tools and war is no longer studied. Verse 5 turns the whole vision into an invitation for the present: come, let us walk in the light of the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: Two things make this more than a hope for peace. First, the peace is a consequence: the swords are recycled because the disputes are being settled at God's throne, so disarmament is the result of his rule rather than a route to it. Second, the nations are not conquered and not summoned — they flow, which is what water does not do uphill. Something is drawing them.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 is the model for how prophecy is meant to work on a reader. The vision is not offered for admiration at a distance; it is turned immediately into a step to take today. The light is coming, therefore walk in it now.

verseByVerse.quote: The word that Isaiah the son of Amoz saw concerning Judah and Jerusalem. It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it, and many peoples shall come, and say: "Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths." For out of Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"It shall come to pass in the latter days that the mountain of the house of the LORD shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be lifted up above the hills; and all the nations shall flow to it."

Zion is not a high mountain. Anyone who has been to Jerusalem knows it is outclassed by the hills around it, and any Israelite knew it too. So this is not a claim about geology. It is a claim about which authority will finally be visibly on top.

And the verb is the surprise: the nations flow to it. Water does not flow uphill. Isaiah has chosen an image that cannot happen in nature to describe peoples moving toward God — not marched, not conquered, not summoned, but pouring upward as if gravity had been reversed.

"And many peoples shall come, and say: 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, to the house of the God of Jacob, that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.'"

Listen to who is speaking. Not Israel inviting the nations — the nations inviting each other. They are recruiting one another to go and be taught by a God who was not theirs.

And what they want is instruction. Not prosperity, not protection, not a share of the land: that he may teach us his ways. The thing the nations turn out to have been starving for is not power but knowing how to live.

"For out of Zion shall go the law, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem."

The traffic runs both ways in the same verse. They come up; the word goes out. Which is what happened, from that city, when men who had been taught there were sent to the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore. O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes for many peoples; and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war anymore."

The most famous sentence in the chapter, and the order inside it is usually missed. The disarmament comes second. First God arbitrates — he shall judge between the nations, and shall decide disputes — and only then do the weapons get melted down.

That is not naive pacifism, and it is not a policy proposal. Nations do not disarm and then discover peace; they disarm because their quarrels are being settled somewhere else by someone whose verdict holds. Take away the judge and the ploughshares go straight back to being swords. Peace here is a by-product of a throne.

And the metalwork is exact. A sword becomes a ploughshare and a spear becomes a pruning hook — the same iron, reheated, hammered into a tool for growing food. Nothing is thrown away. The materials of killing become the materials of feeding.

"Neither shall they learn war anymore." War is a discipline: it is studied, taught, funded, rehearsed. Somewhere in every generation people are being trained in it. Isaiah promises a world where the syllabus is simply dropped.

"O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the LORD."

And then, without a pause, the vision turns into an instruction for this afternoon. The nations said come, let us go up; Isaiah says come, let us walk. If that is where history is going, then start living in that direction now — which is the only proper use of any promise about the future.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–22 — The Day Against Everything Tall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The reversal is total. Where the nations climbed toward God in verse 3, here people burrow into holes to get away from him. Verses 6 to 8 name what filled the land instead: imported divination, silver and gold without end, horses and chariots without number, and idols they made and then bowed to. Verses 10 to 16 announce a day against everything high — cedars, oaks, mountains, towers, walls, ships — with the refrain that the LORD alone will be exalted. Verses 18 to 21 have the idols thrown to moles and bats, and verse 22 draws the practical conclusion.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is principled rather than arbitrary: it falls on height as such, because pride is the sin that makes a creature into a rival. The catalogue moves deliberately from what God grew (cedars, mountains) to what men built (towers, walls, ships), and both come down under the same sentence — which says that the problem was never the thing but the trust placed in it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 20 is one of the sharpest pictures in the prophets: men flinging their silver and gold idols to the moles and the bats as they run. The objects were expensive, carefully made, and worth nothing at the only moment when it mattered — and they are thrown to creatures that live in the dark underground, which is where they belonged all along.

verseByVerse.quote: For you have rejected your people, the house of Jacob, because they are full of things from the east and of fortune-tellers like the Philistines, and they strike hands with the children of foreigners. Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is filled with horses, and there is no end to their chariots. Their land is filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their hands, to what their own fingers have made.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For you have rejected your people, the house of Jacob, because they are full of things from the east and of fortune-tellers like the Philistines, and they strike hands with the children of foreigners."

The vision breaks off and the present arrives. The word full is going to be repeated three times in as many verses, and each time it names something that has taken up the space God should occupy.

Full of things from the east — imported divination, the horoscopes and omen-readers of Mesopotamia. Fortune-tellers like the Philistines. A people who have God's own word are buying their future from anyone who will sell it.

"Their land is filled with silver and gold, and there is no end to their treasures; their land is filled with horses, and there is no end to their chariots."

Full a second time, and a third — and this is the striking part. Silver, gold, horses, chariots: these are not sins. Every one is a blessing, and Isaiah is writing during a period of real prosperity. What he flags is the phrase no end, twice. The problem is not that they have these things. It is that the accumulation has no stopping point, which is the surest sign that something has stopped being useful and started being trusted.

"Their land is filled with idols; they bow down to the work of their own hands, to what their own fingers have made."

And the fourth filling names what the first three were leading to. Notice how carefully Isaiah puts it: the work of their own hands, what their own fingers have made. A man makes a thing and then kneels to it. Every idolatry in the chapter has that shape, and most idolatries since have kept it — we build the thing, and then we need it, and then we serve it.

verseByVerse.quote: So man is humbled, and each one is brought low— do not forgive them! Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty. The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"So man is humbled, and each one is brought low — do not forgive them!"

A hard line, and it is the prophet speaking rather than God: Isaiah has looked at verse 8 and cannot ask for a pardon. Leave it uncomfortable. A man who has watched his own people kneel to what their fingers made does not always find the gracious sentence first.

"Enter into the rock and hide in the dust from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty."

And here is the reversal that governs the rest of the chapter. In verse 3 the nations went up the mountain. Here God's own people go down — into rock crevices, into dust, looking for somewhere low enough to be missed.

It is the same God in both scenes. The difference is not in him; it is entirely in whether his arrival is what you have been waiting for or what you have been avoiding.

"The haughty looks of man shall be brought low, and the lofty pride of men shall be humbled, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day."

That last clause is the refrain of the chapter and it will come round again in verse 17. The LORD alone will be exalted.

Read it as a statement of fact rather than a threat and it becomes something to rest on. There is exactly one throne, and the competition for it is imaginary. Everything currently standing tall — every reputation, empire, portfolio and self-assessment — is scheduled to be levelled, not out of spite, but because only one thing in the universe is actually high, and on that day it will be obvious.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up—and it shall be brought low; against all the cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up; and against all the oaks of Bashan; against all the lofty mountains, and against all the uplifted hills; against every high tower, and against every fortified wall; against all the ships of Tarshish, and against all the beautiful craft.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the LORD of hosts has a day against all that is proud and lofty, against all that is lifted up — and it shall be brought low."

The catalogue that follows is one of the great lists in the prophets, and the sequence matters.

It begins with what God grew. The cedars of Lebanon, lofty and lifted up — the timber kings sent ships for, the wood of palaces and temples, the most magnificent living thing in that world. The oaks of Bashan. All the lofty mountains and all the uplifted hills.

Then it moves to what men built. Every high tower, and every fortified wall — the whole apparatus of security, the things a city puts up so it can sleep. All the ships of Tarshish — the ocean-going merchantmen that ran the length of the Mediterranean, the visible symbol of a trading economy. And all the beautiful craft.

Nature and culture, the grown and the constructed, the military and the commercial. And the same verdict falls on all of it, because Isaiah is not listing bad things. There is nothing wrong with a cedar, a wall, or a ship.

What they have in common is height. Every item on the list is something a person looks up at, and looking up is the problem, because a creature only has so much of it and every bit spent on a cedar or a share price is taken from somewhere else.

God does not have a day against wickedness in this passage. He has a day against tallness — and the reason is given in the next verse.

verseByVerse.quote: And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. And the idols shall utterly pass away. And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the haughtiness of man shall be humbled, and the lofty pride of men shall be brought low, and the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. And the idols shall utterly pass away."

The refrain returns, word for word, and now the reason for the whole catalogue is plain. The cedars and the towers and the ships were never the point; they were what the haughtiness was standing on. Cut down the platform and the pride has nowhere to be.

And then, in half a line, the idols are disposed of: they utterly pass away. Not defeated, not argued with. They simply stop existing, the way a shadow stops existing when the thing casting it is moved. Isaiah gives the gods of the nations five words and does not look back at them.

"And people shall enter the caves of the rocks and the holes of the ground, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth."

The men who were looking up at cedars are now underground looking for a hole.

And notice what drives them there. Not fire, not armies, not a plague — the splendor of his majesty. It is the sheer beauty and weight of God that they cannot stand in front of. The same glory that draws the nations up a mountain in verse 3 sends these men into the rocks in verse 19, and nothing about the glory has changed between the two verses.

What a person does when God finally becomes unmistakable is the most revealing thing about him, and there are only two options in this chapter: climb, or hide.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats, to enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day mankind will cast away their idols of silver and their idols of gold, which they made for themselves to worship, to the moles and to the bats."

The picture is almost comic and entirely serious. Men running for the caves, and as they run, throwing away the gods.

Isaiah keeps every detail that makes it bite. Idols of silver and idols of gold — these cost a great deal. Which they made for themselves to worship — they were not inherited or imposed; each man commissioned his own. And now they are being flung aside as dead weight by the very people who paid for them, because when you are running for a hole in the ground you do not carry anything that cannot help you.

That is the whole argument against idolatry in one gesture, and it needs no theology. The test of what a thing is worth is what you do with it on the worst day.

"To the moles and to the bats." The gods end up with the creatures of the dark, blind things that live under the ground and in the roof space. It is a contemptuous line and it is also a placement: they have finally been put where they belong.

"To enter the caverns of the rocks and the clefts of the cliffs, from before the terror of the LORD, and from the splendor of his majesty, when he rises to terrify the earth."

The verse ends where verse 19 ended, with the same words, because the point does not change with repetition. Everything the chapter has listed — silver, gold, cedars, towers, ships, idols — is being abandoned by men looking for a rock to get behind. Only one thing is standing.

verseByVerse.quote: Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Stop regarding man in whose nostrils is breath, for of what account is he?"

One verse, and it is the practical landing of everything above it. After the mountain, the ploughshares, the catalogue of tall things and the men in the caves, the instruction is short enough to act on: stop.

And the phrase Isaiah chooses is deliberately physical. Man in whose nostrils is breath. Not man who is weak, or foolish, or unreliable — man who is currently breathing, which is a description of everybody and a reminder that the whole arrangement is tenanted. The words go straight back to the second chapter of Genesis, where God breathed into a man's nostrils the breath of life. That is what a human being is: dust with borrowed air in it, and the loan is not disclosed in advance.

"Of what account is he?" The answer expected is none — and it needs a careful hand, because this book insists everywhere that people matter enormously to God. What is being denied is not human worth but human weight: the reliability of a creature as something to build a life on.

Which is a mercy as much as a warning. A great deal of disappointment comes from having put more onto a person than a person can carry — a leader, a spouse, a parent, a mentor, oneself. Verse 22 does not say they are worthless. It says they breathe, and that everything resting on them rests on that.

The chapter began with nations flowing uphill to be taught by God, and ends by telling his own people to stop leaning on men. Between the two stands the sentence it says twice: the LORD alone will be exalted in that day. He is the only one who is not borrowing his next breath.

3.subtitle: Judgment on Jerusalem's Leaders
3.intro: Overview. Chapter 3 works out a specific form of divine judgment: the withdrawal of good leadership. When God removes his blessing from a society, one of the earliest signs is the collapse of wise governance — boys become princes, the incompetent are elevated, the social order unravels from the top. The second half of the chapter turns to the women of Zion — not to single them out but because their pride and extravagance are a precise symptom of a society that has turned entirely inward, using wealth as a measure of worth while justice goes unsought.

keyVerse.quote: “Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.”
keyVerse.note: These two verses in the middle of unrelenting judgment are a reminder that Isaiah's God is not random or arbitrary in his dealings. The moral universe holds. Whatever suffering the righteous endure in a corrupt society, the final word over their lives is well. This is not optimism but eschatological certainty — and it is enough to make perseverance possible.

3.reflection: Chapter 3 is uncomfortable precisely because its diagnoses are recognisable across every generation: bad governance as divine judgment, normalised shamelessness, the powerful exploiting the poor, status-display substituting for character. The pastoral response is not despair but the posture of verses 10–11: keep trusting that it shall be well with the righteous, and keep doing good.
3.text: <sup>1</sup>For behold, the Lord GOD of hosts is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and supply, all support of bread, and all support of water;<sup>2</sup>the mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder,<sup>3</sup>the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms.<sup>4</sup>And I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them.<sup>5</sup>And the people will oppress one another, every one his fellow and every one his neighbor; the youth will be insolent to the elder, and the despised to the honorable.<sup>6</sup>For a man will take hold of his brother in the house of his father, saying: "You have a cloak; you shall be our leader, and this heap of ruins shall be under your rule";<sup>7</sup>in that day he will speak out, saying: "I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me leader of the people."<sup>8</sup>For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their speech and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence.<sup>9</sup>For the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. Woe to them! For they have brought evil on themselves.<sup>10</sup>Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.<sup>11</sup>Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him.<sup>12</sup>My people— infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, your guides mislead you and they have swallowed up the course of your paths.<sup>13</sup>The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples.<sup>14</sup>The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people: "It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses.<sup>15</sup>What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?" declares the Lord GOD of hosts.<sup>16</sup>The LORD said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet,<sup>17</sup>therefore the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts.<sup>18</sup>In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents;<sup>19</sup>the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves;<sup>20</sup>the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets;<sup>21</sup>the signet rings and nose rings;<sup>22</sup>the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags;<sup>23</sup>the mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils.<sup>24</sup>Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty.<sup>25</sup>Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle.<sup>26</sup>And her gates shall lament and mourn; empty, she shall sit on the ground.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — When God Removes the Grown-Ups
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Judgment here does not arrive as an army. It arrives as a withdrawal. Verses 1 to 3 have God removing supply and support and then every kind of competent person — soldier, judge, prophet, elder, craftsman — and verse 4 names what is left: boys as princes. Verses 5 to 8 show the society turning on itself and nobody willing to take charge. Verse 9 says the shame has gone. Verses 10 and 11 hold two steady sentences about outcomes, and verses 13 to 15 have God rising in court to charge the leaders with the spoil of the poor.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology is that competent leadership, wisdom and skill are gifts rather than achievements, and can be withdrawn. A nation does not usually lose them dramatically; it simply finds one day that the serious people are gone and nobody is willing to hold anything. Verse 9 marks the point of no self-correction: when sin is proclaimed rather than hidden, the instinct that made repentance possible has been lost.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 10 and 11 are the most useful thing in the chapter for anyone living through institutional collapse. They do not promise the righteous an exemption from the chaos — the chapter is full of it. They promise that the moral universe has not been suspended, which is exactly what such times make people doubt.

verseByVerse.quote: For behold, the Lord GOD of hosts is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and supply, all support of bread, and all support of water; the mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder, the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms. And I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, the Lord GOD of hosts is taking away from Jerusalem and from Judah support and supply, all support of bread, and all support of water."

Notice the verb the whole chapter turns on. Not sending — taking away. The judgment in this chapter is a subtraction, and it begins with bread and water, the two things a city cannot do without for a week.

"The mighty man and the soldier, the judge and the prophet, the diviner and the elder, the captain of fifty and the man of rank, the counselor and the skillful magician and the expert in charms."

Then the people. Read the list slowly and it is a functioning society being dismantled by category: the men who fight, the men who decide cases, the men who advise, the men who know a trade. Even the fraudulent professions go; a nation losing its charm-sellers has still lost the people it was relying on.

These are not villains being punished. They are competences being removed — and every one of them is a gift, held on loan, which nobody notices until it is gone.

"And I will make boys their princes, and infants shall rule over them."

The result is not tyranny but immaturity in charge. Isaiah is not insulting the young; he is describing leadership without the weight that years and the fear of God are supposed to produce — decisions made by people who have no idea what they are handling, reacting to the last thing that happened.

That is the judgment. Not an invader at the gate, but a room full of people who are not up to it, and no one else available.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people will oppress one another, every one his fellow and every one his neighbor; the youth will be insolent to the elder, and the despised to the honorable. For a man will take hold of his brother in the house of his father, saying: "You have a cloak; you shall be our leader, and this heap of ruins shall be under your rule"; in that day he will speak out, saying: "I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me leader of the people." For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their speech and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence. For the look on their faces bears witness against them; they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. Woe to them! For they have brought evil on themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the people will oppress one another, every one his fellow and every one his neighbor; the youth will be insolent to the elder, and the despised to the honorable."

With nobody holding the structures, the pressure turns sideways. The word is oppress, and the objects are his fellow and his neighbour — not foreigners, not enemies. When a society stops functioning, people do not become cruel to strangers first. They become cruel to whoever is nearest.

"For a man will take hold of his brother in the house of his father, saying: 'You have a cloak; you shall be our leader.'"

The scene is almost comic and entirely desperate. The qualification for high office has become owning a coat. And the man seized replies: "I will not be a healer; in my house there is neither bread nor cloak; you shall not make me leader of the people."

Nobody wants it. That is the mark of a collapse that has gone past a certain point — authority stops being contested and starts being refused, because everyone can see there is nothing left to lead with.

"For Jerusalem has stumbled, and Judah has fallen, because their speech and their deeds are against the LORD, defying his glorious presence."

"They proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it."

And there is the diagnosis, and it is not the size of the sin but the loss of the instinct to conceal it. Shame is an unattractive thing and it is also a signal that somebody still knows the standard. Isaiah's point is that the hiding had stopped — which means the standard had gone, and with it any vocabulary for repentance. It is the same descent Paul traces to its end in Romans 1, where people not only do such things but approve of those who practise them.

verseByVerse.quote: Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him. My people— infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, your guides mislead you and they have swallowed up the course of your paths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Tell the righteous that it shall be well with them, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds. Woe to the wicked! It shall be ill with him, for what his hands have dealt out shall be done to him."

Two verses of daylight, dropped into the middle of a collapsing chapter without explanation, and they are the most useful thing in it.

Note carefully what they do not say. They do not promise the righteous an exemption from the chaos — the boys are still in charge, the bread is still gone, and the righteous are living in the same city as everyone else. What is promised is an outcome: it shall be well with them.

That is precisely the thing that becomes hard to believe when institutions fail and the worst people prosper. The daily evidence says that integrity is a losing strategy and that nobody is keeping accounts. These two verses say the accounts are being kept, and that a person will in the end eat the fruit of what he actually did.

"My people — infants are their oppressors, and women rule over them. O my people, your guides mislead you, and they have swallowed up the course of your paths."

Then back to the ruin, with the tenderest possible address running through it: my people, twice in one verse, of a nation being described as ungovernable. He has not stopped calling them his.

And the charge against the guides is exact. They have swallowed up the course of your paths — not merely given bad directions, but consumed the road, so that there is no longer a way to walk even for those who want to.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples. The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people: "It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses. What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor?" declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD has taken his place to contend; he stands to judge peoples."

The courtroom of chapter 1 reconvenes, and the posture is described twice — he has taken his place, he stands. A judge sitting is deliberating. A judge standing is about to deliver.

"The LORD will enter into judgment with the elders and princes of his people."

And he goes for the leadership. Not the nation in general, not the young men insulting their elders in verse 5 — the elders and princes, the people who had the power to prevent what happened and used it to profit from it instead.

"It is you who have devoured the vineyard, the spoil of the poor is in your houses."

Two images, and both are physical. Devoured the vineyard — chapter 5 is coming, where the vineyard turns out to be Israel itself, and these men have eaten it. And then the sentence that requires no interpretation at all: the spoil of the poor is in your houses.

Not in your policies. In your houses. God names the location of the stolen goods, and it is where these men eat dinner. Every comfortable object in the room came from somebody who could not stop them taking it.

"What do you mean by crushing my people, by grinding the face of the poor? declares the Lord GOD of hosts."

And then a question, which is worse than a verdict. What do you mean by it? — the incredulity of someone who cannot make sense of what he is looking at.

The image is a millstone: a face pressed into the grinding surface and turned. It is one of the most violent pictures in the prophets, and it describes what these men would have called ordinary business — foreclosures, wages withheld, cases quietly not heard. God watches respectable commerce and describes it as a face under a stone.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter narrows to the women of Zion, walking with outstretched necks and tinkling anklets (v. 16), and God answers with a list. Verses 18 to 23 itemise twenty-one articles of finery — anklets, headbands, crescents, pendants, bracelets, scarves, headdresses, sashes, perfume boxes, amulets, signet rings, nose rings, festal robes, cloaks, handbags, mirrors, linen garments, turbans, veils. Verse 24 reverses five of them one by one, and verses 25 and 26 leave the city sitting on the ground.
verseByVerse.theology: This is not disapproval of ornament. Isaiah has spent fifteen verses on judges who took bribes and princes with the spoil of the poor in their houses, and the inventory belongs to that argument: the wealth is on display because the wealth is the point. What is indicted is an economy in which worth is signalled rather than possessed — and the reversals of verse 24 undo it item by item, in the same order.
verseByVerse.examples: The last image is the most affecting in the chapter. After twenty-one named luxuries and five paired reversals, the city has nothing left to say: empty, she shall sit on the ground. Every substitute for God arrives eventually at the same posture.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said: Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet, therefore the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because the daughters of Zion are haughty and walk with outstretched necks, glancing wantonly with their eyes, mincing along as they go, tinkling with their feet."

Isaiah moves from the courts to the street, and what he describes is a walk. Necks stretched to gain height. Eyes working the crowd. Short deliberate steps. And ankle ornaments made to be heard, so that people look before they can see who is coming.

Every detail is about being noticed. This is not a description of women enjoying themselves; it is a description of a performance, and the performance is the point.

Read it in its place in the chapter and the connection is unmistakable. Fifteen verses ago the spoil of the poor was in these houses; now it is walking down the street on display. The finery is the proceeds. What Isaiah objects to is not that these women look good but that a whole economy of worth has been built on looking good, and it is being funded by faces held under a millstone.

"Therefore the Lord will strike with a scab the heads of the daughters of Zion, and the LORD will lay bare their secret parts."

The judgment is deliberately aimed at the display. What was elevated is made repellent; what was arranged to be seen is exposed. It is harsh, and it is the exact shape of the offence: a life organised around being looked at is judged by being looked at.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves; the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; the signet rings and nose rings; the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags; the mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the Lord will take away the finery of the anklets, the headbands, and the crescents; the pendants, the bracelets, and the scarves; the headdresses, the armlets, the sashes, the perfume boxes, and the amulets; the signet rings and nose rings; the festal robes, the mantles, the cloaks, and the handbags; the mirrors, the linen garments, the turbans, and the veils."

Twenty-one items, named one after another with no comment attached, and the effect of the list is the argument. Isaiah could have written "their jewellery". Instead he inventories it, like a bailiff going through a house.

Some of it is unexpectedly specific. Crescents and amulets are religious objects — lunar charms and things worn to ward off harm, which means the idolatry of chapter 2 is being worn as an accessory. Perfume boxes, signet rings, handbags, mirrors: this is not a peasant economy. Somebody is importing.

And the verb governing all twenty-one is the verb the chapter opened with: the Lord will take away. It is the same word used in verse 1 of the bread and the water and the judges. God removes the essentials and the ornaments with the same hand and in the same tone, which puts them, disconcertingly, in one category.

The list is long on purpose. Read at length it stops sounding like wealth and starts sounding like weight — an enormous accumulation of small things, each one acquired to say something about the person wearing it, and the whole collection unable to say anything at all on the day it is itemised.

verseByVerse.quote: Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty. Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle. And her gates shall lament and mourn; empty, she shall sit on the ground.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Instead of perfume there will be rottenness; and instead of a belt, a rope; and instead of well-set hair, baldness; and instead of a rich robe, a skirt of sackcloth; and branding instead of beauty."

Five exchanges, and each one is the exact opposite of the item it replaces. Perfume for rot. A worked belt for a length of rope. Arranged hair for a shaved head. A fine robe for sackcloth. And beauty for a brand — the mark burned into a slave.

The symmetry is the message. Nothing arbitrary is happening; the judgment is shaped precisely to the thing judged, and it works down the same list in the same order. What was put on comes off, and what replaces it is what was underneath the whole time.

"Your men shall fall by the sword and your mighty men in battle. And her gates shall lament and mourn; empty, she shall sit on the ground."

The chapter ends with a single figure. The city, personified as a woman — the one who was walking with an outstretched neck and tinkling anklets — is now on the ground.

Empty, and sitting in the dirt. It is the posture of a mourner, and it is also simply what is left when everything a person was carrying has been taken. No jewellery, no performance, nobody watching, nothing to say.

That is where every substitute for God eventually puts a person, and the chapter is honest enough to stop there rather than hurry to the comfort. But Isaiah has arranged his book so that the next word after this is in that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious — and the beauty in that sentence is not something anyone puts on.

3.theology:
Judgment as subtraction. Nothing invades in this chapter. God takes away — bread, water, and then every competent person in the society, until boys are princes and nobody will accept office. The premise is that leadership, wisdom, skill and even ordinary maturity are gifts held on loan rather than achievements, and their removal is itself the judgment. A nation rarely loses them dramatically; it discovers one day that the serious people have gone.

The end of shame. Verse 9 marks the point past which self-correction is no longer available: they proclaim their sin like Sodom; they do not hide it. Shame is unattractive and it is also evidence that somebody still knows the standard. When the hiding stops, the standard has gone — and with it the vocabulary repentance needs. Paul traces the same descent to the same end in Romans 1.

Two verses that hold. Verses 10 and 11 sit inside the ruin and promise the righteous no exemption from it. What they promise is that outcomes are still real — it shall be well with them — which is precisely what collapse makes people doubt. And the inventory of vv. 18-23 belongs to the same argument rather than to prudishness: fifteen verses earlier the spoil of the poor was in these houses, and now it is walking down the street.

4.subtitle: The Branch of the LORD
4.intro: Overview. Chapter 4 is only six verses — a brief but essential shaft of light after the darkness of chapter 3. Without it, the reader might conclude that Isaiah's God is nothing but a judge. Embedded here is one of the earliest Messianic titles in the book: the Branch of the LORD. The movement is from desolation (v. 1) to beauty and glory (vv. 2–6), from stripping to clothing, from exposure to shelter. What judgment removes, grace restores — and more than restores.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: The title “Branch” introduced here is one of the richest Messianic descriptions in the Old Testament. It suggests organic growth — something that grows naturally from existing roots rather than arriving as an alien intrusion. Jesus is not an afterthought to Israel's story; he grows from it, as a branch from a tree. And in him, what was laid waste becomes beautiful again.

4.theology:
The Branch. Verse 2 introduces the first messianic title in the book — tsemach, a growth or sprout — and later prophets build on it: Jeremiah’s righteous Branch (Jer. 23:5) and Zechariah’s king-priest who builds the temple (Zech. 6:12-13). Here he is beautiful and glorious, which should be held beside 53:2, where the same book describes a servant with no form or majesty that anyone should look at him. Both are said of one person, and the New Testament keeps both.

A remnant that was written down and washed. The survivors of verse 3 are recorded for life — a register, a name entered in advance — and they are called holy on the strength of what verse 4 says was done to them: the Lord washed the filth and cleansed the bloodstains. Every verb belongs to God. This is the smelting of 1:25 applied to people, and it is not gentle: a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.

The canopy. The cloud and fire that led Israel out of Egypt and settled over one tent now cover the whole of Mount Zion and all her assemblies — the presence decentralised from a building and a priesthood to a people. The word for the covering is the one used of a wedding chamber, and the booth for shade and shelter answers the flimsy hut left standing in the stripped field at 1:8. Revelation 21:3 states its final form.
4.reflection: Chapter 4 is the antidote to despair after the severity of chapters 1–3. Judgment is real; the stripping is real. But the Branch of the LORD is also real — and he is coming. The community that will receive him is not the proudest or most impressive, but the survivors: those who have been through the fire and found that God was in it.
4.text: <sup>1</sup>And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach."<sup>2</sup>In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel.<sup>3</sup>And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem,<sup>4</sup>when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning.<sup>5</sup>Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy.<sup>6</sup>There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — Seven Women and One Man
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A single verse, and it belongs with the end of chapter 3 rather than with what follows. Seven women take hold of one man and offer to feed and clothe themselves if he will only let them carry his name and take away their reproach. It is a picture of demographic collapse after a war — the men of verse 25 have fallen — and of what that does to ordinary life.
verseByVerse.theology: The verse exists to be read before verse 2 rather than skipped on the way to it. Isaiah's comfort characteristically arrives into a specific desolation and not over the top of it, and the beauty of the Branch is felt in proportion to the ground it grows out of.
verseByVerse.examples: What the women ask for is telling: not support, which they offer to provide themselves, but a name and the removal of reproach. Childlessness and widowhood carried a public shame in that world, and shame is the thing money cannot settle.

verseByVerse.quote: And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, "We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And seven women shall take hold of one man in that day, saying, 'We will eat our own bread and wear our own clothes, only let us be called by your name; take away our reproach.'"

The chapter division is unhelpful here. This verse finishes chapter 3, where the men of Jerusalem fell by the sword, and it shows what that looks like a year later.

Seven women to one man. Seven is the number of completeness, so this is not an unusual case being reported but a condition being described: a generation of men is gone, and the ordinary machinery of family life has stopped.

Listen to what they offer and what they ask. They will provide their own food and their own clothing — the two things a husband was legally obliged to supply. They are asking for nothing that costs him anything. What they want is his name, and one other thing: take away our reproach.

In that society a woman without a husband and without children carried a public shame, and it is the shame rather than the poverty that these women cannot bear. They have solved the economics themselves. They cannot solve the disgrace.

Pause on that before the glory of the next verse, because Isaiah put it here deliberately. His comfort always arrives into a specific darkness rather than over the top of it, and the ground the Branch grows out of is this one.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–6 — The Branch and the Canopy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything changes at in that day. Verse 2 introduces the Branch of the LORD, beautiful and glorious, with the fruit of the land as the pride of the survivors. Verse 3 says those left in Zion will be called holy, everyone recorded for life. Verse 4 explains how — the Lord washes the filth away by a spirit of judgment and burning. Verses 5 and 6 put a cloud by day and a flaming fire by night over the whole of Mount Zion, with a canopy over the glory, for shade and shelter and a hiding place.
verseByVerse.theology: Branch (Hebrew tsemach) is the first messianic title in the book, and later prophets take it up: Jeremiah's righteous Branch who executes justice (Jer. 23:5), Zechariah's king-priest who builds the temple (Zech. 6:12-13). And recorded for life is election language — the survivors are not the lucky but the written-down, and verse 4 says plainly that they were washed rather than clean.
verseByVerse.examples: The cloud and fire of verses 5 and 6 are the wilderness pillar, and the change is the point: what once stood over one tent now covers a whole community, and it is described as a canopy — the word used of a wedding chamber. Revelation 21:3 gives the final form: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel. And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the branch of the LORD shall be beautiful and glorious, and the fruit of the land shall be the pride and honor of the survivors of Israel."

Three words in and the whole book changes direction. In that day — the same formula that has been introducing disasters since chapter 2 now introduces a person.

The word is tsemach, a sprout or growth, and this is its first appearance as a title in Scripture. Isaiah will develop it into the shoot from the stump of Jesse in chapter 11; Jeremiah will call him a righteous Branch who executes justice in the land (Jer. 23:5); Zechariah will use it of a king who is also a priest and builds the temple of God (Zech. 6:12-13). It starts here, in one line, at the bottom of a ruined chapter.

And what is said about him is beautiful and glorious. Hold that, because forty-nine chapters later the same book will describe a servant with "no form or majesty that we should look at him, and no beauty that we should desire him" (53:2). Both are descriptions of the same person at different points, and the New Testament keeps both: the one who emptied himself, and the one whose face was like the sun shining in full strength.

"And he who is left in Zion and remains in Jerusalem will be called holy, everyone who has been recorded for life in Jerusalem."

The survivors are not survivors by luck. Recorded for life is the language of a register — a name written down in advance — and Scripture keeps using it right to the end, where the book of life is opened. These people are called holy, which is not a description of how they behaved. The next verse explains where the holiness came from.

verseByVerse.quote: when the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning. Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night; for over all the glory there will be a canopy. There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the Lord shall have washed away the filth of the daughters of Zion and cleansed the bloodstains of Jerusalem from its midst by a spirit of judgment and by a spirit of burning."

Here is why they are called holy in verse 3, and it is entirely done to them. The Lord washes; the Lord cleanses. The two things removed are the two things chapter 3 was about — the filth of the daughters of Zion, the display and the status economy behind it, and the bloodstains, which were on the hands lifted in prayer back in 1:15.

And note the instruments: a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning. The cleansing is not gentle and it is not a passing over. It is the smelting of 1:25 applied to people, and what comes out the other side is a community that can be called holy.

"Then the LORD will create over the whole site of Mount Zion and over her assemblies a cloud by day, and smoke and the shining of a flaming fire by night."

Every Israelite knew this picture. The pillar of cloud and fire had gone in front of them out of Egypt, and had settled over the tabernacle — one cloud, over one tent, where the priests went in and everyone else stayed outside.

What is promised here is the same presence over the whole site and over her assemblies — the entire community, not a building and not a caste. The thing that used to be concentrated in a tent is spread over everybody.

"For over all the glory there will be a canopy. There will be a booth for shade by day from the heat, and for a refuge and a shelter from the storm and rain."

The word for canopy is the one used of a wedding chamber, and the word for booth is the same as the flimsy hut in the stripped vineyard back at 1:8 — but now it is God's, and it holds. Shade in the heat, cover in the storm: the two things a person outdoors actually needs.

Where chapter 3 left a city sitting empty on the ground, chapter 4 leaves a people under a canopy with the glory of God overhead. And the last word on it comes at the end of the Bible, in the same imagery: behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and he will dwell with them (Rev. 21:3).

5.subtitle: The Song of the Vineyard and the Six Woes
5.intro: Overview. Chapter 5 is one of Isaiah's most accomplished literary compositions. It opens with a love song that turns into a lawsuit (vv. 1–7), catalogues six specific moral and social sins with the prophetic “Woe” associated with funeral laments (vv. 8–23), and closes with a vision of judgment so swift it leaves no room for delay (vv. 24–30). Jesus knew this chapter intimately; his parable of the tenants in Matthew 21 is a direct retelling of the vineyard song, using the same rhetorical strategy of drawing hearers into passing judgment before they realise they are the ones in the dock.

keyVerse.quote: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!”
keyVerse.note: This woe does not describe a society that has forgotten God's standards but one that has actively inverted them. The triple parallelism (evil/good, darkness/light, bitter/sweet) emphasises that this is comprehensive and deliberate. Once a culture reaches this stage, self-correction from within is almost impossible — the moral vocabulary needed for repentance has been destroyed. Only a word from outside the system can break through.

5.theology:
The song that convicts the audience. Isaiah uses Nathan’s method: sing a charming ballad about somebody else’s vineyard, get the crowd to deliver a verdict, then name the defendant. The question in verse 4 — what more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done in it? — closes every exit in advance, because most excuses for fruitlessness are versions of I was not given enough. And verse 7 turns on two puns: God looked for mishpat and found mispach, for tsedaqah and found tse’aqah. One letter apart — which is the distance between what was planted and what came up. Jesus made this parable his own against the same city (Matt. 21:33-46).

The six woes as a diagnosis. Their order is deliberate. Self-wisdom (v. 21) is what makes the relabelling of good and evil (v. 20) possible, and both grow in ground prepared by the first two woes, where property and pleasure have made a class incapable of noticing what God is doing. Verse 20 is the most transferable: not moral confusion but moral renaming, which destroys the vocabulary repentance would need. Nobody reaches for a light switch that has been relabelled as the darkness.

Judgment as withdrawal, and as an army. The sentence in vv. 5-6 is mostly subtraction — the hedge removed, the wall broken, no pruning, no rain — the same shape as chapter 3. Then verses 26 to 30 show the other side: God whistles and a superpower arrives with not one sandal strap broken. He does not improvise. The chapter ends on darkness, which is the honest answer to verse 4 — and four chapters later the same voice says the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light.
5.reflection: Isaiah 5 asks the question God himself asks of the vineyard: what more could have been done? Everything was provided; nothing more could be given. The chapter is an invitation to honest self-examination — not only about the sins of society, but about the fruit one's own life is bearing for the One who planted it with such care.
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill.<sup>2</sup>He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.<sup>3</sup>And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard.<sup>4</sup>What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?<sup>5</sup>And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down.<sup>6</sup>I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it.<sup>7</sup>For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting; and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!<sup>8</sup>Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land.<sup>9</sup>The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant.<sup>10</sup>For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah."<sup>11</sup>Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them!<sup>12</sup>They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands.<sup>13</sup>Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge;
