verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah begins by singing. It is a love song about a friend's vineyard, and for six lines it is entirely charming: a fertile hillside, the stones cleared, choice vines planted, a watchtower built and a winepress cut, all in expectation of a good crop (vv. 1-2). Then the vineyard yields wild grapes, and the singer turns to the audience and asks them to judge between him and it (vv. 3-4). Verses 5 and 6 pass sentence — the hedge removed, the wall broken, no pruning, no rain. Verse 7 names the vineyard, and it is them.
verseByVerse.theology: The device is the one Nathan used on David: get the hearer to deliver a verdict before he knows he is the defendant. And the question in verse 4 — what more was there to do for my vineyard that I have not done in it? — forecloses every excuse in advance. The failure is not for want of investment, attention, or advantage.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 turns on two puns the English cannot carry. God looked for justice (mishpat) and found bloodshed (mispach); for righteousness (tsedaqah) and found an outcry (tse'aqah). The words are one letter apart, which is exactly the distance between what was planted and what came up. Jesus took this parable and made it his own against the same city (Matt. 21:33-46).

verseByVerse.quote: Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard: My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it; and he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Let me sing for my beloved my love song concerning his vineyard."

Isaiah opens by performing. This is a ballad — the kind of thing sung at a festival or a harvest supper, a song about a friend and his vineyard, and the crowd settles in to enjoy it.

"My beloved had a vineyard on a very fertile hill. He dug it and cleared it of stones, and planted it with choice vines; he built a watchtower in the midst of it, and hewed out a wine vat in it."

Every line raises the expectation. A very fertile hill — the best ground available. Dug it and cleared it of stones, which is the back-breaking part; anyone who has worked stony hill country knows what clearing a slope by hand costs. Choice vines, not ordinary stock. A watchtower, which is what you build when you expect a crop worth guarding. And a wine vat cut into the rock — a permanent installation, made in advance, for a harvest he was confident of.

Nothing has been withheld and nothing has been done cheaply. The audience is entirely on the farmer's side by now, which is the point of spending five clauses on the preparation.

"And he looked for it to yield grapes, but it yielded wild grapes."

And the song stops. The word is small and sour: wild grapes, the useless fruit of an uncultivated vine, hard and bitter and no good for wine. Every advantage, and the crop is what you would have got from ground nobody touched.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard. What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now, O inhabitants of Jerusalem and men of Judah, judge between me and my vineyard."

The singer steps out of the song and puts a question to the room, and the pronouns have quietly changed. It was my beloved's vineyard in verse 1; now it is my vineyard. Somebody else has begun speaking through the singer, and the audience is being asked for a verdict.

This is Nathan's method with David — tell a man a story about somebody else, let him pass judgment, and then tell him whose story it was. It works because moral clarity is easy at a distance. Everyone in that crowd knew exactly what they thought about a vineyard that had been given everything and produced nothing.

"What more was there to do for my vineyard, that I have not done in it? When I looked for it to yield grapes, why did it yield wild grapes?"

The first question is the one that closes every exit. What more was there to do? The honest answer is: nothing. Not more sunlight, not better vines, not a further year, not clearer instructions. The investment was complete and the failure is entirely the vineyard's.

That is a hard place for a reader to stand, and it is where the chapter intends to put him. Most excuses for a fruitless life are versions of I was not given enough — enough teaching, enough advantage, enough grace, enough time. Verse 4 asks what specifically was missing, and waits.

verseByVerse.quote: And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down. I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it. For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting; and he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down."

The sentence is not that the vineyard is uprooted or burned. It is that the protection comes off. God removes the hedge and breaks the wall — the two things that had been keeping the animals and the passers-by out — and then simply lets whatever happens happen.

"I will make it a waste; it shall not be pruned or hoed, and briers and thorns shall grow up; I will also command the clouds that they rain no rain upon it."

Then the care stops. No pruning, no hoeing — and briers and thorns come up, which is what comes up on any ground that is left alone. The last clause gives the game away about who is speaking: I will command the clouds. No farmer can do that.

Judgment in this song is largely the withdrawal of attention. It is the same shape as chapter 3, where God took things away rather than sending anything, and a striking amount of damage is done simply by God ceasing to intervene.

"For the vineyard of the LORD of hosts is the house of Israel, and the men of Judah are his pleasant planting."

Now the identification, and the crowd that just delivered a verdict discovers it was about them.

"And he looked for justice, but behold, bloodshed; for righteousness, but behold, an outcry!"

In Hebrew this line is two puns and it is unforgettable. He looked for mishpat and got mispach. He looked for tsedaqah and got tse'aqah. Each pair differs by a single letter, and that is the whole indictment: what came up looks and sounds almost exactly like what was planted, and it is the opposite of it.

And the last word is the one to sit with — an outcry. It is the noise the oppressed make, the same word used of Israel groaning in Egypt. God went into his vineyard listening for righteousness and heard people screaming.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six sentences beginning woe, and together they are a diagnosis of how a society comes apart. Verses 8 to 10: joining house to house and field to field until nobody else has anywhere to live. Verses 11 and 12: rising early for drink and filling the evening with music, so that nobody regards the deeds of the LORD. Verses 18 and 19: dragging sin along on a rope and daring God to hurry up. Verse 20: calling evil good and good evil. Verse 21: being wise in one's own eyes. Verses 22 and 23: heroes at drinking, who acquit the guilty for a bribe.
verseByVerse.theology: The order is not random. Self-wisdom (v. 21) is what makes the moral inversion of verse 20 possible, and both are downstream of the first two woes, where wealth and pleasure have made a whole class incapable of noticing what God is doing. Isaiah presents these as covenant charges rather than social commentary: Israel was called to be a society that looked like its God.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 20 travels furthest. It is not moral confusion but moral relabelling — a deliberate exchange of the words, so that darkness is filed under light and bitter under sweet. The danger is precise: a society that has renamed evil has removed the vocabulary its own repentance would need. When the switch is called the darkness, nobody goes looking for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: "Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant. For ten acres of vineyard shall yield but one bath, and a homer of seed shall yield but an ephah."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land."

The first woe is about property, and the mechanism matters because it was legal. Under the law every family held its land in perpetuity; it could not be sold away permanently, and at the Jubilee it came back. What these men are doing is buying up distressed neighbours one at a time — a bad harvest here, a debt there — and consolidating, until whole villages belong to one estate.

And Isaiah names the end state precisely: until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone. The successful accumulator finishes in an empty landscape. There is nobody left because he bought them all out, and the isolation he ends in is not a punishment added to the sin. It is the sin, arrived at its destination.

"The LORD of hosts has sworn in my hearing: 'Surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses, without inhabitant.'"

The estates end up empty, which is the only ending available. And then a farming calculation that would have made the audience wince: ten acres of vineyard will produce a single bath of wine, and a homer of seed will yield an ephah — about a tenth of what was sown.

The land itself stops cooperating. A man can acquire ground and cannot make it yield.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them! They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who rise early in the morning, that they may run after strong drink, who tarry late into the evening as wine inflames them!"

The second woe covers a whole day. Rise early and tarry late — this is not the occasional excess of people with lives; it is the entire waking timetable given over to the pursuit. Isaiah is describing dedication.

"They have lyre and harp, tambourine and flute and wine at their feasts, but they do not regard the deeds of the LORD, or see the work of his hands."

And here is the sting, and it is not what a modern reader expects. He does not condemn the music. Four instruments are named and none of them is the problem; feasting, wine and music all appear elsewhere in Scripture as gifts.

The charge is what the occupation costs them: they do not regard the deeds of the LORD. It is a charge of not noticing. God is at work in their own century — Isaiah has been announcing it at the top of his voice for four chapters — and these people have a diary too full to look up.

That is a more searching indictment than drunkenness, and it reaches a great deal further than a drinking culture. It is entirely possible to be surrounded by genuinely good things, enjoying them competently, and to be blind to the one thing happening in the room — not because the good things are evil but because attention is finite, and they have taken all of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst. Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure, and the nobility of Jerusalem and her multitude will go down, her revelers and he who exults in her. Man is humbled, and each one is brought low, and the eyes of the haughty are brought low. But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness. Then shall the lambs graze as in their pasture, and nomads shall eat among the ruins of the rich.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore my people go into exile for lack of knowledge; their honored men go hungry, and their multitude is parched with thirst."

The reason given for the exile is not idolatry or injustice, which are both in the chapter, but lack of knowledge — the same failure Isaiah opened the book with, where the ox knew its owner and Israel did not. Not ignorance of facts: the collapse of knowing whose they are.

And the reversal is exact. Men who rose early to drink are parched. The honoured go hungry. The appetite that ran their calendar in verse 11 is the appetite left unsatisfied here.

"Therefore Sheol has enlarged its appetite and opened its mouth beyond measure."

Isaiah personifies the grave as the one thing in the chapter with a bigger appetite than they had. They stretched their capacity for consumption; death stretches wider, and the nobility and the crowd go down together.

"But the LORD of hosts is exalted in justice, and the Holy God shows himself holy in righteousness."

And then, in the middle of the wreckage, a sentence that lifts. Everything in the chapter so far has been human beings failing at justice and righteousness — the vineyard produced their opposites. Here are the two words again, and this time they belong to God, and they are not failing.

He is exalted in justice. Not in spite of it, and not by suspending it. When everything human collapses, what stands up in the ruins is the holiness of God, and Isaiah puts the line here so the reader has something to look at that is not the damage.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes, who say: "Let him be quick, let him speed his work that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!" Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter! Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of falsehood, who draw sin as with cart ropes."

An odd, brilliant image. These people are not being dragged into sin; they are hauling it, in harness, like a man pulling a loaded cart uphill. Sin here takes effort. It is worked at, maintained, and towed along behind a life at considerable cost.

"Who say: 'Let him be quick, let him hasten his work, that we may see it; let the counsel of the Holy One of Israel draw near, and let it come, that we may know it!'"

And what they are towing it with is a taunt. They are daring God to do something — get on with it, then; let us see this judgment you keep announcing. The fact that nothing has happened yet is being used as evidence that nothing will.

"Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, who put bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter!"

The fourth woe is the one that travels furthest, and it is not describing confusion. Confused people are uncertain. These people are confident; they have simply swapped the labels, deliberately, in all three pairs — moral, visual, and physical.

The danger is precise. A society that has renamed evil has destroyed the vocabulary its own repentance would need. You cannot turn from something you have agreed to call good, and when the light switch has been relabelled as the darkness nobody reaches for it.

"Woe to those who are wise in their own eyes, and shrewd in their own sight!"

And the fifth woe explains the fourth. Nobody relabels good and evil by accident. It takes a settled confidence in one's own judgment, and that confidence is the root the inversion grows from. Isaiah puts them in this order on purpose.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who are heroes at drinking wine, and valiant men in mixing strong drink, who acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right!"

The last woe pairs two things that look unrelated and are not, and the joke in the first half is bitter. Heroes and valiant men are war words — the vocabulary of a soldier who holds the line. This is what the courage of the ruling class has been spent on: an impressive capacity for drink.

Then the second half, and it is where the drinking leads. These are the men who sit as judges. Acquit the guilty for a bribe, and deprive the innocent of his right — both halves of a court going wrong at once, and the second is the worse. Letting a guilty man off is a failure; taking a right away from an innocent one is theft with the law as the instrument.

The six woes are now complete, and read together they are a diagnosis rather than a list. Property accumulated until neighbours vanish. Pleasure pursued until God goes unnoticed. Sin hauled along with effort and God dared to act. Good and evil relabelled. Self-confidence underneath it all. And a bench that can be bought.

Not one of these is spectacular wickedness. Every one is respectable, and most of them are what success looks like from the outside — which is why Isaiah addressed them to a nation that considered itself to be doing rather well.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–30 — He Whistles, and They Come
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with an army on the horizon. Verses 24 and 25 give the reason — they rejected the law of the LORD of hosts — and sound for the first time the refrain that will hammer through chapters 9 and 10: his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still. Verse 26 has God raising a signal and whistling for a nation at the end of the earth. Verses 27 to 29 describe a force that never tires, whose sandal straps do not break and whose arrows are sharp. Verse 30 ends in darkness over the land.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology of the closing section is that God commands the empires he judges his people with. He does not improvise or scramble; he whistles, and a superpower arrives on schedule. That is a hard comfort and it is a comfort: what is coming is not chaos, and it is not outside his hand.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter closes on the word darkness, and it is the honest answer to the unanswerable question of verse 4. But Isaiah has arranged his book so that the same voice says, four chapters later, that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light (9:2). The night at the end of chapter 5 is not the last word and was never meant to be read as one.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel. Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them, and the mountains quaked; and their corpses were as refuse in the midst of the streets. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore, as the tongue of fire devours the stubble, and as dry grass sinks down in the flame, so their root will be as rottenness, and their blossom go up like dust; for they have rejected the law of the LORD of hosts, and have despised the word of the Holy One of Israel."

The image goes to the root, which is where a vineyard chapter has to end. What looked alive at the surface was rotten underneath, and a plant with a rotten root has nothing to be done for it — the blossom that remains goes up as dust at the first heat.

And the cause is stated without ambiguity: they rejected the law and despised the word. Under all six woes is one act. The property, the drinking, the relabelling and the bribes are symptoms of a decision about a book.

"Therefore the anger of the LORD was kindled against his people, and he stretched out his hand against them and struck them... For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still."

Here is the first sounding of a refrain that will become one of the most oppressive sounds in the book. It returns three times in chapter 9 and once more in chapter 10, and it always means the same thing: this is not finished.

The hand is stretched out. It has struck, and it has not gone back down, because the striking has not yet produced what it was sent for. As chapter 9 will say outright, the people did not turn to him who struck them — which is what the hand was reaching for the whole time.

verseByVerse.quote: He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come! None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind. Their roaring is like a lion, like young lions they roar; they growl and seize their prey; they carry it off, and none can rescue. They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He will raise a signal for nations far away, and whistle for them from the ends of the earth; and behold, quickly, speedily they come!"

God whistles, and an empire comes. It is the same gesture as chapter 7, where he whistles for the fly and the bee, and the casualness of it is the point: superpowers are summoned the way you call a dog.

"None is weary, none stumbles, none slumbers or sleeps, not a waistband is loose, not a sandal strap broken; their arrows are sharp, all their bows bent, their horses' hoofs seem like flint, and their wheels like the whirlwind."

Then five verses of terrifying competence. Read the list of what is not wrong: nobody tired, nobody tripping, nobody asleep, no belt working loose, not one sandal strap gone. Anyone who has watched an organisation try to move knows how unlikely that is. This army has no friction in it anywhere.

And it is set directly against the vineyard. There, everything was given and nothing grew. Here, nothing is out of place and everything works. The contrast is deliberate: Israel had every advantage and produced wild grapes; the instrument of her judgment arrives with its sandal straps intact.

"Their roaring is like a lion... they will growl over it and seize their prey; they will carry it off, and none can rescue."

"They will growl over it on that day, like the growling of the sea. And if one looks to the land, behold, darkness and distress; and the light is darkened by its clouds."

And the chapter ends in the dark, which is the only honest answer to what more was there to do? When everything has been given and the fruit is still wild, this is what is left.

But Isaiah has arranged his book, and four chapters further on the same voice says: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. The night at the end of the vineyard song is real and it is not final, and the light that ends it will not be grown out of the vineyard. It will be given, the way everything in that hillside was given from the start.

50.subtitle: The Servant’s Obedience
50.intro:
Overview. The third Servant Song (vv. 4-9) sits between two passages that frame it. First God asks for the divorce certificate and the creditor’s name and finds neither — Israel was not dismissed, she sold herself — and turns the charge of absence around: when God came, nobody was there. Then the servant speaks, and his first claim about himself is that he is taught: given a disciple’s tongue so that he can hold up the weary with a word, and wakened ear-first, morning by morning.

What that obedience costs is itemised in a single verse — the back given to floggers, the cheeks to men pulling out the beard, the face not hidden from spitting — and every verb is active. He gave. He did not hide. Then the face set like flint, and a courtroom in which he invites anyone to bring a charge, because the one who vindicates him is standing next to him. The chapter closes by putting two people in the same darkness: one who trusts a name he cannot see, and one who strikes a light of his own and walks by it.

keyVerse.quote: “But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.”
keyVerse.note: The confidence here is entirely derivative — it flows from God’s help, not the Servant’s constitution. Luke 9:51 applies “set his face” directly to Jesus heading to Jerusalem, and the deliberateness is the point: he is not swept toward the cross by events but walks toward it with resolution, grounded in the certainty that the Father is with him.

50.reflection: The Servant’s day begins with listening before speaking, receiving before giving. This is not merely a spiritual discipline — it is the source of the sustaining word he is able to offer the weary. Where are you most tempted to speak, teach, or act before you have first sat quietly to receive? And where in your life are you lighting your own fire rather than waiting in the dark for God’s?
50.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD: "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away.<sup>2</sup>Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst.<sup>3</sup>I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering."<sup>4</sup>The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.<sup>5</sup>The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward.<sup>6</sup>I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.<sup>7</sup>But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.<sup>8</sup>He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me.<sup>9</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up.<sup>10</sup>Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God.<sup>11</sup>Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God opens with two legal questions and the answer to both is that no such document exists. Verse 1 asks for the mother's certificate of divorce and for the name of the creditor she was sold to, and then states the truth: she was sold for her own iniquities and sent away for her own transgressions. Verse 2 turns the charge of absence round — when God came, nobody was there; when he called, nobody answered — and asks whether his hand has grown too short to redeem. Verse 3 answers with the sky going black at his word.
verseByVerse.theology: The choice of legal category is the mercy in the passage. A wife formally divorced under Deuteronomy 24 has been permanently sent away and cannot simply be taken back; a debtor sold into slavery can always be redeemed by a kinsman with the price. God denies that any divorce was issued or any sale transacted, which leaves the exile in the one category from which return is possible. The door was never legally shut.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 names the pattern that runs through the whole book and through most Christian experience of God's supposed silence: God came and there was no one, God called and no one answered. The complaint of absence is being answered by a counter-complaint of absence, and only one of the two parties had actually gone missing.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away. Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer? Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem? Or have I no power to deliver? Behold, by my rebuke I dry up the sea, I make the rivers a desert; their fish stink for lack of water and die of thirst. I clothe the heavens with blackness and make sackcloth their covering."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: 'Where is your mother's certificate of divorce, with which I sent her away? Or which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you?'"

Two legal questions, and the answer to each is that the document does not exist. But notice which two categories God chooses, because the mercy of the whole passage is in the choice.

Under the law, a man who divorced his wife had to write her a certificate and put it in her hand, and once she had gone and married another, he could never take her back — the door was legally sealed (Deut. 24:1-4). A debtor sold into slavery was in a different position entirely: a slave sold for debt could always be bought out, by a kinsman with the price in his hand, at any time.

God denies both. There was no certificate, so she is not permanently dismissed. There was no creditor, so nobody holds a legal claim on her that has to be honoured. What is left is the one situation from which return is possible, and Isaiah has arranged the question so that the exiles find themselves standing in it.

"Behold, for your iniquities you were sold, and for your transgressions your mother was sent away." The cause is named without cruelty and without evasion. Nobody sold Israel; Israel sold herself. That is worse in one way and much better in another, because a problem you created is a problem God can undo without anybody's permission.

"Why, when I came, was there no man; why, when I called, was there no one to answer?"

Now the charge is reversed, and it is the sentence to sit with. The exiles' complaint was that God had gone. God's reply is that he came, and the house was empty. He called, and nothing came back. The silence everyone was blaming him for was measured from the wrong end.

"Is my hand shortened, that it cannot redeem?" It is the standing idiom for a reach that will not stretch far enough, and the answer is given in creation: by a rebuke he dries up the sea, and he clothes the heavens in black. The hand that parted the water at the exodus has not shrunk in the interval. What has changed is not the arm. It is who is at home when he calls.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Taught Tongue and the Set Face
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant speaks, and his first word about himself is not power but teachability: he has been given the tongue of those who are taught, so that he can sustain the weary with a word, and morning by morning his ear is wakened (v. 4). Verse 5 has the ear opened and no rebellion following. Verse 6 itemises what obedience cost — back, cheeks, beard, face, spitting — and says he gave them. Verse 7 sets his face like flint on the strength of God's help. Verses 8 and 9 turn the whole thing into a courtroom and dare anyone to bring a charge.
verseByVerse.theology: This song introduces suffering into the servant material for the first time in explicit terms, and it insists that the suffering is chosen. The verbs are active: I gave my back, I hid not my face. That distinction between a victim and a volunteer is what the New Testament preserves when Jesus says no one takes his life from him but he lays it down of his own accord. And the confidence in verse 7 is entirely derivative: not I am strong, but the Lord GOD helps me.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 6 lists physical particulars that the Gospels later record as events: the flogging, the blows, the spitting (Matt. 26:67; 27:26-30). Luke describes Jesus turning toward Jerusalem in the language of verse 7 — he set his face to go (Luke 9:51) — which makes the journey a decision rather than a drift. And Paul takes the courtroom of verses 8 and 9 and gives it to every believer: who shall bring any charge against God's elect? (Rom. 8:33).

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The Lord GOD has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary."

The servant begins to speak, and the first thing he says about himself is startling. Not that he has authority, or power, or a commission. That he has been taught. The word is limmudim — learners, disciples — and it is the same word Isaiah used of his own followers back in 8:16. The servant's opening credential is that he is a pupil.

And the purpose of the taught tongue is specific: to sustain with a word him who is weary. Not to win arguments. Not to make pronouncements. To hold up somebody who is tired, with a word — one word, if that is all it takes — placed exactly where the weight is.

Anyone who has been on the receiving end of that knows how rare it is and how unmistakable. Most speech aimed at an exhausted person makes things worse: advice, cheer, comparison, the wrong verse at the wrong moment. Knowing how to sustain the weary is a skill, and Isaiah says it is a taught skill.

"Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught."

Here is where it is learned, and the repetition is the method. Not once, at a call. Morning by morning, which means most of those mornings were unremarkable and none of them were skipped. And what is wakened is not the man but the ear — God's first act each day is to open the servant's hearing, and everything he will say later that day comes out of what he took in first.

The order is not negotiable and it is the reverse of every instinct. Reception before speech, listening before ministry, the ear before the tongue. The servant who sustains the weary of the whole world is a man who sat still every morning and let God talk to him first.

verseByVerse.quote: The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward. I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious; I turned not backward."

The opened ear is the same picture as verse 4, and here it produces obedience. Two negatives carry it: not rebellious, not turning back. Isaiah does not say the servant was enthusiastic. He says he did not refuse and he did not retreat — which is what obedience actually looks like from inside, when the thing being asked is hard.

"I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting."

Read the verbs before the injuries. I gave. I hid not. Every one of them is active. This is not a man describing what was done to him; it is a man describing what he handed over. The distinction is the whole theology of the passage, and the New Testament keeps it exactly: no one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord (John 10:18).

Then the injuries themselves, and their specificity should stop the reader. The back given to those who strike — flogging. The cheeks to those who pull out the beard, which in that world was not merely painful but the deliberate stripping of a man's dignity; you did it to humiliate, and the humiliation lasted as long as the beard took to grow back. And the face not hidden from spitting, which is the most contemptuous thing one human being can do to another and requires no weapon at all.

Matthew records all three as events. They spat in his face and struck him; some slapped him (Matt. 26:67). They scourged him, and they spat on him again (Matt. 27:26, 30). Isaiah wrote the list seven hundred years earlier, and a Roman guardroom filled it in item by item.

He gave his back. Nobody prised his face round; he did not turn it away. Every blow that landed, landed on someone who had decided in advance not to move, and he had decided it in the light of what it was for.

verseByVerse.quote: But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the Lord GOD helps me; therefore I have not been disgraced; therefore I have set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be put to shame."

Everything in this verse hangs off the first clause, and the two therefores make the logic impossible to miss. The servant is not resolute because he is a resolute sort of person. He is resolute because the Lord GOD helps him. Take the help away and the flint face goes with it.

That matters for anyone trying to imitate him. The endurance in this passage is not a temperament some people have and others do not. It is derivative — a strength drawn down from somewhere else, available to whoever draws on the same source.

"I have set my face like a flint." Flint is the stone you strike to make fire: hard, unyielding, and used precisely because it does not give. The face is the part of a person that shows what he intends, and this one has been set — a deliberate act, done once, not a mood that happened to hold.

Luke uses the phrase. When the time drew near for Jesus to be taken up, "he set his face to go to Jerusalem" (Luke 9:51), and everything after that in Luke's Gospel is a journey toward the city that would kill him. He was not swept there by events, or cornered by his enemies, or overtaken by a plot he had failed to anticipate. He turned his head and walked.

And the last clause is the ground of it: I know that I shall not be put to shame. Not that it will not hurt. Not that it will be brief. That the end of it will not be humiliation — which is exactly what it would look like to everyone watching on the day, and exactly what it turned out not to be.

verseByVerse.quote: He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me. Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He who vindicates me is near. Who will contend with me? Let us stand up together. Who is my adversary? Let him come near to me."

The scene changes to a courtroom, and the servant is on his feet, inviting prosecution. Let us stand up together — the posture of two parties rising to have the case heard. He is not defending himself. He is asking whether anybody wants to try.

The confidence rests on the first four words: he who vindicates me is near. The word is the courtroom verb for declaring in the right — the same root the New Testament uses for justification — and the point is proximity. The one who will pronounce the verdict is not distant, not neutral and not undecided. He is standing next to the defendant.

"Behold, the Lord GOD helps me; who will declare me guilty? Behold, all of them will wear out like a garment; the moth will eat them up."

And there is the fate of the prosecution. Not defeated in argument — simply outlasted. The accusers will go the way of an old coat left in a cupboard: not torn, not burned, quietly eaten through until there is nothing left to put on. Every charge in the room has a shelf life, and the moth is already in the cloth.

Paul takes this courtroom and hands it to ordinary Christians. "Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies. Who is to condemn?" (Rom. 8:33-34). The structure is identical — the accusation invited, the Judge standing near, the verdict already settled — and Paul's ground for extending it is that the one who first stood in that dock stood there for us.

So the accusations a believer knows best about himself, the true ones, the ones with dates attached, are in a room where the Judge has already spoken and the prosecutor is being eaten by moths.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — Two Ways of Walking in the Dark
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends by putting two people side by side in the same darkness. Verse 10 describes someone who fears the LORD, obeys the servant's voice, and has no light at all — and gives him one instruction: trust in the name of the LORD and lean on his God. Verse 11 describes someone who solves the darkness himself, striking a light and walking by it, and gives the verdict: this you have from my hand, you shall lie down in torment.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 is one of the most pastorally important sentences in the Old Testament because of who it is about. The man in the dark is not backslidden. He fears God and obeys the servant, and he still has no light — which forecloses the idea that darkness is always evidence of sin or of some failure of faith. What is asked of him is not a feeling but a decision to lean.
verseByVerse.examples: The two verses describe a choice everybody faces in a season of unanswered prayer: wait in the dark holding a name, or manufacture some light of your own and walk by that. The fire in verse 11 is not wickedness dressed up — it is the perfectly understandable refusal to stand still in the dark, and the sober warning is that a self-made light leads to a bed nobody would have chosen.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who among you fears the LORD and obeys the voice of his servant? Let him who walks in darkness and has no light trust in the name of the LORD and rely on his God."

Read carefully who is being described, because everything depends on it. This man fears the LORD. He obeys the voice of his servant. By every measure the book has offered, he is where he should be. And he walks in darkness and has no light.

Not dim light. Not light he is failing to notice. No light.

That single verse dismantles an assumption that does enormous damage: that darkness is evidence — that if a Christian cannot see, something must have gone wrong, some sin unconfessed, some faith insufficiently exercised, some technique not applied. Isaiah puts an obedient, God-fearing man in total darkness and does not suggest for a moment that he has made a mistake.

What is asked of him is not a feeling and not an explanation. Two verbs: trust in the name of the LORD, and rely on his God. The second is the word for leaning, putting your weight on something. He is not told to find the light, or to work out why it went, or to generate an assurance he does not have. He is told to put his weight on a name in the dark.

And notice the order in the chapter. The servant has just walked through blows and spitting with a face like flint and no visible vindication, trusting a God who did not intervene. Verse 10 is the invitation to do the same thing. The path the servant took is not merely admired here; it is handed over.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, all you who kindle a fire, who equip yourselves with burning torches! Walk by the light of your fire, and by the torches that you have kindled! This you have from my hand: you shall lie down in torment."

Here is the other man in the same darkness, and it is important to see that he is not a villain. He is doing the sensible thing. It is dark, he has no light, and rather than standing still he strikes a spark and makes one. Anyone would.

That is exactly why the warning is needed. The fire in this verse is not gross wickedness; it is self-supply — the entirely understandable refusal to wait in the dark holding nothing but a name. It looks like initiative. It produces real light, for a while, and you can genuinely see by it.

The invitation is bitter: walk by the light of your fire. Go on, then. Use it. God does not put the fire out or argue about whether it burns. He lets the man have exactly what he made and lets it take him where it goes.

"You shall lie down in torment." The last word of the chapter is a bed — the place you end up when you finally stop walking. The torches got him through the night and they did not get him anywhere he wanted to be.

So the chapter closes on two men in identical darkness, and everything hangs on what each does with his hands. One holds a name he cannot see; the other holds a light he made himself. Only one of them is being led — and the one being led is the one who looks, from the outside, to have nothing at all.

50.theology:
Chosen suffering, not endured misfortune. This song brings the servant’s suffering into the open for the first time, and it insists on the grammar: I gave my back, I hid not my face. He is a volunteer, not a victim, and the distinction is preserved exactly when Jesus says that no one takes his life from him (John 10:18). His confidence is equally carefully sourced — not I am strong but the Lord GOD helps me — which is what makes it imitable rather than admirable.

The courtroom, handed over. Verses 8 and 9 have the servant on his feet inviting prosecution because his vindicator is near, and the accusers are dismissed not by argument but by moths. Paul gives the same courtroom to every believer — who shall bring any charge against God’s elect? (Rom. 8:33-34) — on the ground that the one who first stood in that dock stood there for us.

Darkness is not always evidence. The man in verse 10 fears the LORD and obeys the servant’s voice and has no light. Isaiah does not treat that as a symptom of sin or of deficient faith, and neither should anyone using this chapter pastorally. He is given two verbs rather than an explanation: trust the name, lean on the God. Verse 11 shows the alternative and is careful not to caricature it — a self-made light is the reasonable response to darkness, it genuinely works, and it ends in a bed nobody would have chosen.

51.subtitle: Look to the Rock from Which You Were Cut
51.intro: Overview. Chapter 51 is a sustained call to remembrance — look back to Abraham, look back to the exodus, look up to the heavens God made — as the ground for present courage. God’s salvation will last when the heavens vanish; his righteousness endures forever. The chapter ends with the cup of wrath taken from Israel’s lips and placed in the hand of her oppressors.

sections.title: Look to Abraham
sections.commentary:
Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were cut, to the quarry from which you were hewn. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you — when he was but one I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. One man, childless, and from him came a nation. The logic of the call is: if God can do that from one, he can rebuild Zion from its ruins.

v. 6 — “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.” The contrast is between two kinds of permanence. The heavens and earth feel maximally stable — but they are contingent and will pass. God’s salvation is not contingent; it will outlast the cosmos. 2 Pet. 3:10–13 and Rev. 21:1 describe this passing from the outside.

sections.title: The Arm of the LORD
sections.commentary:
Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in the days of old. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who dried up the sea, who made the depths into a road for the redeemed? The appeal to the exodus is not nostalgia but argument: the same arm that acted then can act now.

God promises to comfort Zion and silence the one who taunts. Then the reversal: the cup of staggering — the bowl of God’s wrath that Jerusalem has been drinking — will be taken from her hand and placed in the hand of those who afflicted her. The suffering is not permanent; the oppressors’ temporary power is not the final arrangement.

keyVerse.quote: “Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment… but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed.”
keyVerse.note: The permanence of God’s salvation is grounded in the impermanence of everything else. When even the heavens and earth are revealed as contingent, the one thing that stands is what God has declared. This is not escapism but realism: the most stable-seeming things will pass; the apparently fragile promise will not.

51.reflection: God says: look to Abraham — I called one man and multiplied him. Where in your situation does the evidence look like “only one” or “only remnant”? What would it mean to draw courage from the Abraham-logic: that God specializes in beginnings that look statistically impossible?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–23 — Awake, Awake: the Arm of the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three times the chapter calls for awakening — first to Israel (vv.1, 7), then to the arm of the LORD (v.9), then to Jerusalem herself (v.17). God points to Abraham and Sarah as the prototype of fruitfulness from barrenness. His salvation and righteousness are everlasting. The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drank is taken from her hand and given to her tormentors.
verseByVerse.theology: Memory and hope: the call to look to Abraham and Sarah (v.2) grounds hope in precedent — a barren couple became a multitude. Similarly the exiled community, few and scattered, will become many. The arm of the LORD (v.9) is personified as a warrior who slew Rahab and dried the sea. The same arm will lead a new exodus. The cup of divine wrath (vv.17-23) passes from Israel to her oppressors — God's justice works in both directions.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer identifies the three-fold 'awake' (vv.9, 17; 52:1) as structuring the chapter and its sequel. The arm of the LORD that the exiles call upon becomes the suffering arm of the servant (53:1) — the very arm of God's salvation is the servant's sacrificial death. The cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks becomes the cup the servant drains in her place.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, you who pursue righteousness, you who seek the LORD: look to the rock from which you were hewn, and to the quarry from which you were dug. Look to Abraham your father and to Sarah who bore you; for he was but one when I called him, that I might bless him and multiply him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exiles who pursue righteousness are called to historical memory. The rock from which Israel was hewn is Abraham — one person, barren wife, no descendants when God called. Yet God blessed and multiplied them into a nation. Oswalt: the precedent of Abraham and Sarah is God's pastoral argument from pattern. If God created a nation from a barren couple, he can restore a nation from a scattered remnant. Faith is always partly retrospective — looking at what God has already done.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will comfort Zion; he will comfort all her waste places and will make her wilderness like Eden, her desert like the garden of the LORD; joy and gladness will be found in her, thanksgiving and the voice of song. Give attention to me, my people, and give ear to me, my nation; for a law will go out from me, and I will set my justice for a light to the peoples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Comfort transforms the physical landscape — waste becomes Eden, desert becomes garden. The creation language (Eden, garden of the LORD) signals new creation: God is not merely restoring what was but making something that was never before. Joy and song replace mourning and silence. Then the universal note: God's law and justice will be a light to the peoples — reaching beyond Israel's restoration to the world's illumination. Childs: the comfort of Zion is not an end in itself but the first act of the universal restoration.

verseByVerse.quote: My righteousness draws near, my salvation has gone out, and my arms will judge the peoples; the coastlands hope for me, and for my arm they wait. Lift up your eyes to the heavens, and look at the earth beneath; for the heavens vanish like smoke, the earth will wear out like a garment, and they who dwell in it will die in like manner; but my salvation will be forever, and my righteousness will never be dismayed. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The contrast between creation's transience and God's eternal salvation: heavens like smoke, earth wearing out like an old garment, its inhabitants dying. But God's salvation is forever; his righteousness will never be dismayed. This is cosmic eschatology — the created order will end, but the redemptive order will not. Jesus echoes this in Matt 24:35: heaven and earth will pass away, but my words will not pass away. Motyer: the permanence of God's salvation makes it the only reliable investment — everything else depreciates to zero.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, you who know righteousness, the people in whose heart is my law; fear not the reproach of man, nor be dismayed at their revilings. For the moth will eat them up like a garment, and the worm will eat them like wool, but my righteousness will be forever, and my salvation to all generations. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The second address — to those who have God's law in their hearts (Jer 31:33, the new covenant). The reproach and reviling of persecutors is temporary: moth and worm consume them, as they do all created things. But God's righteousness and salvation persist to all generations. This is the pastoral logic of the eternal: the temporary opposition of the wicked does not threaten the permanent salvation of God. Young: fear not the reproach of man is addressed to those who feel the weight of being a minority in a hostile culture.

verseByVerse.quote: Awake, awake, put on strength, O arm of the LORD; awake, as in days of old, the generations of long ago. Was it not you who cut Rahab in pieces, who pierced the dragon? Was it not you who dried up the sea, the waters of the great deep, who made the depths of the sea a way for the redeemed to pass over? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The community's prayer: Awake, arm of the LORD! — an urgent cry for divine action. The arm is personified as a warrior who defeated Rahab (a chaos-monster, here a name for Egypt) and dried the Red Sea. The exodus is the paradigm act of divine strength. This prayer will be answered in ch53 where the arm of the LORD is revealed — in the servant's suffering. Motyer: the connection between this prayer for the arm and the servant's identity as the arm (53:1) is the structural heart of chs51-53.

verseByVerse.quote: And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away. I, I am he who comforts you; who are you that you are afraid of man who dies, of the son of man who is made like grass, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: V.11 nearly quotes 35:10 — the Highway of Holiness refrain — joining the return of the ransomed with everlasting joy. Then God's self-identification: I, I am he who comforts you. The doubled I is emphatic. And the rebuke: who are you that you are afraid of man who dies? The transience of human oppressors (made like grass) makes fear of them disproportionate. Oswalt: the comfort of God is the antidote to the fear of man. When God fills the foreground, every human threat shrinks to proper size.

verseByVerse.quote: and have forgotten the LORD, your Maker, who stretched out the heavens and laid the foundations of the earth, and you fear continually all the day because of the wrath of the oppressor, when he sets himself to destroy? And where is the wrath of the oppressor? He who is bowed down shall speedily be released; he shall not die and go down to the pit; neither shall his bread fail. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The diagnosis: you have forgotten the LORD your Maker and therefore fear the oppressor continuously. The forgetfulness is the root; the fear is the fruit. The remedy is not psychological but theological — remember who your God is. The liberator's promise: the bowed-down one shall speedily be released, shall not die, shall not starve. Every specific fear is addressed. Young: the pastoral genius of Isaiah is to address specific anxieties with specific promises grounded in specific truths about God's character.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar — the LORD of hosts is his name. And I have put my words in your mouth and covered you in the shadow of my hand, establishing the heavens and laying the foundation of the earth, and saying to Zion, 'You are my people.' (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The LORD who stirs up the sea (sovereign over nature's most terrifying force) has put his words in Israel's mouth and covered them with the shadow of his hand. The creator who established heavens and earth claims his people in the simplest covenant formula: You are my people. Childs: the movement from creation (establishing heavens and earth) to covenant (you are my people) is the movement of biblical theology — the Creator becomes the Covenant-Maker.

verseByVerse.quote: Wake yourself, wake yourself, stand up, O Jerusalem, you who have drunk from the hand of the LORD the cup of his wrath, who have drunk to the dregs the bowl, the cup of staggering. There is none to guide her among all the sons she has borne; there is none to take her by the hand among all the sons she has brought up. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The third awakening command — now addressed to Jerusalem herself. She has drunk the cup of divine wrath to the dregs — the exile was no half-measure but the full weight of judgment. And she has been left without help: sons born and raised, yet none to guide or lead. The desolation is complete. But the command wake presupposes recovery — you are called to rise, which means rising is possible. Motyer: the cup of wrath that Jerusalem drinks in judgment is the same cup that the servant will drain in ch53, taking it from her hand.

verseByVerse.quote: These two things have happened to you — who will console you? — devastation and destruction, famine and sword; who will comfort you? Your sons have fainted; they lie at the head of every street like an antelope in a net; they are full of the wrath of the LORD, the rebuke of your God. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The two pairs of disaster — devastation and destruction, famine and sword — describe the fall of Jerusalem with graphic simplicity. Sons fainted in the streets like netted antelopes: helpless, trapped, exhausted. Who will comfort you? — the question that will be answered by God himself (40:1, 51:3, 12). The depth of the desolation makes the coming comfort all the more glorious. Young: the lament of vv.17-20 must be heard fully before the promise of vv.21-23 can land with its proper weight.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear this, you who are afflicted, who are drunk, but not with wine: Thus says your Lord, the LORD, your God who pleads the cause of his people: 'Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering; the bowl of my wrath you shall drink no more; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The reversal begins: the cup of staggering is taken from Jerusalem's hand. God himself has pleaded her cause — the advocate becomes the judge who rules in her favor. Drink no more — the sentence is complete, the judgment exhausted. The same hand that held out the cup of wrath now takes it away. This is the shape of atonement: someone must drain the cup. The servant will do this in ch53. Oswalt: the transfer of the cup from Israel to her oppressors in v.23 is a picture of what the servant accomplishes — the righteous bearing what the guilty deserved.

verseByVerse.quote: and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors, who have said to you, 'Bow down, that we may pass over'; and you have made your back like the ground and like the street for them to pass over. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The cup passes to the tormentors who forced prostration — who treated Jerusalem as pavement. The humiliation is precisely reversed: those who walked over God's people will themselves be brought low. The justice is poetic and exact. Motyer: the oppressor's cruelty — using human beings as a road — is itself the measure of their judgment. God does not invent a new punishment; he simply applies the same measure they used. The chapter ends with promise: the cup of wrath has been redirected, and the ransomed will return with singing (v.11).

52.subtitle: How Beautiful Are the Feet
52.intro:
Overview. Chapter 52 is a wake-up call and a homecoming. Zion is told to get up out of the dust, put on festival clothes and untie her own neck — commands grounded in a redemption already accomplished, since she was sold for nothing and will be bought back without money. God gives his reason plainly: his name is being despised all day long among the nations. Then a runner appears on the ridge above the city with the most famous feet in Scripture, and his whole message reduces to two words — your God reigns. The rubble is told to sing, God rolls up his sleeve in front of every nation, and the people walk out of Babylon unhurried, with God in front of the column and God behind it.

The last three verses begin the fourth and greatest Servant Song, which runs on into chapter 53. God gives away the ending first — the servant will be high and lifted up, in the language used of the Lord enthroned in chapter 6 — and then says why people stared at him: his appearance was marred beyond human semblance. Kings will shut their mouths in front of the man they could not bear to look at.

keyVerse.quote: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace… who says to Zion, ‘Your God reigns.’”
keyVerse.note: Paul’s use of this verse in Romans 10:15 extends the herald imagery to every Christian witness. The feet are beautiful not because the herald is but because of what they carry. Every announcement of the gospel is an echo of this verse: “your God reigns” is the irreducible content of Christian proclamation.

52.reflection: Zion is told to shake off the dust and put on beautiful garments — before she sees the full deliverance. The command to rise precedes the visible evidence that rising makes sense. Where in your life is God calling you to rise and dress for freedom before you can yet see the liberation he has promised?
