And the upgrade is real, not rhetoric. Mud brick was what ordinary houses were made of — cheap, quick, and what you use when you cannot afford stone. Dressed stone is quarried, cut square and expensive. Sycamore-fig was the common tree of the lowlands, useful and unimpressive; cedar came from Lebanon by ship and by ox-cart and was what kings panelled palaces with. They are answering a disaster by trading up.

Not one word about why the bricks fell.

That is the whole indictment, and it is why the sentence is so unnerving. There is no defiance of God here, no denial, no atheism — just a people who have taken a blow, absorbed it as a setback, and moved straight to the rebuild. The event was meant to produce a question. It produced a procurement plan.

Ask what the reflex is when something in a life falls down. The instinct to repair, improve and press on is a virtue nearly everywhere else. Here it is the thing that damns them, because they used it to avoid the one question the collapse was sent to raise.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But the LORD raises the adversaries of Rezin against him, and stirs up his enemies. The Syrians on the east and the Philistines on the west devour Israel with open mouth."

The answer to the building programme is not a lecture. It is more pressure. God raises and stirs up — both verbs have him as the subject, moving nations the way chapter 7 had him whistling for flies and bees.

Enemies on both sides at once: Syrians from the east, Philistines from the west. That is the shape of a nation being squeezed rather than invaded, and "devour with open mouth" is the image of an animal that does not need to hurry.

"For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still."

Here is the refrain. It closes this section, and it will close the next two as well — three times in this chapter, hammering. Isaiah wants the reader to feel the judgment not as a single event but as something that keeps not finishing.

And the image deserves care, because it is usually read as pure menace and it is more than that. A hand stretched out is the posture of a man about to strike. It is also the posture of a man reaching for someone. Both are in the picture, and the next verse tells you which is being frustrated: the people did not turn to him who struck them.

The hand stays out because the turning has not happened. Judgment continues, in this chapter, precisely because it has not yet accomplished what judgment in Scripture is nearly always sent to accomplish. It is the strangest kind of mercy — a God who will not let the consequences stop while there is still a chance they might work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Head and Tail Cut Off
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 13 gives the diagnosis in one line: they did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD. Verse 14 removes head and tail, palm branch and reed, in one day. Verse 15 identifies them — the elder and honoured man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail. Verse 16 has the guides leading people astray and the guided swallowed up. Verse 17 reaches the point where even the young men and the fatherless and widows receive no compassion, because the corruption has gone everywhere, and sounds the refrain a second time.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment falls on leadership first and hardest, and Isaiah is careful to say that the followers go down with them rather than instead of them: the guides are culpable and the guided are swallowed. Verse 15 puts the lying prophet at the tail, which is the humiliating end of the animal — a man who speaks in God's name and points the wrong way is not merely wrong, he is the least of what a nation has.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is the hardest sentence in the section, because the fatherless and widows are the very people God repeatedly commands his people to protect. When even they are outside compassion, Isaiah is not saying God has changed his mind about the vulnerable. He is saying the corruption has reached the point where there is no innocent class left to appeal to.

verseByVerse.quote: The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts. So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day— the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The people did not turn to him who struck them, nor inquire of the LORD of hosts."

One verse, and it is the diagnosis for the whole chapter. Not that they were struck, but that they did not turn to him who struck them — which assumes something a modern reader will resist: that the hand causing the pain is the right place to go with it.

That is the instinct being described as missing. When something falls in on a person, the options are to blame, to rebuild, to endure, or to turn to God about it. This nation rebuilt. And nor inquire of the LORD — they did not even ask. There was no consultation, no seeking, nothing sent upward at all.

"So the LORD cut off from Israel head and tail, palm branch and reed in one day — the elder and honored man is the head, and the prophet who teaches lies is the tail."

Isaiah uses a merism, a way of saying "everything" by naming the two ends: head and tail, the tall palm and the low reed. The whole animal, the whole marsh, the entire social order from top to bottom, removed in one day.

Then he interprets his own image, and the interpretation is where it bites. The head is the elder and honoured man — the establishment, the respected figures whose judgment a nation relies on. And the tail is the prophet who teaches lies.

Putting the false prophet at the tail is a deliberate insult; the tail is the least dignified end of an animal. But it is also exactly right about the damage such a man does. He speaks in God's name, so people follow where he points, and he is pointing at the ground. A nation can survive bad politicians. It has much more trouble surviving men who tell it, religiously and reassuringly, that nothing is wrong.

verseByVerse.quote: for those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up. Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For those who guide this people have been leading them astray, and those who are guided by them are swallowed up."

The verbs are set against each other deliberately. The guides lead astray — that is an active thing, done by people whose whole function was to do the opposite. The guided are swallowed up — passive, consumed, disappearing into something.

And both groups go. Isaiah does not offer the followers the exemption a modern reader expects. Being badly led is a real misfortune and it is not, in this chapter, an excuse; these are people who had the law, the prophets and the covenant available and took their directions from men who found it convenient to lie. Somebody chose the guides.

"Therefore the Lord does not rejoice over their young men, and has no compassion on their fatherless and widows; for everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly."

This is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it should not be smoothed over. The fatherless and the widow are the two groups God commands his people to protect on almost every page of the law. He calls himself their defender. And here they are named as outside his compassion.

Read the reason Isaiah gives, because he does give one: everyone is godless and an evildoer, and every mouth speaks folly. The point is not that God has changed his mind about the vulnerable. It is that the corruption has gone everywhere, so there is no longer an innocent class to appeal to. Ordinarily you could plead for a nation on the grounds that the widows and orphans in it are not to blame. Isaiah is saying that plea is no longer available.

"For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still." The second sounding of the refrain, and the reach is still unanswered.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — The Fire That Eats Itself
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last movement describes wickedness as a fire that starts in the scrub and ends in the forest, with the people themselves as the fuel (vv. 18-19). Verses 20 and 21 show what it looks like on the ground: a nation eating and never satisfied, each man devouring the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh against Ephraim and Ephraim against Manasseh, and both of them united only in being against Judah. The refrain sounds a third and final time.
verseByVerse.theology: The theology here is that sin is self-consuming rather than merely punishable. Isaiah does not describe God importing a fire; he describes wickedness burning like one, feeding on the society that houses it, until brothers are eating each other and a body politic is chewing its own arm. Judgment in this passage is largely God handing a people over to what they have chosen and letting it run.
verseByVerse.examples: The detail in verse 21 is the bleakest political observation in the book: two halves of one nation at war with each other and in agreement about nothing except hostility to a third. Shared enmity is the only unity available to people who have lost every other kind, and it is a counterfeit — they were still devouring each other while they did it.

verseByVerse.quote: For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke. Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For wickedness burns like a fire; it consumes briers and thorns; it kindles the thickets of the forest, and they roll upward in a column of smoke."

Notice the subject of that sentence. It is not God who burns; it is wickedness. Isaiah has changed the way he is describing judgment, and this is the deepest thing in the chapter's second half: sin is not merely an offence that gets punished, it is a fire, and fires do not need anyone to keep them going.

Watch how it spreads. First briers and thorns — the dry scrub, the rubbish at the edge of a field, the stuff nobody values. That is where it always starts: in the parts of a life or a nation that seem too minor to matter. Then the thickets. Then the forest, and a column of smoke going up.

"Through the wrath of the LORD of hosts the land is scorched, and the people are like fuel for the fire; no one spares another."

And now both are said at once, which is what makes the passage honest. The fire is wickedness burning on its own, and it is the wrath of the LORD. There is no contradiction: God's judgment here largely consists of handing a people over to what they have chosen and declining to put it out. What burns them is their own.

"The people are like fuel for the fire." Not victims of it. Fuel. The very thing feeding the blaze is the population, which means every person in it is both burning and burning.

"No one spares another." That is the first sign of a society properly alight — not atrocity, just the quiet universal withdrawal of forbearance. Nobody lets anybody off anything any more.

verseByVerse.quote: They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied; each devours the flesh of his own arm, Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They slice meat on the right, but are still hungry, and they devour on the left, but are not satisfied."

The picture is a man eating in both directions at once and getting no fuller. Isaiah has moved from fire to appetite, and appetite is the better image for what he wants to say, because a fire can be starved of fuel and a hunger like this cannot be fed at all. The more it consumes, the emptier it is.

"Each devours the flesh of his own arm."

And then the sentence the whole passage has been building toward. A man so hungry that he eats himself, starting with the limb he would need to feed himself with. It is grotesque on purpose. Isaiah wants the reader to flinch, because he is describing a nation doing exactly this, and nations do it without noticing.

"Manasseh devours Ephraim, and Ephraim devours Manasseh; together they are against Judah."

Here is the arm, named. Manasseh and Ephraim were the two sons of Joseph, and their tribes were the twin heartland of the northern kingdom. They were not neighbours; they were brothers, one household. That is the flesh of the same arm, and they are eating each other.

Then the last, bitterest clause: together they are against Judah. Two peoples tearing at one another can still find one thing to agree on, and it is a shared enemy. That is the only unity left to them — the counterfeit kind, produced by hostility rather than love, which holds people together exactly as long as the third party is in the room.

"For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still."

The refrain a third time, and the chapter simply stops on it. No resolution, no closing comfort. The hand is still out and nobody has taken it.

Which is why verses 6 and 7 stand where they do. Isaiah put the child and the four names at the top of this chapter, before a word of the ruin below — so that when the reader arrives here, at brothers eating each other under an outstretched hand, the answer has already been given and is sitting fourteen verses back. A child is born. The government is on his shoulder. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.

10.subtitle: Woe to Unjust Laws — Assyria the Rod of God
10.intro: Overview. Chapter 10 operates on two levels simultaneously. The first is immediate and political: God will use Assyria as his instrument of judgment against Israel, but Assyria's own arrogance means it will then be judged in turn. The second level is theological and universal: how does God govern history through the free actions of wicked human agents? The chapter offers no evasion of this question. God is sovereign over the nations; the nations are morally responsible for their own actions; both are fully true.

keyVerse.quote: “Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!”
keyVerse.note: God is not reacting to Assyria's power by co-opting it; he is directing it. The world's dominant military superpower is a tool in the hand of the LORD. This does not make Assyria innocent — verses 12–19 make clear they will be judged for their pride. But it does make God sovereign over the most frightening human powers of every age.

10.theology:
Sovereignty and responsibility, both asserted. God calls Assyria the rod of my anger and says I send him and I command him (vv. 5-6). Two verses later: but he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think (v. 7). The emperor is acting entirely out of his own ambition, every decision genuinely his, and he is judged for it. Isaiah states both and reconciles neither. The New Testament does exactly the same about the cross: delivered up according to the definite plan of God, and crucified by the hands of lawless men, in one sentence (Acts 2:23).

The axe. Verse 15 deflates an empire with a question about tools. The conquests were real and the axe was genuinely sharp; what an axe cannot do is take the credit, because the whole account of what happened is contained in a man’s arm. Assyria’s sin was not incompetence but the assumption that its success was self-generated — the standing error of every power that mistakes being used for being in charge.

Leaning, and the two names in verse 21. The remnant will lean no longer on the one who struck them but on the LORD, in truth — the qualifier that separates this from the scrupulous, hollow religion of chapter 1. And verse 21 fastens three chapters together: a remnant will return is the name of the boy who stood beside Isaiah before Ahaz (7:3), and the mighty God is El Gibbor, the throne-name given to the child in 9:6. Paul applies the promise to his own generation (Rom. 9:27-28).
10.reflection: The two temptations this chapter addresses are the same ones Israel faced: leaning on the overwhelming power that threatens you, and despairing when that power seems unstoppable. God's word to the remnant (v. 24) is simply “do not be afraid.” The basis for that courage is not a better military assessment but a theological one: the LORD of hosts has a purpose, and no human empire is the last word in any situation. What is the ‘Assyria’ in your own life — the overwhelming power you are tempted either to appease or to despair before?
10.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression,<sup>2</sup>to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey!<sup>3</sup>What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?<sup>4</sup>Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.<sup>5</sup>Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!<sup>6</sup>Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets.<sup>7</sup>But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few;<sup>8</sup>for he says: "Are not my commanders all kings?<sup>9</sup>Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?<sup>10</sup>As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria,<sup>11</sup>shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?"<sup>12</sup>When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes.<sup>13</sup>For he says: "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones.<sup>14</sup>My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been forsaken, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped."<sup>15</sup>Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood!<sup>16</sup>Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire.<sup>17</sup>The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame, and it will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day.<sup>18</sup>The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the LORD will destroy, both soul and body, and it will be as when a sick man wastes away.<sup>19</sup>The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down.<sup>20</sup>In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth.<sup>21</sup>A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God.<sup>22</sup>For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness.<sup>23</sup>For the Lord GOD of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth.<sup>24</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD of hosts: "O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrians when they strike with the rod and lift up their staff against you as the Egyptians did.<sup>25</sup>For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction.<sup>26</sup>And the LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt.<sup>27</sup>And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat."<sup>28</sup>He has come to Aiath; he has passed through Migron; at Michmash he stores his baggage;<sup>29</sup>they have crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodge for the night; Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled.<sup>30</sup>Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth!<sup>31</sup>Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety.<sup>32</sup>This very day he will halt at Nob; he will shake his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.<sup>33</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low.<sup>34</sup>He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–4 — Woe to Those Who Write the Laws
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The sixth woe of chapter 5 gets a seventh, and it is aimed at legislators. Verses 1 and 2 describe men who write oppressive statutes so as to turn the needy away from justice and make widows and the fatherless their plunder. Verse 3 asks what they will do on the day of reckoning and where they will leave their wealth. Verse 4 leaves them crouching among prisoners, and sounds the refrain for the last time: his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.theology: What is indicted here is not corruption but legality. These men are not breaking the law; they are drafting it, and the injustice is being done through the proper channels with the paperwork in order. That is a harder thing to see and a harder thing to repent of, because everyone involved can point to a statute.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 asks the only question such a system cannot answer: what will you do on the day of punishment? Legal skill is precisely the asset that is worthless in front of a judge who is not subject to the legislation. Nothing drafted in Jerusalem has jurisdiction there.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey! What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth? Nothing remains but to crouch among the prisoners or fall among the slain. For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who decree iniquitous decrees, and the writers who keep writing oppression, to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right, that widows may be their spoil, and that they may make the fatherless their prey."

Chapter 5 pronounced six woes. Here is a seventh, and it is aimed at the people who draft the legislation.

Read what is actually being described, because it is worse than corruption. These men are not taking bribes in dark corners; they are writing. There is a legislature, there are clerks, there is a process, and the output is oppression with a seal on it. The phrase the writers who keep writing has the sound of an industry — a steady output of statutes, each one narrowing somebody's rights a little further.

And the intended result is stated with no euphemism: to turn the needy away from justice, to rob the poor of their right — not their charity, their right — and to make widows and orphans into plunder.

That is a harder thing to repent of than ordinary theft, because everyone involved can point to a statute. The judge is following the law. The clerk is filing correctly. The system is working as designed, and the design is the crime.

"What will you do on the day of punishment, in the ruin that will come from afar? To whom will you flee for help, and where will you leave your wealth?"

Three questions, and the first is the one with no answer. Legal skill is exactly the asset that is worthless in front of a judge who is not subject to the legislation. Nothing drafted in Jerusalem has jurisdiction in that court.

"For all this his anger has not turned away, and his hand is stretched out still." The refrain sounds for the fifth and final time in the book — 5:25, three times in chapter 9, and here. It has been reaching since the vineyard, and nobody has taken it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 5–19 — The Axe and the Man Who Swings It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls Assyria the rod of his anger and sends it against a godless nation (vv. 5-6) — and then says flatly that Assyria does not see it that way and has no such intention (v. 7). Verses 8 to 11 give the emperor's boast in his own voice: my commanders are all kings, I have taken city after city, shall I not do to Jerusalem as I did to Samaria? Verse 12 announces that when God has finished his work he will turn and punish that arrogance. Verses 13 and 14 quote the boast again, and verse 15 answers it with a question about carpentry. Verses 16 to 19 burn the forest down until a child could count the trees.
verseByVerse.theology: This passage states the hardest thing in theology and refuses to soften either half. God is genuinely directing Assyria — it is his rod, sent on his errand. Assyria is genuinely responsible — it is judged, and judged for the pride and cruelty with which it did what God used it to do. Isaiah asserts both and explains neither, and the New Testament does exactly the same thing about a crucifixion (Acts 2:23).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 deflates an empire with a question about tools: shall the axe boast over the man who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against the one who wields it? Assyria's error was not incompetence — the conquests were real. It was the assumption that the success was self-generated. Every human power that has ever mistaken being used for being in charge is in that verse.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury! Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets. But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, Assyria, the rod of my anger; the staff in their hands is my fury!"

The most powerful empire on earth is described as a stick.

God is not saying he permits Assyria, or that he will make the best of what Assyria does. He calls it my rod, and the fury in the Assyrian hand is mine. The invasion that is about to devastate the region is an instrument being used deliberately, and God says so in the first person.

"Against a godless nation I send him, and against the people of my wrath I command him, to take spoil and seize plunder, and to tread them down like the mire of the streets."

Two verbs: I send, I command. The orders are specific and the target is God's own people.

"But he does not so intend, and his heart does not so think; but it is in his heart to destroy, and to cut off nations not a few."

And now the hardest verse in the chapter, and one of the most important in the Bible for thinking about how God governs the world.

Assyria has no idea. The emperor is not serving God, does not believe in him, and has never received an instruction. He is doing what emperors do — expanding, destroying, annexing — entirely out of his own ambition and his own appetite, and every decision is genuinely his.

Both sentences in this passage are true at once. God sent him. He does not so intend. Isaiah puts them two verses apart and does not attempt a reconciliation, and neither does the rest of Scripture: the clearest parallel is Peter saying of the cross that Jesus was delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, and that you crucified and killed him by the hands of lawless men — in one sentence (Acts 2:23).

verseByVerse.quote: for he says: "Are not my commanders all kings? Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus? As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria, shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For he says: 'Are not my commanders all kings? Is not Calno like Carchemish? Is not Hamath like Arpad? Is not Samaria like Damascus?'"

Isaiah now lets the emperor speak for himself for four verses, and it is a masterpiece of self-portraiture. Nobody had to caricature this man; he only had to be quoted.

The first boast is about staff: are not my commanders all kings? The men who work for me outrank the men who rule other countries. It is the brag of an organisation so large that its middle management is more powerful than the neighbours.

Then a list of six cities, arranged as a set of equations. Calno fell like Carchemish; Hamath like Arpad; Samaria like Damascus. Each pair is a bigger city matched with one that had already gone, and the point is the pattern: it makes no difference how large or well-defended a place is, they all end the same way.

"As my hand has reached to the kingdoms of the idols, whose carved images were greater than those of Jerusalem and Samaria, shall I not do to Jerusalem and her idols as I have done to Samaria and her images?"

And here the boast becomes theology, and gets it exactly wrong. The emperor has noticed that gods do not stop him. He has surveyed the temples of the nations he has taken, ranked them by the quality of the statuary, and concluded that Jerusalem's God is simply another one — and, judging by the workmanship, not a leading example.

The mistake is the one every conqueror makes. He is arguing from an unbroken record of success to a conclusion about ultimate reality, and the record is unbroken because God has been holding the handle.

verseByVerse.quote: When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes. For he says: "By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones. My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been forsaken, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the Lord has finished all his work on Mount Zion and on Jerusalem, he will punish the speech of the arrogant heart of the king of Assyria and the boastful look in his eyes."

Note the order and the timing. When the Lord has finished all his work — the judgment on Judah runs its full course first, and only then does God turn to the instrument. Assyria's day comes second, and it comes.

And notice what is punished. Not the conquests — the speech and the look. God's charge against this empire is the arrogance with which it did what he used it to do, which is precisely the point at which the emperor's own responsibility sits.

"For he says: 'By the strength of my hand I have done it, and by my wisdom, for I have understanding; I remove the boundaries of peoples, and plunder their treasures; like a bull I bring down those who sit on thrones.'"

Three times in one verse: my hand, my wisdom, I have understanding. The man is not merely proud of the results; he is certain about the cause.

"My hand has found like a nest the wealth of the peoples; and as one gathers eggs that have been forsaken, so I have gathered all the earth; and there was none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped."

The image he chooses for himself is chilling because it is so casual. Taking the wealth of nations was like reaching into an abandoned nest for eggs. No resistance, no noise — none that moved a wing or opened the mouth or chirped.

He is describing the conquest of the civilised world as an errand a boy could run, and he is not exaggerating. That is what makes the next verse so effective.

verseByVerse.quote: Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood! Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire. The light of Israel will become a fire, and his Holy One a flame, and it will burn and devour his thorns and briers in one day. The glory of his forest and of his fruitful land the LORD will destroy, both soul and body, and it will be as when a sick man wastes away. The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Shall the axe boast over him who hews with it, or the saw magnify itself against him who wields it? As if a rod should wield him who lifts it, or as if a staff should lift him who is not wood!"

The whole empire is answered with a question about carpentry, and it is unanswerable.

An axe does real work. Trees genuinely come down, and the axe is genuinely sharp, and none of that is in dispute. What the axe cannot do is take the credit, because the entire account of what happened is contained in a man's arm — and no amount of felled timber changes which of the two is holding the other.

Isaiah pushes it to absurdity in the second half: a rod that wields the man, a stick that picks up a person. Once stated plainly, the imperial self-understanding is not frightening. It is ridiculous.

The reason for stating it carefully is that Assyria's conquests were real. This is not a claim that the empire was weak or that its victories were illusions. It is a claim about what those victories establish, which is nothing at all about the one holding the axe.

"Therefore the Lord GOD of hosts will send wasting sickness among his stout warriors, and under his glory a burning will be kindled, like the burning of fire."

The judgment is fire, and it is comprehensive: thorns and briers in one day, and then the glory of his forest and his fruitful land consumed both soul and body.

"The remnant of the trees of his forest will be so few that a child can write them down."

Which is the perfect ending for a chapter about a boast. The army that gathered the earth like eggs from a nest is reduced to a number a child could get onto a slate — and the counting is the humiliation, because a thing you can count is a thing that has stopped being immeasurable.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–34 — The Remnant Leans, and the Forest Falls
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone turns. Verses 20 to 23 promise that a remnant will stop leaning on the power that struck them and lean on the LORD instead — in truth — and Paul quotes those verses about his own generation. Verses 24 to 27 tell Zion not to be afraid of Assyria, because the yoke will be broken as it was at Midian and at the sea. Verses 28 to 32 track the invader town by town along the northern road until he stands shaking his fist at Jerusalem. Verses 33 and 34 have God take an axe to the forest.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 21 stitches three chapters together. A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God — the first phrase is the name of the son who stood beside Isaiah in front of Ahaz (7:3), and the last two words are El Gibbor, the name given to the child in 9:6. The doctrine of the remnant and the deity of the coming king are fastened together in a single line.
verseByVerse.examples: The march in vv. 28-32 is a piece of terrifying local geography: a dozen villages named in the order an army would reach them, ending three miles from the city with a fist shaken at the mountain. And then verses 33-34 answer it — the forest comes down, and the very next verse of the book is a green shoot out of a stump.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth. A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God. For though your people Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant of them will return. Destruction is decreed, overflowing with righteousness. For the Lord GOD of hosts will make a full end, as decreed, in the midst of all the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the remnant of Israel and the survivors of the house of Jacob will no more lean on him who struck them, but will lean on the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, in truth."

The verb is lean, and it is used twice in one sentence to make the contrast exact. They had been leaning on Assyria — that was Ahaz's whole policy in chapter 7, and it is the thing that struck them. Now they lean on God.

The two words at the end matter: in truth. Isaiah has spent nine chapters describing religion that was scrupulous and hollow — the festivals God could not bear, the prayers he would not hear. This leaning is not that. It is the real thing, and the phrase is there because the difference is not visible from outside.

"A remnant will return, the remnant of Jacob, to the mighty God."

Two names are hidden in that line, and together they tie three chapters into one.

A remnant will return is Shear-jashub — the name of the boy Isaiah was told to bring with him when he went out to meet Ahaz at the conduit (7:3). The child who walked beside his father as a living sign now turns out to be a sentence in a promise.

And the mighty God is El Gibbor — the second of the four throne-names given to the child in 9:6. If anyone doubted that the name in that verse meant what it said, here is the same phrase, fifteen verses later, unmistakably of God himself.

So the remnant returns, and what it returns to is the one the child was named. Paul quotes the next two verses about his own generation: though the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, only a remnant will be saved (Rom. 9:27-28).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD of hosts: "O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrians when they strike with the rod and lift up their staff against you as the Egyptians did. For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction. And the LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt. And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke will be broken because of the fat."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD of hosts: 'O my people, who dwell in Zion, be not afraid of the Assyrians when they strike with the rod and lift up their staff against you as the Egyptians did.'"

The address is tender in the middle of an invasion: O my people, who dwell in Zion. And the instruction is not that the striking will not happen — it will, with the rod and the staff — but that they are not to be afraid of it.

The comparison is chosen deliberately. As the Egyptians did. Everyone hearing this knew how the Egyptian version ended.

"For in a very little while my fury will come to an end, and my anger will be directed to their destruction."

The anger has a term. It has been stretched out through five chapters and it is not permanent, and when it ends it turns — not on them, but on the instrument.

"And the LORD of hosts will wield against them a whip, as when he struck Midian at the rock of Oreb. And his staff will be over the sea, and he will lift it as he did in Egypt."

Two rescues are named, and both are the sort where the numbers made no difference: Gideon against Midian, and the staff over the sea. Isaiah keeps reaching for these two because they are the occasions when Israel contributed nothing and the result was total.

"And in that day his burden will depart from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck."

The picture at the end is a farm animal being unharnessed — the weight lifted off the shoulder, the yoke off the neck. It is the same yoke that gets broken in 9:4, on the day of Midian, in the passage about the child. Isaiah's promises keep converging on the same gesture: somebody taking a load off a neck that could not remove it.

verseByVerse.quote: He has come to Aiath; he has passed through Migron; at Michmash he stores his baggage; they have crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodge for the night; Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled. Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth! Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety. This very day he will halt at Nob; he will shake his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He has come to Aiath; he has passed through Migron; at Michmash he stores his baggage; they have crossed over the pass; at Geba they lodge for the night; Ramah trembles; Gibeah of Saul has fled."

Five verses of place names, and the effect is entirely dependent on knowing the map — so here it is. These are villages on the northern approach to Jerusalem, listed in the order an invading army would reach them, and they get closer with every clause.

The detail is what makes it frightening. At Michmash he stores his baggage — the army is stripping down for the final push, leaving the heavy gear behind. At Geba they lodge for the night, which means people in the next village lay awake knowing where the camp fires were.

"Cry aloud, O daughter of Gallim! Give attention, O Laishah! O poor Anathoth! Madmenah is in flight; the inhabitants of Gebim flee for safety."

Now the villages are named as they panic. This is a road most of Isaiah's hearers had walked; Anathoth is a couple of hours from the city and would one day be Jeremiah's home town. It reads like a list of ordinary places on a familiar route, going one by one.

"This very day he will halt at Nob; he will shake his fist at the mount of the daughter of Zion, the hill of Jerusalem."

And there he stops — at Nob, on the last ridge, within sight of the city. Close enough to make a gesture, which is what he does: not an assault, a raised fist at a hill.

Isaiah has taken twelve place names to walk an army to the edge of everything, and left it there, arm in the air. The next verse is what answers the fist.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low. He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the Lord GOD of hosts will lop the boughs with terrifying power; the great in height will be hewn down, and the lofty will be brought low."

The answer to the raised fist is a woodsman.

Assyria has been a forest through this chapter — the glory of his forest consumed, the trees so few a child could count them — and now God comes into it with an axe. Lop the boughs. Hewn down. Brought low. Three verbs, all of them downward.

And the phrase the great in height reaches back to chapter 2, where the day of the LORD was against the cedars of Lebanon and everything tall. The principle has not changed since: there is one thing in the universe that is high, and everything else is timber.

"He will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One."

The chapter ends in a clearing. Great trunks on the ground, the sound stopped, the man with the axe still standing there. It is a complete ending, and it is the end of the Assyrian question in the book.

But it is not the end of the sentence. Isaiah wrote the next line without a break, and a chapter division has hidden the join: there shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse.

Out of the same felled ground, at the bottom of the same picture, something green. The axe that ends the empire is the axe that clears the way — and the shoot is not an afterthought to the felling but the reason a stump was left standing at all.

11.subtitle: The Root of Jesse and the Peaceable Kingdom
11.intro:
Overview. Chapter 10 ends with God taking an axe to a forest, and chapter 11 begins in the clearing: out of a cut stump, a green shoot. It is the same stump as 6:13, where the felled tree was left with the promise that the holy seed is its stump. And Isaiah names Jesse rather than David — reaching back past the whole monarchy to the Bethlehem farmer it started from, as though the line had to begin again from nothing.

The Spirit does not visit this king but rests on him, which is exactly the sign John the Baptist was given (John 1:32-33). He judges neither by appearance nor by hearsay — the two ways every human court fails — and gets the cases of the poor and the meek right, striking the earth with nothing but the rod of his mouth. Then the most reproduced verses in the book: the wolf living with the lamb, the lion eating straw, a baby playing at a cobra’s hole, and no hurting or destroying anywhere — because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. The chapter closes with the nations walking toward a raised banner, an old two-hundred-year grievance simply taken away, and a highway home running out of Assyria along the very road the exiles left by.

keyVerse.quote: “And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The Spirit's resting on the Messiah is not temporary or intermittent but permanent — he rests on him. At Jesus' baptism, the Spirit descends and remains (John 1:32–33). The full range of Spirit-gifts needed for the Messiah's work — wisdom to teach, counsel to govern, might to deliver, knowledge and fear of God to judge rightly — are all present in him simultaneously and without measure (John 3:34).

11.theology:
The stump. The image is humiliating before it is glorious, and that is the doctrine. Not a bough of a flourishing tree but a shoot from cut wood, and from Jesse rather than David — which is why the New Testament makes so much of a birth in Bethlehem to people of no standing, six centuries after the house of David had lost the throne. The dynasty being a stump was never the obstacle to the promise; it was the shape of it. Isaiah lays the thread deliberately: the holy seed in the stump at 6:13, the shoot here, and a root out of dry ground with no form or majesty at 53:2.

The Spirit who rests. The judges of Israel had the Spirit rush upon them and leave again. Here the verb is rest — settle and stay — and the sixfold description supplies precisely what every leader in chapters 1 to 10 lacked: wisdom and understanding, counsel and might (rarely found in one person), knowledge and the fear of the LORD. The Spirit does not supplement his deity; he equips his humanity for the work.

Peace by saturation, not by restraint. The lion is not fenced from the ox — it eats straw, which is a change in what a lion is. And verse 9 makes the cause explicit: they do not hurt or destroy for the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea. The new creation is not policed into harmony but flooded into it, which means every present hurt is downstream of a place where that knowledge is thin. Isaiah returns to the whole vision at 65:25, set in the new heavens and new earth, and Habakkuk borrows verse 9 whole (Hab. 2:14).
11.reflection: The shoot from Jesse's stump grows from a situation that looks finished. The dynasty is reduced; the forest has been cut down; the stump is all that remains. If you are in a season that feels like a stump — where what you had hoped for seems to have been cut off — Isaiah 11 is written for you. God's most significant growth often comes from the most apparently finished starting points.
11.text: <sup>1</sup>There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.<sup>2</sup>And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.<sup>3</sup>And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear,<sup>4</sup>but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.<sup>5</sup>Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins.<sup>6</sup>The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them.<sup>7</sup>The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox.<sup>8</sup>The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den.<sup>9</sup>They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.<sup>10</sup>In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.<sup>11</sup>In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea.<sup>12</sup>He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.<sup>13</sup>The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim.<sup>14</sup>But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals.<sup>16</sup>And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Shoot from the Stump
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapter 10 ended with God taking an axe to a forest. Verse 1 begins in the clearing: out of a cut stump, a shoot. Verse 2 has the Spirit of the LORD resting on him, in a sixfold description that has been counted as seven since the earliest centuries. Verses 3 and 4 describe how he judges — not by what his eyes see or his ears hear, but with righteousness for the poor and equity for the meek, striking the earth with nothing but the rod of his mouth. Verse 5 dresses him: righteousness and faithfulness are the belt he is bound with.
verseByVerse.theology: The image is deliberately humiliating before it is glorious. Not a branch from a flourishing tree but a shoot from a stump, and not from David but from Jesse — reaching back past the dynasty to the Bethlehem farmer it started with, as though the monarchy were being begun again from nothing. And the Spirit does not visit him; the verb is rest, a settled dwelling. John records the sign given to the Baptist in exactly those terms: the Spirit descended and remained (John 1:32-33).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 describes a judge who cannot be deceived by appearance or by testimony — which is what every court in chapters 1 to 10 could be, and was. And verse 4 is the answer to every generation that assumes righteousness needs an army: he strikes the earth with the rod of his mouth. Paul takes that clause and applies it to the return of Christ (2 Thess. 2:8).

verseByVerse.quote: There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"There shall come forth a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and a branch from his roots shall bear fruit."

Read the last two verses of chapter 10 before this one, because they are one picture cut in half by a chapter division that did not exist when Isaiah wrote. God has just gone through Assyria's army like a woodsman: "he will cut down the thickets of the forest with an axe, and Lebanon will fall by the Majestic One" (10:34). Great trees on the ground, the axe still in his hand.

And then, in the silence after the felling, a green shoot.

The word is netser — a sprout, the thin growth that comes off a stump nobody expected anything from. It is not a bough of a standing tree. It comes out of the cut, at ground level, from wood that everyone walking past has written off.

Isaiah has used this image before and it is the same stump. At the end of his call vision, when he asked how long the judgment would last and was told until cities lie waste without inhabitant, the answer ended with a tree felled and this promise: "the holy seed is its stump" (6:13). That was the seed. This is what came up.

Now notice whose stump it is, because Isaiah could have said David and did not. He says Jesse — David's father, a farmer in Bethlehem with a lot of sons, a man of no importance whatever until a prophet turned up at his door. To name Jesse is to reach back past the whole monarchy to the point before it began, as if the royal line had been cut down so completely that the only way forward was to start again from the family it started from.

Which is why the New Testament makes so much of a birth in Bethlehem to people of no standing, in a reign when a foreigner sat on the throne and the house of David had been out of power for six hundred years. The dynasty had long since been a stump. That was never the obstacle. It was the point.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD."

The first thing said about the shoot is not what he will do but who is on him.

And the verb matters. The Spirit does not come upon him, or rush upon him, which is the language used of the judges — the Spirit rushed on Samson, on Gideon, on Saul, and then left again. Here the word is rest: settle, alight, stay. It is the difference between a bird landing on a branch and a bird passing overhead.

That is exactly the sign John the Baptist was given, and he says so. "I saw the Spirit descend from heaven like a dove, and it remained on him. I myself did not know him, but he who sent me to baptise with water said to me, 'He on whom you see the Spirit descend and remain, this is he'" (John 1:32-33). The identifying mark was not the descending. Other men had that. It was that it stayed.

Then three pairs, which with "the Spirit of the LORD" at the head make the seven that Christian tradition has counted since the early centuries.

Wisdom and understanding — knowing what is true and seeing how it fits together. Counsel and might — knowing what to do and being able to do it, which are almost never found in the same person. Most who see clearly cannot act, and most who can act do not see. Knowledge and the fear of the LORD — and it ends there deliberately, because in this book the fear of the LORD is where knowledge begins rather than a pious afterthought appended to it.

Set the list against the leaders Isaiah has been describing for ten chapters: rulers who could not judge, elders who took bribes, prophets who lied, a king who would not ask God for a sign. Every single item is the thing they lacked. The shoot arrives fully equipped with precisely what the forest ran out of.

verseByVerse.quote: And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear, but with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth; and he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And his delight shall be in the fear of the LORD."

Not his duty. His delight. The Hebrew has a physical flavour to it — the verb is related to smelling, taking something in with pleasure — and what he takes pleasure in is reverence for God. Everything that follows about his justice comes out of that, which is the right order: a judge is only as good as what he loves.

"He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide disputes by what his ears hear."

That sounds like a criticism of the senses and it is not. It is a description of the two ways every human court goes wrong. Judging by the eyes is judging on appearance — who looks respectable, who is well dressed, whose face fits. Deciding by the ears is judging on testimony and rumour — who tells the better story, who has the louder advocate, what everybody says about the man.

No human judge can get past those two, because they are the only evidence available. Samuel could not, until God told him that man looks on the outward appearance but the LORD looks on the heart — and then sent him to Jesse's house, where the shoot in verse 1 comes from. This king sees the thing itself.

"But with righteousness he shall judge the poor, and decide with equity for the meek of the earth."

And look who is named. Not "he shall judge rightly" in general — the poor and the meek, the two groups whose cases go wrong in every court in history, because they cannot afford representation and have nobody to speak for them. In chapter 10 Isaiah denounced men who wrote laws "to turn aside the needy from justice and to rob the poor of my people of their right" (10:2). Here is the reversal, named at the same people.

"And he shall strike the earth with the rod of his mouth, and with the breath of his lips he shall kill the wicked."

No army. No sword. He speaks, and it is done — which is how the world was made and how it will be judged. Paul takes this clause and applies it to the return of Christ, who will kill the lawless one "with the breath of his mouth" (2 Thess. 2:8). The strongest thing in the universe turns out to be a sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Righteousness shall be the belt of his waist, and faithfulness the belt of his loins."

A small verse doing structural work. Everything before it described what he does; this describes what holds him together.

The belt in that world was not decoration. A man wore a long robe, and to do anything strenuous — fight, run, work — he had to gather it up and bind it at the waist. The belt was what turned a loose garment into something you could move in. Without it you were tripping over yourself. "Gird up your loins" is the same idea, and it means: get ready to act.

So Isaiah is not saying the king is decorated with righteousness. He is saying righteousness is the thing that gathers him and makes him able to move at all. Take it away and he could not function.

The two words are chosen as a pair. Righteousness is being right — doing what conforms to God's own character. Faithfulness is the word behind amen, which chapter 7 built its great pun on: reliability, being the sort of thing you can put your weight on. He is right, and he is dependable, and the second is what makes the first useful to anybody else.

Every ruler in this book has been girded with something. Ahaz with an Assyrian treaty. The elders of chapter 3 with what they could take. Isaiah looks at the coming king and finds that the thing binding him is his own righteousness — which cannot be bought off, cannot be frightened, and does not come loose.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The famous verses. The wolf lodges with the lamb, the leopard lies down with the young goat, the calf and the lion feed together and a small child herds them (v. 6). The cow and the bear graze side by side and the lion eats straw like an ox (v. 7). An infant plays over a cobra's hole and a toddler puts his hand into the adder's den (v. 8). And verse 9 gives both the scope and the cause: no hurting and no destroying anywhere on God's holy mountain, because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
verseByVerse.theology: What is described is transformation rather than restraint. The lion is not fenced off from the ox; it eats straw, which is a change in what the lion is. And verse 9 makes the cause explanatory rather than decorative: the peace is the effect of the knowledge of God saturating everything. Creation is not policed into harmony; it is flooded into it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is a quiet reversal of Genesis 3. The serpent that struck at the woman's offspring is now a hole a baby plays over, and this chapter's answer to that ancient enmity is a child — which is what verse 6 has leading the animals, and what 9:6 has on the throne. Isaiah returns to the whole vision at 65:25 in almost the same words, where it is set in the new heavens and the new earth.

verseByVerse.quote: The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them. The cow and the bear shall graze; their young shall lie down together; and the lion shall eat straw like the ox. The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat, and the calf and the lion and the fattened calf together; and a little child shall lead them."

These are the most reproduced verses in the book, and familiarity has flattened them. So read what is actually being claimed. Not that the wolf is restrained from the lamb, or penned separately, or fed elsewhere so it leaves the lamb alone. It dwells with it — the word for settling, living at the same address.

"The lion shall eat straw like the ox." That is the sentence that makes the point unmistakable. A lion cannot digest straw. Its whole body — teeth, gut, instinct — is built around killing something. To say it eats straw is not to say it has been tamed; it is to say it has been remade. What is promised here is not better behaviour in a fallen creation but a different creation.

"And a little child shall lead them." The herdsman is a toddler. In a world where a boy with a flock needed a sling and a stick and sometimes had to fight a lion — as one boy from Jesse's house did — the child here is simply walking in front, and everything follows.

"The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den."

Two children, one just younger than the other, and Isaiah has picked the two most helpless humans available and put them at the two most lethal spots in the landscape. A baby playing at a snake hole. A toddler with his hand down an adder's den — the exact gesture that would empty a room.

And go back to the third chapter of the Bible, where the enmity was set: between the serpent and the woman, between his offspring and hers, and he shall bruise your head and you shall bruise his heel (Gen. 3:15). A heel is what a snake strikes on a child at a hole in the ground. Here the ancient hostility is simply over — not because the child is protected from the serpent, but because the war has already been won somewhere else, by another child of the woman's offspring.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea."

The vision is summarised in six words and then explained, and the explanation is the more remarkable half.

They shall not hurt or destroy. Two verbs, and between them they cover nearly everything wrong with the world. To hurt is to damage what is there. To destroy is to end it. Take both out of a marriage, a workplace, a nation, a species, and there is almost nothing left of what we mean by trouble.

And the scope grows in the same line. It begins at my holy mountain — Zion, one hill — and by the end of the sentence it is the earth. The peace does not stay in the sanctuary. It spreads out from it until it has covered everything.

Then the cause, and this is the sentence to keep: for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

The peaceable kingdom is not produced by law, or by force, or by removing the dangerous animals. It is produced by knowledge of God saturating the world. Wolves lie down with lambs because the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD — that is the causal for, and it means every hurt and every destruction now happening is downstream of a place where that knowledge is thin.

And the measure is the sea. Not rain on the sea, or a tide across it — the waters covering it, which is to say the sea is water all the way down and all the way across, with no dry spot anywhere in it and no possibility of one. Habakkuk found the line and used it again (Hab. 2:14). That is the promised saturation: not that many people will know God, but that the world will be full of the knowledge of him the way the ocean is full of water.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–16 — The Signal, and the Second Exodus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verse 10 raises the root of Jesse as a signal that the nations come to enquire of, and calls his resting place glorious. Verse 11 has God stretching out his hand a second time to recover a remnant from eight named countries; verse 12 raises a banner and gathers the banished from the four corners of the earth. Verses 13 and 14 heal the oldest wound in the nation — Ephraim will stop being jealous of Judah, and Judah will stop harassing Ephraim. Verses 15 and 16 dry a sea and split a river and lay a highway home from Assyria, as there was for Israel coming out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: The second time in verse 11 is the interpretive key: the first was the exodus from Egypt, and everything here is deliberately built on that template — a sea destroyed, a river struck, a highway, a people walking across. God's later acts of rescue are made to look like his earlier ones so that his people can recognise them. Paul quotes verse 10 as the warrant for preaching to Gentiles (Rom. 15:12).
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 is easy to skim and it is the most personally applicable line in the section. The jealousy of the north and the harassment of the south had run for two centuries and had brought the coalition of chapter 7 to Jerusalem's walls. Isaiah puts the healing of that division in the same breath as the drying of the sea — both are things only God does, and one is not obviously easier than the other.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples—of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the root of Jesse, who shall stand as a signal for the peoples — of him shall the nations inquire, and his resting place shall be glorious."

The shoot of verse 1 has become the root, which is a quiet change and a large one. In verse 1 he grew out of Jesse's stump; here he is what Jesse's family grew out of. Both are true, and the New Testament says so in one breath: "I am the root and the descendant of David" (Rev. 22:16).

"A signal for the peoples." The word is nes — a standard raised on a hill so an army knows where to gather, or a pole set up as a rallying point visible from a distance. It is not a decoration; it is a thing you can see from far away and walk toward.

And the traffic is the surprise. In this book the nations have been the problem for ten chapters — coalitions, invasions, empires, the flies and bees of chapter 7. Now they arrive, and they arrive to enquire. Not to attack, not to trade, not to demand tribute: to ask. The banner goes up and the enemy comes over to find out what it means.

Paul quotes this verse at the end of his argument in Romans, as the last of four Scriptures proving that Gentiles were always in the plan: "The root of Jesse will come, even he who arises to rule the Gentiles; in him will the Gentiles hope" (Rom. 15:12). What Isaiah saw as a banner on a hill, Paul was doing for a living.

"And his resting place shall be glorious." A strange last clause for a chapter about a king, until you notice what it does not say. Not his throne, or his palace, or his battlefield. His resting place — the place where he stops. Everything in this chapter has been moving toward something settled, and the glory is finally located not in his conquering but in his rest.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people, from Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea. He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the Lord will extend his hand yet a second time to recover the remnant that remains of his people."

Everything in the rest of the chapter turns on two words: a second time.

There was a first. God stretched out his hand once before, over Egypt, and brought a people out of slavery through a sea, and every Israelite alive knew the story by heart. By calling this the second, Isaiah tells his readers exactly what kind of event to expect and gives them the pattern to recognise it by.

"From Assyria, from Egypt, from Pathros, from Cush, from Elam, from Shinar, from Hamath, and from the coastlands of the sea."

Eight places, and they are not a list so much as a compass. Assyria and Elam and Shinar away to the east. Egypt, Pathros and Cush to the south, running up the Nile into Africa. Hamath to the north. And the coastlands — Isaiah's phrase for everywhere across the water that he has no name for.

The first exodus came out of one country. This one comes out of everywhere, because by now the scattering has gone everywhere. God's rescue is shaped to the size of the loss.

"He will raise a signal for the nations and will assemble the banished of Israel, and gather the dispersed of Judah from the four corners of the earth."

Two words for the lost, and they should be kept apart. The banished are those who were driven out — the ones judgment removed. The dispersed are those simply scattered, blown about, who ended up far away without any single moment of expulsion. Both get gathered. It makes no difference whether a person left under judgment or merely drifted; the same banner is raised and the same hand collects them.

verseByVerse.quote: The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim. But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east. They shall put out their hand against Edom and Moab, and the Ammonites shall obey them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The jealousy of Ephraim shall depart, and those who harass Judah shall be cut off; Ephraim shall not be jealous of Judah, and Judah shall not harass Ephraim."

This is the least quoted verse in the chapter and one of the most striking, because of where Isaiah has put it: in the middle of drying up seas and gathering nations, as though it belonged in the same category of difficulty.

The wound is old. The kingdom split after Solomon, and for two centuries the two halves had been rivals — north jealous of the south's temple and dynasty, south contemptuous of the north's shrines and coups. Four chapters ago that rivalry had put an army from Ephraim outside Jerusalem's walls, trying to pull down the house of David (7:1). This is not an abstraction. It is the specific quarrel that shaped everything in chapters 7 to 10.

And notice that both sides are named, with the right fault attached to each. Ephraim's sin is jealousy — the resentment of the one who feels overlooked. Judah's is harassment — the needling of the one who feels superior. Neither is let off, and neither is asked to admit the other was right.

Isaiah does not say they negotiate, or that a treaty is signed, or that the issues are resolved. He says the jealousy departs. It is taken away, in the same passage and by the same hand that splits a river into seven channels — which is a fair estimate of how hard it is to remove a two-hundred-year-old grievance between people who share a history.

"But they shall swoop down on the shoulder of the Philistines in the west, and together they shall plunder the people of the east." United, they turn outward. The energy that two factions spend on each other is not small, and it is astonishing what becomes possible when it stops being spent there.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals. And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the LORD will utterly destroy the tongue of the Sea of Egypt, and will wave his hand over the River with his scorching breath, and strike it into seven channels, and he will lead people across in sandals."

The exodus is being staged again, deliberately, with the same props. A sea destroyed — the tongue of the Sea of Egypt is the northern arm of the Red Sea, the exact water Moses stood in front of. A river struck — the River, with no further identification, is always the Euphrates, the far boundary and the road home from Assyria. God waves his hand over it, as Moses lifted his staff, and it opens into seven fords.

"And he will lead people across in sandals." The detail is small and it is the point. At the first crossing they went through in haste, at night, with the Egyptian chariots behind them. This time they walk over dry-shod, in their shoes, at a normal pace. The same miracle, with the panic taken out.

"And there will be a highway from Assyria for the remnant that remains of his people, as there was for Israel when they came up from the land of Egypt."

A highway from Assyria. That is the road the deportations went out on — the route by which Zebulun and Naphtali were emptied, the long march east that families disappeared down and did not come back. Isaiah says the same road will carry them home.

God does not build a new route to avoid the memory. He turns the road of the exile into the road of the return, so that the way out becomes the way back, and nobody walking it can mistake who arranged it.

So the chapter that began with an axe in a cleared forest ends with a highway full of people. The stump was not the end of the tree. Out of it came a shoot with the Spirit resting on him, who judged the poor rightly and killed the wicked with a word, under whom the lion eats straw and a baby plays at the snake's hole, whose banner the nations walk toward, and whose road runs home from the place of exile. The holy seed was in the stump the whole time, and it always was, and the woodsman knew.

12.subtitle: A Song of Salvation
12.intro: Overview. Chapter 12 is a short hymn of praise — only six verses — that brings the first major section of Isaiah (chapters 1–12) to a doxological close. After eleven chapters of judgment, warning, and Messianic promise, the redeemed community breaks into song. The language draws on the Exodus (v. 2 quotes from the Song of Moses in Exodus 15) and looks forward to the gathering described at the end of chapter 11. This is what the people of God sound like when they have arrived at where God was always taking them.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation.”
keyVerse.note: The word translated salvation is Yeshua — the same name as Jesus. “God is my Yeshua” is, in retrospect, a name as much as a statement. The song that brings the first section of Isaiah to a close is a song about the one who will bring all of God's purposes to their close.

12.reflection: Chapter 12 ends the first major section of Isaiah at the highest point imaginable: the redeemed community singing with joy, drawing from wells of salvation, declaring God's name among the nations. This is the destination God has been aiming at through all eleven chapters of judgment and promise. Whatever stage of the journey you are on, this is where it ends.
