12.text: <sup>1</sup>You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me.<sup>2</sup>"Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation."<sup>3</sup>With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.<sup>4</sup>And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted.<sup>5</sup>"Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth.<sup>6</sup>Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — You Were Angry, and You Comforted Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Eleven chapters of indictment and judgment end in a hymn. Verse 1 begins where honest praise has to begin — you were angry with me — and then reports that the anger turned away and comfort came. Verse 2 states the confidence in words lifted from the Song of Moses at the Red Sea: God is my salvation, I will trust and not be afraid. Verse 3 turns it into an image: with joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.
verseByVerse.theology: The song does not open by claiming innocence. It opens by acknowledging that the anger was real and deserved and is now gone, which is the only foundation praise can actually stand on. A worship that has to pretend nothing was wrong is thin; this one knows exactly what it was rescued from and is therefore able to be glad without qualification.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 is almost word for word what Israel sang after the sea closed (Exod. 15:2). Isaiah puts the old song in the mouth of a new generation because the rescue is the same rescue and the Redeemer is the same Redeemer — which is why the church has always been able to sing songs written by people it never met.

verseByVerse.quote: You will say in that day: "I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me. "Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You will say in that day: 'I will give thanks to you, O LORD, for though you were angry with me, your anger turned away, that you might comfort me.'"

Eleven chapters of vineyard and woes and Assyrian armies, and the twelfth is a song. It is very short, and it is the hinge on which the whole first movement of the book turns.

Look at how it opens, because it would be easy to write this differently. The first thing said is not I was innocent or it was a misunderstanding. It is you were angry with me — stated plainly, in the past tense, as a fact about which there is now no argument.

That is what makes the rest of it sing. Praise that has to pretend nothing was wrong is always slightly thin, because everyone involved knows better. This song knows exactly what it was rescued from, which is why it can be glad without qualification.

And the purpose clause is the loveliest thing in the verse: the anger turned away that you might comfort me. Not so that accounts could be settled or order restored. God turned his anger away in order to get to the comforting.

"Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the LORD GOD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation."

Any Israelite would have recognised this immediately, because it is what their ancestors sang on the far bank of the Red Sea: the LORD is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation (Exod. 15:2).

Isaiah puts the old words in a new mouth, and the effect is to say that nothing has changed about how God rescues people. Same song, same Redeemer, different century.

And notice the order in I will trust, and will not be afraid. The trusting comes first and the fearlessness follows from it. Nobody in this verse is told to stop being frightened by an act of will.

verseByVerse.quote: With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation."

One line, and it is the most quoted verse in the chapter.

The picture belongs to a country where water is the daily problem. A well is not a scenic feature; it is the thing a household walks to every morning, and the difference between a village with one and a village without is the difference between life and leaving. To be told there are wells — plural — is to be told the supply is not going to run out.

And the word Isaiah chooses for salvation is yeshuah, which is the name that would one day be given to a boy in Nazareth.

Centuries later, at the Feast of Tabernacles, priests carried water in golden pitchers from the pool of Siloam up to the temple and poured it out while the crowd recited the songs of salvation — and this verse was among them. On the last day of that feast, with the water ceremony fresh in everyone's memory, a man stood up in the temple courts and shouted: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37-38).

He was not introducing a new idea. He was standing in front of people who had just sung about wells of salvation and telling them where the well was.

The word to keep is joy. Not duty, not relief — drawing water here is a glad thing, the way a homecoming is glad. Whatever else the Christian life is, it is meant to involve going back to the same source repeatedly and being pleased about it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Make Known His Deeds Among the Peoples
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second stanza turns outward. Verses 4 and 5 stack up imperatives — give thanks, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted, sing, let this be made known in all the earth. Verse 6 ends with a shout: sing for joy, inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel.
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation received becomes salvation announced, and the movement is treated as natural rather than commanded reluctantly. Nothing in these verses suggests that worship and mission are separate activities: the same gladness that sings turns round and tells, because a report this good does not stay in a room.
verseByVerse.examples: The last line brings the book's opening vision full circle. In chapter 6 the seraphim called the LORD of hosts holy and Isaiah said he was undone. Here the same title — the Holy One of Israel — is shouted by ordinary forgiven people as the reason for their joy. The holiness that once destroyed a man is now what his neighbours are singing about.

verseByVerse.quote: And you will say in that day: "Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted. "Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth. Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And you will say in that day: 'Give thanks to the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the peoples, proclaim that his name is exalted.'"

The second stanza begins the way the first did — you will say in that day — but everything now faces outward.

Count the verbs: give thanks, call, make known, proclaim. The first two are directed to God and the second two are directed at everybody else, and Isaiah puts them in one sentence without a seam. There is no moment in this song where the community finishes worshipping and starts evangelising. The same breath does both.

"Sing praises to the LORD, for he has done gloriously; let this be made known in all the earth."

And the reason given for the singing is not the experience of the singers but the quality of what God did. He has done gloriously — and a thing done that well cannot reasonably be kept in one country.

"Shout, and sing for joy, O inhabitant of Zion, for great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel."

The last line takes the book back to its beginning, and the reader who has come this far should feel it.

In chapter 6 a young man stood in the temple while creatures with six wings called to one another, Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts, and the building shook and he said, Woe is me, for I am lost. That is what the holiness of God did to the best man in Jerusalem.

Here the same title is on the lips of ordinary people, and it is the reason they are shouting with joy. Nothing has changed about the holiness. What has changed is that a coal came from the altar, and the guilt was taken away, and the anger turned aside so that comfort could get through.

Great in your midst is the Holy One of Israel. He is not distant and not diminished — he is holy, and he is in the middle of them, and they are singing about it. That is the whole arc of the gospel in one line: the holiness that ought to undo a sinner becomes the thing he cannot stop celebrating.

12.theology:
Praise that names what it was rescued from. The song opens with you were angry with me — not a claim of innocence but an acknowledgment, in the past tense, that the anger was real and deserved and has turned. That is the only ground authentic praise can stand on, and it is why the gladness here needs no qualification. The purpose clause is the tender part: the anger turned away that you might comfort me.

The same song as the sea. Verse 2 is almost word for word what Israel sang on the far bank of the Red Sea (Exod. 15:2). Isaiah puts the old words in a new generation’s mouth because the rescue and the Redeemer are the same — the reason the church has always been able to sing hymns written by people it never met. And the order inside the verse matters: I will trust, and will not be afraid. The trust comes first and the fearlessness follows.

The wells, and the circle closed. Yeshuah — salvation — is the name later given to a boy in Nazareth, and at the Feast of Tabernacles, when water from Siloam was poured out and these songs were sung, a man stood up in the temple and told the crowd where the well was (John 7:37-38). The chapter then ends by returning the trisagion of chapter 6 to ordinary lips: the holiness that made Isaiah say I am undone is here the reason forgiven people are shouting for joy.

13.subtitle: The Oracle Against Babylon
13.intro: Overview. Chapters 13–23 contain a series of oracles against the nations, beginning with Babylon. This is significant: Isaiah is prophesying the fall of Babylon more than a century before Babylon became a dominant power, and roughly two centuries before Cyrus of Persia conquered it in 539 BC. The oracle against Babylon serves a dual purpose — it announces specific historical judgment on a specific empire, and it uses that judgment as a lens through which to see the ultimate Day of the LORD against all that opposes God.

keyVerse.quote: “I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.”
keyVerse.note: The oracle against one specific historical empire has this universal horizon: “I will punish the world.” Babylon is the instance; the world's arrogance is the charge. Every empire that mistakes its power for permanence is, in Isaiah's vision, standing where Babylon stood — and heading where Babylon went.

13.reflection: The oracles against the nations in Isaiah 13–23 are not comfortable reading, but they answer an urgent question: does God see what the nations are doing? Is there accountability beyond the reach of any earthly court? The answer of this chapter is unambiguous. The pomp of the arrogant has an expiry date set by God himself.
13.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw.<sup>2</sup>On a bare hill raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles.<sup>3</sup>I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones.<sup>4</sup>The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle.<sup>5</sup>They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land.<sup>6</sup>Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come!<sup>7</sup>Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt.<sup>8</sup>They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame.<sup>9</sup>Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it.<sup>10</sup>For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light.<sup>11</sup>I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless.<sup>12</sup>I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir.<sup>13</sup>Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger.<sup>14</sup>And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land.<sup>15</sup>Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword.<sup>16</sup>Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–16 — Why There Are Eleven of These
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Chapters 13 to 23 are a block of oracles against the nations, and Babylon comes first. Verses 1 to 5 have God mustering an army — his consecrated ones, his mighty men — from the end of the heavens. Verses 6 to 8 turn the hearers to water: hands go limp, hearts melt, faces blaze. Verses 9 to 13 lift the language out of any single battle into the Day of the LORD, with the sun dark at its rising and the heavens trembling. Verses 14 to 16 describe what a sacked city actually looks like, and do not spare the reader.
verseByVerse.theology: The point of the whole block, stated once: these oracles are not foreign policy. They exist to say that the God of a small hill kingdom governs every empire on the map, that no power is outside his jurisdiction, and that his people therefore never have to negotiate with history as though God were absent from it. Each oracle also carries a turn toward mercy somewhere in it — watch for it, because it is the pattern rather than the exception.
verseByVerse.examples: Babylon is placed first although Assyria was the present danger, because Babylon is more than a country in this book: it is the standing name for human empire that makes itself ultimate. Revelation takes chapters 13 and 47 as its template for Babylon the great (Rev. 17-18), and the cosmic darkness of verse 10 is the vocabulary Jesus uses of the last day (Matt. 24:29).

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw. On a bare hill raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger, my proudly exulting ones. The sound of a tumult is on the mountains as of a great multitude! The sound of an uproar of kingdoms, of nations gathering together! The LORD of hosts is mustering a host for battle. They come from a distant land, from the end of the heavens, the LORD and the weapons of his indignation, to destroy the whole land. Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come! Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning Babylon which Isaiah the son of Amoz saw."

A new block begins here and runs to chapter 23: eleven oracles against foreign nations. Before going in, it helps to know what they are for, because a reader can be forgiven for wondering why a book about Judah spends eleven chapters on other people's politics.

They are here to say that the God of a small hill kingdom governs the whole map. Not that he takes an interest in it — that he rules it, appoints its dates, and holds every empire accountable. Which means Judah never has to treat history as a room God is not in. That is the pattern, and it will not be repeated at every stop.

"On a bare hill raise a signal; cry aloud to them; wave the hand for them to enter the gates of the nobles. I myself have commanded my consecrated ones, and have summoned my mighty men to execute my anger."

The striking phrase is my consecrated ones. It is temple vocabulary — people set apart for a holy purpose — and it is being used of a pagan army. They have no idea they are consecrated. God calls them his anyway, exactly as he will call Assyria his rod in the next chapter but one.

"Wail, for the day of the LORD is near; as destruction from the Almighty it will come!"

And then the human response, in three physical details: hands drop, hearts melt, faces turn to flame. Isaiah does not describe fear as a feeling. He describes what it does to a body when the news arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it. For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light. I will punish the world for its evil, and the wicked for their iniquity; I will put an end to the pomp of the arrogant, and lay low the pompous pride of the ruthless. I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir. Therefore I will make the heavens tremble, and the earth will be shaken out of its place, at the wrath of the LORD of hosts in the day of his fierce anger. And like a hunted gazelle, or like sheep with none to gather them, each will turn to his own people, and each will flee to his own land. Whoever is found will be thrust through, and whoever is caught will fall by the sword. Their infants will be dashed in pieces before their eyes; their houses will be plundered and their wives ravished.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the day of the LORD comes, cruel, with wrath and fierce anger, to make the land a desolation and to destroy its sinners from it."

The language now outgrows the subject. Everything so far could describe the sack of a city; what follows could not.

"For the stars of the heavens and their constellations will not give their light; the sun will be dark at its rising, and the moon will not shed its light."

The lights go out. Not clouds — the sun dark at its rising, which is the one moment it can be relied on. Isaiah has moved from a military campaign to the end of the world, and he does it without a seam, because in prophetic sight the fall of Babylon and the last day are the same event at different distances: one is a rehearsal for the other, and both are the Day of the LORD.

Jesus uses this vocabulary of his own return — the sun darkened, the moon not giving its light, the stars falling (Matt. 24:29) — and John uses it again in Revelation. The imagery began here.

"I will make people more rare than fine gold, and mankind than the gold of Ophir."

A terrible way of counting. In a sacked city gold is what becomes scarce; Isaiah says people will be scarcer.

Verses 15 and 16 then describe what conquest did to civilians in that world, and it is not softened: the thrust through, the infants dashed, the houses plundered. The Bible does not present war as clean, and it does not spare the reader the cost of the judgment it announces.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–22 — Owls Where the Palaces Were
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names the instrument: the Medes, who do not care for silver or delight in gold — an enemy that cannot be bought off (v. 17). Verses 19 and 20 promise that the glory of kingdoms will go the way of Sodom and Gomorrah and never be inhabited again, with not even a shepherd making a fold there. Verses 21 and 22 fill the ruins with wild animals: desert creatures, owls, ostriches, jackals howling in the towers.
verseByVerse.theology: The prophecy is dated and it landed. Babylon fell to a Median-Persian coalition in 539 BC, and the city that was the wonder of the ancient world declined into exactly the emptiness described here. What Isaiah offers is not a general warning about pride but a specific, checkable claim about a named city, made while it was still rising.
verseByVerse.examples: The detail that lands hardest is the silence. No Arab pitching a tent, no shepherd resting a flock — not even the casual, temporary use that ruins usually get. Only animals, in the palaces. Every empire believes it is the exception, and the ruins of every empire are eventually somebody's nesting site.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold. Their bows will slaughter the young men; they will have no mercy on the fruit of the womb; their eyes will not pity children. And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them. It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there. But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces; its time is close at hand and its days will not be prolonged.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, I am stirring up the Medes against them, who have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold."

God names the executioner a century and a half before the event, and the detail he selects is the one that matters. The Medes cannot be bought. Babylon's entire security apparatus — wealth, tribute, the ability to pay anyone off — is useless against an enemy that does not want money.

It happened in 539 BC, when a Median-Persian coalition took the city.

"And Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the splendor and pomp of the Chaldeans, will be like Sodom and Gomorrah when God overthrew them."

Isaiah gives Babylon its full titles — the glory of kingdoms — before he demolishes it. The city had walls wide enough to drive chariots along and gardens counted among the wonders of the world. He is not underestimating it.

"It will never be inhabited or lived in for all generations; no Arab will pitch his tent there; no shepherds will make their flocks lie down there."

And here is the sentence that gets under the skin. Not destruction — disuse. Ruins usually get some casual afterlife: a traveller camps in them, a shepherd pens sheep in a broken courtyard. Isaiah says not even that. Nobody will find it worth stopping at.

"But wild animals will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures; there ostriches will dwell, and there wild goats will dance. Hyenas will cry in its towers, and jackals in the pleasant palaces."

The last picture is of animals in the throne rooms, and it is the standing answer to every empire that believes it is the exception. Babylon was the greatest of them, and God told a small nation, in advance, exactly what would eventually be nesting in it.

13.theology:
Why eleven chapters about other nations. The oracles of chapters 13-23 exist to say that the God of a small hill kingdom governs the whole map — not that he takes an interest in the empires but that he rules them, appoints their dates and holds them to account. The pastoral effect is that God’s people never have to treat history as a room he is absent from. Each oracle also turns toward mercy somewhere in it; that is the pattern rather than the exception.

Babylon first, and why. Assyria was the present danger and Babylon was still rising, yet Babylon leads the block — because in this book it is more than a country. It is the standing name for human empire that makes itself ultimate, and Revelation takes these chapters as its template for Babylon the great (Rev. 17-18). The prophecy is also specific and checkable: a named enemy who cannot be bought (v. 17), and a fall that came in 539 BC.

The Day of the LORD. At verse 10 the language outgrows any sack of any city — the sun dark at its rising, the stars withholding their light. Isaiah moves from a military campaign to the end of the world without a seam, because in prophetic sight the two are one event at different distances. Jesus uses this exact vocabulary of his own return (Matt. 24:29).

14.subtitle: The Taunt Against the King of Babylon
14.intro: Overview. Chapter 14 continues the Babylon oracle with a taunt song addressed to the king of Babylon — one of the most dramatically vivid passages in all of Isaiah. The king who exalted himself to the heavens is brought down to Sheol; those who once cowered before him now mock him in death. The famous passage in verses 12–15 has been interpreted from the earliest centuries as a description of the fall of Satan, behind the earthly king. The chapter also contains brief oracles against Assyria and Philistia.

keyVerse.quote: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high… I will make myself like the Most High.’”
keyVerse.note: The five “I will” statements are the grammar of pride at its most naked. Behind every act of human arrogance lies this claim: I will be my own ultimate authority. The king of Babylon is the extreme form of what is present in every sinful heart. This is why pride is not just a character flaw but a theological rebellion — it is the assertion of the self in the place of God.

14.reflection: The taunt song of Isaiah 14 is a meditation on the vanity of earthly greatness. The king who made the world tremble lies without a burial, mocked by those he once terrified. The chapter asks a searching question: in what are you tempted to place your ultimate confidence and identity? Because whatever it is, it has the same trajectory as the king of Babylon unless it is anchored in something that cannot fall.

For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks.<sup>32</sup>What will one answer the messengers of the nation? "The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — The Song Belongs to People Who Got Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Before a word of the taunt, Isaiah says who sings it. The LORD will have compassion on Jacob, will again choose Israel, and will settle them in their own land; foreigners will join them, and those who took them captive will be taken (vv. 1-2). Verse 3 sets the scene precisely: on the day the LORD gives you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service you were made to serve.
verseByVerse.theology: The placement matters. This is not a song of bitterness sung by people still in chains; it is sung by people who have been given rest, looking back. That distinction keeps the chapter from being gloating — the fall of the oppressor and the freeing of the captives are one event seen from two sides, and only the freed are allowed to sing about it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 1 quietly widens the promise: sojourners will join them and attach themselves to the house of Jacob. In the middle of an oracle about a foreign empire, foreigners are being folded into the people of God — which is where this book always ends up going.

verseByVerse.quote: For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land, and sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. And the peoples will take them and bring them to their place, and the house of Israel will possess them in the LORD's land as male and female slaves. They will take captive those who were their captors, and rule over those who oppressed them. When the LORD has given you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the LORD will have compassion on Jacob and will again choose Israel, and will set them in their own land."

Before the famous song begins, Isaiah tells you who is singing it, and everything depends on that.

The singers are not prisoners spitting at a wall. They are people God has already had compassion on, already chosen again, already brought home — and verse 3 dates the song exactly: on the day when the LORD gives you rest from your pain and turmoil and the hard service with which you were made to serve.

So this is a song sung after the rest arrives. That keeps it from being what it would otherwise obviously be, which is gloating. The freeing of the captive and the fall of the captor are one event, and only the freed have the right to sing about it.

And there is a quiet enlargement in verse 1 that is easy to read past: sojourners will join them and will attach themselves to the house of Jacob. In the middle of an oracle about the destruction of a foreign empire, foreigners are being brought in. Isaiah cannot go five chapters without the nations arriving.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The taunt-song proper. Verses 4 to 8 have the whole earth at rest and even the trees of Lebanon glad, because nobody comes to cut them now. Verses 9 to 11 take the reader down to Sheol, where the dead kings stir themselves to greet the new arrival. Verses 12 to 15 give the five great I will boasts and the one-line answer to them. Verses 16 to 20 have onlookers staring at a corpse and asking whether this is the man who shook kingdoms — a man with no grave. Verses 21 to 23 close the account: no descendants, and owls and swamp where the city was.
verseByVerse.theology: The five I wills of verses 13 and 14 are the anatomy of pride, and they end at the only place they can: I will make myself like the Most High. The answer is one sentence long. This is the sin that has no ceiling and therefore no floor either — it climbs until it falls, and both the climbing and the falling are its own doing.
verseByVerse.examples: Since the early church these verses have been read as showing the shape of an older fall behind the Babylonian one — the Day Star cast down — and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). The text is about a human king; what it exposes is the pride that lies behind every throne that makes itself ultimate.

verseByVerse.quote: you will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: "How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased! The LORD has broken the staff of the wicked, the scepter of rulers, that struck the peoples in wrath with unceasing blows, that ruled the nations in anger with unrelenting persecution. The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, 'Since you were laid low, no woodcutter comes up against us.' Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations. All of them will answer and say to you: 'You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!' Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You will take up this taunt against the king of Babylon: 'How the oppressor has ceased, the insolent fury ceased!'"

The word is taunt, and this is a recognised form — a mocking funeral song, sung with the rhythm of a lament and the content of a celebration.

"The whole earth is at rest and quiet; they break forth into singing. The cypresses rejoice at you, the cedars of Lebanon, saying, 'Since you were laid low, no woodcutter comes up against us.'"

The trees are glad. It is a wonderful touch: the great cedar forests of Lebanon, stripped for generations to build imperial palaces and warships, are pictured breathing out because the logging has stopped. Even the landscape was a victim, and even the landscape is relieved.

"Sheol beneath is stirred up to meet you when you come; it rouses the shades to greet you, all who were leaders of the earth; it raises from their thrones all who were kings of the nations."

Then the scene shifts underground, and Isaiah writes the strangest and most effective passage in the chapter. The dead kings of the earth get up.

They have been sitting on shadowy thrones, and the arrival of the great one causes a stir — and what they say is: "You too have become as weak as we! You have become like us!" It is the greeting of a club nobody wants to join, delivered with grim satisfaction by members who were once told they were nothing beside him.

"Your pomp is brought down to Sheol, the sound of your harps; maggots are laid as a bed beneath you, and worms are your covers."

And the bedding. The man who slept in the finest room in the world is given a mattress of maggots and a blanket of worms. Isaiah is not being gratuitous; he is answering magnificence in its own currency, item for item.

verseByVerse.quote: "How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low! You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.' But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"How you are fallen from heaven, O Day Star, son of Dawn! How you are cut down to the ground, you who laid the nations low!"

Day Star, son of Dawn — in Hebrew helel ben shachar, the morning star, the last light left in the sky before the sun comes up and puts it out. It is a brilliant title for a king who thought he outshone everything, and a brilliant thing to watch fall.

"You said in your heart, 'I will ascend to heaven; above the stars of God I will set my throne on high; I will sit on the mount of assembly in the far reaches of the north; I will ascend above the heights of the clouds; I will make myself like the Most High.'"

Five sentences, each beginning I will, and they are the anatomy of pride laid out in order. Ascend. Set my throne. Sit. Ascend again. And then the last one, which is where every one of the others was always heading: I will make myself like the Most High.

Notice where the whole thing happens: you said in your heart. Not in a speech, not in a decree. This is a private sentence that nobody heard, and it is the sentence God answers.

"But you are brought down to Sheol, to the far reaches of the pit."

One line, and it is deliberately the same shape as the boast — the far reaches of the north answered by the far reaches of the pit. He aimed at the top of the sky and reached the bottom of the ground, and the distance between them is exactly the measure of the ambition.

Christian readers have long seen an older fall showing through this one, and with reason: Jesus told his disciples he saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven (Luke 10:18). The passage is about a king of Babylon. What it exposes is the thing behind every throne that makes itself ultimate, which had been falling a long time before Babylon was built.

verseByVerse.quote: Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: 'Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?' All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch, clothed with the slain, those pierced by the sword, who go down to the stones of the pit, like a dead body trampled underfoot. You will not be joined with them in burial, because you have destroyed your land, you have slain your people. "May the offspring of evildoers nevermore be named! Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth, and fill the face of the world with cities." "I will rise up against them," declares the LORD of hosts, "and will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, descendants and posterity," declares the LORD. "And I will make it a possession of the hedgehog, and pools of water, and I will sweep it with the broom of destruction," declares the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Those who see you will stare at you and ponder over you: 'Is this the man who made the earth tremble, who shook kingdoms, who made the world like a desert and overthrew its cities, who did not let his prisoners go home?'"

Isaiah brings the reader back up to ground level, and the scene is a crowd around a body.

They stare and ponder — the slow double-take of people trying to match what is in front of them with what they remember. Is this him? The question is asked with four clauses of achievement attached, and every one of them was true, and none of them helps.

The last charge is the human one: who did not let his prisoners go home. Among all the shaken kingdoms, the thing the crowd names last is the men he kept.

"All the kings of the nations lie in glory, each in his own tomb; but you are cast out, away from your grave, like a loathed branch."

And here is the point of the passage. Other kings got tombs. This one is thrown out like a lopped limb, trampled underfoot, not joined with them in burial. In a world where a proper grave was the last dignity a great man could count on, the king who wanted to sit above the stars ends without a plot of ground.

"Prepare slaughter for his sons because of the guilt of their fathers, lest they rise and possess the earth."

The line is hard, and it belongs to the world of dynasties, where a surviving son meant a restored regime. The intention is stated plainly in verses 22 and 23: God will cut off from Babylon name and remnant, and turn it into a possession of the hedgehog and pools of water.

The greatest city on earth becomes a swamp with birds in it. That is the end of the "I will" of verse 13.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two short oracles close the chapter. Verses 24 to 27 turn to Assyria — the power actually at the door — with an oath: as I have planned, so shall it be; I will break him in my land; and who will annul it? Verses 28 to 31 warn Philistia not to celebrate the death of the king whose rod struck her, because something worse is coming from the north. Verse 32 answers the messengers of the nations with a single sentence about Zion.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 27 is the load-bearing line of the whole oracle block: the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back? Every nation in chapters 13 to 23 is being measured against that question, and the expected answer is nobody.
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the one to keep. Asked what to tell the envoys of the nations, the answer is not a military assessment but this: the LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge. In a chapter full of thrones and corpses, the final word is about a shelter for people with nothing.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD of hosts has sworn: "As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand, that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot; and his yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder." This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations. For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD of hosts has sworn: 'As I have planned, so shall it be, and as I have purposed, so shall it stand, that I will break the Assyrian in my land, and on my mountains trample him underfoot; and his yoke shall depart from them, and his burden from their shoulder.'"

The chapter turns from Babylon, which was still rising, to Assyria, which was at the door — and it does so with an oath.

Look at the structure of the promise: as I have planned, so shall it be; as I have purposed, so shall it stand. Two clauses, both saying that with God the distance between the intention and the event is nil. That is the whole difference between his plans and everyone else's in this chapter, where a man said five things in his heart and none of them happened.

"This is the purpose that is purposed concerning the whole earth, and this is the hand that is stretched out over all the nations."

Notice the widening. What began as a promise about one invasion is immediately extended to the whole earth and all the nations — because the oracles in this block are not eleven separate policies but one hand over one world.

"For the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? His hand is stretched out, and who will turn it back?"

And this is the sentence the entire block rests on. Two questions, both rhetorical, and the expected answer to each is nobody.

It is also the answer to a fear older than Assyria. Whatever is currently stretched out over a life — a diagnosis, a government, a decline that seems unstoppable — there is exactly one hand in the universe that cannot be turned back, and it belongs to somebody who is for his people.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: Rejoice not, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken, for from the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent. And the firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay. Wail, O gate; cry out, O city; melt in fear, O Philistia, all of you! For smoke comes out of the north, and there is no straggler in his ranks. What will one answer the messengers of the nation? "The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the year that King Ahaz died came this oracle: Rejoice not, O Philistia, all of you, that the rod that struck you is broken."

Philistia is celebrating a death — some Assyrian king, or possibly Ahaz himself — and reading it as the end of the pressure. Isaiah tells them to stop.

"For from the serpent's root will come forth an adder, and its fruit will be a flying fiery serpent."

The image is a family tree of snakes, each generation worse than the last. That is the warning: the relief is temporary, and the successor is more dangerous than the man who died. Anyone who has watched a bad situation improve slightly and concluded it is over knows the shape of Philistia's mistake.

"And the firstborn of the poor will graze, and the needy lie down in safety; but I will kill your root with famine, and your remnant it will slay."

Two futures side by side in one verse, and they could not be further apart. The poor lie down in safety; the proud lose even their root. It is the pattern of the whole book in a sentence.

"What will one answer the messengers of the nation? 'The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge.'"

The chapter ends with a diplomatic question and a theological answer. Envoys arrive — presumably looking for an alliance, which is what envoys did — and ask what Judah's position is.

The reply says nothing about armies or treaties. The LORD has founded Zion, and in her the afflicted of his people find refuge.

That is the last word of a chapter that has been full of thrones, boasts, corpses and empires: a founded city, and in it a shelter for the afflicted. Everything the king of Babylon tried to build for himself, God simply provides — and he provides it to people who have nothing to bring.

14.theology:
Who is allowed to sing it. Isaiah dates the taunt before he quotes it: it belongs to the day God gives his people rest from their hard service (v. 3). It is not sung by prisoners at a wall but by people already brought home, which is what keeps a mocking funeral song from being mere gloating. The fall of the oppressor and the freeing of the captive are one event, and only the freed sing about it.

The five I wills. Verses 13 and 14 lay out the anatomy of pride in order, ending where it was always heading: I will make myself like the Most High. And it happens in his heart — a private sentence nobody heard, which is the one God answers. The reply is a single line shaped like the boast: the far reaches of the north answered by the far reaches of the pit. Since the early church these verses have been read as showing an older fall behind the Babylonian one, and Jesus says he saw Satan fall like lightning (Luke 10:18).

The purpose nobody annuls. Verse 27 is the line the whole oracle block rests on — the LORD of hosts has purposed, and who will annul it? — and it is deliberately widened from one invasion to the whole earth and all the nations. The chapter then ends, after all its thrones and corpses, on a founded city and a refuge for the afflicted (v. 32): everything the king of Babylon tried to build for himself, given free to people with nothing to bring.

15.subtitle: The Oracle Against Moab
15.intro: Overview. Chapters 15–16 form a single oracle against Moab, the nation east of the Dead Sea descended from Lot. The oracle is unusual in its tone: there is genuine mourning over Moab's destruction (15:5 — “My heart cries out for Moab”), and a remarkable invitation in 16:3–5 for Moab's fugitives to find shelter under Judah's king. Even in the oracles against the nations, Isaiah's God is not without compassion for the perishing.

keyVerse.quote: “My heart cries out for Moab.”
keyVerse.note: The brevity of this verse is part of its power. In the middle of an oracle announcing destruction, God's own heart cries out. Judgment and compassion are not mutually exclusive in God's character — they are simultaneously present. This is why the cross is simultaneously the most severe expression of divine justice and the most profound expression of divine love.

15.reflection: The oracles against the nations are often read only for their political and historical content. But Isaiah 15:5 breaks through that register entirely: God's heart cries out for the people he is judging. This should shape how God's people relate to those under judgment — not with triumph or indifference, but with the same broken compassion their God displays.
15.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone.<sup>2</sup>He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn;<sup>3</sup>in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears.<sup>4</sup>Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles.<sup>5</sup>My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction;<sup>6</sup>the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more.<sup>7</sup>Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows.<sup>8</sup>For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim.<sup>9</sup>For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Prophet Weeps for the Enemy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moab falls in a night, and Isaiah walks the reader through it town by town: Ar, Kir, Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz, Zoar, Horonaim, Nimrim, Eglaim, Beer-elim, Dimon. Heads are shaved and beards cut off; people go about in sackcloth and weep on the rooftops and in the streets (vv. 1-3). Fugitives run for the border with whatever they could carry (v. 7). And in the middle of it, unexpectedly, a voice says my heart cries out for Moab (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Moab was an old enemy and a blood relative — descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew (Gen. 19:37) — and had a long record of hostility toward Israel. What makes this oracle remarkable is its tone. It is not a victory announcement; it is a lament, and the grief in verse 5 is most naturally God's own. He judges Moab and he mourns Moab, and the two are not in tension.
verseByVerse.examples: That refuses a division most religious people find comfortable: our nation whom God loves, their nation whom he does not. The God who deals with sin in justice also grieves over those who go down under it — which is why the same book can end with all flesh worshipping, and why Jesus wept over the city that was about to kill him.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone. He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn; in the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears. Heshbon and Elealeh cry out; their voice is heard as far as Jahaz; therefore the armed men of Moab cry aloud; his soul trembles. My heart cries out for Moab; her fugitives flee to Zoar, to Eglath-shelishiyah. For at the ascent of Luhith they go up weeping; on the road to Horonaim they raise a cry of destruction;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"An oracle concerning Moab. Because Ar of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone; because Kir of Moab is laid waste in a night, Moab is undone."

Two cities, both gone in a night, and the sentence repeats itself with almost the same words — which is how people talk when they cannot take something in.

What follows is a litany of place names, and there is no need to look any of them up. The effect is what matters: Dibon, Nebo, Medeba, Heshbon, Elealeh, Jahaz — ordinary towns where ordinary people lived, named one after another the way a local would name them, each one now a place where somebody is weeping.

"He has gone up to the temple, and to Dibon, to the high places to weep; over Nebo and over Medeba Moab wails. On every head is baldness; every beard is shorn."

Shaved heads and cut beards were the visible signs of grief in that world — a man did to his own body what the disaster had done to his life. Isaiah is describing a whole country in mourning dress.

"In the streets they wear sackcloth; on the housetops and in the squares everyone wails and melts in tears."

Public grief, in the two places where a town is most itself: the flat roofs where families slept and talked in the evening, and the squares where they did business.

"My heart cries out for Moab."

And then, without warning, this. In the middle of a judgment oracle against a hostile neighbour, somebody is grieving — and the most natural reading is that it is God.

He is not conflicted. He has judged Moab justly and he is heartbroken about it, and Scripture never treats those two as needing to be reconciled. It is the same voice that would one day stand on a hill outside Jerusalem, look at the city that was arranging his death, and weep over it.

verseByVerse.quote: the waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more. Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows. For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim. For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more, a lion for those of Moab who escape, for the remnant of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The waters of Nimrim are a desolation; the grass is withered, the vegetation fails, the greenery is no more."

The disaster reaches the water, which in that country is the end of the argument. Grass gone, vegetation failed, nothing green — and a place named for its waters is now named ironically.

"Therefore the abundance they have gained and what they have laid up they carry away over the Brook of the Willows."

Here is one of the saddest sentences in the prophets, and it is about luggage. Everything a family had built up and put by — the abundance they gained, the things they laid up, the whole slow accumulation of a life — is now what they can carry across a stream while running away.

It is a picture worth sitting with, because it measures possessions by the only test that finally applies to them: what happens to them on the day you have to leave.

"For a cry has gone around the land of Moab; her wailing reaches to Eglaim; her wailing reaches to Beer-elim."

The sound travels to the borders. Isaiah has been tracking the grief geographically, and now it has filled the whole country and is arriving at the edges.

"For the waters of Dibon are full of blood; for I will bring upon Dibon even more."

The chapter ends without relief, and the last words are God's: even more. There is no turn here, no comfort in the final line.

The turn is coming — the very next chapter opens by telling Moab's refugees where to run and offering them shelter under a throne in Judah. But Isaiah does not hurry to it. He lets a chapter end in blood and weeping, because that is honest, and because the offer of refuge means nothing to anyone who has not first been allowed to see what is being fled from.

15.theology:
The prophet weeps for the enemy. Moab was an old adversary and a blood relative, descended from Lot (Gen. 19:37), with a long record of hostility toward Israel. What makes this oracle remarkable is not its content but its tone: it is a lament rather than a victory announcement, and the grief in verse 5 — my heart cries out for Moab — is most naturally God’s own.

Justice and grief together. God judges Moab and mourns Moab, and Scripture never treats those as needing reconciliation. That refuses a division religious people find comfortable — our nation whom God loves, their nation whom he does not. The same voice would one day look at the city arranging his own death and weep over it.

What possessions weigh on the day you leave. Verse 7 is the quietest devastation in the chapter: everything a family gained and laid up is now what they can carry across a stream while fleeing. And the chapter is allowed to end in blood with no comfort in the last line — the offer of refuge in chapter 16 means nothing to a reader who has not been made to see what is being fled from.

16.subtitle: Moab's Pride and the Promise of the Throne
16.intro: Overview. Chapter 16 concludes the Moab oracle, moving from a remarkable offer of shelter for Moab's fugitives (vv. 1–5) through the description of Moab's pride (vv. 6–12) to the announcement of Moab's judgment within three years (vv. 13–14). The passage in verses 4–5 — describing a king who will judge in faithfulness and seek justice — is another of Isaiah's quiet Messianic insertions, pointing beyond any immediate political solution to the one king who will fully embody these qualities.

keyVerse.quote: “Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.”
keyVerse.note: The four qualities named — steadfast love, faithfulness, justice, righteousness — are the covenant attributes of God himself applied to the coming king. Every good king in Israel's history embodied them partially; the Messiah will embody them fully. This is the throne that will have no end (9:7).

16.reflection: Moab's refusal of the shelter offered in verse 3 is a parable of the pride that refuses grace. The offer is genuine; the shelter is real; the king on the throne of steadfast love is ready to receive. What prevents the fugitive from entering is not the absence of welcome but the presence of pride. This is always the obstacle.
16.text: <sup>1</sup>Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion.<sup>2</sup>Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon.<sup>3</sup>"Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive;<sup>4</sup>let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land,<sup>5</sup>then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness."<sup>6</sup>We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right.<sup>7</sup>Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth.<sup>8</sup>For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea.<sup>9</sup>Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased.<sup>10</sup>And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting.<sup>11</sup>Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth.<sup>12</sup>And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail.<sup>13</sup>This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past.<sup>14</sup>But now the LORD has spoken, saying, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracle turns from lament to counsel. Moab's refugees are told to send tribute to Zion and to come like fluttering birds pushed from the nest to the fords of the Arnon (vv. 1-2). Verses 3 and 4 are addressed to Judah, and they are an instruction: give counsel, grant justice, hide the outcasts, do not betray the fugitive, let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you, be a shelter to them. Verse 5 grounds the whole offer in a throne established in steadfast love, with someone seated on it who seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness.
verseByVerse.theology: The direction of the counsel is the surprise. Refugees from a nation under God's judgment are told to run toward God's people, and God's people are told to take them in and not hand them back. The instruction is given as an obligation rather than as generosity — hide the outcasts, do not betray the fugitive — and it is the standing shape of how Israel was to treat the displaced.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 cannot be satisfied by any king Judah actually had. A throne established in steadfast love, occupied in faithfulness, by one swift to do righteousness, is the throne of 9:7 — and Isaiah reaches for it here because the offer of refuge is only as good as the character of the one on the seat.

verseByVerse.quote: Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion. Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon. "Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer. When the oppressor is no more, and destruction has ceased, and he who tramples underfoot has vanished from the land, then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Send the lamb to the ruler of the land, from Sela, by way of the desert, to the mount of the daughter of Zion."

The chapter opens with advice, and it is addressed to the fugitives of chapter 15. Send tribute; go to Jerusalem; put yourselves under Judah's king.

"Like fleeing birds, like a scattered nest, so are the daughters of Moab at the fords of the Arnon."

The image is birds knocked out of a nest, still in the air, with nowhere yet to land. That is a refugee column: people in motion who have not stopped being in motion.

"Give counsel; grant justice; make your shade like night at the height of noon; shelter the outcasts; do not reveal the fugitive; let the outcasts of Moab sojourn among you; be a shelter to them from the destroyer."

Now Judah is being addressed, and the instructions are stacked without pause. Note that none of them is optional-sounding. Shelter the outcasts. Do not reveal the fugitive. That second one assumes somebody is looking for them and expects Judah to say nothing.

And the image in the middle is beautiful: make your shade like night at the height of noon. In that climate the middle of the day is dangerous, and the only mercy is shadow. God asks his people to be, for the frightened, what a wall of shade is at noon — a patch of night in the worst part of the day.

"Then a throne will be established in steadfast love, and on it will sit in faithfulness in the tent of David one who judges and seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness."

And the ground of the offer is a throne. Read the description and ask which king of Judah it fits: established in steadfast love, occupied in faithfulness, by a man who seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness. None of them. It is the throne of 9:7, and Isaiah reaches for it here because a refuge is only as good as the character of whoever is sitting at the centre of it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The offer is refused, and verse 6 says why in one word repeated four ways: we have heard of the pride of Moab — how proud he is — of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence. Verses 7 to 11 return to lament: the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth, the vines of Sibmah that once reached the sea, the shouting over the harvest silenced, and God saying his own heart throbs like a lyre for Moab. Verses 12 to 14 have Moab wearing itself out at the high place with no result, and set a three-year term on the whole prophecy.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the most theologically useful thing in the two chapters. The refuge was genuinely available, the throne was genuinely established in steadfast love, and Moab did not go — not because the offer was withdrawn but because accepting it required stooping. Pride is not primarily an unpleasant character trait here; it is the thing that makes grace impossible to receive.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 is the picture that stays: Moab presenting himself at the high place, wearying himself, praying, and getting nothing. There is no shortage of religion in this chapter. There is only a shortage of the humility that would have walked to Zion instead.

verseByVerse.quote: We have heard of the pride of Moab— how proud he is!— of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right. Therefore let Moab wail for Moab, let everyone wail. Mourn, utterly stricken, for the raisin cakes of Kir-hareseth. For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert; its shoots spread abroad and passed over the sea. Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears, O Heshbon and Elealeh; for over your summer fruit and your harvest the shout has ceased. And joy and gladness are taken away from the fruitful field, and in the vineyards no songs are sung, no cheers are raised; no treader treads out wine in the presses; I have put an end to the shouting. Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab, and my inmost self for Kir-hareseth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"We have heard of the pride of Moab — how proud he is! — of his arrogance, his pride, and his insolence; in his idle boasting he is not right."

The offer of verses 3 and 4 is not taken, and this verse is the whole explanation. Isaiah says the same thing four times over in one line, which is his way of indicating that there was nothing else to say.

Moab did not refuse shelter because the shelter was inadequate, or because the terms were humiliating in any objective sense, or because Judah was untrustworthy. Moab refused because going would have meant arriving as a supplicant at the door of a smaller neighbour and admitting it needed help.

That is the most important thing in these two chapters, and it should be said plainly: pride is not chiefly an unattractive trait. It is the faculty that makes grace impossible to accept. Everything in verses 3 to 5 was free and available, and the one qualification for receiving it was the willingness to stoop.

"Therefore let Moab wail for Moab — let everyone wail... For the fields of Heshbon languish, and the vine of Sibmah; the lords of the nations have struck down its branches, which reached to Jazer and strayed to the desert."

Then the grief returns, and it is agricultural. The vines of Sibmah were famous; Isaiah describes them as having reached all the way to Jazer and wandered out into the desert — a picture of extravagant growth, now cut down by foreigners.

"Therefore I weep with the weeping of Jazer for the vine of Sibmah; I drench you with my tears... Therefore my inner parts moan like a lyre for Moab."

And God grieves again, more physically than in chapter 15. His inner parts moan like a lyre — a low vibration in the body, the way a struck string goes on sounding. He offered the refuge, it was refused out of pride, the judgment fell, and he is not detached about any of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail. This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. But now the LORD has spoken, saying, "In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt, in spite of all his great multitude, and those who remain will be very few and feeble."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And when Moab presents himself, when he wearies himself on the high place, when he comes to his sanctuary to pray, he will not prevail."

This is the picture the two chapters have been building toward, and it should be read slowly, because it is not what most people expect the end of a judgment oracle to look like.

Moab is not being described as irreligious. He presents himself. He goes up to the high place. He wearies himself there — the word suggests real effort, prolonged and exhausting. He comes to his sanctuary to pray.

And nothing happens.

There was no shortage of devotion in Moab. There was a shortage of the one thing that would have made devotion useful, which was the humility to walk to Zion when the door was open. A man can spend enormous energy on religion at the wrong address, and Isaiah has just shown us what that costs.

"This is the word that the LORD spoke concerning Moab in the past. But now the LORD has spoken, saying, 'In three years, like the years of a hired worker, the glory of Moab will be brought into contempt.'"

And then a date. Three years, like the years of a hired worker — a labourer counting off a fixed contract, who knows exactly how long is left and is not inclined to be generous with the arithmetic.

Isaiah stakes the oracle on a verifiable timetable, as he did with the child in chapter 8. He is not offering a general reflection on the fate of proud nations. He is naming a country, a cause, and a number of years, and inviting his hearers to check.

16.theology:
Refuge offered to the enemy. The counsel in vv. 1-4 runs in the direction nobody expects: refugees from a nation under God’s judgment are told to run toward God’s people, and God’s people are told to take them in, hide them, and not betray the fugitive. It is framed as an obligation rather than as generosity, and the image at its centre is one of the loveliest in the book: make your shade like night at the height of noon.

A throne that no king of Judah fitted. Verse 5 grounds the whole offer in a throne established in steadfast love, occupied in faithfulness, by one who seeks justice and is swift to do righteousness. No historical Davidic king answers that description; it is the throne of 9:7. Isaiah reaches for it because a refuge is only as good as the character of whoever sits at the centre of it.

Pride as the thing that cannot receive. The offer is refused, and verse 6 gives the reason four times in one line. Moab did not decline because the shelter was inadequate but because accepting it meant arriving as a supplicant. That is the most useful thing in these two chapters: pride is not chiefly an unattractive trait but the faculty that makes grace impossible to accept. And verse 12 shows the alternative — a nation wearying itself in prayer at the wrong address, with no shortage of religion and no result.

17.subtitle: The Oracle Against Damascus — and a Remnant Who Returns
17.intro: Overview. Chapter 17 contains an oracle against Damascus (the capital of Syria) and its ally Ephraim (the northern kingdom of Israel), who together formed the anti-Assyrian coalition of chapter 7. Their destruction is announced with the stark brevity of verses 1 and 3. But within the oracle of judgment, Isaiah inserts one of his characteristic remnant promises: a few survivors will look to their Maker, and those survivors will be like gleaned olives, like the stalk left after a harvest. The judgment produces a purified people.

keyVerse.quote: “In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.”
keyVerse.note: This is the goal of all of Isaiah's prophecy compressed into one verse. The point of every judgment oracle is not destruction but redirection — turning eyes that have been fixed on everything else back to the only one worth looking at. The Holy One of Israel is the beginning and end of all genuine recovery.

17.reflection: Chapter 17 sets the pattern that runs through all of Isaiah's national oracles: judgment that aims at restoration. The stripping of idols from the remnant is not punishment for its own sake but the loving removal of everything that was substituting for God. Where in your own life have you experienced the stripping of something you relied on — and found, on the other side, that your eyes were clearer for it?
17.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins.<sup>2</sup>The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid.<sup>3</sup>The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts.<sup>4</sup>And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean.<sup>5</sup>And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>6</sup>Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel.<sup>7</sup>In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.<sup>8</sup>He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense.<sup>9</sup>In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation.<sup>10</sup>For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger,<sup>11</sup>though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain.<sup>12</sup>Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters!<sup>13</sup>The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm.<sup>14</sup>At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Two or Three Berries on the Highest Bough
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Damascus ceases to be a city and becomes a heap of ruins; its towns are abandoned to flocks that lie down undisturbed (vv. 1-2). Ephraim loses its fortress and Syria its kingdom, and the glory of Jacob is brought low and its fat body made lean (vv. 3-4). Verses 5 and 6 give two pictures of what is left: a reaper gathering standing grain in the Valley of Rephaim, and an olive tree that has been beaten — two or three berries at the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches.
verseByVerse.theology: These are the two powers whose coalition made the house of David shake like trees in a wind (7:2), and the oracle is their answer. Damascus fell in 732 BC and Samaria in 722. The terror of chapter 7 turns out to have had about a decade left in it.
verseByVerse.examples: The gleanings image is the remnant doctrine at its most honest. What survives is not impressive: a few berries the beaters could not reach, at the very top of the tree. But they are there, and they are there because they were out of reach — which is a fair description of how God has preserved his people in every century.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Damascus. Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins. The cities of Aroer are deserted; they will be for flocks, which will lie down, and none will make them afraid. The fortress will disappear from Ephraim, and the kingdom from Damascus; and the remnant of Syria will be like the glory of the children of Israel, declares the LORD of hosts. And in that day the glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean. And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears, and as when one gleans the ears of grain in the Valley of Rephaim. Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten— two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree, declares the LORD God of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, Damascus will cease to be a city and will become a heap of ruins."

The oracle is aimed at the two powers whose alliance made Ahaz's heart and his people's hearts shake like trees in a forest wind (7:2). Isaiah answers that terror here, and the answer is short.

Damascus will cease to be a city. Not be defeated — cease. And its towns will be given over to flocks, which will lie down there with none to frighten them: a picture of sheep dozing in the streets of an empire's capital.

It happened in 732 BC, and Samaria followed in 722. The coalition that had a king of Judah emptying the temple treasury in panic had about a decade left.

"The glory of Jacob will be brought low, and the fat of his flesh will grow lean."

Ephraim is included, because Ephraim chose the alliance. The image is a well-fed body losing its condition — not killed, reduced.

"And it shall be as when the reaper gathers standing grain and his arm harvests the ears ... Gleanings will be left in it, as when an olive tree is beaten — two or three berries in the top of the highest bough, four or five on the branches of a fruit tree."

And here is the remnant, described more honestly than anywhere else in the book. Olives were harvested by beating the tree with poles, and what survived a beating was whatever the poles could not reach: a few berries at the very top, a handful on the outer branches.

That is what is left of the northern kingdom. Not a faithful core that stood firm — two or three berries that happened to be out of reach. Isaiah does not flatter the remnant. It survives because of where it was kept, not because of what it was.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–11 — In That Day a Man Will Look
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Verses 7 and 8 describe the conversion the disaster was for: a man will look to his Maker and his eyes will look to the Holy One of Israel, and he will not look to the altars, the work of his own hands. Verses 9 and 10 name the cause of the ruin — you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge — and verse 11 has the pleasant plantings and imported vine-slips flowering in the morning and yielding nothing on the day of grief.
verseByVerse.theology: The two verbs in vv. 7-8 are the same verb: look. What changes is the direction. Judgment in Isaiah is very often simply the removal of everything else worth looking at, until a man's eyes come to rest where they should have been. And what he stops looking at is described precisely as the work of his own hands.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 diagnoses the whole thing as forgetting, which is not an intellectual failure. Nobody forgot that God existed; they forgot to remember him — the slow, unremarkable neglect of someone always available. And the gardens of verse 11 are the substitute: carefully planted, expensively stocked, flowering on schedule, and worth nothing on the day the grief arrives.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel.
