He will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made, either the Asherim or the altars of incense. In that day their strong cities will be like the deserted places of the wooded heights and the hilltops, which they deserted because of the children of Israel, and there will be desolation. For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge; therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day man will look to his Maker, and his eyes will look on the Holy One of Israel; he will not look to the altars, the work of his hands, and he will not look on what his own fingers have made."

One verb, used three times, and the whole conversion is in which way it points. Look.

The man in this verse does not acquire new information. He turns his head. He had been looking at altars he built and objects his own fingers made, and now he is looking at the one who made him — and the contrast between his Maker and the work of his hands is doing all the work in the sentence.

That is what the disaster was for. Judgment in this book is very often nothing more complicated than the removal of everything else worth looking at, continued until a man's eyes come to rest where they should have been all along.

"For you have forgotten the God of your salvation and have not remembered the Rock of your refuge."

And the cause is named, and it is not rebellion. It is forgetting.

Nobody in Israel had concluded that God did not exist. They had simply stopped remembering him — which is the quiet, unremarkable neglect that happens to anything permanently available, and which requires no decision at any point.

"Therefore, though you plant pleasant plants and sow the vine-branch of a stranger, and though you make them grow on the day that you plant them, and make them blossom in the morning that you sow, yet the harvest will flee away in a day of grief and incurable pain."

The substitute is a garden: fashionable imported stock, expertly planted, and it comes up beautifully. Isaiah grants it every success — it grows the same day, it blossoms the same morning.

And then the day of grief arrives, and there is no harvest. Which is the exact test that any substitute for God eventually fails: not whether it flourishes, but whether it is still there on the worst morning of your life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–14 — At Evening, Terror; Before Morning, Gone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter closes with a sound. The thunder of many peoples and the roaring of nations, like the roaring of mighty waters (v. 12). God rebukes them and they flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before a storm (v. 13). And then the timing: at evening time, sudden terror; before morning, they are no more (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole threat of the international situation is reduced to weather in three verses. What roars like the sea is answered with a rebuke and blows away like chaff — not defeated in a campaign, simply gone. And the last line names the principle the oracles exist to establish: this is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is the most usable sentence in the chapter for anyone going to bed frightened. At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more. That is exactly what happened to Sennacherib's army outside Jerusalem (37:36), and it is the standing shape of what God does with what terrifies his people overnight.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters! The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm. At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more! This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, the thunder of many peoples; they thunder like the thundering of the sea! Ah, the roar of nations; they roar like the roaring of mighty waters!"

The chapter ends with noise. Isaiah does not describe the armies of the nations; he describes the sound they make, and he compares it twice to the sea — which for an inland people was the standing image of a force that could not be reasoned with or stopped.

"The nations roar like the roaring of many waters, but he will rebuke them, and they will flee far away, chased like chaff on the mountains before the wind and whirling dust before the storm."

And the answer is one word: he will rebuke them. No battle is described, no army is raised. God speaks sharply and the sea turns out to have been chaff all along — the light husk left after threshing, which a hillside wind takes without effort.

"At evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more!"

This is the sentence to take out of the chapter, and it repays memorising for the right kind of night.

Isaiah puts the two times side by side with nothing in between. Evening: terror, present tense, immediate, with behold in front of it because it is right there in the room. Morning: gone. Not defeated after a long campaign — simply not there any more when the light comes.

Twenty chapters later that is exactly what happens outside the walls of Jerusalem, where an Assyrian army camps in the evening and in the morning the survivors are burying it (37:36).

"This is the portion of those who loot us, and the lot of those who plunder us." The chapter closes by naming that as a settled arrangement rather than a single incident. What has terrified God's people through the night has an appointment with the morning.

17.theology:
Two or three berries. Verse 6 is the remnant doctrine at its most honest. Olives were harvested by beating the tree, and what survived was whatever the poles could not reach — two or three berries at the top of the highest bough. Isaiah does not flatter the survivors: they are not a faithful core that stood firm, but a handful that happened to be out of reach. They exist because of where they were kept.

Judgment as the clearing of the view. In verses 7 and 8 the same verb is used three times — look — and the conversion consists entirely of a change of direction: away from altars and the work of his hands, toward his Maker. Judgment in this book is very often nothing more complicated than the removal of everything else worth looking at. And the cause of the ruin is named as forgetting (v. 10), which is not an intellectual failure but the unremarkable neglect that happens to anything permanently available.

Evening and morning. The roaring of the nations, twice compared to the sea, is answered by a rebuke and becomes chaff. Then verse 14 sets two times side by side with nothing in between: at evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more. That is precisely what happened to Sennacherib’s army outside Jerusalem (37:36), and the chapter names it as a settled arrangement rather than an incident.

18.subtitle: The Oracle Against Cush
18.intro: Overview. Chapter 18 is a brief oracle addressed to the land of Cush (ancient Ethiopia/Sudan), the nation from which Judah might have been tempted to seek military help against Assyria. The oracle is unusual in that it contains no explicit condemnation — it is more of a description of events, addressed to the distant Cushites, announcing that God is watching events unfold from his heavenly throne and will act at the right moment. The chapter ends with the remarkable promise that Cush will one day bring gifts to the LORD on Mount Zion.

keyVerse.quote: “For thus the LORD said to me: I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.”
keyVerse.note: The image of God watching quietly from his dwelling is one of the most calming pictures of divine sovereignty in Scripture. It is not passivity — the harvest is coming and the pruning shears are ready (v. 5). It is the quiet confidence of one who is never caught off guard, never reactive, always working toward his own purposes at exactly the right pace.

18.reflection: Chapter 18 is a reminder that God's apparent silence is not absence. He is watching — quietly, intently, from his dwelling — and he will act at exactly the right moment. The temptation in every crisis is to rush ahead of God, to seek the Cushite alliance when God has told us to wait. The chapter invites trust in the God who watches before he acts.
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush,<sup>2</sup>which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide.<sup>3</sup>All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!<sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest."<sup>5</sup>For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away.<sup>6</sup>They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them.<sup>7</sup>At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Envoys arrive from Cush — the African power that then ruled Egypt — almost certainly proposing an alliance against Assyria (vv. 1-2). They are sent straight home with a message for their own tall, smooth-skinned nation. Verse 4 gives God's posture: I will quietly look from my dwelling, like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. Verses 5 and 6 have him pruning the vine just before the harvest and leaving the cuttings to the birds. Verse 7 brings that same distant people to Mount Zion with a gift.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is the chapter, and the word that carries it is quietly. God is not inactive and not agitated. The two similes are of conditions a farmer watches for — steady heat, and dew in harvest weather — things that do their work without noise while everyone else is busy negotiating.
verseByVerse.examples: Judah is being told, by way of a message to Cush, that the diplomacy is beside the point. And the chapter that begins with envoys arriving to propose an alliance ends with the same nation arriving to bring a gift to the LORD of hosts — which is the turn toward mercy these oracles keep making.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters! Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide. All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, land of whirring wings that is beyond the rivers of Cush, which sends ambassadors by the sea, in vessels of papyrus on the waters!"

Cush is roughly modern Sudan, and in Isaiah's day its kings had taken Egypt and ruled both. It was a serious power a long way off, and its envoys have come up the coast in reed boats to see whether Judah will join a coalition against Assyria.

"Go, you swift messengers, to a nation tall and smooth, to a people feared near and far."

The description is respectful rather than mocking — a tall people, feared near and far, whose land the rivers divide. Isaiah is not belittling them. He is sending them home without an answer, which is a different thing.

"All you inhabitants of the world, you who dwell on the earth, when a signal is raised on the mountains, look! When a trumpet is blown, hear!"

And the audience widens abruptly from one embassy to everybody alive. There is a signal coming that will be visible from anywhere and a trumpet that will be audible to all, and when it goes the diplomatic question this delegation has travelled so far to ask will have answered itself.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the LORD said to me: "I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest." For before the harvest, when the blossom is over, and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away. They shall all of them be left to the birds of prey of the mountains and to the beasts of the earth. And the birds of prey will summer on them, and all the beasts of the earth will winter on them. At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth, from a people feared near and far, a nation mighty and conquering, whose land the rivers divide, to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus the LORD said to me: 'I will quietly look from my dwelling like clear heat in sunshine, like a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest.'"

Here is the sentence the chapter exists for, and everything is in one adverb. Quietly.

Ambassadors are rowing up the coast, coalitions are being assembled, and the great question of the decade is being urgently negotiated — and God says he is watching from home without raising his voice.

The two pictures are both agricultural and both chosen with care. Clear heat in sunshine is the steady warmth that ripens a crop: nothing dramatic, no storm, just the conditions doing their work day after day. A cloud of dew in the heat of harvest is the moisture that settles overnight in the hottest weeks. Neither makes any noise. Both are irresistible.

That is the answer to the panic of the chapter. God is not indifferent and he is not scrambling; he is watching the way a farmer watches a ripening field, waiting for the exact day.

"For before the harvest, when the blossom is over and the flower becomes a ripening grape, he cuts off the shoots with pruning hooks, and the spreading branches he lops off and clears away."

And then he moves. The timing is precise — not at the blossom, not at the harvest, but at the moment the fruit is setting — and the cutting is thorough. The birds and the beasts get the summer and the winter out of what is left on the ground.

"At that time tribute will be brought to the LORD of hosts from a people tall and smooth ... to Mount Zion, the place of the name of the LORD of hosts."

The chapter began with that nation sending ambassadors to Judah to talk politics. It ends with the same people arriving at Zion with a gift for God. That is what these oracles keep doing: the nations turn up first as a threat or a temptation, and eventually as worshippers.

18.theology:
Quietly. The chapter turns on a single adverb in verse 4. Envoys are rowing up the coast, coalitions are being assembled, and God says he is watching from home without raising his voice. Both similes are agricultural and both describe forces that work without noise: clear heat in sunshine, and dew in harvest weather. Neither is dramatic; neither can be resisted. God is not inactive and not agitated — he is watching a ripening field and waiting for the exact day.

The timing of the cut. When he moves (vv. 5-6) it is neither at the blossom nor at the harvest but at the moment the fruit is setting, and it is thorough. The point for a nation tempted to solve its problem by treaty is that the diplomacy is beside the point: the decisive act has a date, and the date is not being set in any of the capitals involved.

Threat, then worshipper. The chapter opens with a distant people sending ambassadors to talk politics and closes with the same people arriving at Mount Zion with a gift. That is the turn these oracles keep making, and it is why the block is not merely a catalogue of judgments.

19.subtitle: The Oracle Against Egypt — and Egypt's Redemption
19.intro: Overview. Chapter 19 is one of the most astonishing chapters in all of Isaiah. It opens with a severe oracle against Egypt — civil war, failed Nile, economic collapse, foolish counsellors — and then pivots, in its second half, to one of the most remarkable promises in the Old Testament: Egypt will know the LORD, worship him, and be called “my people.” The chapter that begins with God riding on a swift cloud against Egypt ends with Egypt, Assyria, and Israel forming a threefold blessing in the earth.

keyVerse.quote: “Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my heritage.”
keyVerse.note: The terms “my people” and “my heritage” are covenant terms used exclusively of Israel throughout the Old Testament. Here they are extended to Egypt and Assyria. This is not the abolition of Israel's election but its expansion — the covenant blessings flowing outward to the nations, exactly as God promised Abraham: “in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed” (Gen 12:3).

19.theology:
Judgment aimed at what a nation trusts. God does not attack Egypt’s army. He dries the Nile and confuses the counsellors — the river that was the country, and the wisdom that was proverbial across the ancient world. That is how a civilisation is dismantled rather than merely defeated, and verse 3 shows the reflex that follows: when real guidance fails, the appetite for it goes shopping, and the most sophisticated state on earth ends up consulting the dead.

The exodus, performed for Egypt. In verse 20 the Egyptians cry out under oppressors, God hears, and he sends them a saviour and delivers them. Isaiah has written that sentence deliberately in the shape of Exodus 2-3. The rescue that was carried out against Egypt is to be carried out for Egypt — the same mercy, extended to the old enemy, with an altar in the middle of the land of bondage.

The three titles of verse 25. Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance. Egypt enslaved Israel; Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom; both are given covenant names, and Israel is not displaced but stands as one of three. The nations are not absorbed into Israel — they are blessed as themselves, by name. It is the promise to Abraham arriving, and the same trajectory that ends with a dividing wall pulled down.
19.reflection: Chapter 19 moves from “the LORD is coming against Egypt” to “blessed be Egypt my people” — from judgment to adoption, from terror to worship. This is the arc of the gospel for every human soul. The God who rides on a swift cloud against his enemies is the same God who says to those same enemies, “You are mine.” The distance between those two verses is the cross.
19.text: <sup>1</sup>An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them.<sup>2</sup>And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom;<sup>3</sup>and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers;<sup>4</sup>and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.<sup>5</sup>And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched,<sup>6</sup>and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away.<sup>7</sup>There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more.<sup>8</sup>The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water.<sup>9</sup>The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton.<sup>10</sup>Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved.<sup>11</sup>The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings"?<sup>12</sup>Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt.<sup>13</sup>The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger.<sup>14</sup>The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit.<sup>15</sup>And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do.<sup>16</sup>In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them.<sup>17</sup>And the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them.<sup>18</sup>In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction.<sup>19</sup>In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border.<sup>20</sup>It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them.<sup>21</sup>And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them.<sup>22</sup>And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them.<sup>23</sup>In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians.<sup>24</sup>In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth,<sup>25</sup>whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–15 — The Wisdom of Egypt Fails
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God rides into Egypt on a swift cloud and the idols tremble (v. 1). The judgment works downward through everything the country was: civil war, Egyptian against Egyptian and city against city (v. 2); the spirit of the nation emptied out and its counsel confounded, so that it turns to idols, mediums and necromancers (v. 3); the Nile itself failing, with canals dry, reeds rotting and fishermen mourning (vv. 5-10). And finally the princes of Zoan and Memphis, the sons of ancient kings, exposed as fools who have made Egypt stagger like a drunk in his own vomit (vv. 11-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is aimed with precision at the two things Egypt was famous for: its river and its wisdom. The Nile was the country — take it away and there is no Egypt — and Egyptian counsel was proverbial across the ancient world. God does not attack the army. He dries the water and confuses the advisers, which is how you dismantle a civilisation rather than merely defeat one.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 is the pattern seen everywhere in this book: when the true source of guidance is gone, the appetite for guidance does not disappear, it goes shopping. A nation that prided itself on wisdom ends up consulting the dead — exactly as Judah does at 8:19.

verseByVerse.quote: An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them. And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom; and the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers; and I will give over the Egyptians into the hand of a hard master, and a fierce king will rule over them, declares the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"An oracle concerning Egypt. Behold, the LORD is riding on a swift cloud and comes to Egypt; and the idols of Egypt will tremble at his presence, and the heart of the Egyptians will melt within them."

The image is a war-chariot, and the cloud is it. God comes into Egypt personally, and the first things to react are the statues.

Egypt had more gods than any nation in the region and had held them for three thousand years. Isaiah gives them one verb: they tremble. Nothing is argued and nothing is disproved; the room simply becomes one in which they cannot stand still.

"And I will stir up Egyptians against Egyptians, and they will fight, each against another and each against his neighbor, city against city, kingdom against kingdom."

The judgment begins as civil war, which is the worst thing that can happen to a country and the hardest to blame on anyone outside it. Neighbour against neighbour, city against city — a nation coming apart along its own seams.

"And the spirit of the Egyptians within them will be emptied out, and I will confound their counsel; and they will inquire of the idols and the sorcerers, and the mediums and the necromancers."

Then the nerve. The spirit of the nation is emptied out — its confidence, its sense of itself — and its counsel is confounded.

And the reflex is the one Isaiah has already described in Judah (8:19). When real guidance fails, the appetite for guidance does not go away; it goes shopping. The most sophisticated civilisation on earth ends up asking questions of the dead.

verseByVerse.quote: And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, and its canals will become foul, and the branches of Egypt's Nile will diminish and dry up, reeds and rushes will rot away. There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more. The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton. Those who are the pillars of the land will be crushed, and all who work for pay will be grieved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the waters of the sea will be dried up, and the river will be dry and parched, and its canals will become foul, and the branching streams of Egypt will diminish and dry up."

Now the Nile, and to feel this you have to know that Egypt was the Nile. The country is a green ribbon a few miles wide with desert on both sides; everything — the food, the trade, the calendar, the religion — ran off one river that flooded on schedule every year for millennia. It was the most reliable thing in the ancient world.

Isaiah says it will fail.

"Reeds and rushes will rot away. There will be bare places by the Nile, on the brink of the Nile, and all that is sown by the Nile will be parched, will be driven away, and will be no more."

He follows the drying down through the ecosystem: the reed beds rot, the sown ground goes bare, the crops blow away.

"The fishermen will mourn and lament, all who cast a hook in the Nile; and they will languish who spread nets on the water. The workers in combed flax will be in despair, and the weavers of white cotton."

And then the trades, one by one. Line fishermen. Net fishermen. Flax workers. Weavers. Isaiah takes the disaster out of the palace and puts it in the hands of men who get up early — because that is where a failed river is actually felt, and because a judgment described only in national terms is a judgment nobody can picture.

verseByVerse.quote: The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, "I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings"? Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Zoan have become fools, and the princes of Memphis are deluded; those who are the cornerstones of her tribes have made Egypt stagger. The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit. And there will be nothing for Egypt that head or tail, palm branch or reed, may do.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The princes of Zoan are utterly foolish; the wisest counselors of Pharaoh give stupid counsel. How can you say to Pharaoh, 'I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings'?"

The second target after the river is the wisdom, and it is chosen just as carefully. Egyptian counsel was proverbial: the schools of Egypt trained the region's advisers, and their wisdom literature was old before Israel existed. When Solomon is praised, he is said to have surpassed the wisdom of Egypt.

Isaiah's charge is not that these men are unintelligent but that they are trading on an inheritance. I am a son of the wise, a son of ancient kings — a credential rather than a judgment, and credentials are exactly what fail when something genuinely new arrives.

"Where then are your wise men? Let them tell you that they might know what the LORD of hosts has purposed against Egypt."

And there is the test, and it is one no adviser in this chapter can pass. The question is not whether they are clever. It is whether any of them can tell you what God intends — and no amount of accumulated human wisdom has ever been able to answer that question, which is why it has to be told to us rather than worked out.

"The LORD has mingled within her a spirit of confusion, and they will make Egypt stagger in all its deeds, as a drunken man staggers in his vomit."

The final picture is undignified on purpose. The most sophisticated state in the world lurching about like a drunk who has fallen in his own mess — and verse 15 says there is nothing left for Egypt to do, head or tail, palm branch or reed.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Six paragraphs beginning in that day turn the chapter completely round. Egypt trembles before the LORD of hosts (vv. 16-17); five cities speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to him (v. 18); an altar to the LORD stands in the middle of Egypt and a pillar at its border (vv. 19-20); Egyptians cry out under oppression and God sends them a saviour who defends and delivers them (v. 20); the LORD makes himself known to Egypt and they know him, worship, and keep their vows (v. 21); and a highway runs from Egypt to Assyria, with Israel a third alongside them (vv. 23-25).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 25 is one of the most startling sentences in the Old Testament: Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance. Egypt enslaved Israel. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom. Both are given covenant titles, and Israel is not displaced but placed alongside them as one of three. The nations do not become Israel; they are blessed as themselves, and blessed by name.
verseByVerse.examples: Notice how God saves Egypt in verse 20: they cry out because of oppressors, and he sends them a saviour and delivers them. That is the exodus, performed for Egypt — and the exodus was performed against Egypt. The mercy is not a different kind of mercy from Israel's. It is the same rescue, extended to the old enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them. And the land of Judah will become a terror to the Egyptians. Everyone to whom it is mentioned will fear because of the purpose that the LORD of hosts has purposed against them. In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts. One of these will be called the City of Destruction. In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border. It will be a sign and a witness to the LORD of hosts in the land of Egypt. When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them. And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering, and they will make vows to the LORD and perform them. And the LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing, and they will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas for mercy and heal them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the Egyptians will be like women, and tremble with fear before the hand that the LORD of hosts shakes over them."

Six paragraphs now begin with in that day, and between the first and the last the chapter turns completely round. Watch it happen, because there is nothing else quite like it in the prophets.

It begins where chapter 19 has been: Egypt terrified. Then:

"In that day there will be five cities in the land of Egypt that speak the language of Canaan and swear allegiance to the LORD of hosts."

Five Egyptian cities speaking Hebrew and swearing loyalty to Israel's God. Not conquered — converted.

"In that day there will be an altar to the LORD in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to the LORD at its border."

An altar in the middle of Egypt. For a people whose entire national memory of Egypt was slavery, brick quotas and a drowned army, this is close to unthinkable: the place of bondage becomes a place of sacrifice.

"When they cry to the LORD because of oppressors, he will send them a savior and defender, and deliver them."

And now read that sentence with Exodus in mind, because Isaiah has written it deliberately. Israel cried out under oppression, and God heard, and sent a deliverer. Here the Egyptians cry out under oppression, and God hears, and sends them a saviour.

It is the same rescue, with the old enemy in Israel's place. The exodus was performed against Egypt; God intends to perform it for Egypt.

"And the LORD will make himself known to the Egyptians, and the Egyptians will know the LORD in that day and worship with sacrifice and offering... They will return to the LORD, and he will listen to their pleas and heal them."

The book opened by saying Israel did not know its owner as well as an ox knows its master (1:3). Here Egypt knows him.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians. In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth, whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, "Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day there will be a highway from Egypt to Assyria, and Assyria will come into Egypt, and Egypt into Assyria, and the Egyptians will worship with the Assyrians."

A road runs between the two superpowers, and the traffic on it is not military.

These two states had spent centuries marching armies along that corridor, and Judah was the ground they marched over — the whole political agony of the book comes from being the small country between them. Isaiah sees the same road with worshippers on it, going both ways.

"In that day Israel will be the third with Egypt and Assyria, a blessing in the midst of the earth."

And Israel is the third. Not the centre with two satellites — one of three, in the middle of the earth, as a blessing. That is the promise to Abraham arriving: in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.

"Whom the LORD of hosts has blessed, saying, 'Blessed be Egypt my people, and Assyria the work of my hands, and Israel my inheritance.'"

Read the three titles slowly, because they are given to the wrong nations.

My people is Israel's phrase, running through the whole Bible — and it is given to Egypt, the house of slavery, the nation of the brick pits and the drowned chariots. The work of my hands is the language of creation and craftsmanship, and it is given to Assyria, the empire that destroyed the northern kingdom and stood outside Jerusalem's walls. And Israel keeps its own title, my inheritance, alongside them.

Nothing is taken from Israel. Something is given to everybody else, and the two nations that between them account for most of Israel's suffering are named with covenant affection.

This is where the oracles against the nations have been going all along. They begin as judgments on empires and end with God calling his oldest enemies his people, and it is the same trajectory that runs out through Ephesians to a church made of Jew and Gentile with the dividing wall pulled down.

20.subtitle: The Sign of Isaiah's Nakedness
20.intro: Overview. Chapter 20 is a brief but vivid narrative. For three years, at God's command, Isaiah walked naked and barefoot as a living sign — a prophecy enacted in the prophet's own body. The sign had a specific target: Judah's temptation to rely on an Egyptian-Cushite military coalition against Assyria. Isaiah's three-year acted parable announced that Egypt and Cush would be led away by Assyria as naked prisoners, and therefore they were no foundation to build on.

keyVerse.quote: “And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, ‘Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?’”
keyVerse.note: The question “how shall we escape?” is the exact question every misplaced confidence eventually produces. When the thing we trusted — whether Egypt, an alliance, a financial plan, a relationship — fails, we are left with the question Isaiah has been asking from chapter 1: to whom are you actually looking? The answer the book provides is always the same: “Look to the rock from which you were hewn” (51:1).

20.reflection: Isaiah's three-year acted sign is a reminder that God sometimes calls his servants to costly, public, apparently undignified forms of witness. The prophet did not get to choose a more respectable way to deliver this message. The question the chapter poses is both historical and personal: what is the Egypt or Cush in your own life — the security that looks impressive but will one day be led away in chains?
20.text: <sup>1</sup>In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it—<sup>2</sup>at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.<sup>3</sup>Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush,<sup>4</sup>so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast.<sup>6</sup>And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Prophet's Body Becomes the Sermon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter is dated by an Assyrian campaign against Ashdod under Sargon II, about 711 BC (v. 1). God tells Isaiah to take the sackcloth off his body and the sandals off his feet, and he does, and walks that way for three years (v. 2). Verses 3 and 4 give the meaning: as Isaiah has walked stripped and barefoot, so the king of Assyria will lead away Egyptian and Cushite captives, young and old, naked and barefoot. Verses 5 and 6 name the target — not Egypt but everyone in the coastlands who had been counting on Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: This is a sign-act, and the cost is the point. Prophets were sometimes told to do strange things briefly; this one ran for three years, in public, in the capital, and destroyed Isaiah's dignity for the duration. The message could have been preached in a sentence. God required it to be worn.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 3 calls him my servant Isaiah, which is the title this book will later give to someone else. A servant who accepts public shame in order to deliver God's word is a small rehearsal of the one who was stripped in earnest, and whose clothes were divided at the foot of a cross.

verseByVerse.quote: In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it— at that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, "Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet," and he did so, walking naked and barefoot.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the year that the commander in chief, who was sent by Sargon the king of Assyria, came to Ashdod and fought against it and captured it."

The chapter opens with a date stamp, and it is unusually specific even for Isaiah: Sargon II's campaign against the Philistine city of Ashdod, about 711 BC. Ashdod had rebelled against Assyria, counting on Egyptian support, and the support did not come.

That is the background the whole chapter is about, and it explains why the sign is needed.

"At that time the LORD spoke by Isaiah the son of Amoz, saying, 'Go, and loose the sackcloth from your waist and take off your sandals from your feet,' and he did so, walking naked and barefoot."

The instruction is four words long and it costs everything. Sackcloth was the prophet's garment — rough, dark, the visible sign of his office. He is told to take it off, along with his sandals.

Whether "naked" here means completely unclothed or stripped to a loincloth is disputed and does not much matter; what is not disputed is that this was the appearance of a prisoner of war being marched away, and that Isaiah adopted it in public in Jerusalem.

And the response is three words: and he did so. No argument is recorded, no request for an alternative. It is the shortest sentence in the chapter and the hardest one.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush, so shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt. Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we, how shall we escape?'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then the LORD said, 'As my servant Isaiah has walked naked and barefoot for three years as a sign and a portent against Egypt and Cush.'"

Three years. That is the detail that changes what kind of story this is.

Prophets were sometimes told to do arresting things — break a jar, bury a belt, lie on one side. Those are gestures; they take an afternoon. This ran for three years, in the capital, in front of neighbours and children and the people he had grown up with. There was no moment when it was over and he could go back to being a respected man.

The message itself could have been preached in one sentence: Egypt will not save you. God did not want it preached. He wanted it worn.

"So shall the king of Assyria lead away the Egyptian captives and the Cushite exiles, both the young and the old, naked and barefoot, with buttocks uncovered, the nakedness of Egypt."

And there is what the costume meant. The great powers everyone was banking on would be walking that road themselves, in exactly that condition, old and young together. Isaiah was not dressed as a madman. He was dressed as the future.

"Then they shall be dismayed and ashamed because of Cush their hope and of Egypt their boast. And the inhabitants of this coastland will say in that day, 'Behold, this is what has happened to those in whom we hoped and to whom we fled for help to be delivered from the king of Assyria! And we — how shall we escape?'"

The sign was never aimed at Egypt. It was aimed at everyone watching Egypt — including Judah, which was being urged into exactly that alliance.

The last line is the one to keep: and we — how shall we escape? It is the sound a person makes when the thing he was relying on turns out to need rescuing itself, and the only cure for it is to have relied on something else.

One word in verse 3 should not be passed over. God calls him my servant Isaiah — the title this book will spend chapters 42 to 53 giving to somebody else. A servant who accepts public humiliation to make God's word visible is a small rehearsal of the one who was stripped in earnest, outside a city wall, while soldiers divided what he had been wearing.

20.theology:
The message God would not let be spoken. The content of this sign is one sentence long — Egypt will not save you — and God required three years of public humiliation to deliver it. Sign-acts elsewhere in the prophets take an afternoon; this one had no moment at which Isaiah could go back to being a respected man. The cost is not incidental to the message. It is the message’s weight made visible.

Aimed at the watchers, not the subject. The sign is against Egypt and Cush and is performed in Jerusalem, because the target was never Egypt but everyone banking on Egypt — including a Judah being urged into exactly that alliance. The closing line is the sound of misplaced trust collapsing: and we — how shall we escape?

My servant Isaiah. The title in verse 3 is the one this book will later give to another figure entirely. A servant who accepts public shame in order to make God’s word visible is a small rehearsal of the one who was stripped in earnest outside a city wall while soldiers divided his clothes.

21.subtitle: Oracles Against Babylon, Edom, and Arabia
21.intro: Overview. Chapter 21 contains three short oracles, each addressed to a different nation. The first and longest (vv. 1–10) is a vision of Babylon’s fall, delivered with such physical intensity that the prophet reels under it. The second (vv. 11–12) is a night-watchman exchange with Edom — poetic, cryptic, unresolved. The third (vv. 13–17) turns to the desert caravans of Arabia, where the commerce of the ancient world will be silenced within a year. Together they form a triptych: the great empire, its anxious neighbor, and the ordinary trader — all subject to the same sovereign word.

keyVerse.quote: “Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night? The watchman says: ‘Morning comes, and also the night.’”
keyVerse.note: The exchange is one of the strangest moments in prophetic literature. But its strangeness is the point: history does not move in simple arcs from darkness to light. Morning and night come together. The right response is not resignation but inquiry — keep asking, keep returning.

21.reflection: Isaiah reeled physically under the vision of Babylon’s fall. The prophets were not spectators of history but participants in God’s grief over it. Is there a situation in the world right now that you have allowed yourself to feel — not just analyze? And what does it mean to keep “inquiring” in the darkness when the watchman can only say that morning and night will both come?
21.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land.<sup>2</sup>A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end.<sup>3</sup>Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see.<sup>4</sup>My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling.<sup>5</sup>They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!<sup>6</sup>For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees.<sup>7</sup>When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently."<sup>8</sup>Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights.<sup>9</sup>And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground."<sup>10</sup>O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you.<sup>11</sup>The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?"<sup>12</sup>The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again."<sup>13</sup>The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites.<sup>14</sup>To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema.<sup>15</sup>For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle.<sup>16</sup>For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end.<sup>17</sup>And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — The Watchman, and the Cost of Seeing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A storm sweeps out of the desert (v. 1) and a stern vision is announced: Elam and Media are to go up and besiege (v. 2). Verses 3 and 4 are the prophet's own body — anguish like a woman in labour, too dismayed to hear, too appalled to see, the twilight he longed for turned into trembling. Verse 5 sets a banquet table and then breaks it up with an order to oil the shields. Verses 6 to 9 post a watchman who stands at his post day after day until riders come with the news, and verse 10 addresses a threshed and winnowed people.
verseByVerse.theology: The message is one line long — fallen, fallen is Babylon — and Isaiah spends nine verses on what it cost to receive it. That is unusual and deliberate. He is not a detached analyst reporting the collapse of an oppressor; the vision doubles him over, and the night he had been waiting for arrives as terror rather than relief.
verseByVerse.examples: The banquet in verse 5 is a picture of how such a fall actually happens: a table spread, rugs laid, people eating and drinking, and then an order to arm shouted across it. Daniel 5 records exactly that night. And John takes the watchman's sentence and repeats it twice over the last empire (Rev. 14:8; 18:2).

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land. A stern vision is told to me; the traitor betrays, and the destroyer destroys. Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end. Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see. My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling. They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea. As whirlwinds in the Negeb sweep on, it comes from the wilderness, from a terrible land."

The title is a riddle — the wilderness of the sea — and Babylon is meant, sitting on its marshy plain between two rivers. What comes is described as desert whirlwinds, which arrive without warning and cannot be argued with.

"Go up, O Elam; lay siege, O Media; all the sighing she has caused I bring to an end."

The last clause deserves a moment. God is not merely toppling a power; he is ending the sighing she has caused — the accumulated groaning of everybody Babylon has hurt. The judgment is measured against suffering that has been recorded.

"Therefore my loins are filled with anguish; pangs have seized me, like the pangs of a woman in labor; I am bowed down so that I cannot hear; I am dismayed so that I cannot see."

And now something unusual. Isaiah stops describing Babylon and starts describing himself.

He is doubled over. He cannot hear; he cannot see. The image is childbirth, which is the standard biblical picture for pain that cannot be postponed or escaped — and he is not the one being judged. He is the one being shown it.

"My heart staggers; horror has appalled me; the twilight I longed for has been turned for me into trembling."

That last line is the saddest in the chapter. Twilight is what a tired man waits for — the end of the day, the cool, the rest. He had been longing for evening, and when it came it brought this.

"They prepare the table, they spread the rugs, they eat, they drink. Arise, O princes; oil the shield!"

Then a scene, in six short clauses. A banquet in progress — table, rugs, food, wine — and across it an order to grease the leather shields for battle. Daniel 5 describes that night from inside the room, with writing appearing on a wall while the cups are still full.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the Lord said to me: "Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees. When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently." Then he who saw cried out: "Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights. And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs!" And he answered, "Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground." O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus the Lord said to me: 'Go, set a watchman; let him announce what he sees.'"

The scene changes to a lookout post, and the instruction is minimal. Not interpret, not advise. Announce what you see.

"When he sees riders, horsemen in pairs, riders on donkeys, riders on camels, let him listen diligently, very diligently."

"Then he who saw cried out: 'Upon a watchtower I stand, O Lord, continually by day, and at my post I am stationed whole nights.'"

And here is the watchman's own report of the job, which is mostly waiting. Continually by day and whole nights — a man standing on a tower for an indefinite period, watching an empty road, with no way of knowing when or whether anything will come.

That is a fair description of a great deal of faithful work. Most of what God asks of people is not dramatic action but staying at a post while nothing visible happens, and the watchman is the Bible's standing image for it.

"And behold, here come riders, horsemen in pairs! And he answered, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon; and all the carved images of her gods he has shattered to the ground.'"

The waiting ends and the message is five words. After the anguish, the sleeplessness and the strain, the whole content of the vision is a single sentence: fallen, fallen is Babylon.

The doubling is not decoration — it is how a runner speaks when he has been running. And John hears it again at the end of the Bible and repeats it twice, over the last empire that thought it was permanent (Rev. 14:8; 18:2).

"O my threshed and winnowed one, what I have heard from the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel, I announce to you."

The last line names the audience: a people who have been threshed and winnowed — beaten on a floor and thrown into the air. To them, and only to them, the news is worth the telling.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11–12 — Watchman, What Time of the Night?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two verses, and they are the most enigmatic in the book. A voice calls from Seir — that is Edom — asking the watchman how much of the night is left. He asks twice, which is the mark of someone who cannot wait for the answer. And the reply comes back: morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again.
verseByVerse.theology: The answer refuses to be simple, and its refusal is the point. Morning is coming — that is real. And night is coming too. Anyone who wants a promise of dawn with no darkness in it will not get one here, and anyone who concludes that the darkness is all there is has stopped reading half way through the sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Come back again is the mercy in it. The door is not shut on Edom's question; the enquirer is told to keep enquiring and to return. For a reader in the middle of a long night with no clear answer, being told to come back and ask again is not a brush-off. It is an invitation to keep asking the one who actually knows what time it is.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, "Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?" The watchman says: "Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning Dumah. One is calling to me from Seir, 'Watchman, what time of the night? Watchman, what time of the night?'"

A voice out of Edom, and the question is asked twice.

Anyone who has been awake through a bad night knows why. You do not ask what time it is because you want the information. You ask because you want to be told that it is nearly over, and asking twice is what people do when the first answer is taking too long to arrive.

Edom is not a friendly nation in Scripture. But the question here is not hostile; it is exhausted, and it is the most human sentence in the oracle block.

"The watchman says: 'Morning comes, and also the night. If you will inquire, inquire; come back again.'"

And the answer refuses to be simple, which is why it has puzzled readers for twenty-seven centuries.

Morning comes. That is a real promise, and it is the first thing said. And also the night. That is real too. The watchman will not sell a dawn with no darkness in it, and he will not pretend the darkness is final.

That is an honest answer to give someone in the middle of a long night, and it is more useful than either of the comfortable alternatives. Morning is coming. There is also more night. Both.

"If you will inquire, inquire; come back again."

And here is the mercy in it. The door is not shut. The enquirer is not told he has had his answer and should go away; he is told to keep asking and to come back.

For anyone who has put a question to God and received something less than a full answer, that is the shape of what is on offer. Not a schedule — an open invitation to return with the same question to the one who actually knows what time it is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–17 — Bring Water to the Thirsty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last oracle turns to Arabia. Caravans of Dedan are camping rough in the scrub (v. 13); the people of Tema are told to bring water to the thirsty and meet the fugitive with bread (v. 14); people are fleeing from swords, bent bows and the press of battle (v. 15). And then a date: within a year, measured like the year of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will end, and few of its famous archers will be left (vv. 16-17).
verseByVerse.theology: Kedar was known for its bowmen. The oracle is precise about what will be gone: not the tribe as such but the thing it was proud of. That is the pattern in the whole block — God does not merely reduce nations, he takes away the specific thing each one trusted in.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is the human instruction inside a judgment oracle, and it is easy to miss: bring water to the thirsty; meet the fugitive with bread. The prophecy announces the disaster and, in the same breath, tells the neighbouring people what to do about the refugees it produces.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites. To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema. For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle. For thus the Lord said to me, "Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end. And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few, for the LORD, the God of Israel, has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning Arabia. In the thickets in Arabia you will lodge, O caravans of Dedanites."

The last of the three oracles, and it opens with people sleeping rough. The Dedanites were traders; caravans of that kind normally camped at known stops with wells and shelter. These are in the scrub, off the route, hiding.

"To the thirsty bring water; meet the fugitive with bread, O inhabitants of the land of Tema."

And then, in the middle of a judgment oracle, an instruction about hospitality.

It is easy to read past and it should not be. God is announcing a disaster and, in the same breath, telling the people next door what to do about the refugees it will produce. Bring water. Bring bread. Meet them — the verb means to go out toward, rather than to wait for them to arrive at your door.

Prophecy in this book is never only information. When it describes trouble coming to somebody, it tends to turn immediately to the people who will be in a position to help.

"For they have fled from the swords, from the drawn sword, from the bent bow, and from the press of battle."

Four short phrases, and every one of them is a reason somebody left home in a hurry.

"For thus the Lord said to me, 'Within a year, according to the years of a hired worker, all the glory of Kedar will come to an end. And the remainder of the archers of the mighty men of the sons of Kedar will be few.'"

The oracle ends with a date and a specific loss. Kedar's archers were famous — that was the thing the tribe was known for across the region — and it is precisely the famous thing that goes.

That is the pattern running through all eleven of these chapters. God does not simply reduce a nation. He takes away the particular thing it trusted in and was proud of, because the trust was the actual problem and the rest is only the arithmetic.

21.theology:
The cost of seeing. The message of the first oracle is five words long — fallen, fallen is Babylon — and Isaiah spends nine verses on what receiving it did to him: anguish like labour, unable to hear or see, the twilight he had longed for turned into trembling. He is not a detached analyst reporting an oppressor’s collapse. And the watchman’s own account of the work is mostly waiting — continually by day, whole nights — which is a fair description of most faithful service. John repeats the sentence twice over the last empire (Rev. 14:8; 18:2).

Morning comes, and also the night. The reply to Edom’s twice-asked question refuses both comfortable answers. It will not sell a dawn with no darkness in it, and it will not pretend the darkness is final. And the last clause is the mercy: if you will inquire, inquire; come back again. The enquirer is not dismissed but invited to return with the same question to the one who knows what time it is.

Water and bread inside a judgment. Verse 14 interrupts an oracle of disaster to tell the neighbouring people what to do about the refugees it will create — and the verb means to go out toward them rather than wait at the door. Prophecy here is never only information. And verse 16 shows the block’s consistent aim: what ends is Kedar’s archers, the thing the tribe was proud of, because the trust was the problem.

22.subtitle: The Valley of Vision
22.intro: Overview. Chapter 22 is unique in the oracles-against-the-nations sequence: it is addressed not to a foreign power but to Jerusalem itself, here called “the valley of vision.” The city that has received more revelation than any other is judged precisely for what it did with it. The occasion appears to be a near-miss — perhaps Sennacherib’s siege in 701 BC, when the city was threatened and then inexplicably spared. But instead of weeping and repentance, Jerusalem breaks out in celebration. The chapter also contains a striking personal oracle against the arrogant royal steward Shebna, and a promise about a better servant, Eliakim.

keyVerse.quote: “I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open.”
keyVerse.note: What begins as a personnel change in Hezekiah’s court becomes one of the richest Christological images in the Old Testament. Rev. 3:7 places this language on the lips of the risen Christ. No one approaches the Father except through him; no one is excluded who comes through him.

22.reflection: Jerusalem celebrated survival without repentance. The near-miss became a party rather than a turning point. Is there a situation in your life where God has been merciful and you have responded with relief rather than return? What would true repentance look like in that situation now?
