verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of eleven chapters about foreign nations, one is about Jerusalem. The city is on its roofs, full of shouting and revelry (vv. 1-2) — and Isaiah points out that its dead were not killed in battle: the leaders fled and were captured without a bow being drawn (vv. 2-3). Verse 4 has him refusing to be comforted and asking to be left alone to weep. Verses 8 to 11 list the city's impressive preparations — the armoury inspected, the houses counted and demolished for wall repairs, a reservoir built between the walls — and end with the charge: you did not look to him who did it. Verses 12 to 14 have God calling for weeping and getting a party.
verseByVerse.theology: The point of placing this chapter here is that the reader has spent nine chapters watching God judge other people. Isaiah drops Jerusalem into the same list, under the same heading, and does not mark the transition. Whatever has been enjoyable about the oracles against the nations stops being enjoyable at chapter 22.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 11 is the indictment and it is not about incompetence. The engineering was excellent — the tunnel Hezekiah cut to bring water inside the walls can still be walked through today. They did everything right and never once consulted the one whose city it was. It is possible to respond to a crisis with total competence and complete godlessness, and the two look identical from outside.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What do you mean that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops, you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town? Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured. All of you who were found were captured, though they had fled far away. Therefore I said: "Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning the valley of vision. What do you mean that you have gone up, all of you, to the housetops, you who are full of shoutings, tumultuous city, exultant town?"

Stop at the title before anything else. Nine chapters of oracles against Babylon, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Arabia — and now one against the valley of vision, which is Jerusalem. The city that has been reading over God's shoulder while he judged the neighbours is in the list.

Isaiah does not announce the change of subject. He simply gives Jerusalem an oracle heading like everybody else's, and lets the reader discover that the seat he has been sitting in is in the dock.

The city is on its flat roofs, shouting. Something has apparently gone well — a siege lifted, a threat withdrawn — and the whole town is celebrating.

"Your slain are not slain with the sword or dead in battle. All your leaders have fled together; without the bow they were captured."

And Isaiah punctures it in one line. Look at your dead: they did not fall fighting. The leadership ran, and was picked up on the road without the bow — nobody even had to shoot at them.

There is nothing here to celebrate. The party on the roofs is being held over a disgrace that the celebrants have decided to read as a deliverance.

"Therefore I said: 'Look away from me; let me weep bitter tears; do not labor to comfort me concerning the destruction of the daughter of my people.'"

One man in a shouting city is crying, and he asks to be left alone to do it. Do not labour to comfort me — the comfort on offer would be false, and accepting it would mean joining a celebration he can see through.

verseByVerse.quote: For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains. And Elam bore the quiver with chariots and horsemen, and Kir uncovered the shield. Your choicest valleys were full of chariots, and the horsemen took their stand at the gates. He has taken away the covering of Judah. In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many. You collected the waters of the lower pool, and you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool. But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the Lord GOD of hosts has a day of tumult and trampling and confusion in the valley of vision, a battering down of walls and a shouting to the mountains."

Isaiah describes the siege as it will be: Elam with the quiver, Kir uncovering the shield, the best valleys full of chariots, horsemen drawn up at the gate, and the covering of Judah taken away.

"In that day you looked to the weapons of the House of the Forest, and you saw that the breaches of the city of David were many, and you collected the waters of the lower pool."

Now the preparations, and it is important to see that they are good ones. The armoury is checked. The walls are surveyed and the breaches counted. The water supply is secured.

"And you counted the houses of Jerusalem, and you broke down the houses to fortify the wall. You made a reservoir between the two walls for the water of the old pool."

They even demolish houses for stone to close the gaps, and build a reservoir inside the defences. This is decisive, competent crisis management. The tunnel Hezekiah cut to bring the spring water inside the city can still be walked through today, and it is a genuinely impressive piece of engineering.

"But you did not look to him who did it, or see him who planned it long ago."

And there is the charge, and it is not incompetence.

Notice the verb: you looked to the weapons in verse 8, and you did not look to him in verse 11. The same action, aimed in two directions. They surveyed everything except the one who had arranged the crisis, and had planned it, Isaiah says, long ago.

That is a searching thing for capable people. It is entirely possible to meet a disaster with total competence and complete godlessness, and the two are indistinguishable from outside. Everything gets done. Nobody prays.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth; and behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine. "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die." The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: "Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die," says the Lord GOD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the Lord GOD of hosts called for weeping and mourning, for baldness and wearing sackcloth."

God's response to the crisis is a summons, and it is a summons to grief. Weeping, mourning, shaved heads, sackcloth — the four visible signs of a nation that has understood something.

"And behold, joy and gladness, killing oxen and slaughtering sheep, eating flesh and drinking wine."

And what he gets is a barbecue.

The contrast is set out without a word of comment: he called for one thing, and behold, here is the other. They are killing the animals that would have fed them through a siege and eating them tonight.

"'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.'"

This is the sentence the chapter is remembered for, and Paul quotes it (1 Cor. 15:32) as the only rational conclusion if there is no resurrection. Here it is the motto of people who have looked at the situation, decided it is hopeless, and chosen to spend what is left on enjoyment.

It is fatalism dressed as festivity, and it is the exact opposite of the response God asked for. Grief would have been an admission that something could still be done. The party is the sound of a city that has stopped believing that.

"The LORD of hosts has revealed himself in my ears: 'Surely this iniquity will not be atoned for you until you die.'"

And the verdict is the heaviest sentence in the chapter. Not that the sin is too large for atonement — this book has said that scarlet becomes snow — but that these people, having been called to mourn and having thrown a feast instead, will not be dealt with until they are dead. Refusal has consequences, and one of them is the loss of the moment when repentance was on offer.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–25 — Two Stewards and a Key
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The oracle narrows to one man. Shebna, the palace steward, is found cutting himself a grand tomb in the rock while the city is under threat (vv. 15-16). God promises to bundle him up and hurl him like a ball into a wide country, where he will die, and his splendid chariots will be the shame of his master's house (vv. 17-19). In his place God calls Eliakim, clothes him with the robe and sash, commits authority to his hand, and hangs on his shoulder the key of the house of David: he shall open and none shall shut, shut and none shall open (vv. 20-23). Verses 24 and 25 warn that even this peg, loaded with the whole weight of a family, will eventually give way.
verseByVerse.theology: Shebna's sin is a tomb. With an army coming he is investing in a monument to himself — the perfect picture of a public servant whose real project is his own memory. The judgment fits exactly: he dies far from home and the expensive tomb stands empty.
verseByVerse.examples: The key of the house of David hung on Eliakim's shoulder is taken up by the risen Christ in Revelation 3:7 — the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens. And verses 24-25 are why the type was never enough: hang the weight of a whole house on any human peg and it will come out of the wall. Only one shoulder has ever held it.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the Lord GOD of hosts, "Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself, you who cut out a tomb on the height and carve a dwelling for yourself in the rock? Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land. There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house. I will thrust you from your office, and you will be pulled down from your station.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come, go to this steward, to Shebna, who is over the household, and say to him: 'What have you to do here, and whom have you here, that you have cut out here a tomb for yourself?'"

The oracle now stops addressing a city and addresses one man by name, which it has not done before.

Shebna is over the household — the highest official under the king, chief of staff of the palace. And he is found doing something specific: cutting a tomb for himself in the rock, on the heights, in the good burial ground.

The questions God asks are the right ones. What have you to do here, and whom have you here? — which most naturally means Shebna is not even a native of Jerusalem. He has no family plot and no claim on that hillside, and he is quarrying himself a monument in it while an empire moves toward the city.

"Behold, the LORD will hurl you away violently, O you strong man. He will seize firm hold on you and whirl you around and around, and throw you like a ball into a wide land."

The judgment is almost comic in its physicality. God winds him up and throws him. A man obsessed with where his body will lie is going to die in a wide land — somewhere with no boundaries, far from the hillside he was carving.

"There you shall die, and there shall be your glorious chariots, you shame of your master's house."

And the expensive tomb will still be there, empty, in the good ground, with somebody else's name eventually on it.

Shebna is the standing portrait of a public servant whose actual project is his own memory. The city is in danger and he is thinking about how he will be remembered, which is a temptation for anyone who holds office of any kind.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah. And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open. And I will fasten him like a peg in a secure place, and he will become a throne of honor to his father's house. And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons. In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off, for the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day I will call my servant Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, and I will clothe him with your robe, and will bind your sash on him, and will commit your authority to his hand."

A replacement is named, and the transfer is done by God rather than by the palace. He takes the robe off one man and puts it on another, ties the sash himself, and hands over the authority.

"And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem and to the house of Judah."

The job description is the striking part. Not administrator or chief officer — a father to the inhabitants. That is what the office was always supposed to be, and what Shebna had made into a platform.

"And I will place on his shoulder the key of the house of David. He shall open, and none shall shut; and he shall shut, and none shall open."

The key of a great house was a substantial object, carried on the shoulder, and whoever carried it decided who came in. It is the visible sign of complete access authority.

And this sentence went somewhere. On Patmos, the risen Christ introduces himself to a struggling church as "the holy one, the true one, who has the key of David, who opens and no one will shut, who shuts and no one opens" (Rev. 3:7). He takes the words spoken over a palace steward in Jerusalem and applies them to himself.

"And they will hang on him the whole honor of his father's house, the offspring and issue, every small vessel, from the cups to all the flagons."

"In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, the peg that was fastened in a secure place will give way, and it will be cut down and fall, and the load that was on it will be cut off."

And then the chapter does something unexpected: it takes the promise back. Eliakim is a peg driven into a wall, and everything gets hung on him — the whole family, the honour, every cup and flagon — until the peg pulls out of the wall and the lot comes down.

That is not cynicism about Eliakim. It is honesty about pegs. Load a whole household's weight onto any human being — a leader, a father, a pastor, yourself — and eventually the fixing gives. The key of David needed a shoulder that could carry it, and this chapter is the record of the two men who could not.

22.theology:
The oracle against us. Nine chapters of judgment on foreign nations, and then one on Jerusalem with the same heading and no announcement of the change. Isaiah lets the reader discover that the seat he has been reading from is in the dock. Whatever was enjoyable about watching God judge the neighbours stops being enjoyable here.

Competence without God. The preparations in vv. 8-11 are excellent — armoury inspected, breaches counted, houses demolished for stone, a reservoir cut between the walls. Hezekiah’s water tunnel can still be walked through. The charge is not incompetence but the same verb pointed two ways: you looked to the weapons, and you did not look to him who did it. A crisis can be met with total competence and complete godlessness, and from outside the two are indistinguishable. When God then called for weeping (v. 12) he got a barbecue and a slogan — let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die — which Paul quotes as the only rational motto if there is no resurrection (1 Cor. 15:32).

The key, and the peg. Shebna is cutting himself a tomb while the city is threatened — a public servant whose real project is his own memory — and dies far away with the monument standing empty. Eliakim receives the key of the house of David on his shoulder, words the risen Christ later takes for himself (Rev. 3:7). And then vv. 24-25 pull the promise down: hang the whole weight of a house on any human peg and the fixing gives way. That is why the type was never sufficient.

23.subtitle: The Oracle Against Tyre
23.intro: Overview. Tyre was the commercial capital of the ancient world — the great Phoenician port whose ships connected Egypt, Canaan, Spain, and the Greek islands. Its fall would be like the collapse of a global financial center. Isaiah’s oracle against it (the last of the series begun in chapter 13) is not merely a military prediction but a theological meditation: what happens when the city that made itself indispensable is removed? The chapter ends with a surprising note: after seventy years, Tyre’s commerce will resume — and its profits will be consecrated to the LORD.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth.”
keyVerse.note: The oracles against the nations are not vindictive but clarifying. God is not against cities or commerce; he is against the pride that refuses to acknowledge him as the source of all prosperity. Every judgment in chapters 13–23 is a reorientation of glory toward its proper object.

23.reflection: Tyre’s commerce was eventually consecrated rather than abolished. God’s goal is not the destruction of human achievement but its reorientation. What gifts, skills, or resources in your life are currently operating for self-glorification — and what would it look like to consecrate them?
23.text: <sup>1</sup>The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–14 — The City That Made Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last oracle takes on Tyre, the Phoenician port that ran Mediterranean trade. Ships coming home from Tarshish find no harbour and no house (v. 1); the merchants of Sidon who crossed the sea are silenced (vv. 2-4); Egypt writhes at the news (v. 5). Verses 8 and 9 ask who planned this against the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, and answer: the LORD of hosts, to defile the pride of all glory and dishonour all the honoured of the earth. Verses 10 to 14 have the trade routes broken and the ships of Tarshish told to wail.
verseByVerse.theology: Tyre is not judged for being commercial. It is judged for the pride that made commerce ultimate — and Isaiah names it precisely: the bestower of crowns, a city rich enough to make kings. The charge in verse 9 is against the pride of all glory, which is the same principle as the day against everything tall in chapter 2, applied to money rather than to cedars.
verseByVerse.examples: The detail that dates the passage is that verse 8 asks who purposed it, and gets a name. Trade routes do not simply shift; markets do not merely turn. Behind the collapse of an economy that everyone had come to depend on stands a decision, and the decision is God's.

verseByVerse.quote: The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor! From the land of Cyprus it is revealed to them. Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. And on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations. Be ashamed, O Sidon, for the sea has spoken, the stronghold of the sea, saying: "I have neither labored nor given birth, I have neither reared young men nor brought up young women." When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre. Cross over to Tarshish; wail, O inhabitants of the coast! Is this your exultant city whose origin is from days of old, whose feet carried her to settle far away?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The oracle concerning Tyre. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for Tyre is laid waste, without house or harbor!"

The last of the eleven oracles, and the target is not an empire with an army but a port with a fleet.

Tyre was the commercial capital of the Mediterranean world: a Phoenician city on an island, effectively unbesiegeable, whose ships ran from Spain to Egypt and whose colonies included Carthage. It made the purple dye that kings wore. If you wanted a modern comparison, it is not a conquering nation but a financial centre.

And the news reaches the fleet at sea. Ships of Tarshish were the big ocean-going vessels; they are coming home from the far west and being told, before they can see the coast, that there is no harbour to come into.

"Be still, O inhabitants of the coast; the merchants of Sidon, who cross the sea, have filled you. And on many waters your revenue was the grain of Shihor, the harvest of the Nile; you were the merchant of the nations."

Isaiah describes the business accurately: Phoenician ships buying Egyptian grain and selling it round the sea. The verb he uses of the coast is be still — a trading shore going quiet is the sound of an economy stopping.

"When the report comes to Egypt, they will be in anguish over the report about Tyre."

And the anguish is not sympathy. Egypt is Tyre's supplier. When a trading partner of that size fails, everyone connected to it discovers how connected they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth? The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pompous pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth. Cross over your land like the Nile, O daughter of Tarshish; there is no restraint anymore. He has stretched out his hand over the sea; he has shaken the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds. And he said: "You will no more exult, O oppressed virgin daughter of Sidon; arise, cross over to Cyprus, even there you will have no rest." Behold the land of the Chaldeans! This is the people that was not; Assyria destined it for wild beasts. They erected their siege towers, they stripped her palaces bare, they made her a ruin. Wail, O ships of Tarshish, for your stronghold is laid waste.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who has purposed this against Tyre, the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes, whose traders were the honored of the earth?"

The question is the centre of the chapter, and the titles in it are the point.

The bestower of crowns. Tyre was rich enough to make kings — to fund a claimant, install a dynasty, decide who ruled somewhere else. Whose merchants were princes: the commercial class in that city had the standing of nobility. Money had become the aristocracy.

So the question is a real one. Who takes down a power like that? Not an army; it sat on an island. Something else has to be at work.

"The LORD of hosts has purposed it, to defile the pride of all glory, to dishonor all the honored of the earth."

And there is the answer, with the reason attached. God did it, and the target named is not trade but the pride of all glory.

Isaiah is careful here, and the care matters. Tyre is not condemned for being a trading city. Ships, cargoes and commerce are nowhere in Scripture treated as evil, and the last verse of this chapter will have Tyre trading again with God's approval. What is judged is the pride that made commerce ultimate — the assumption that a city which can buy anything is answerable to nobody.

It is the same principle as the day against every high tower and every ship of Tarshish in chapter 2, applied now to money rather than to cedars. God has a day against everything tall, and wealth is one of the tallest things there is.

"He stretched out his hand over the sea; he shook the kingdoms; the LORD has given command concerning Canaan to destroy its strongholds."

The hand over the sea is the exodus gesture. The God who reached over water once before, for slaves, reaches over it again — and this time the thing that goes down is a market.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–18 — Her Profit Will Be Holy
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seventy years pass — the length of a king's life, and the number Jeremiah will use for Babylon's dominion — and Tyre is forgotten (v. 15). Then she is remembered, and the image is deliberately undignified: an old prostitute taking up her harp, going about the city, singing well to be noticed again (vv. 16-17). She returns to her trade with all the kingdoms of the world. And then verse 18 turns the whole thing round: her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD, not stored or hoarded, but supplying abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before him.
verseByVerse.theology: The restoration is not a compliment. Isaiah refuses to ennoble commerce simply because it resumes: the city goes straight back to what it was, and he says so in the least flattering image available. What changes is not the trade but where the profit ends up.
verseByVerse.examples: This is where the whole block has been going since chapter 13, and the currency is the surprise. The wealth of the nations, purged of its pride, is not destroyed but redirected — it ends up feeding and clothing the people of God. It is a small seed of the vision at the end of the book, where the nations bring their glory in, and of the city whose gates never shut.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute: "Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered." At the end of seventy years, the LORD will visit Tyre, and she will return to her wages and will prostitute herself with all the kingdoms of the world on the face of the earth. Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day Tyre will be forgotten for seventy years, like the days of one king. At the end of seventy years, it will happen to Tyre as in the song of the prostitute."

Seventy years is a working lifetime — a generation and a bit — and it is the number Jeremiah will use for the length of Babylon's dominion. Long enough that the people who remembered the city at its height are gone.

"Take a harp; go about the city, O forgotten prostitute! Make sweet melody; sing many songs, that you may be remembered."

The image is deliberately unflattering, and Isaiah chose it rather than a gentler one. An ageing prostitute nobody calls for any more, walking the streets with an instrument, singing well in the hope of being noticed.

He is refusing to ennoble commerce simply because it resumes. Tyre comes back and goes straight back to what she was, hiring herself out to all the kingdoms on the face of the earth. Nothing about the return is presented as redemption.

"Her merchandise and her wages will be holy to the LORD. It will not be stored or hoarded, but her merchandise will supply abundant food and fine clothing for those who dwell before the LORD."

And then the last verse of the last oracle does something nobody could have predicted from the previous seventeen.

The profits are not destroyed and the trade is not shut down. The money is redirected. What Tyre earns will be holy to the LORD — the technical term for something set apart for God's use — and the two things specified are food and clothing for the people who live in his presence.

Note the clause in the middle: it will not be stored or hoarded. That is the whole difference between the city in verse 8 and the city in verse 18. The commerce is identical; the accumulation has stopped. What was piled up is now passing through.

So the block that opened with Babylon's palaces full of owls closes with the wealth of a trading empire buying dinner for the people of God. Chapter 13 said these oracles always turn toward mercy somewhere, and here is the turn, in the most unexpected currency in the book. The nations arrive at Zion not only as worshippers but as suppliers, and everything they bring is holy.

23.theology:
Not commerce, but the pride that made it ultimate. Tyre is titled with precision — the bestower of crowns, whose merchants were princes — a city rich enough to make kings and a class in which money had become the aristocracy. Verse 9 names the target: to defile the pride of all glory. Trade itself is not condemned anywhere here; the last verse has Tyre trading again with God’s approval. What is judged is the assumption that a city which can buy anything answers to nobody — the day against everything tall (ch. 2), applied to money rather than cedars.

Somebody purposed it. Verse 8 asks who did this and gets a name. Trade routes do not simply shift and markets do not merely turn; behind the failure of an economy everyone had come to depend on stands a decision, and the hand stretched over the sea (v. 11) is the exodus gesture.

Redirected, not destroyed. Isaiah refuses to ennoble the restoration — Tyre returns to exactly what she was, in the least flattering image available. What changes is not the trade but the destination of the profit: it becomes holy to the LORD, and the clause that carries the whole difference is it will not be stored or hoarded. The commerce is identical; the accumulation has stopped, and what was piled up is now passing through to feed and clothe God’s people. The block that opened with owls in Babylon’s palaces closes with the wealth of the nations buying their dinner.

24.subtitle: The LORD’s Devastation of the Earth
24.intro: Overview. With chapter 24 the focus widens dramatically from individual nations to the whole earth. Sometimes called the “Isaiah Apocalypse,” chapters 24–27 form a distinct unit dealing with universal judgment and ultimate renewal. Chapter 24 describes the desolation of the earth in terms that deliberately echo the flood narrative — a covenant broken, creation undone — before closing with a vision of the LORD reigning on Mount Zion. It is not primarily about a specific historical event but about the logic of history itself: what happens when human civilization persistently violates the terms of its existence.

keyVerse.quote: “The LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders, for the LORD of hosts will reign.”
keyVerse.note: After a chapter of comprehensive devastation, this sentence arrives like a foundation stone. The point of all the undoing is not nihilism but preparation — the clearing of the earth for the reign that cannot be shaken. It is the same movement John sees in Revelation: the bowls of wrath followed by the marriage supper of the Lamb.

24.theology:
An earlier covenant than Sinai. The charge in verse 5 is that the inhabitants of the earth have broken the everlasting covenant — which cannot be Sinai, since most of the earth never received it and cannot break what it never had. It is the covenant made after the flood with Noah, with every living creature and with the ground itself. That is why the whole planet is answerable in these four chapters, and not only the nations with prophets.

The levelling of verse 2. Six pairs, each naming a relationship in which one party holds the advantage — priest over layman, master over slave, creditor over debtor — and in every case the verdict is the same: so with. The distinctions people spend their lives establishing have no purchase whatever on the day described.

Songs and grief, unreconciled. Praise rises from the ends of the earth (vv. 14-16) and the prophet interrupts it to say he is wasting away. Isaiah does not smooth that out, and it should not be smoothed out for him: the songs are deserved and the grief is warranted, and they sit in adjacent sentences. It is the honest position of anyone living between the two comings. The chapter then ends with the sun and moon not destroyed but ashamed — outshone rather than abolished, as in Revelation 21:23.
24.reflection: Isaiah hears songs of praise and immediately collapses in grief — both responses are appropriate to the same reality. How do you hold together genuine worship with honest lament over the state of the world? Which comes more naturally to you, and which do you need to cultivate?

For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed."<sup>17</sup>Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth!<sup>18</sup>He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble.<sup>19</sup>The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken.<sup>20</sup>The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again.<sup>21</sup>On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth.<sup>22</sup>They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished.<sup>23</sup>Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lens pulls back from named nations to the earth itself. God empties it and twists its surface (v. 1), and verse 2 levels every social distinction in six pairs — priest and people, master and slave, buyer and seller, lender and borrower, creditor and debtor. Verse 5 gives the reason: the earth lies defiled under its inhabitants, who have transgressed the laws and broken the everlasting covenant. Verses 7 to 12 take the joy out of the world one item at a time: the wine dries up, the music stops, the city is broken, and every house is shut. Verse 13 leaves gleanings on a beaten olive tree even here.
verseByVerse.theology: The judgment is universal in a way nothing before it in the book has been, and its grounds are pre-Israelite. The everlasting covenant of verse 5 is not Sinai, which most of the earth never received, but the covenant God made with Noah and every living creature — which is why the whole planet is answerable here.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 is the levelling that makes the chapter uncomfortable. Every pair names a relationship in which one party has the advantage, and in each case Isaiah says as with — it will go the same for both. The distinctions people spend their lives establishing turn out to have no purchase at all on the day being described.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants. And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor. The earth shall be utterly empty and utterly plundered; for the LORD has spoken this word. The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and withers; the highest people of the earth languish. The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant. Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt; therefore the inhabitants of the earth are scorched, and few men are left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the LORD will empty the earth and make it desolate, and he will twist its surface and scatter its inhabitants."

Eleven chapters have named nations one at a time. This one names none, because the subject is now the earth, and the four chapters that follow keep it there.

The verb in the middle is unusual and physical: God will twist the surface of the world, the way you would wring out a cloth.

"And it shall be, as with the people, so with the priest; as with the slave, so with his master; as with the maid, so with her mistress; as with the buyer, so with the seller; as with the lender, so with the borrower; as with the creditor, so with the debtor."

Six pairs, and every one names a relationship where somebody has the advantage. The priest over the layman. The master over the slave. The lender over the borrower, the creditor over the debtor — which in that economy could mean owning a man's future outright.

And in every case the verdict is the same three words: so with. The gap between them, which is the thing both parties have organised their lives around, turns out to make no difference whatever on the day being described.

"The earth lies defiled under its inhabitants; for they have transgressed the laws, violated the statutes, broken the everlasting covenant."

Here is the charge, and the last phrase is the one that widens it. This cannot be Sinai; most of the earth never received Sinai and could not break what it never had.

The everlasting covenant is the one God made after the flood with Noah and with every living creature and with the ground itself — the arrangement under which human beings hold the world. That is what has been broken, and it is why the whole planet is answerable in this chapter and not only the nations with prophets.

"Therefore a curse devours the earth, and its inhabitants suffer for their guilt."

verseByVerse.quote: The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh. The mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled. No more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it. The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter. There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished. Desolation is left in the city; the gates are battered into ruins. For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The wine mourns, the vine languishes, all the merry-hearted sigh."

What follows is a careful, patient removal of every source of ordinary human gladness, and Isaiah takes seven verses over it because the loss is cumulative.

The wine goes first. Then the mirth of the tambourines is stilled, the noise of the jubilant has ceased, the mirth of the lyre is stilled — three instruments, silenced one after another. Then the drinking songs: no more do they drink wine with singing; strong drink is bitter to those who drink it.

Note that last clause. The drink is still available. It has simply stopped working — which is a more desolate thing than not having it, and anyone who has tried to enjoy something during a season of grief knows the exact taste being described.

"The wasted city is broken down; every house is shut up so that none can enter."

Then the town. Doors shut, nobody going in or out — a street with people behind every door and no life in it.

"There is an outcry in the streets for lack of wine; all joy has grown dark; the gladness of the earth is banished."

All joy has grown dark. The chapter is not describing violence at this point; it is describing a world with the pleasure taken out of it, which is its own kind of judgment.

"For thus it shall be in the midst of the earth among the nations, as when an olive tree is beaten, as at the gleaning when the grape harvest is done."

And the same image as chapter 17 closes the section: the beaten olive tree, with a few things left at the top. Even here, in the widest judgment in the book so far, Isaiah cannot describe a devastation without leaving gleanings in it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–23 — Songs, and a Prophet Wasting Away
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Voices lift from the west and the east and the coastlands, glorifying the LORD and shouting the majesty of the Righteous One (vv. 14-16a) — and in the middle of the singing Isaiah breaks in: I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! Verses 17 to 20 have terror, pit and snare closing on the inhabitants of the earth, which staggers like a drunkard and sways like a hut. Verses 21 to 23 gather the host of heaven and the kings of the earth into a pit, shame the sun and moon, and end with the LORD of hosts reigning on Mount Zion before his elders in glory.
verseByVerse.theology: The praise and the grief are both real and Isaiah refuses to resolve them. Somewhere on the earth people are already singing glory to the Righteous One, and the prophet in the middle of it is undone by the treachery still going on around him. That is a fair description of the position of any believer between the two comings.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter that opened with the earth emptied ends with God enthroned and his glory before his elders — and the sun and moon ashamed, not destroyed, because everything that gave light is outshone. John sees the same city needing neither sun nor moon, because the glory of God is its light (Rev. 21:23).

verseByVerse.quote: They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel. From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One. But I say, "I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They lift up their voices, they sing for joy; over the majesty of the LORD they shout from the west. Therefore in the east give glory to the LORD; in the coastlands of the sea, give glory to the name of the LORD, the God of Israel."

Singing breaks out, and it comes from the compass points — west, east, the coastlands. In a chapter about the earth being emptied, some of the earth is already worshipping.

"From the ends of the earth we hear songs of praise, of glory to the Righteous One."

That is a remarkable thing to hear in the middle of this. The ends of the earth are the places furthest from Jerusalem, and the title they use is not one Israel had taught them. Judgment is running and praise is running at the same time, in the same world.

"But I say, 'I waste away, I waste away. Woe is me! For the traitors have betrayed, with betrayal the traitors have betrayed.'"

And then the prophet interrupts his own vision.

He is not singing. He says twice that he is wasting away, and then uses one root three times over — traitors, betrayal, betrayed — the sound of a man who cannot get past what he is looking at.

Isaiah does not smooth this out, and it should not be smoothed out for him. The songs are real and deserved; his grief is real and warranted; and the two are in adjacent sentences with no attempt to reconcile them.

That is the honest position of anybody living between the first coming and the second. Christ has risen and the praise from the ends of the earth is genuine; the treachery is still going on and it is right to be undone by it. Anyone who feels only one of those has stopped paying attention to half the evidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare. For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble. The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut; its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth! He who flees at the sound of the terror shall fall into the pit, and he who climbs out of the pit shall be caught in the snare."

Three dangers in sequence, and the sequence is the point. The man runs from the first and lands in the second; he climbs out of the second and is taken by the third.

In Hebrew the three words chime — pachad, pachat, pach — so the sentence sounds like what it describes: one thing after another, each escape leading into the next trap. It is the experience of a bad year rendered as three syllables.

"For the windows of heaven are opened, and the foundations of the earth tremble."

The windows of heaven were opened once before, at the flood, and Isaiah uses the phrase deliberately. He has already grounded the judgment in the covenant God made after that flood; now he reaches for the flood's own vocabulary.

"The earth is utterly broken, the earth is split apart, the earth is violently shaken. The earth staggers like a drunken man; it sways like a hut."

Three clauses beginning with the earth, and then two images that are almost comic if they were not terrible: the planet lurching like a drunk, and swaying like the flimsy watchman's hut from chapter 1.

"Its transgression lies heavy upon it, and it falls, and will not rise again."

The last line names what is doing the damage, and it is not the shaking. The earth falls because its own transgression is heavy upon it — a weight it has been carrying and can no longer hold up.

verseByVerse.quote: On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth. They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished. Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven, in heaven, and the kings of the earth, on the earth."

Two categories, and both are in the sentence for a reason. The host of heaven is the spiritual powers; the kings of the earth is the political ones. Scripture keeps them close together, because the second so often draws its confidence from the first.

God deals with both on the same day and in the same clause, which is a considerable comfort to anybody who has ever felt that the trouble in the world has more behind it than the people visibly causing it.

"They will be gathered together as prisoners in a pit; they will be shut up in a prison, and after many days they will be punished."

Note the interval. They are shut up, and after many days they are dealt with. There is a holding period built into the sentence — which is exactly what the New Testament describes when it speaks of spirits kept until judgment, and it explains the delay that troubles every reader of this book.

"Then the moon will be confounded and the sun ashamed, for the LORD of hosts reigns on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and his glory will be before his elders."

And here is the ending of a chapter that began with the earth emptied and twisted.

The sun and moon are not destroyed. They are ashamed — put out of countenance, the way a lamp is when a door opens onto daylight. Nothing is wrong with them; something brighter has arrived, and the two great lights that have measured every day and month since creation are simply outshone.

John saw the end of it: a city with no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God gives it light and its lamp is the Lamb (Rev. 21:23).

The chapter that opened with a world wrung out like a cloth closes with God on his throne, his glory in front of his elders, and the sun embarrassed. The devastation was never the last word, and it never is in this book.

25.subtitle: A Feast on the Mountain
25.intro: Overview. Chapter 25 is one of the high points of Isaiah — a psalm of praise for what God has done and will do, including two of the most stunning promises in the Old Testament: the abolition of death and the wiping away of every tear. After the cosmic devastation of chapter 24, God throws a banquet. The chapter also contains a compact oracle against Moab (vv. 10–12), which serves as a foil to highlight the contrast between those who trust in the LORD and those who trust in their own strength.

keyVerse.quote: “He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth.”
keyVerse.note: This is one of the clearest resurrection promises in the entire Old Testament. “Swallow up death forever” is the language of total, permanent defeat — not death postponed but death ended. Paul places it at the climax of his resurrection argument (1 Cor. 15:54), and John plants it at the center of the new creation (Rev. 21:4). The whole trajectory of redemptive history bends toward this sentence.

25.theology:
Three things swallowed. Verses 7 and 8 name what is wrong with the world in order, and remove each one: the veil spread over all nations that stops people seeing; death, swallowed up forever with a violent verb and no possibility of return; and the reproach that clings to God’s people, taken from all the earth. Paul quotes verse 8 as the sentence fulfilled at the resurrection of the body (1 Cor. 15:54), and John hears the tear-wiping again at the very end (Rev. 21:4).

For all peoples. The phrase is used twice and all nations once in four verses. This is not Israel’s feast with guests admitted but a table spread by God himself for everybody, and the menu is not relief rations: rich food full of marrow, and aged wine well refined — the honoured guest’s portion, laid down years in advance. It is the meal Jesus kept describing and the marriage supper John was told to write down (Rev. 19:9).

Two places to be. The chapter ends by naming somebody absent from a feast spread for all peoples — the nation offered shelter under David’s throne in chapters 15-16, which refused out of pride. Verse 11 puts him in a dung-pit, swimming with real technique, and lays low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. The two go down together: Moab is not incompetent but expert, and every bit of the expertise is deployed in a medium no skill makes clean.
25.reflection: God’s response to the devastation of chapter 24 is a banquet. Not a repair program or a recovery plan — a feast. What does it tell you about God that his ultimate answer to the brokenness of the world is abundance and celebration? And which promise from this chapter do you most need to hold onto right now: the feast, the lifted veil, or the end of death and tears?
25.text: <sup>1</sup>O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure.<sup>2</sup>For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt.<sup>3</sup>Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you.<sup>4</sup>For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall,<sup>5</sup>like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down.<sup>6</sup>On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined.<sup>7</sup>And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations.<sup>8</sup>He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken.<sup>9</sup>It will be said on that day, "Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation."<sup>10</sup>For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill.<sup>11</sup>And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands.<sup>12</sup>And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Shelter in the Storm
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the widest vision in the book, the response is personal: O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you, I will praise your name (v. 1). The grounds are specific — wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. Verses 2 and 3 have the fortified city made a heap so that strong peoples glorify God, and verses 4 and 5 name what he has been to those with nothing: a stronghold to the poor and the needy, a shelter from the storm, a shade from the heat.
verseByVerse.theology: Notice the direction. It runs from the cosmic to the personal rather than the other way round: having seen what God will do to the whole earth, the prophet says my God. Big theology in this book does not produce distance; it produces possessives.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 4 and 5 use two weathers, and both are what a poor man cannot escape. A storm, when the ruthless come like rain against a wall; and heat, when there is no shade in an open country. God is described not as removing either but as being the wall and the shadow — which is what shelter actually means.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure. For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin; the foreigners' palace is a city no more; it will never be rebuilt. Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you. For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat; for the breath of the ruthless is like a storm against a wall, like heat in a dry place. You subdue the noise of the foreigners; as heat by the shade of a cloud, so the song of the ruthless is put down.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"O LORD, you are my God; I will exalt you; I will praise your name, for you have done wonderful things, plans formed of old, faithful and sure."

After twelve chapters of nations and one of the whole earth being wrung out, the first word of this chapter is my.

The movement runs the opposite way from what most people expect. It is not that private faith gradually widens into a concern for the world; it is that having seen what God will do with the world, the prophet turns and says you are my God. Large theology in this book does not produce distance. It produces possessives.

And the grounds are specific: plans formed of old, faithful and sure. What has just been described was not improvised. It was decided long ago and has been kept.

"For you have made the city a heap, the fortified city a ruin... Therefore strong peoples will glorify you; cities of ruthless nations will fear you."

The unnamed city is every fortified city in the book — the human project of walls and self-security. And the result of its fall is not that the nations are destroyed but that strong peoples will glorify you. They lose the walls and gain the God.

"For you have been a stronghold to the poor, a stronghold to the needy in his distress, a shelter from the storm and a shade from the heat."

Then the ground of the praise, and it is not the cosmic engineering. It is what God has been to people with nothing.

Two weathers are named, and both are the kind a poor man cannot get away from. A storm, when the ruthless come like a storm against a wall. And heat, in a country where shade is the difference between working and collapsing.

Notice that God does not stop the weather in these verses. He is the wall and he is the shadow. That is what shelter has always meant: not the absence of the storm, but something solid between you and it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — He Will Swallow Up Death Forever
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The summit of these four chapters, and of a good deal else. On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food and well-aged wine (v. 6). On this mountain he will swallow up the covering cast over all peoples, the veil spread over all nations (v. 7). He will swallow up death forever, wipe away tears from all faces, and take the reproach of his people from all the earth (v. 8). And verse 9 is what the redeemed say when it happens: behold, this is our God; we have waited for him.
verseByVerse.theology: The three things swallowed are the three things wrong with the world, in order: the veil that stops people seeing, death that ends them, and the shame that clings to them. Paul takes verse 8 as the sentence fulfilled at the resurrection of the body — death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54) — and John hears the tear-wiping again at the very end (Rev. 21:4).
verseByVerse.examples: For all peoples is said twice and all nations once, in four verses. The feast is not Israel's with guests admitted; it is spread for everybody, on the mountain, by God himself — and the menu is not survival rations but rich food and aged wine. It is the meal Jesus kept describing, and the marriage supper John was told to write down (Rev. 19:9).

verseByVerse.quote: On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined. And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged wine well refined."

Read that slowly, because it is one of the great sentences in the Old Testament and almost every word is doing something.

On this mountain — the same hill on which the hand of the LORD rests in verse 10, the place where God reigns. The LORD of hosts — the commander of armies is the one cooking. Will make — he prepares it himself; nobody contributes a dish.

And then for all peoples, which in a book written for one nation is the astonishing phrase. Not Israel's feast with a few guests admitted. A table spread for everybody.

The menu is the last surprise. This is not relief food or survival rations. Rich food full of marrow is the fat, the best part of the animal, the portion reserved for honoured guests. Aged wine well refined is wine that has been kept for years and then strained clear. God's provision at the end of the story is not adequate. It is lavish, and it has been laid down in advance.

"And he will swallow up on this mountain the covering that is cast over all peoples, the veil that is spread over all nations."

Before the eating, something has to be removed. There is a covering over the human race — a shroud spread across all nations — and it has to go before anybody can see what is on the table.

It is the same word used for a funeral shroud, and it is also the veil Paul says lies over the heart until it turns to the Lord (2 Cor. 3:14-16). The trouble with the world in this verse is not first that people refuse to look but that something is over their faces. And God does not lift it politely. He swallows it.

verseByVerse.quote: He will swallow up death forever; and the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth, for the LORD has spoken. It will be said on that day, "Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He will swallow up death forever."

Four words, and there is nothing like them in the Old Testament before this point.

The verb is the same one used of the veil, and it is deliberately violent: not death managed, not death survived, not death made less frightening — death swallowed, taken in and gone, the way the ground swallowed Korah and the sea swallowed the Egyptians. And forever, so that it cannot come back.

Every religion has something to say about death. Almost all of them are strategies for coping with it, and the honest ones admit it. This verse says the thing itself will be removed from the world, and the surrounding chapters say who will do it and where.

Paul quotes this line at the climax of his argument about the resurrection of the body, when what has been sown perishable is raised imperishable: then shall come to pass the saying that is written, "Death is swallowed up in victory" (1 Cor. 15:54). He is saying that Isaiah's sentence has a date and an occasion.

"And the Lord GOD will wipe away tears from all faces, and the reproach of his people he will take away from all the earth."

Then something more intimate than the cosmic verb before it. God wipes away tears — a hand on a face, one person at a time. Whatever else the end of the world is, it includes God stooping to do that.

And the reproach of his people: the shame, the long humiliation of having been on the losing side. That goes too, from all the earth.

"It will be said on that day, 'Behold, this is our God; we have waited for him, that he might save us. This is the LORD; we have waited for him; let us be glad and rejoice in his salvation.'"

And here is what the redeemed actually say, and notice that it is not a prayer or a request. It is recognition, twice over: this is our God... this is the LORD.

The clause repeated in the middle is we have waited for him. All the waiting of this book — the watchman on his tower through whole nights, Edom asking what time it is, the prophet wasting away in chapter 24 — is gathered into one sentence and answered by a face.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends abruptly and harshly. The hand of the LORD rests on this mountain, and Moab is trodden down as straw is trodden down in a dung-pit (v. 10). Moab spreads out his hands in the middle of it as a swimmer spreads his hands to swim, and God brings down his pride along with the skill of his hands (v. 11). The high fortifications of his walls are laid low, cast to the ground, to the dust (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The placement is deliberate rather than vindictive. Isaiah has just spread a table for all peoples, and immediately names somebody who is not at it — the nation of chapters 15 and 16, which was offered shelter under the throne of David and refused it out of pride. The feast is for all peoples and Moab is a people; the only thing keeping him out is what kept him out before.
verseByVerse.examples: The picture in verse 11 is grotesque and exact: a man swimming in a dung-pit, spreading his hands with real skill. Effort, technique and self-sufficiency, applied vigorously in the wrong place. It is the alternative to the feast, and Isaiah declines to make it look dignified.

verseByVerse.quote: For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill. And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands. And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For the hand of the LORD will rest on this mountain, and Moab shall be trampled down in his place, as straw is trampled down in a dunghill."

The chapter turns abruptly, and the abruptness is the point.

Isaiah has just spread a table for all peoples on this mountain. In the next breath he names somebody who is not at it — and the reader who has been paying attention knows exactly why, because chapters 15 and 16 told the story. Moab was offered shelter under the throne of David, in verses of extraordinary tenderness, and refused it. The reason was given four times in one line: pride.

So the feast is for all peoples, and Moab is a people, and the only thing keeping him outside is the thing that kept him outside before.

"And he will spread out his hands in the midst of it as a swimmer spreads his hands out to swim, but the LORD will lay low his pompous pride together with the skill of his hands."

The image is grotesque and exact: a man swimming in a dung-pit, and doing it well — arms spread properly, technique intact, real effort.

Isaiah puts pride and the skill of his hands in the same clause because they go down together. Moab is not incompetent. He is capable, energetic and expert, and every bit of it is being deployed in the wrong place, in a medium that no amount of skill makes clean.

That is the alternative to the feast, and Isaiah refuses to let it look dignified. There are two places to be at the end of this chapter: at a table on a mountain, eating food you did not provide, with the shroud taken off your face — or in the pit, swimming strongly.

"And the high fortifications of his walls he will bring down, lay low, and cast to the ground, to the dust."

26.subtitle: The Song of the Strong City
26.intro: Overview. Chapter 26 is a sustained song — partly communal, partly prophetic — celebrating the security of those who trust in the LORD while the lofty city of the nations lies in the dust. It includes one of the clearest Old Testament anticipations of bodily resurrection (v. 19), framed within a meditation on the contrast between God’s reliable character and human weakness. The chapter invites Israel to enter her chambers and wait while God’s judgment passes — an echo of Passover, a foretaste of the final hiding.

keyVerse.quote: “You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.”
keyVerse.note: The doubled shalom — peace-peace — is not accidental. It indicates completeness: there is no dimension of a person’s life that this peace does not reach. And it is entirely relational — it belongs to the one whose imagination is anchored in God, not in circumstances. Philippians 4:7 is the New Testament cognate: the peace of God that guards heart and mind in Christ Jesus.

26.reflection: The people in this chapter are told to enter their chambers and hide “for a little while.” There is a season of patient waiting in the darkness that belongs to the life of faith. Where are you right now — in a waiting season, a labor season, or a morning-after season? And what does “staying your mind on God” actually look like in the middle of it?
26.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks.<sup>2</sup>Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in.<sup>3</sup>You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you.<sup>4</sup>Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock.<sup>5</sup>For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust.<sup>6</sup>The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy."<sup>7</sup>The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous.<sup>8</sup>In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul.<sup>9</sup>My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.<sup>10</sup>If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD.<sup>11</sup>O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them.<sup>12</sup>O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works.<sup>13</sup>O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance.<sup>14</sup>They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them.<sup>15</sup>But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land.<sup>16</sup>O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them.<sup>17</sup>Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD;<sup>18</sup>we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.<sup>19</sup>Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead.<sup>20</sup>Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by.<sup>21</sup>For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A song sung in Judah: we have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks (v. 1). The gates are opened for a righteous nation that keeps faith (v. 2). Verse 3 gives the chapter's most quoted line — perfect peace for the mind stayed on God — and verse 4 the reason: in the LORD is an everlasting rock. Verses 5 and 6 have the lofty city brought down and trampled by the feet of the poor. Verses 7 to 9 turn personal: the path of the righteous is level, and my soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you.
verseByVerse.theology: The strong city of this chapter is set against the fortified city of chapter 25, and the difference is not masonry. What makes it strong is that God is its wall — he sets up salvation as walls — and what its citizens do is trust. The Hebrew of verse 3 is literally peace, peace: a doubled word, which is how that language says complete.
verseByVerse.examples: The word behind stayed in verse 3 means propped or leaned, as a beam is leaned against a wall. The peace is not the absence of trouble — the chapter is full of trouble — but a stability the trouble cannot reach, and it belongs specifically to a mind that keeps putting its weight somewhere.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: "We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in. You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you. Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day this song will be sung in the land of Judah: 'We have a strong city; he sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks.'"

One chapter ago a fortified city was made a heap. Here is another city, and the singers call it strong — but read the second half of the line before deciding what the strength consists of.

He sets up salvation as walls and bulwarks. The masonry is not mentioned. What stands between this city and the world is not stone but salvation, and God is the one who put it there.

"Open the gates, that the righteous nation that keeps faith may enter in."

And the gates are opened rather than defended. A city whose walls are God can afford to have its doors standing open, which is where the book eventually ends up: a city whose gates are never shut, because there is nothing left to keep out.

"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you."

The most quoted verse in the chapter, and the Hebrew is more emphatic than the English. There is no adjective; the phrase is simply shalom shalom, peace repeated — which is how that language says complete. Doubled peace.

And the verb behind stayed is architectural: to prop, to lean, to rest weight against. It is what you do with a beam. So the promise is not to the mind that thinks calm thoughts about God but to the mind that keeps putting its weight on him.

Notice what is not promised. Not the absence of trouble — this chapter has a trampled city, a confession of total failure and a call to hide behind closed doors. It is stability that the trouble cannot get at, which is a different and better thing.

"Trust in the LORD forever, for the LORD GOD is an everlasting rock."

verseByVerse.quote: For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy." The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous. In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul. My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you. For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For he has humbled the inhabitants of the height, the lofty city. He lays it low, lays it low to the ground, casts it to the dust. The foot tramples it, the feet of the poor, the steps of the needy."

The other city, and the way it comes down. God lays it low — the phrase is repeated, and then a third verb piles on: casts it to the dust.

And then the detail that makes the verse. Who walks on the ruins? Not an army. The feet of the poor, the steps of the needy — the people the lofty city was built by and paid for with. They are not described as conquering it. They are just walking over what is left, which is the quietest reversal in the book.

"The path of the righteous is level; you make level the way of the righteous."

"In the path of your judgments, O LORD, we wait for you; your name and remembrance are the desire of our soul."

Now the song turns personal, and what it says it wants is not rescue but your name and remembrance. That is a striking thing for people in the middle of a judgment to say.

"My soul yearns for you in the night; my spirit within me earnestly seeks you."

This is one of the most honest sentences about desire in the Old Testament, and the setting is the important part. In the night — the hours when there is nothing to do, nothing to distract, and whatever a person actually wants surfaces without being asked.

What surfaces here is God. Not an answer, not an outcome — him. Anyone who has lain awake knows how reliably the night exposes what the heart is really after, and this verse sets the standard for what it should be.

"For when your judgments are in the earth, the inhabitants of the world learn righteousness."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The middle section is unsparing about human limits. Verse 10 observes that grace shown to the wicked does not teach him righteousness. Verses 12 to 15 confess that whatever has been done for us, God did it, and that other lords have ruled but are dead and will not rise. Verses 16 to 18 give the confession its most honest form: we were pregnant, we writhed, and we gave birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the emptying that has to happen before verse 19 can be said. Israel is not confessing laziness but the failure of genuine effort — labour pains, real and prolonged, that produced nothing. The reason the deliverance in the next verse comes entirely from God is that human strength has been spent to exhaustion trying and has delivered wind.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 is the sentence to keep from this section: O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. Everything that was ever actually accomplished turns out, on inspection, to have been his — which is humbling and, for anyone tired of carrying it, an enormous relief.

verseByVerse.quote: If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD. O LORD, your hand is lifted up, but they do not see it. Let them see your zeal for your people, and be ashamed. Let the fire for your adversaries consume them. O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works. O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise; to that end you have visited them with destruction and wiped out all remembrance of them. But you have increased the nation, O LORD, you have increased the nation; you are glorified; you have enlarged all the borders of the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"If favor is shown to the wicked, he does not learn righteousness; in the land of uprightness he deals corruptly and does not see the majesty of the LORD."

A sober observation, and it corrects a sentimental assumption. Kindness does not automatically produce goodness. Show a man favour, put him in a decent society, and he may simply take the advantage and go on as before — not because kindness is wasted, but because the problem was never a shortage of it.

The last clause names the root: he does not see the majesty of the LORD. That is the faculty that is out, and no improvement in circumstances repairs it.

"O LORD, you will ordain peace for us, for you have indeed done for us all our works."

And here is one of the most quietly devastating sentences in the chapter. You have done for us all our works.

Not you helped us with our works. Everything on the list of things Israel had accomplished turns out, when the accounts are opened, to have been done by God. That is humbling to read and, for anybody tired of carrying the weight of his own record, an enormous relief.

"O LORD our God, other lords besides you have ruled over us, but your name alone we bring to remembrance. They are dead, they will not live; they are shades, they will not arise."

An honest admission — there have been other lords, and Israel served them — and then a flat statement about where they are now. They are dead. They will not arise.

Hold that sentence, because in four verses the same book will say the exact opposite about somebody else, and the contrast is the point of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them.
