Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD; we were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"O LORD, in distress they sought you; they poured out a whispered prayer when your discipline was upon them."

The phrase is exact and gentle: a whispered prayer. Not eloquence, not liturgy. The sound a person makes under pressure, half audible, when there is nothing left to say properly.

"Like a pregnant woman who writhes and cries out in her pangs when she is near to giving birth, so were we because of you, O LORD."

"We were pregnant, we writhed, but we have given birth to wind. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth, and the inhabitants of the world have not fallen."

This is the most honest confession in the book and one of the bleakest images in Scripture.

Every part of the labour was real. They carried something, they went into pains, they cried out, they laboured to the point where a birth should have happened — and what came out was wind. Nothing to hold. Nothing to show anyone. All the agony of production and no product.

Note carefully what is being confessed. Not laziness. Not failure to try. This is the failure of genuine, exhausting effort, which is a far harder thing to admit and a far more common experience. We have accomplished no deliverance in the earth.

Anyone who has poured years into something — a marriage, a ministry, a child, a work — and watched it come to nothing knows this verse from the inside, and Isaiah does not offer a word of consolation about it here. He lets the confession stand.

Because it has to stand before the next verse can be said. What follows does not come as an encouragement to try harder. It comes to people who have just admitted that everything they had was spent, and that it produced air.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Into that confession of futility God speaks. Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! — because God's dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead (v. 19). Verses 20 and 21 tell God's people to go into their rooms, shut the doors and hide for a little while until the fury has passed, because the LORD is coming out of his place to punish the earth, and the ground will disclose the blood shed on it.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 19 is the earliest unambiguous promise of bodily resurrection in Isaiah, and it is emphatically physical: bodies, dust, awaking. Daniel says the same (Dan. 12:2) and Paul builds on it (1 Cor. 15). And note the placement — a people who have just admitted they gave birth to wind are told that the earth will give birth to the dead. The verb is the same; the mother is different.
verseByVerse.examples: The instruction in verse 20 is unexpectedly domestic. Go inside, shut the door, wait a little while. It is what Israel did on the night of the Passover, and it is what God's people are given to do in the interval — not a strategy, not a defence, just staying inside the room while something passes over.

verseByVerse.quote: Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy! For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead. Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by. For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Your dead shall live; their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust, awake and sing for joy!"

Into that confession, God speaks — and this is the first unambiguous promise of bodily resurrection in the book.

Read how physical it is. Your dead: particular people, belonging to somebody. Their bodies shall rise. You who dwell in the dust — addressed directly to the dead, in the second person, which is a startling thing to do. And the instruction given to them is not merely to get up but to sing for joy.

Four verses ago the other lords were dead, would not live, were shades and would not arise. Here is the same vocabulary with the verdict reversed for God's own. The difference between the two is not the quality of the dead. It is whose they are.

"For your dew is a dew of light, and the earth will give birth to the dead."

And the verb is the one from verse 18. They gave birth to wind; the earth will give birth to the dead. Same word, different mother. What human labour could not produce, the ground will hand over when God's dew falls on it.

Daniel says it plainly a few centuries later — many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake (Dan. 12:2) — and Paul builds fifteen chapters of argument on it, answering the question of what kind of body with the answer that it is sown perishable and raised imperishable.

"Come, my people, enter your chambers, and shut your doors behind you; hide yourselves for a little while until the fury has passed by."

Then the instruction, and after resurrection it is unexpectedly domestic. Go inside. Shut the door. Wait a little while.

Every Israelite would have recognised it: that is the night of the Passover, with the blood on the doorposts and the families indoors while something passed over. It is not a strategy or a defence. It is staying in the room, on the authority of somebody who said the fury would pass.

"For behold, the LORD is coming out from his place to punish the inhabitants of the earth for their iniquity, and the earth will disclose the blood shed on it, and will no more cover its slain."

And the last line answers every murder that was got away with. The ground has been absorbing blood since Abel, and it has been keeping the record. On that day it gives the evidence up.

26.theology:
Peace as leaning. Verse 3 has no adjective in Hebrew — it reads shalom shalom, peace doubled, which is how that language says complete. And stayed is an architectural word: propped, leaned, as a beam rests against a wall. The promise is not to a mind that thinks calm thoughts about God but to one that keeps putting its weight on him, and it is not the absence of trouble — this chapter is full of trouble — but a stability the trouble cannot reach.

Giving birth to wind. Verses 17-18 are the most honest confession in the book: real labour, real pains, real crying out, and nothing produced. What is admitted is not laziness but the failure of genuine effort — we have accomplished no deliverance in the earth. That emptying is what makes verse 19 sayable, and verse 12 has already conceded the wider point: whatever was actually accomplished, you have done for us all our works.

Your dead shall live. Verse 19 is the first unambiguous promise of bodily resurrection in Isaiah, and it is emphatically physical: bodies, dust, awaking, and the dead addressed in the second person and told to sing. Four verses earlier the other lords were dead and would not arise; the difference is not the quality of the dead but whose they are. And the verb in the earth will give birth to the dead is the one from verse 18: human labour produced wind, the ground will produce the dead. Same word, different mother.

27.subtitle: The Great Harvest
27.intro: Overview. Chapter 27 concludes the Isaiah Apocalypse (chs. 24–27) with three movements: the defeat of the serpentine powers (v. 1), the song of the vineyard revisited (vv. 2–6), and the ingathering of scattered Israel (vv. 12–13). It stands in deliberate contrast with chapter 5’s vineyard song — the same vineyard, but now God tends it with care and there is fruit. The chapter is eschatological: it looks to the final outcome of history.

keyVerse.quote: “In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.”
keyVerse.note: The vine that was stripped in chapter 5 becomes the vine that fills the earth. This is the covenantal logic of Isaiah in miniature: judgment clears the way for new growth, and the new growth exceeds the old. It is also a Christological verse: Jesus declares himself the true vine (John 15:1), and his fruitfulness fills the world through those who abide in him.

27.reflection: God says “I have no wrath” and doubles the invitation: “let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me.” There is urgency in the repetition — not threat, but longing. In what area of your life have you been treating God’s patience as distance rather than invitation?
27.text: <sup>1</sup>In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.<sup>2</sup>In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it!<sup>3</sup>I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day;<sup>4</sup>I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together.<sup>5</sup>Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me."<sup>6</sup>In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.<sup>7</sup>Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain?<sup>8</sup>Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind.<sup>9</sup>Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing.<sup>10</sup>For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches.<sup>11</sup>When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor.<sup>12</sup>In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel.<sup>13</sup>And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Sword and the Serpent
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse, and it is a thunderclap. In that day the LORD, with his hard and great and strong sword, will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and will slay the dragon that is in the sea.
verseByVerse.theology: Leviathan is the ancient symbol of chaos — the sea-monster that stands in Near Eastern imagination for everything disordered, untamable and hostile to creation, and in Scripture for the power behind hostile empires. Three names are given for one creature, which is how a decisive victory gets described: every version of the thing, dealt with at once.
verseByVerse.examples: John identifies the figure when he sees it: the great dragon, that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan (Rev. 12:9). The sword in this verse ends what began with a serpent in a garden — and it belongs beside 11:8, where a baby plays over the hole of an adder because the war is already over.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day the LORD with his hard and great and strong sword will punish Leviathan the fleeing serpent, Leviathan the twisting serpent, and he will slay the dragon that is in the sea."

One verse, and it changes the register of everything around it.

Leviathan was a figure every reader in that world knew. In the mythologies of the region it is the sea-monster of chaos — the thing that was there before order, that heaves under the water, that no one can hunt or bridle. The book of Job spends most of a chapter on the impossibility of catching it. It stands for everything untamable and hostile to creation, and behind the empires that behave the same way.

Isaiah gives it three names in one line: the fleeing serpent, the twisting serpent, the dragon that is in the sea. That is how a decisive victory gets described — not one aspect dealt with, but every version of the thing, in a single sentence.

And the weapon is described before the target: his hard and great and strong sword. Three adjectives for the sword and three names for the monster. It is a fair fight described in a way that makes clear it is not one.

John saw who this was. In his vision the great dragon is thrown down — "that ancient serpent, who is called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world" (Rev. 12:9). The sword in this verse finishes what a serpent started in a garden.

Set it beside 11:8, where a nursing child plays over the hole of a cobra and comes to no harm. That verse is only possible because of this one. The reason a baby can put his hand in the adder's den in the peaceable kingdom is that somewhere behind the scene the dragon has already been dealt with.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–11 — The Vineyard Song, Sung Again
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In that day, a pleasant vineyard, sing of it! Chapter 5 opened with a vineyard song that ended with the wall broken and briers let in. Here the song begins again and the owner has changed his posture entirely: I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day (v. 3). Verse 4 has him saying he has no wrath, and pressing an offer twice over — let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me. Verse 6 has Jacob taking root and filling the whole world with fruit. Verses 7 to 11 measure the discipline and name what still has to go: by verse 9 the altar stones are crushed to chalk and no Asherim or incense altars are left standing, and vv. 10-11 leave the fortified city empty with a calf grazing in it.
verseByVerse.theology: The change between chapter 5 and this one is not in the vineyard. It is in what God is doing with it: there he was the disappointed owner who looked for grapes and walked away; here he is the keeper who waters it every moment and guards it night and day. Between the two songs stands everything the book has been promising.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is the most surprising sentence in the chapter. I have no wrath — said by the God of chapters 1 to 23 — and then an invitation repeated in the same breath, as people repeat things they badly want to be heard. God is not waiting to be asked here. He is pressing the offer.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day, "A pleasant vineyard, sing of it! I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day; I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me." In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day, 'A pleasant vineyard, sing of it!'"

Anyone who has read chapter 5 should stop here, because Isaiah is starting the same song over.

That one began as a love song about a friend's vineyard on a fertile hill, described every care the owner had taken, and ended with wild grapes, a broken wall, and briers and thorns growing where the vines had been. It was the saddest thing in the first third of the book.

Here is the song again, and the first thing said about the vineyard is that it is pleasant.

"I, the LORD, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and day."

And here is what has changed, and it is not the vineyard. It is the owner's posture.

In chapter 5 he dug it, planted it, built a tower, cut a winepress — and then looked for fruit, found none, and removed the hedge. Here he does not plant and step back. He waters it every moment and keeps it night and day, and the reason given is protective: lest anyone punish it. The disappointed owner has become the watchman over his own field.

"I have no wrath. Would that I had thorns and briers to battle! I would march against them, I would burn them up together. Or let them lay hold of my protection, let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me."

Four words that should stop a reader who has come this far through the book: I have no wrath. Said by the God of the vineyard song, the six woes, the outstretched hand and the emptied earth.

And then the sentence is repeated: let them make peace with me, let them make peace with me. People repeat things when they badly want to be heard. This is not a God waiting to be approached and considering whether to receive the approach. He is pressing the offer, twice, in one verse.

"In days to come Jacob shall take root, Israel shall blossom and put forth shoots and fill the whole world with fruit."

And the vineyard that produced wild grapes fills the whole world with fruit. The song that ended in briers ends here in a harvest big enough for everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain? Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind. Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing. For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches. When its boughs are dry, they are broken; women come and make a fire of them. For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them; he who formed them will show them no favor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Has he struck them as he struck those who struck them? Or have they been slain as their slayers were slain?"

Two questions, both expecting the answer no, and together they make an important distinction. God has struck his people. He has not struck them the way he struck their enemies.

The difference between discipline and destruction is not the pain; it is the intention and the limit, and this verse says the limit was there all along.

"Measure by measure, by exile you contended with them; he removed them with his fierce breath in the day of the east wind."

Measure by measure. The judgment was weighed out, not poured. Even at its worst it was rationed — which is a thing to hold on to for anyone who has felt that a hard providence had no bottom to it.

"Therefore by this the guilt of Jacob will be atoned for, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin: when he makes all the stones of the altars like chalkstones crushed to pieces, no Asherim or incense altars will remain standing."

And here is what the whole discipline was for. Not punishment discharged but idols removed — the altar stones ground to chalk, the Asherah poles and incense stands gone from the landscape.

Isaiah is precise about the mechanism: the fruit of the removal of sin is that the apparatus of the old religion is physically destroyed. God was not merely making Israel sorry. He was getting the alternatives out of the country.

"For the fortified city is solitary, a habitation deserted and forsaken, like the wilderness; there the calf grazes; there it lies down and strips its branches."

The fortified city appears again, empty, with a calf browsing in it — and verses 10 and 11 note that when its boughs are dry, women come and use them for firewood. Even the ruins are only good for kindling.

"For this is a people without discernment; therefore he who made them will not have compassion on them." A hard sentence, and it names the failure once more as a failure to understand — the same charge as 1:3, where the ox knew more than Israel did.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The apocalypse ends not in wreckage but in a harvest and a procession. God threshes from the Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt, and the people of Israel are gleaned one by one (v. 12). Then a great trumpet is blown, and those who were perishing in Assyria and driven out to Egypt come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: One by one is the phrase to keep. After four chapters of the whole earth being emptied, twisted, shaken and levelled, the gathering is done individually — not swept up in a mass but picked out singly, each one known and retrieved by name.
verseByVerse.examples: The two countries named in verse 13 are the two that had swallowed God's people: Assyria, which deported the north, and Egypt, where refugees had fled. Both give their people back at the sound of a trumpet — the instrument Paul and John both reach for when they describe the last gathering of all.

verseByVerse.quote: In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel. And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were lost in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In that day from the river Euphrates to the Brook of Egypt the LORD will thresh out the grain, and you will be gleaned one by one, O people of Israel."

The apocalypse ends in a field at harvest.

The two boundaries named are the whole territory ever promised — from the great river in the north-east to the wadi at the Egyptian border — and God works across all of it. Thresh is the beating that separates grain from husk, so the judgment is still in the picture; but what it produces is grain, and the grain is collected.

And then the phrase that redeems four chapters of cosmic scale: you will be gleaned one by one.

After the earth emptied and twisted, the host of heaven shut in a pit, the sun ashamed, death swallowed and the dragon killed — after all of that, the actual gathering is done singly. Not swept up in a mass. Picked out, one at a time, each one seen and known and lifted.

Set that against the scale of everything else in these chapters. God is not too large for the individual. The same hand that wrings out a planet gleans a field one grain at a time.

"And in that day a great trumpet will be blown, and those who were perishing in the land of Assyria and those who were driven out to the land of Egypt will come and worship the LORD on the holy mountain at Jerusalem."

The two countries are the two that had swallowed God's people: Assyria, which deported the northern tribes, and Egypt, where the frightened had run. Both give them back.

And the summons is a trumpet — the instrument used to call an assembly, to announce a jubilee, and to gather a scattered people. Paul reaches for it when he describes the last gathering of all, at the sound of the last trumpet, when the dead are raised imperishable (1 Cor. 15:52).

So the four chapters that began with God emptying the earth end with people walking up a hill to worship, called by a horn, gathered one by one from the countries that took them. The devastation was never the destination. It was the road to a mountain with a feast on it.

27.theology:
The dragon dealt with. Leviathan is the ancient figure of chaos — untamable, hostile to creation, standing behind the empires that behave the same way. Isaiah gives it three names in one verse, which is how a decisive victory is described: every version of the thing, at once. John identifies it when he sees it thrown down (Rev. 12:9). And it is what makes 11:8 possible: a baby can play at a cobra’s hole in the peaceable kingdom because the dragon has already been killed.

The vineyard song, sung again. Chapter 5’s song ended with the wall broken and briers let in. Here the same song begins with the vineyard called pleasant, and what has changed is the owner’s posture: not the disappointed proprietor who looked for fruit and walked away, but a keeper who waters it every moment and guards it night and day. Verse 4 then says the unthinkable — I have no wrath — and repeats the invitation twice in one breath, the way people repeat what they badly want heard.

Discipline measured, and gathered one by one. Verses 7-9 distinguish God’s striking of his people from his striking of their enemies: it was measure by measure, rationed even at its worst, and its aim was not punishment discharged but idols physically removed. And after four chapters of cosmic scale the harvest is gleaned one by one — the same hand that wrings out a planet picks up a field one grain at a time.

28.subtitle: Woe to the Drunkards of Ephraim
28.intro: Overview. With chapter 28, Isaiah moves from the oracles-against-the-nations and the apocalypse into a new section of woes (chs. 28–33), directed primarily against Judah’s leaders for their catastrophic political strategy: seeking alliance with Egypt against Assyria rather than trusting in the LORD. Chapter 28 opens with a woe against the northern kingdom (Ephraim/Samaria), already fallen or falling, then turns to Jerusalem’s leaders — drunk priests and prophets who have made a “covenant with death.” It contains the foundational cornerstone promise (vv. 16–17) and the unforgettable image of a bed too short to stretch out on.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold, I am the one who has laid in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation. Whoever believes will not be in haste.”
keyVerse.note: The stone’s primary characteristic is that it has been tested — proven under pressure. The one who builds on it will not need to run in panic. Peter and Paul both identify the stone as Christ, and the New Testament adds the layer of stumbling: the same stone is a rock of offense to those who reject him. Cornerstone or stumbling-block — the stone is the same; the relationship to it makes all the difference.

28.reflection: The leaders of Jerusalem made a “covenant with death” because they could not bear to trust in something invisible when a visible alliance was available. Where in your life are you reaching for a bed that’s too short rather than resting on the tested cornerstone? What would it look like to believe without being in haste?
28.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine!<sup>2</sup>Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand.<sup>3</sup>The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot;<sup>4</sup>and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand.<sup>5</sup>In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people,<sup>6</sup>and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate.<sup>7</sup>These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment.<sup>8</sup>For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left.<sup>9</sup>"To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast?<sup>10</sup>For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little."<sup>11</sup>For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people,<sup>12</sup>to whom he has said, "This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear.<sup>13</sup>And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.<sup>14</sup>Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem!<sup>15</sup>Because you have said, "We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement, when the overwhelming whip passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter";<sup>16</sup>therefore thus says the Lord GOD, "Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.'<sup>17</sup>And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter."<sup>18</sup>Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it.<sup>19</sup>As often as it passes through it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night; and it will be sheer terror to understand the message.<sup>20</sup>For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in.<sup>21</sup>For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed—strange is his deed! and to work his work—alien is his work!<sup>22</sup>Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land.<sup>23</sup>Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech.<sup>24</sup>Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground?<sup>25</sup>When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cumin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border?<sup>26</sup>For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him.<sup>27</sup>Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin, but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod.<sup>28</sup>Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it.<sup>29</sup>This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The woe falls first on Samaria: a drunkard's garland on a fading flower, admired the way the first ripe fig of summer is admired — seen and swallowed on the spot (vv. 1-4). Verses 5 and 6 promise that God himself will be a crown of glory to the remnant. Then the oracle turns to Judah and finds the priests and prophets drunk too, reeling in their visions and staggering in their judgments, with vomit on every table (vv. 7-8). Verses 9 and 10 quote their mockery of Isaiah — is he teaching toddlers? tsav latsav, qav laqav, precept upon precept — and verses 11 to 13 answer that if they will not hear plain speech they will hear it in a foreign tongue.
verseByVerse.theology: The mockery in verse 10 is the heart of the passage. The Hebrew is nonsense syllables, the sound of adults imitating baby talk, and it is aimed at a prophet for speaking too simply. God's reply is to send them a language they really cannot understand — Assyrian — which is what happens when plain instruction is despised.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 12 names what was on offer and refused: this is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose — and they would not hear. What the drunk leaders were mocking was an invitation to lie down. Compare the far more famous invitation to the weary from a later teacher whose yoke is easy.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine! Behold, the Lord has one who is mighty and strong; like a storm of hail, a destroying tempest, like a storm of mighty, overflowing waters, he casts down to the earth with his hand. The proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim will be trodden underfoot; and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand. In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people, and a spirit of justice to him who sits in judgment, and strength to those who turn back the battle at the gate. These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink, they are swallowed by wine, they stagger with strong drink, they reel in vision, they stumble in giving judgment. For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, the proud crown of the drunkards of Ephraim, and the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley of those overcome with wine!"

Samaria sat on a hill above a fertile valley, and Isaiah looks at it and sees a wreath on a drunk man's head — the garland worn at a banquet, already wilting while the party is still going.

"And the fading flower of its glorious beauty, which is on the head of the rich valley, will be like a first-ripe fig before the summer: when someone sees it, he swallows it as soon as it is in his hand."

The image is precise and unpleasant. The first ripe fig of the season is irresistible; a man who spots one does not put it in a basket, he eats it standing there. Isaiah says that is what an empire will do with the northern kingdom — not besiege it, just see it and swallow it.

"In that day the LORD of hosts will be a crown of glory, and a diadem of beauty, to the remnant of his people."

And there is the contrast the chapter is built on. Two crowns: the fading wreath on a drunk head, and God himself as the diadem of those who are left. One is worn and wilting; the other wears them.

"These also reel with wine and stagger with strong drink; the priest and the prophet reel with strong drink... they stagger in giving judgment. For all tables are full of filthy vomit, with no space left."

Then the oracle crosses the border into Judah, and finds the same condition in worse company. Not the political class this time: the priest and the prophet — the two offices responsible for knowing what God thinks and saying so.

They reel in their visions and stagger in their verdicts, which is exactly where it matters: a drunk prophet still prophesies and a drunk judge still decides. And Isaiah gives the scene one detail he does not need and includes anyway — every table covered in vomit, no clean space left. He wants the reader in the room.

verseByVerse.quote: "To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast? For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little." For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people, to whom he has said, "This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear. And the word of the LORD will be to them precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little, that they may go, and fall backward, and be broken, and snared, and taken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To whom will he teach knowledge, and to whom will he explain the message? Those who are weaned from the milk, those taken from the breast?"

Now the drunk clergy answer back, and it is one of the few places in Scripture where we hear a prophet's opponents mimicking him.

Their complaint is that Isaiah talks down to them. Who does he think he is teaching — babies just off the breast? These are trained men with offices, and they resent being addressed as though they needed things spelled out.

"For it is precept upon precept, precept upon precept, line upon line, line upon line, here a little, there a little."

In Hebrew this is tsav latsav tsav latsav, qav laqav qav laqav, and it is not really language at all. It is the sound of adults doing an impression of baby talk — blah blah, blah blah — and it is aimed at a man preaching the word of God.

Sit with that, because the charge is one the church still attracts. Plain teaching, repeated, in small pieces, sounds simplistic to people who consider themselves past it. The mockery in this verse is directed at exactly the thing that would have saved them.

"For by people of strange lips and with a foreign tongue the LORD will speak to this people."

And here is the answer, and it fits the crime exactly. You found my plain speech childish? Then you will hear from me in a language you genuinely cannot understand — Assyrian, shouted in your streets by soldiers.

"To whom he has said, 'This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose'; yet they would not hear."

And this is what they were mocking. Not a complicated doctrine — an invitation to lie down. This is rest. The word being ridiculed as baby talk was the offer of rest to tired people, and they laughed at it.

Seven hundred years later another teacher stood up and said come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, and educated men found that simplistic too.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–22 — A Covenant with Death, and a Stone
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rulers of Jerusalem are addressed as scoffers, and God quotes their own boast back at them: we have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement — so the overwhelming whip will pass by and not touch us (vv. 14-15). Against that, verse 16 sets a stone laid in Zion: tested, precious, a sure foundation, and whoever believes will not be in haste. Verses 17 to 22 measure the city with justice as the line and righteousness as the plumb, sweep away the refuge of lies, and describe a bed too short and a blanket too narrow. Verses 21 and 22 call the whole business God's strange and alien work.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 is Isaiah naming a policy for what it actually is. The rulers had made a treaty with Egypt; he calls it a covenant with death, because that is the effect of buying security from a power that cannot give it. Political arrangements get theological names in this book, and the names are usually more accurate than the communiqués.
verseByVerse.examples: The cornerstone of verse 16 is quoted three times in the New Testament and always of Christ — by Peter (1 Pet. 2:6) and twice by Paul (Rom. 9:33; 10:11). Note what the verse promises the believer: not that he will not be shaken but that he will not be in haste. A man standing on something that will hold does not have to panic.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem! Because you have said, "We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement, when the overwhelming whip passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter"; therefore thus says the Lord GOD, "Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: 'Whoever believes will not be in haste.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore hear the word of the LORD, you scoffers, who rule this people in Jerusalem!"

"Because you have said, 'We have made a covenant with death, and with Sheol we have an agreement, when the overwhelming whip passes through it will not come to us, for we have made lies our refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter.'"

The rulers are quoted, and the question is whether anyone actually said this. Almost certainly not in these words. What they had done was sign a treaty with Egypt and conclude that it would keep the Assyrians off.

Isaiah gives the policy its true name. A deal that buys safety from a power which cannot provide it, made in order to avoid trusting God, is a covenant with death — and the men who made it would have described it as prudent foreign policy.

That is one of the most useful things this book does. It puts theological names on practical arrangements, and the theological name is usually the accurate one. Nobody ever draws up a covenant with death under that heading. It is always called security, or realism, or keeping our options open.

"Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: 'Behold, I am the one who has laid as a foundation in Zion, a stone, a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, of a sure foundation: whoever believes will not be in haste.'"

Against the refuge of lies, God sets a stone, and every word of the description is answering something in verse 15. Their shelter is falsehood; this is tested. Theirs is an arrangement; this is a foundation. Theirs will be swept away by the hail; this one is sure.

The New Testament takes this verse three times and always of one person: Peter, writing about a living stone rejected by men but chosen and precious in God's sight (1 Pet. 2:6), and Paul twice (Rom. 9:33; 10:11).

And notice what is promised to the believer. Not that he will be spared the storm — the next verses have hail sweeping away the refuge of lies. He will not be in haste. He will not panic. A man standing on rock does not have to run about, and the absence of hurry is the visible mark of somebody who knows what is under him.

verseByVerse.quote: And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter." Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it. As often as it passes through it will take you; for morning by morning it will pass through, by day and by night; and it will be sheer terror to understand the message. For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in. For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed—strange is his deed! and to work his work—alien is his work! Now therefore do not scoff, lest your bonds be made strong; for I have heard a decree of destruction from the Lord GOD of hosts against the whole land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And I will make justice the line, and righteousness the plumb line; and hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter."

God comes to the building site with a builder's tools. The measuring line and the plumb are not weapons; they are instruments for finding out whether a wall is straight, and the standards being applied are justice and righteousness.

The wall does not survive the measurement.

"Then your covenant with death will be annulled, and your agreement with Sheol will not stand; when the overwhelming scourge passes through, you will be beaten down by it."

The treaty is cancelled by the very thing it was signed to prevent. What they bought protection from is what arrives, and the protection is not merely inadequate — it is annulled, as though the paper had never been valid.

"For the bed is too short to stretch oneself on, and the covering too narrow to wrap oneself in."

And here is the best image in the chapter, and one anybody has experienced. A bed you cannot straighten out on. A blanket that will not cover you — pull it up and your feet come out, cover your feet and your shoulders are cold. A night of that, and no way to solve it.

That is what trusting an inadequate refuge feels like from inside. Not sudden catastrophe: a permanent, low-grade inability to rest, with constant small adjustments and nothing ever quite right. Anyone lying awake managing an arrangement that does not quite work knows the mattress being described.

"For the LORD will rise up as on Mount Perazim; as in the Valley of Gibeon he will be roused; to do his deed — strange is his deed! and to work his work — alien is his work!"

Two of David's victories are named, and then the unsettling phrase: God's deed is strange, his work is alien. He is doing at Jerusalem what he once did for Israel against her enemies — and Judah is on the wrong end of it. That is foreign to his character and he says so — which is not a comfort exactly, but hold on to it: judgment on his own people is the work God himself calls alien.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23–29 — The Farmer Knows When to Stop
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends with a parable from a field, and it is the gentlest thing in it. Does a farmer plough continually, and never sow? He breaks the ground, and then he plants — dill here, cumin there, wheat in rows, barley in its place, spelt at the border (vv. 23-25). And when it is harvested he does not thresh everything the same way: dill is beaten with a stick, cumin with a rod, and bread grain is crushed but not for ever, because the cart wheel is not driven over it endlessly (vv. 27-28). Twice Isaiah says where the farmer learned this — his God instructs him (v. 26), and this also comes from the LORD of hosts (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: The argument is subversive and consoling at once. If God taught a farmer to match the tool to the crop and to stop when the grain is ready, does anyone imagine he is less careful with people? The ploughing is not endless, the threshing is proportioned, and neither is the point — the bread is.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the answer to the drunk mockery of verse 10 and to everyone since who has found a season of discipline apparently arbitrary. There is a method, it varies with what is being handled, and it has a stopping point that was decided before it began.

verseByVerse.quote: Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech. Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground? When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cumin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border? For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him. Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin, but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever; when he drives his cart wheel over it with his horses, he does not crush it. This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Give ear, and hear my voice; give attention, and hear my speech. Does he who plows for sowing plow continually? Does he continually open and harrow his ground?"

The chapter that has had drunk priests, vomit on the tables and a covenant with death ends in a field, and the change of tone is deliberate.

The first question answers itself. No farmer ploughs for ever. Ploughing is violent — the ground is cut open and turned over — and it is also brief, because it is not the point. It is what you do before you sow.

"When he has leveled its surface, does he not scatter dill, sow cumin, and put in wheat in rows and barley in its proper place, and emmer as the border?"

And then the sowing, and it is not one action but five, each crop in the place and manner that suits it. Dill scattered, cumin sown, wheat in rows, barley in its plot, spelt round the edge. A farmer does not treat everything the same.

"For he is rightly instructed; his God teaches him."

Isaiah stops to say where the knowledge came from, and it is a striking claim: ordinary agricultural competence is God teaching a man. He will say it again at the end of the chapter.

"Dill is not threshed with a threshing sledge, nor is a cart wheel rolled over cumin; but dill is beaten out with a stick, and cumin with a rod. Does one crush grain for bread? No, he does not thresh it forever."

Now the harvest, and the same principle. Threshing is heavy work with heavy tools — a weighted sledge, a cart wheel — and you would ruin dill and cumin with either. Those get a stick. And even the bread grain, which does need crushing, is not crushed forever: there is a point at which the wheels come off and the man stops.

"This also comes from the LORD of hosts; he is wonderful in counsel and excellent in wisdom."

And here is the argument, and it is aimed at everyone who has found a hard season apparently arbitrary.

If God taught a farmer to match the tool to the crop, to use a stick where a sledge would destroy, and to know the moment the grain is ready and stop — is he going to be less careful with people? The ploughing in a life is not endless. The threshing is proportioned to what is being threshed. And neither of them is the object of the exercise.

The object is bread.

28.theology:
Baby talk, and the offer inside it. The mockery in verse 10 is nonsense syllables in Hebrew — tsav latsav, qav laqav, the sound of adults imitating a child — aimed at a prophet for speaking too plainly. And verse 12 says what he had been speaking: this is rest; give rest to the weary. The thing being ridiculed as simplistic was an invitation to lie down. God’s answer fits the crime: they will hear from him in a language they genuinely cannot understand.

Theological names for practical arrangements. The rulers had signed a treaty with Egypt. Isaiah calls it a covenant with death (v. 15), because that is the effect of buying safety from a power that cannot provide it in order to avoid trusting God. Nobody ever files such a deal under that heading; it is always called security or realism. Against it God lays a stone — tested, precious, sure — and the promise to the one who believes is not that he will escape the storm but that he will not be in haste. Peter and Paul both apply the verse to Christ (1 Pet. 2:6; Rom. 9:33; 10:11).

The farmer. The chapter ends by arguing from agriculture to providence, and twice names the source of the farmer’s skill as God himself (vv. 26, 29). No one ploughs for ever; dill is beaten with a stick rather than crushed under a cart wheel; and even bread grain is not threshed endlessly. If God taught a man to match the tool to the crop and to know when to stop, he is not less careful with people. The ploughing is not the point. The bread is.

29.subtitle: Ariel in Distress
29.intro: Overview. Chapter 29 continues the woes with an oracle against Jerusalem, here called Ariel — a word meaning either “lion of God” or “altar hearth,” both rich with associations. The chapter moves through three great movements: the distress and siege of Jerusalem (vv. 1–8), the spiritual blindness of prophets and people (vv. 9–16), and then a surprising turn to hope (vv. 17–24). It contains two of the most-quoted passages in the New Testament from Isaiah: the lip-service condemnation (v. 13) and the potter-clay image (vv. 15–16).

keyVerse.quote: “This people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.”
keyVerse.note: Jesus’ application of this verse to the Pharisees makes it timelessly diagnostic. The Pharisees were the most religiously serious people of their generation — and the most thoroughly described by Isaiah’s warning. The danger is not irreligion but religion that has become self-referential: honoring God with forms that protect the heart from actual encounter with him.

29.reflection: Isaiah describes a form of blindness that is self-inflicted: “blind yourselves, and be blind.” The spiritual numbness he diagnoses is not simply ignorance but the accumulated result of not wanting to see clearly. Is there something God has been trying to show you that you have been sealing and covering? What would it cost to open the book?
29.text: <sup>1</sup>Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round.<sup>2</sup>Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel.<sup>3</sup>And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you.<sup>4</sup>And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper.<sup>5</sup>But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly,<sup>6</sup>you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire.<sup>7</sup>And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night.<sup>8</sup>As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion.<sup>9</sup>Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink!<sup>10</sup>For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers).<sup>11</sup>And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot, for it is sealed."<sup>12</sup>And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot read."<sup>13</sup>And the Lord said: "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men,<sup>14</sup>therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden."<sup>15</sup>Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, "Who sees us? Who knows us?"<sup>16</sup>You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"?<sup>17</sup>Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest?<sup>18</sup>In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see.<sup>19</sup>The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel.<sup>20</sup>For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off,<sup>21</sup>who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right.<sup>22</sup>Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: "Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale.<sup>23</sup>For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jerusalem is addressed by a strange name — Ariel, which can mean lion of God or altar hearth — and told to let the feasts run their annual round (v. 1). Then God says he will besiege it himself, with siegeworks and towers (vv. 2-3), until the city speaks from the ground, its voice coming out of the dust like a ghost's whisper (v. 4). And then, without transition, the besieging horde becomes fine dust blown away in an instant (vv. 5-7) — and verse 8 compares them to a hungry man who dreams he is eating and wakes with nothing in him.
verseByVerse.theology: The shock of the passage is who is doing the besieging. Judah assumed God was on the inside of the walls with them because the festivals were being kept on schedule. Isaiah says he is outside, building ramps. And the purpose is stated in verse 4: to bring the city low enough to whisper — not to destroy it but to reduce it to a voice from the dust, which is where prayer starts.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is one of the most exact images in the book. A starving man dreams a full meal and wakes hungrier for having dreamt it. That is what the nations massed against Zion will turn out to have been: a vivid appetite that produced nothing, and a waking with the mouth still empty.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. Yet I will distress Ariel, and there shall be moaning and lamentation, and she shall be to me like an Ariel. And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you. And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper. But the multitude of your foreign foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, you will be visited by the LORD of hosts with thunder and with earthquake and great noise, with whirlwind and tempest, and the flame of a devouring fire. And the multitude of all the nations that fight against Ariel, all that fight against her and her stronghold and distress her, shall be like a dream, a vision of the night. As when a hungry man dreams, and behold, he is eating, and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams, and behold, he is drinking, and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched, so shall the multitude of all the nations be that fight against Mount Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, Ariel, Ariel, the city where David encamped! Add year to year; let the feasts run their round."

The name is a riddle. Ariel can mean lion of God, which suits a royal city, and it can mean altar hearth — the place on top of the altar where the fire burns and the sacrifice is consumed. Isaiah uses it of Jerusalem, and by verse 2 he plainly wants the second meaning: the city will become what its own altar is.

And the instruction in verse 1 is sardonic. Add year to year; let the feasts run their round. Carry on. The calendar is working perfectly — Passover, Weeks, Tabernacles, every year, on time — and that is precisely the problem, because the machinery is running and nobody is thinking about it.

"And I will encamp against you all around, and will besiege you with towers and I will raise siegeworks against you."

Here is the shock of the passage, and it is in the pronoun. I will besiege you. Not Assyria, not Babylon — God, outside the walls, building ramps.

Judah's whole assumption was that God was inside with them, guaranteed by the festivals. Isaiah puts him in the siege lines.

"And you will be brought low; from the earth you shall speak, and from the dust your speech will be bowed down; your voice shall come from the ground like the voice of a ghost, and from the dust your speech shall whisper."

And then the purpose, which is not destruction. The city is brought down to the point of whispering from the ground.

That is a humiliation and it is also where prayer begins. A city that shouts its festivals cannot be heard by God; a city whispering out of the dust can. Isaiah has already watched a nation consult the dead (8:19); now the nation itself sounds like one, and for the first time it is talking to the right person.

"And the multitude of your foes shall be like small dust, and the multitude of the ruthless like passing chaff. And in an instant, suddenly, you will be visited by the LORD of hosts."

Then the turn, with no transition at all. The besieging horde becomes dust and blows away, in an instant, suddenly.

"As when a hungry man dreams he is eating and awakes with his hunger not satisfied, or as when a thirsty man dreams he is drinking and awakes faint, with his thirst not quenched — so shall the multitude of all the nations be."

And the closing image is exact. A starving man dreams a meal, and the dream is vivid, and he wakes emptier for having had it. That is what the armies against Zion amount to: a strong appetite, a convincing dream, and a waking with nothing in the mouth.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God has poured out a spirit of deep sleep, closing the eyes of the prophets and covering the heads of the seers (vv. 9-10). The whole vision has become a sealed book: hand it to a man who can read and he says it is sealed; hand it to one who cannot and he says he cannot read (vv. 11-12). Verse 13 gives the reason — this people draw near with their mouths and honour God with their lips while their hearts are far from him, and their fear of him is a commandment taught by men. Verses 15 and 16 catch them making plans in the dark and turning things upside down, as if the clay could say of the potter, he did not make me.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the most quoted verse of this chapter in the New Testament. Jesus reads it to Pharisees who have just asked him about hand-washing (Matt. 15:8-9; Mark 7:6-7) and applies every clause: nearness of mouth, distance of heart, and a religion whose content is human instruction. What is described here is not irreligion. It is religion working perfectly with nobody home.
verseByVerse.examples: The sealed book of verses 11 and 12 is a picture of how revelation fails on a closed heart, and it is deliberately even-handed. The educated man cannot read it because it is shut; the uneducated cannot read it at all. Neither is stupid and neither is helped, because the problem was never literacy.

verseByVerse.quote: Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink! For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers). And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot, for it is sealed." And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, "Read this," he says, "I cannot read."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Astonish yourselves and be astonished; blind yourselves and be blind! Be drunk, but not with wine; stagger, but not with strong drink!"

The imperatives are ironic. God is not commanding them to do this; he is telling them to carry on doing what they have already done to themselves, which is the bleakest form a command can take.

And the drunkenness is the one from chapter 28, now diagnosed without the wine. They stagger, and there is nothing in the cup.

"For the LORD has poured out upon you a spirit of deep sleep, and has closed your eyes (the prophets), and covered your heads (the seers)."

The judicial hardening of chapter 6 returns, and it lands on the professionals. The eyes of the nation are closed and the heads of the nation are covered — the men whose whole function was to see and to say.

"And the vision of all this has become to you like the words of a book that is sealed. When men give it to one who can read, saying, 'Read this,' he says, 'I cannot, for it is sealed.' And when they give the book to one who cannot read, saying, 'Read this,' he says, 'I cannot read.'"

And here is the picture of how revelation fails, and it is scrupulously even-handed.

Two men are offered the same book. The first is literate and the book is sealed, so he cannot get at it. The second is handed it unsealed, and cannot read.

Neither man is stupid, and neither is being mocked. Isaiah's point is that the barrier is not competence — the educated and the uneducated fail identically. The revelation is present, in the room, in their hands, and it does not get in.

That should be sobering for anyone who assumes that better teaching or more study would solve a spiritual problem. Sometimes it would. In this chapter the book is available and the issue is a hundred per cent elsewhere, and the next verse says where.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Lord said: "Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men, therefore, behold, I will again do wonderful things with this people, with wonder upon wonder; and the wisdom of their wise men shall perish, and the discernment of their discerning men shall be hidden." Ah, you who hide deep from the LORD your counsel, whose deeds are in the dark, and who say, "Who sees us? Who knows us?" You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, "He did not make me"; or the thing formed say of him who formed it, "He has no understanding"?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the Lord said: 'Because this people draw near with their mouth and honor me with their lips, while their hearts are far from me, and their fear of me is a commandment taught by men.'"

Here is the diagnosis, and it is the most quoted sentence in the chapter for good reason.

Read what is being described, because it is not irreligion. These people draw near. They honour God. There is nothing wrong with the words coming out of their mouths — the liturgy is orthodox and the attendance is excellent.

The failure is a distance: mouths near, hearts far. And the third clause names the cause: their fear of God has become a commandment taught by men — a set of learned behaviours, correctly performed, passed on by other people, with nothing at the centre of it that came from God directly.

That is a religion that works perfectly and has nobody home, and it is the specific danger of the well-taught rather than the ignorant. Nothing in this verse could be fixed by better catechesis, because good catechesis is what produced it.

Jesus quotes this verse. Pharisees have come from Jerusalem to ask him why his disciples do not wash their hands according to the tradition of the elders, and he answers, "Well did Isaiah prophesy of you hypocrites, as it is written: 'This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching as doctrines the commandments of men'" (Mark 7:6-7; Matt. 15:8-9).

He applies every clause and adds nothing. The verse was already exact.

"You turn things upside down! Shall the potter be regarded as the clay, that the thing made should say of its maker, 'He did not make me'?"

And the last image is the inversion behind all of it: a pot arguing that it made itself. Paul takes the same picture up in Romans 9, and it is the standing answer to the creature who wants a vote on the terms of his own existence.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns. In a very little while Lebanon becomes a fruitful field and the field a forest (v. 17). The deaf hear the words of a book and the blind see out of gloom and darkness (v. 18) — which reverses, item by item, everything wrong in the middle of the chapter. The meek get fresh joy and the poor exult in the Holy One of Israel (v. 19); the ruthless and the scoffer are gone, along with everyone who watched for a chance to condemn (vv. 20-21). And verses 22 to 24 have Jacob no longer ashamed, his children sanctifying the Holy One, and those who went astray in spirit coming to understanding.
verseByVerse.theology: The reversals are exact. The sealed book of verse 11 is heard by the deaf in verse 18; the eyes God covered in verse 10 are opened in verse 18; the hearts far away in verse 13 come to understanding in verse 24. Isaiah undoes his own diagnosis clause by clause, which is his standard way of showing that judgment was never the destination.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 21 names a specific and recognisable evil: those who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate. That is the practice of catching somebody in a phrase in order to discredit him — which is precisely what was being done to Jesus by the men he quoted verse 13 at.

verseByVerse.quote: Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest? In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see. The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel. For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate, and with an empty plea turn aside him who is in the right.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Is it not yet a very little while until Lebanon shall be turned into a fruitful field, and the fruitful field shall be regarded as a forest?"

The turn begins, and it begins with a landscape rearranging itself: forest becomes farmland, farmland becomes forest. Everything fixed turns out to be provisional.

"In that day the deaf shall hear the words of a book, and out of their gloom and darkness the eyes of the blind shall see."

Now read that against the middle of the chapter, because Isaiah is undoing his own diagnosis item by item.

Verse 11 had a sealed book that nobody could read. Verse 18 has the deaf hearing the words of a book. Verse 10 had God closing the eyes of the prophets. Verse 18 has the blind seeing out of gloom and darkness.

The reversal is not a general improvement in circumstances. It is the specific undoing of the specific judgment, and the people it happens to are the ones least equipped: not the literate man who could not open the seal, but the deaf and the blind.

"The meek shall obtain fresh joy in the LORD, and the poor among mankind shall exult in the Holy One of Israel."

And the beneficiaries are named. The meek and the poor — the two groups whose cases never reached the bench back in chapter 1.

"For the ruthless shall come to nothing and the scoffer cease, and all who watch to do evil shall be cut off, who by a word make a man out to be an offender, and lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate."

Verse 21 names an evil precisely enough to be uncomfortable. Who by a word make a man out to be an offender — the practice of catching somebody in a phrase, taking it badly on purpose, and using it to discredit him. And lay a snare for him who reproves in the gate: trapping the man who says the unpopular true thing in public.

Remember who Jesus was quoting verse 13 at, and what they were doing while he did it. They were watching him to catch him in his words.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: "Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale. For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel. And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore thus says the LORD, who redeemed Abraham, concerning the house of Jacob: 'Jacob shall no more be ashamed, no more shall his face grow pale.'"

God introduces himself here as the one who redeemed Abraham, which is an unusual title and a deliberate one. Before there was a nation, a law, a temple or a festival calendar, there was a man in Mesopotamia whom God went and got. The chapter that has spent sixteen verses on the failure of institutional religion reaches back past all of it to the beginning.

And the promise is about shame. No more shall his face grow pale — which is what a face does when a person is caught, or humiliated, or found out. The whole physical vocabulary of disgrace is removed.

"For when he sees his children, the work of my hands, in his midst, they will sanctify my name; they will sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and will stand in awe of the God of Israel."

The children are described as the work of my hands, which answers verse 16 directly. There the clay was denying that the potter made it; here the same people are named as his handiwork, and they are the evidence Jacob sees.

"And those who go astray in spirit will come to understanding, and those who murmur will accept instruction."

And the last verse of the chapter is the quietest and best of it.

Two groups are named, and they are the two the chapter has been describing. Those who go astray in spirit — the drunk without wine, the staggering, the ones with a spirit of deep sleep poured over them. And those who murmur — the complainers, the plotters of verse 15 who made their plans in the dark.

Neither group is destroyed. The first comes to understanding, which is the faculty that was missing in 1:3 when the ox knew its owner and Israel did not. The second accepts instruction — and instruction is exactly what was being mocked in chapter 28 as baby talk.

So the chapter that began with a besieged city whispering from the dust, and ran through sealed books and lips without hearts, ends with people who could not understand understanding, and people who would not be taught being taught. That is not an improvement in their situation. It is a repair to them.

29.theology:
God on the outside of the walls. The shock of vv. 1-4 is the pronoun: I will encamp against you. Judah assumed God was inside the city with them, guaranteed by a festival calendar running perfectly on schedule. Isaiah puts him in the siege lines — and states the purpose, which is not destruction but reduction: the city is brought low until it speaks from the dust in a whisper. That is a humiliation, and it is where prayer starts.

Lips near, hearts far. Verse 13 does not describe irreligion. These people draw near, honour God, and say the right words; the liturgy is orthodox and the attendance excellent. The failure is a distance, and the cause is named: their fear of God has become a commandment taught by men — learned behaviour, correctly performed, with nothing at the centre that came from God directly. It is the specific danger of the well-taught rather than the ignorant, and better catechesis cannot fix what good catechesis produced. Jesus quotes the verse at Pharisees asking about hand-washing and applies every clause (Mark 7:6-7; Matt. 15:8-9).

The diagnosis undone clause by clause. The sealed book nobody could read (v. 11) is heard by the deaf (v. 18); the eyes God closed (v. 10) are opened (v. 18); the hearts far away (v. 13) come to understanding (v. 24). Isaiah reverses his own indictment item by item, and gives the reversals to the least equipped — not to the literate man who could not break the seal but to the deaf and the blind.

30.subtitle: The Rebellious Children
30.intro: Overview. Chapter 30 contains the fullest treatment in the woes section of Judah’s Egyptian alliance — the plan to go to Pharaoh for protection against Assyria. God calls them “rebellious children” who carry out a plan but not his, who weave a web but not of his Spirit. The chapter is also one of the richest sources of comfort in Isaiah, closing with a remarkable promise about God’s waiting, his gracious response when his people turn, and the coming day when idols will be thrown away like menstrual rags.

keyVerse.quote: “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”
keyVerse.note: The verse is both a promise and a rebuke, because it was rejected. The strength on offer was completely counterintuitive — not cavalry but quietness, not diplomacy but trust. Alistair Begg often noted that God’s strategy always appears inadequate until it is the only strategy left. The tragedy of verse 16 is that Judah never found out whether it worked, because they refused to try.

30.reflection: God is described as waiting to be gracious — not holding back, but oriented toward the moment of your return. What would returning and resting actually look like in whatever you are currently trying to manage by your own strength? And what are the “horses” you keep reaching for instead?

In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures,<sup>24</sup>and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork.<sup>25</sup>And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall.<sup>26</sup>Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.<sup>27</sup>Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire;<sup>28</sup>his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck; to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads astray.<sup>29</sup>You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones.<sup>31</sup>The Assyrians will be terror-stricken at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod.<sup>32</sup>And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres.
