verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to rebellious children who carry out a plan that is not God's and make an alliance without consulting him (v. 1). They go down to Egypt without asking, to take refuge in Pharaoh's protection (v. 2) — and the treasures go with them, on donkeys and camels, through a wilderness of lions and vipers, to a people who cannot help (vv. 6-7). Verses 8 to 11 have the oracle written down as a permanent witness, and quote what the people actually want from their prophets: speak to us smooth things. Verses 15 to 17 give God's alternative in eight words, and the refusal that met it.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 gives Egypt a nickname that is the whole argument: Rahab who sits still. Rahab was the mythic sea-monster, the name of raw chaotic power — and Isaiah says this one is sitting down. All the reputation, none of the motion. Buying protection from an impressive thing that does not move is the specific folly the chapter exists to name.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 15 is the chapter's centre: in returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength. Four words for what God offered — return, rest, quietness, trust — every one of them passive, and every one refused. But you were unwilling, and the alternative chosen was speed: we will ride on swift horses.

verseByVerse.quote: "Ah, stubborn children," declares the LORD, "who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin; who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt! Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation. For though his officials are at Zoan and his envoys reach Hanes, everyone comes to shame through a people that cannot profit them, that brings neither help nor profit, but shame and disgrace." An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them. Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her "Rahab who sits still."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, stubborn children, declares the LORD, who carry out a plan, but not mine, and who make an alliance, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin."

Notice that the charge is not that they have no plan. They have one, and it is competent: a defensive alliance with the only power in the region capable of standing up to Assyria. Isaiah's objection is contained in two words — not mine.

"Who set out to go down to Egypt, without asking for my direction, to take refuge in the protection of Pharaoh and to seek shelter in the shadow of Egypt!"

Without asking. That is the whole indictment, and it is the same failure as chapter 22: not incompetence, not even disobedience to a stated command, but a decision of enormous consequence taken without the question being put.

"Therefore shall the protection of Pharaoh turn to your shame, and the shelter in the shadow of Egypt to your humiliation."

"An oracle on the beasts of the Negeb. Through a land of trouble and anguish, from where come the lioness and the lion, the adder and the flying fiery serpent, they carry their riches on the backs of donkeys, and their treasures on the humps of camels, to a people that cannot profit them."

And here is the journey, and Isaiah lets the reader watch it go past.

A caravan crosses the Negeb — lion country, snake country, a land of trouble and anguish — with the wealth of Judah loaded on donkeys and camels. Everything the temple and the treasury could raise is going south, through danger, at speed.

To a people who cannot profit them. The whole enterprise is described in one long sentence so the reader feels the distance and the risk and the expense, and then the destination is dismissed in four words.

"Egypt's help is worthless and empty; therefore I have called her 'Rahab who sits still.'"

And the nickname is the argument. Rahab was the name of the sea-monster of chaos — raw, mythic, terrifying power, the same figure as Leviathan in chapter 27. It is what Egypt's reputation amounted to.

And Isaiah says: Rahab who sits still. The monster is sitting down. All the name, all the legend, all the terror — and no motion.

That is the exact shape of the folly. Judah did not buy nothing; they bought something genuinely impressive that was never going to get up.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, go, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever. For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; who say to the seers, "Do not see," and to the prophets, "Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions, leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel." Therefore thus says the Holy One of Israel, "Because you despise this word and trust in oppression and perverseness and rely on them, therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant; and its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now, go, write it before them on a tablet and inscribe it in a book, that it may be for the time to come as a witness forever."

The oracle is to be written down and kept, and the reason given is for the time to come. Isaiah expects this to be needed again, which is why it is in the Bible and why it still reads like current affairs.

"For they are a rebellious people, lying children, children unwilling to hear the instruction of the LORD; who say to the seers, 'Do not see,' and to the prophets, 'Do not prophesy to us what is right; speak to us smooth things, prophesy illusions.'"

And here is a nation stating exactly what it wants from its clergy. Let them say it in their own words.

Not do not speak — they want the prophets in business. What they want is a change of content: speak to us smooth things. Pleasant, frictionless, comfortable things. Prophesy illusions — and the word means deceptions, so they are asking, knowingly, to be told what is not true.

"'Leave the way, turn aside from the path, let us hear no more about the Holy One of Israel.'"

The last clause is the most honest thing they say. The trouble is not the news; it is the person the news is about. They want the subject changed.

"Therefore this iniquity shall be to you like a breach in a high wall, bulging out and about to collapse, whose breaking comes suddenly, in an instant."

The image is precise. A high wall with a bulge in it — anyone who has seen an old wall going out of true knows the look. It does not fall for a long time. It sits there bulging, and everyone gets used to it, and then one day it goes all at once.

"And its breaking is like that of a potter's vessel that is smashed so ruthlessly that among its fragments not a shard is found with which to take fire from the hearth, or to dip up water out of the cistern."

And when it goes, the pieces are too small to be useful. Not one fragment big enough to carry an ember or scoop water — the two most basic domestic tasks. Total loss, described by what can no longer be done with the wreckage.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, "In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"; therefore you shall flee away; and, "We will ride upon swift steeds"; therefore your pursuers shall be swift. A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus said the Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel: 'In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.'"

Here is the centre of the chapter, and possibly of this whole section of the book.

God's alternative to the Egyptian treaty is four words, and every one of them is passive. Returning — turning round and coming back, which requires no resources. Rest — stopping. Quietness — not speaking. Trust — leaning on somebody else.

Nothing on that list is a strategy. There is no journey, no treasure loaded onto camels, no negotiation, no fast horses. It is the complete opposite of everything the nation had been doing since verse 1, and it is offered as the way to be saved and as their strength.

"But you were unwilling."

Four words, and they land like a door closing. Not you could not. Not you misunderstood. You were unwilling — which locates the failure precisely in the will, and which is the honest diagnosis of most refusals of God's help.

Ask why. Rest and quietness sound easy and are not. They require a person to stop managing the situation, and the managing is where the sense of control lives. A caravan across the Negeb is exhausting, expensive and dangerous, and it feels like doing something. Sitting still feels like negligence.

"And you said, 'No! We will flee upon horses'; therefore you shall flee away; and, 'We will ride upon swift steeds'; therefore your pursuers shall be swift."

And the judgment is simply the request granted. You want speed? You shall have speed — you will be the one running, and the people chasing you will be quick.

"A thousand shall flee at the threat of one; at the threat of five you shall flee, till you are left like a flagstaff on the top of a mountain, like a signal on a hill."

The last image is a bare pole on a summit: one thing left standing, visible for miles, with nothing around it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The turn comes in one of the most surprising sentences in the book: therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you (v. 18). What follows is a description of the day it arrives — God answering the sound of a cry (v. 19); a Teacher who will not hide himself any more, and a voice behind you saying this is the way, walk in it (vv. 20-21); the silver and gold idols thrown out like a menstrual cloth (v. 22); rain for the seed, rich pasture, oxen eating seasoned fodder, streams on every hill (vv. 23-25); and the moon shining like the sun and the sun seven times brighter (v. 26). Verses 27 to 33 close with the Name coming from far away, burning, and Assyria terror-struck at the voice of the LORD, with the blows of verse 32 falling to the sound of tambourines and verse 33 lighting Topheth.
verseByVerse.theology: The verb in verse 18 is the astonishing thing. God waits — not reluctantly delayed but actively poised, watching for the moment he can pour out grace, the way somebody waits at a window. And the same verse ends by pronouncing blessed all those who wait for him. Both parties are waiting, which is a very different picture of the delay from the one most people carry.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 21 is the most quoted promise here and is often misapplied. The voice is behind you and speaks when you turn to the right or the left — which is guidance given in the walking rather than in advance, and correction rather than an itinerary. It is preceded by verse 20, where the Teacher stops hiding himself: the guidance is a person before it is a direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you. For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him. For a people shall dwell in Zion, in Jerusalem; you shall weep no more. He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you. And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher. And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, "This is the way, walk in it," when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left. Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver and your gold-plated metal images. You will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, "Be gone!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Therefore the LORD waits to be gracious to you, and therefore he exalts himself to show mercy to you."

The therefore is the most surprising word in the chapter. Everything before it is a nation refusing help, insisting on horses, and asking for lies from its prophets. Therefore — because of that — God waits to be gracious.

And the verb is the astonishing part. God waits. Not is delayed, not withholds. He is in the posture of somebody at a window, watching for the moment when grace can be given — and the reason it has not been given yet is not reluctance on his side.

The second half is stranger still: he exalts himself to show mercy. He rises up — the language of a king standing to act — and what he stands up to do is have compassion.

"For the LORD is a God of justice; blessed are all those who wait for him."

And now both parties are waiting. God waits to be gracious; blessed are those who wait for him. That puts a very different construction on a delay: not an absence at one end and frustration at the other, but two waitings, pointed at each other.

"He will surely be gracious to you at the sound of your cry. As soon as he hears it, he answers you."

"And though the Lord give you the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, yet your Teacher will not hide himself anymore, but your eyes shall see your Teacher."

Note that the adversity is not removed. Bread and water of affliction are still on the table — and in the middle of it the Teacher stops hiding. What is promised is not the end of hardship but the end of God's apparent absence in it.

"And your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, 'This is the way, walk in it,' when you turn to the right or when you turn to the left."

This is the most quoted promise in the chapter and it is often misread as a map. Look where the voice is. It is behind you, and it speaks when you turn aside. That is not an itinerary given in advance; it is correction given in the walking, by somebody following you closely enough to see which way you drifted.

"Then you will defile your carved idols overlaid with silver... you will scatter them as unclean things. You will say to them, 'Be gone!'"

And the response to seeing the Teacher is throwing the idols out, using a word for something ceremonially filthy. Nothing argues an idol away like the arrival of the real thing.

verseByVerse.quote: And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous. In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork. And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he will give rain for the seed with which you sow the ground, and bread, the produce of the ground, which will be rich and plenteous."

What follows is a farm, and after twenty-two verses of politics that is the point. The consequences of returning to God are described in terms of weather, soil and livestock rather than in terms of the Assyrian question.

"In that day your livestock will graze in large pastures, and the oxen and the donkeys that work the ground will eat seasoned fodder, which has been winnowed with shovel and fork."

The detail here is remarkable and easy to miss: the working animals get seasoned fodder, winnowed with shovel and fork. That is prepared feed — salted, cleaned, better than animals normally get.

Isaiah's picture of the restored world includes an ox eating well. God's generosity in this passage reaches past the people to the beasts that pull their ploughs, which is a small detail and says a great deal about him.

"And on every lofty mountain and every high hill there will be brooks running with water, in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall."

Water on the tops of hills, which is where water never is. And note the phrase tucked into the middle: this happens in the day of the great slaughter, when the towers fall. The mercy and the judgment are the same day.

"Moreover, the light of the moon will be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, as the light of seven days, in the day when the LORD binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow."

The last verse turns the lights up: the moon as bright as the sun is now, and the sun seven times brighter than that.

And then the reason, in the plainest language in the chapter: God binds up the brokenness of his people, and heals the wounds inflicted by his blow.

Read that last clause carefully, because Isaiah does not soften it. The wounds being healed are the ones God inflicted. He does not pretend somebody else struck them, and he does not apologise. The same hand that struck binds up, and the binding is why the lights go to seven times.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire; his breath is like an overflowing stream that reaches up to the neck; to sift the nations with the sieve of destruction, and to place on the jaws of the peoples a bridle that leads astray. You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD, to the Rock of Israel. And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones. The Assyrians will be terror-stricken at the voice of the LORD, when he strikes with his rod. And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres. Battling with brandished arm, he will fight with them. For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready, its pyre made deep and wide, with fire and wood in abundance; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the name of the LORD comes from afar, burning with his anger, and in thick rising smoke; his lips are full of fury, and his tongue is like a devouring fire."

The chapter ends with a theophany, and what comes is the name of the LORD — which in Hebrew usage means God himself in the character he has revealed. He is described entirely in terms of speech: lips, tongue, breath. The weapon is what he says.

"And the LORD will cause his majestic voice to be heard and the descending blow of his arm to be seen, in furious anger and a flame of devouring fire, with a cloudburst and storm and hailstones."

"And every stroke of the appointed staff that the LORD lays on them will be to the sound of tambourines and lyres."

An extraordinary detail. The blows fall to music — tambourines and lyres, which are festival instruments. Judgment on the empire is scored as a celebration by the people it had been crushing, and Isaiah does not apologise for that either.

"You shall have a song as in the night when a holy feast is kept, and gladness of heart, as when one sets out to the sound of the flute to go to the mountain of the LORD."

And here is the sound of the redeemed in the same passage: the singing of a festival night, and the gladness of a pilgrim walking up to the temple behind a flute player.

That is the last picture of a chapter which began with a caravan going the wrong way across a desert, carrying treasure to a monster that sits still. Both are journeys, and both are undertaken with everything the nation has. One goes south, in fear, at speed, and ends in shame. The other goes up a hill, at walking pace, to a flute.

"For a burning place has long been prepared; indeed, for the king it is made ready... the breath of the LORD, like a stream of sulfur, kindles it."

The chapter closes on Topheth, the burning ground in the valley outside Jerusalem — prepared, deep, wide, and lit by the breath of God. It is a sober ending, and it is the place whose name later became the standing word for hell.

30.theology:
Rahab who sits still. The chapter’s argument is compressed into a nickname (v. 7). Rahab was the sea-monster of chaos — raw mythic power, the same figure as Leviathan — and that is what Egypt’s reputation amounted to. Isaiah adds two words: who sits still. All the name and none of the motion. Judah did not buy nothing; they bought something genuinely impressive that was never going to get up. And the charge against them is not incompetence but that they went without asking.

Four passive words, and an unwilling people. Verse 15 is the centre: in returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength. Not one of those four is a strategy — no journey, no treasure on camels, no negotiation. And the reply is four words that land like a door: but you were unwilling. Not unable, not confused. Rest and quietness are hard because they require a person to stop managing the situation, and the managing is where the sense of control lives.

God waits. After all that, verse 18 begins therefore — and says the LORD waits to be gracious, and rises up to show mercy. He is poised at a window, not reluctantly delayed, and the same verse blesses those who wait for him. Both parties are waiting, pointed at each other, which recasts the delay entirely. Verse 21’s famous voice is behind and speaks when you have already turned aside — correction in the walking rather than an itinerary — and verse 26 ends with God healing the wounds inflicted by his blow, which Isaiah states without softening.

31.subtitle: Woe to Those Who Go Down to Egypt
31.intro: Overview. Chapter 31 is the sharpest, most compressed of the Egyptian-alliance woes. It drives the contrast between horses and the Holy One to a single question: do you not look to him? But it closes with a promise — Assyria will fall, and not by a human sword — and an image of God as a lion and a mother bird over Jerusalem. The chapter is brief but theologically dense.

keyVerse.quote: “The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.”
keyVerse.note: The verse does not disparage military preparation as such but exposes the category error of treating flesh as if it were spirit — of giving to Egypt the trust that belongs only to God. This is the idol-structure in practical form: not a carved image but a military alliance functioning as ultimate security.

31.reflection: The leaders of Judah were not irreligious people — they went to the temple, kept the feasts, consulted prophets. They simply also went to Egypt. The problem was not the absence of religion but its compartmentalization. In what area of your life do you practice religion in one compartment while making practical decisions in another, as if God were not involved?
31.text: <sup>1</sup>Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD!<sup>2</sup>And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity.<sup>3</sup>The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.<sup>4</sup>For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill.<sup>5</sup>Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it."<sup>6</sup>Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel.<sup>7</sup>For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you.<sup>8</sup>"And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor.<sup>9</sup>His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help, relying on horses and trusting chariots because there are many of them and horsemen because they are very strong — but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD (v. 1). Verse 2 answers with an unexpected compliment to God: he too is wise, and he does not call back his words. Verse 3 states the whole matter in one line: the Egyptians are man and not God, and their horses are flesh and not spirit — and when God stretches out his hand, helper and helped fall together.
verseByVerse.theology: The argument is not that the chariots are useless. Egypt's cavalry was the best in the region and Isaiah does not dispute it. The argument is about category: everything on the Egyptian side of the ledger is flesh, and flesh is not the kind of thing that can hold when God stretches out his hand.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 2 contains a piece of quiet sarcasm that is easy to miss. And yet he is wise — said of God, in the middle of a passage about clever policy. The planners in Jerusalem had weighed the options and produced a sophisticated strategy, and Isaiah observes that God has some competence in this area too.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD! And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or consult the LORD!"

The same policy as chapter 30, stated in a single sentence, and the structure of the verse is the argument. Four clauses about what they do rely on, and then two about what they do not: look and consult.

Note that both of the missing actions are small. Looking is not a campaign. Consulting is not a commitment. What Judah omitted was not obedience but a question, and the omission is the entire charge.

"And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words."

There is a dry edge here that is easy to miss. And yet he is wise — said of God, in the middle of a chapter about a clever policy produced by capable men.

The planners in Jerusalem had assessed the strategic picture and reached a sophisticated conclusion. Isaiah observes, mildly, that God also has some competence in this area, and adds the detail that distinguishes his planning from theirs: he does not call back his words. Human policy is revised constantly. His is not.

"The Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit."

And here is the whole matter in one line, and it should be read as a statement about categories rather than about quality.

Isaiah is not saying the chariots are bad. Egyptian cavalry was the finest in the region and everybody knew it. He is saying that no quantity of an inferior category adds up to the superior one. Man is not God; flesh is not spirit; and no number of horses crosses that line, because it is not a line of degree.

"When the LORD stretches out his hand, the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together."

The last clause is the sober one. They will all perish together. The nation that bought the protection goes down with the protection it bought — which is what always happens when a person ties himself to something that cannot stand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–9 — The Lion and the Birds
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two images of God defending Zion, and they could hardly be less alike. Verse 4 has him as a lion growling over its prey, unbothered by the shouting of shepherds called out against him — he will come down to fight on Mount Zion and nothing will move him off it. Verse 5 has him as birds hovering: protecting, delivering, passing over and rescuing. Verses 6 and 7 call for a return and promise that on that day everyone will throw away the idols his own hands made. Verses 8 and 9 announce that Assyria will fall by a sword that is not man's.
verseByVerse.theology: The pair covers everything. A lion is what you want between you and a threat; a bird over the nest is what you want when the threat is above you. Together they say that there is no direction from which danger can reach the people God is covering — and passing over in verse 5 is the Passover verb, which puts a night in Egypt behind the promise.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 names the manner of the deliverance precisely: Assyria shall fall by a sword, not of man. Judah will not win this. Six chapters later that is exactly what happens outside the walls, with no Judean casualties because there was no Judean battle.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus the LORD said to me, "As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him he is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill. Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus the LORD said to me: 'As a lion or a young lion growls over his prey, and when a band of shepherds is called out against him is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, so the LORD of hosts will come down to fight on Mount Zion and on its hill.'"

The first picture is a lion standing over a kill.

Every detail matters. Shepherds have come out in a group — that is what you do about a lion, you gather men and make noise — and they are shouting and banging. And the lion does not look up. He is not terrified by their shouting or daunted at their noise, because the arithmetic that frightens shepherds does not apply to him.

Isaiah is describing what God is like when he decides to defend Jerusalem: entirely unimpressed by the size and volume of what is arrayed against him, and not moving off the hill.

"Like birds hovering, so the LORD of hosts will protect Jerusalem; he will protect and deliver it; he will spare and rescue it."

And then the second picture, which could not be more different. A bird over the nest, wings out, hovering.

The pair is deliberate and it covers the whole compass. A lion is what you want standing between you and the thing coming at you on the ground. A bird over the nest is what you want when the danger is above. Between them there is no direction left from which anything can arrive.

And four verbs are stacked in one verse: protect, protect, spare, rescue. Isaiah is not being repetitive; he is doing what an anxious person needs, which is saying the same reassurance several ways.

One of those verbs deserves attention. Spare is the Passover word — the verb used when the LORD passed over the houses with blood on the doorposts and did not let the destroyer in. Behind this promise about Jerusalem stands a night in Egypt when the same God went through a country and stepped over particular doors.

verseByVerse.quote: Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel. For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you. "And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor. His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic," declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Turn to him from whom people have deeply revolted, O children of Israel."

The application, and it is one word: turn. Not build, not negotiate, not prepare. Come back — and the phrase from whom people have deeply revolted admits how far there is to come.

"For in that day everyone shall cast away his idols of silver and his idols of gold, which your hands have sinfully made for you."

And the sign of the turning is a hand opening. The idols are described the way this book always describes them — which your hands have made — and the same hands throw them out.

Nothing argues an idol away as effectively as the arrival of something real. In chapter 30 it was seeing the Teacher that made them scatter the images; here it is turning to the one they had revolted from.

"And the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man; and a sword, not of man, shall devour him; and he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be put to forced labor."

The manner of the rescue is stated twice over in one verse, and it is the point: a sword, not of man.

Judah will not win this battle. There will not be a heroic defence, a brilliant commander, or a well-timed alliance. The empire that no human force in the region could stop will fall to something that is not a human force, which is why the horses in verse 1 were beside the point from the beginning.

Six chapters later, that is precisely what happens. An Assyrian army camps outside Jerusalem, and in the morning it is not there, and no Judean sword is mentioned because no Judean sword was drawn.

"His rock shall pass away in terror, and his officers desert the standard in panic, declares the LORD, whose fire is in Zion, and whose furnace is in Jerusalem."

The last line is quietly devastating. His rock — the thing Assyria stood on, its confidence, whatever it called its foundation — shall pass away in terror. And officers abandon the flag, which is the one thing a professional army does not do.

Every side in this chapter has a rock. Judah has been trying to buy one in Egypt; Assyria has one and it dissolves; and God's fire is in Zion, where the only unmoveable thing in the book has been sitting the whole time.

31.theology:
A statement about categories, not quality. Verse 3 is the chapter compressed: the Egyptians are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. Isaiah does not dispute that Egyptian cavalry was the best in the region. He says no quantity of an inferior category adds up to the superior one — the line between flesh and spirit is not a line of degree, and no number of horses crosses it. And what Judah actually omitted was small: they did not look, and they did not consult. Not disobedience to a stated command — a question never asked.

The lion and the birds. Two pictures of God defending Zion that could hardly be less alike, and together they cover the compass. A lion growling over prey, unmoved by a band of shepherds shouting and banging, because the arithmetic that frightens shepherds does not apply to him. And birds hovering over a nest, which is what you want when the danger comes from above. Four verbs are stacked in verse 5 — protect, protect, spare, rescue — and spare is the Passover verb, which puts a night in Egypt behind the promise.

A sword, not of man. Verse 8 says it twice in one verse, and it settles why the horses were beside the point from the beginning. There will be no heroic defence and no brilliant commander; the empire no human force in the region could stop falls to something that is not a human force. Six chapters later an Assyrian army camps outside Jerusalem and in the morning is not there, and no Judean sword is mentioned because none was drawn.

32.subtitle: A King Who Reigns in Righteousness
32.intro: Overview. Chapter 32 pivots from the woes to a vision of what good leadership looks like — a king who reigns in righteousness and princes who rule in justice. It is partly a description of Hezekiah as a contrast to the current failed leaders, and partly a messianic vision of the coming king whose reign will be characterized by true sight, true hearing, and true speech. The chapter also includes a striking oracle to the complacent women of Jerusalem, and closes with a vision of the Spirit poured out.

keyVerse.quote: “Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest.”
keyVerse.note: The word until carries the whole weight of chapters 28–32: all the woes, all the warnings, all the distress are the “until” before God acts. This verse is one of Isaiah’s clearest anticipations of Pentecost — the Spirit-outpouring that makes the wilderness bloom.

32.reflection: Isaiah pictures good government as creating conditions where people can hide from the wind and find water in the desert. Whether you are in any kind of leadership — parent, boss, pastor, elder — are you creating those conditions for the people around you? And what would it look like to wait more consciously for the Spirit, rather than trying to produce the fruit of righteousness through effort alone?
32.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice.<sup>2</sup>Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land.<sup>3</sup>Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will give attention.<sup>4</sup>The heart of the hasty will understand and know, and the tongue of the stammerers will hasten to speak distinctly.<sup>5</sup>The fool will no more be called noble, nor the scoundrel said to be honorable.<sup>6</sup>For the fool speaks folly, and his heart is busy with iniquity, to practice ungodliness, to utter error concerning the LORD, to leave the craving of the hungry unsatisfied, and to deprive the thirsty of drink.<sup>7</sup>As for the scoundrel— his devices are evil; he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right.<sup>8</sup>But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands.<sup>9</sup>Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech.<sup>10</sup>In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come.<sup>11</sup>Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; strip, and make yourselves bare, and tie sackcloth around your waist.<sup>12</sup>Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine,<sup>13</sup>for the soil of my people growing up in thorns and briers, yes, for all the joyous houses in the exultant city.<sup>14</sup>For the palace is forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks;<sup>15</sup>until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest.<sup>16</sup>Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field.<sup>17</sup>And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.<sup>18</sup>My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places.<sup>19</sup>And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low.<sup>20</sup>Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Each One a Hiding Place
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A king will reign in righteousness and princes rule in justice (v. 1) — and verse 2 describes what that does to ordinary people: each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, streams of water in a dry place, the shade of a great rock in a weary land. Verses 3 and 4 reverse the blindness and deafness of chapter 29: eyes will see, ears will listen, the rash will understand and the stammering tongue will speak readily. Verses 5 to 8 restore the vocabulary — the fool will no longer be called noble — and set the scoundrel's schemes against the noble man's.
verseByVerse.theology: The remarkable thing about verse 2 is the subject. It is not the king who is the hiding place and the shade; it is each one under his rule. Good government in this chapter does not merely protect people, it turns them into shelters for each other — and every image chosen is of something you get behind rather than something you admire.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 undoes the moral relabelling of 5:20, where evil was called good. Here the names go back on the right things: the fool stops being called noble and the scoundrel stops being honoured. A society is in serious trouble when its vocabulary stops tracking reality, and part of what the coming king restores is accurate speech.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice. Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land. Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will give attention. The heart of the hasty will understand and know, and the tongue of the stammerers will hasten to speak distinctly.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, a king will reign in righteousness, and princes will rule in justice."

After five chapters of woes against the rulers Judah actually had, here is one who governs properly — and the emphasis falls not on his power but on the two qualities every previous administration in this book has lacked.

"Each will be like a hiding place from the wind, a shelter from the storm, like streams of water in a dry place, like the shade of a great rock in a weary land."

Read the subject of that sentence carefully, because it is the surprise. It is not the king who is the hiding place. It is each — each of the princes, each person under this reign.

Good government here does not merely protect people. It turns them into shelters for one another, which is a considerably higher claim: the effect of a righteous ruler is a society of people you can get behind in bad weather.

And look at the four images, because every one is functional rather than decorative. A hiding place from the wind. A shelter from a storm. Water in a dry place. The shade of a great rock in a weary land — and anyone who has walked in that country knows that a rock big enough to sit against is not scenery, it is survival.

None of these is something you admire. They are all things you get behind, drink, or sit under. That is what a person becomes under a good king.

"Then the eyes of those who see will not be closed, and the ears of those who hear will give attention. The heart of the hasty will understand and know, and the tongue of the stammerers will speak readily and distinctly."

And here the diagnosis of chapter 29 is reversed item by item. Eyes that were closed open; ears that would not attend listen; the heart that could not understand understands. Even the stammering tongue speaks clearly.

Isaiah keeps doing this — announcing the cure in exactly the vocabulary of the disease, so nobody can mistake which problem is being solved.

verseByVerse.quote: The fool will no more be called noble, nor the scoundrel said to be honorable. For the fool speaks folly, and his heart is busy with iniquity, to practice ungodliness, to utter error concerning the LORD, to leave the craving of the hungry unsatisfied, and to deprive the thirsty of drink. As for the scoundrel— his devices are evil; he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right. But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The fool will no more be called noble, nor the scoundrel said to be honorable."

This is the undoing of one of the six woes. Back in 5:20 the charge was against those who call evil good and good evil — the deliberate relabelling that destroys a society's ability to repent, because you cannot turn from something you have agreed to call good.

Here the names go back on the right things. It is a small-sounding promise and it is enormous: under this king, words mean what they mean again.

"For the fool speaks folly, and his heart is busy with iniquity, to practice ungodliness, to utter error concerning the LORD, to leave the craving of the hungry unsatisfied, and to deprive the thirsty of drink."

And then Isaiah defines his terms, and the definition is not what a modern reader expects. The fool in Scripture is not unintelligent. His heart is busy — he is working at this — and the list of what he does runs straight from theology to catering: he says wrong things about God, and he leaves the hungry hungry and the thirsty dry.

Those two belong together in this book and are never separated. Error about God and neglect of the poor are the same failure appearing at two ends of a life.

"As for the scoundrel — his devices are evil; he plans wicked schemes to ruin the poor with lying words, even when the plea of the needy is right."

The scoundrel is more deliberate: he plans, using lying words, against people whose case is actually good. That last clause is the sting — even when the plea of the needy is right. He knows.

"But he who is noble plans noble things, and on noble things he stands."

And the contrast is not activity against passivity. The noble man also plans. The difference is the content of the planning, and the fact that he stands on it — which is what the scoundrel cannot do, because a scheme built on lies is not a place to stand.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah addresses women who are at ease and complacent, and tells them to listen (v. 9). In a little more than a year they will shudder, because the vintage will fail and the harvest will not come (v. 10). He tells them to strip, put on sackcloth, and beat their breasts for the pleasant fields and the fruitful vine (vv. 11-12). Verses 13 and 14 have thorns coming up over the soil of his people, over every joyful house in the exultant city — the palace forsaken, the hill and watchtower turned into dens for wild donkeys.
verseByVerse.theology: The charge is not luxury but complacency, and the two are different. These women are not accused of cruelty or excess; the word used of them twice means secure, untroubled, confident that next year will be like this year. It is the specific danger of people who have been comfortable long enough to forget what the comfort was resting on.
verseByVerse.examples: The timescale is what makes it bite: in little more than a year. Isaiah does not warn about a distant reckoning but about the next harvest but one, which is close enough to check and far enough away to ignore. Complacency is rarely argued out of a person; it is usually taken out by a season.

verseByVerse.quote: Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech. In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come. Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; strip, and make yourselves bare, and tie sackcloth around your waist. Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine, for the soil of my people growing up in thorns and briers, yes, for all the joyous houses in the exultant city. For the palace is forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Rise up, you women who are at ease, hear my voice; you complacent daughters, give ear to my speech."

The address needs care, because it is easy to misread as a complaint about women. It is not. Isaiah picks out one group as a specimen, and the diagnosis is in the two adjectives: at ease and complacent. The word means secure, untroubled, confident that things will go on as they have.

That is a condition, not a gender, and it is the specific condition of people who have been comfortable long enough to forget what the comfort was resting on.

"In little more than a year you will shudder, you complacent women; for the grape harvest fails, the fruit harvest will not come."

And the timescale is what makes it land. Not a distant reckoning — in little more than a year, close enough to be checked and far enough off to be ignored.

Notice how the security is dismantled: not by an army but by a failed harvest. The complacent are not usually argued out of complacency. They are taken out of it by a season that does not do what seasons have always done.

"Tremble, you women who are at ease, shudder, you complacent ones; strip, and make yourselves bare, and tie sackcloth around your waist. Beat your breasts for the pleasant fields, for the fruitful vine."

The instruction is to start mourning now, before the loss arrives — which is Isaiah's characteristic way of asking people to take a warning seriously enough to feel it in advance.

"For the soil of my people growing up in thorns and briers, yes, for all the joyous houses in the exultant city. For the palace is forsaken, the populous city deserted; the hill and the watchtower will become dens forever, a joy of wild donkeys, a pasture of flocks."

The thorns and briers are the vineyard of chapter 5 again. And the ending is the one Isaiah keeps reaching for: not rubble, but wildlife. Wild donkeys enjoying themselves where the watchtower was, and sheep grazing in the streets.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–20 — Until the Spirit Is Poured Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Everything hangs on the first three words of verse 15: until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high. Then the wilderness becomes a fruitful field and the fruitful field is counted a forest; justice dwells in the wilderness and righteousness abides in the field (vv. 15-16). Verse 17 gives the sequence — the effect of righteousness is peace, and its result is quietness and trust for ever. Verse 18 puts God's people in peaceful homes, secure dwellings and quiet resting places; and verse 20 blesses those who sow beside all waters and let the ox and the donkey range free.
verseByVerse.theology: The turn does not come from better policy, a stronger alliance or a reformed leadership — all of which the last five chapters have tried. It comes from the Spirit being poured out, and the word until tells you that nothing before that is going to work. This is the first time in the book that the transformation is explicitly attributed to the Spirit's outpouring, and Joel, Ezekiel and Acts 2 all stand downstream of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Keep verse 17 for its order: righteousness produces peace, and peace produces quietness and trust. Those are the same two words God offered in 30:15 and Judah refused. What could not be adopted as a policy turns out to be available as a fruit — which is the difference the Spirit makes.

verseByVerse.quote: until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest. Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field. And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Until the Spirit is poured upon us from on high, and the wilderness becomes a fruitful field, and the fruitful field is deemed a forest."

Everything in the chapter turns on the first word, and it is a small one. Until.

That word says the desolation of verses 13 and 14 has a terminus, and it says something else as well: nothing before that point is going to work. Five chapters of Egyptian alliances, competent crisis management, walls surveyed and reservoirs cut have produced exactly nothing, and Isaiah now names what will actually change the situation.

Not a policy. Not a better king — though one has just been described. The Spirit poured upon us from on high.

This is the first time in the book that the transformation is explicitly credited to the Spirit being poured out, and everything downstream depends on it: Joel promising the same outpouring on all flesh, Ezekiel promising a new heart and a new spirit, and a room in Jerusalem where it happened.

And the effect is agricultural, which in this book means real. Wilderness becomes farmland; farmland becomes forest. Everything moves up one category.

"Then justice will dwell in the wilderness, and righteousness abide in the fruitful field."

Justice takes up residence in the desert. The two words the whole book has been asking for — the ones the vineyard failed to produce in 5:7, and the ones the coming king brings in verse 1 — are here described as living somewhere, which is what they do when the Spirit has been poured out rather than when a policy has been adopted.

"And the effect of righteousness will be peace, and the result of righteousness, quietness and trust forever."

Read the sequence, because the order cannot be rearranged. Righteousness produces peace. Peace produces quietness and trust.

And those last two words should stop anyone who read chapter 30. Quietness and trust is exactly what God offered Judah in 30:15 as the way to be saved — and they were unwilling.

What could not be adopted as a policy turns out here to be available as a fruit. They could not manufacture quietness and trust by deciding to; it grows, at the end of a chain that begins with the Spirit poured out and righteousness arriving. That is the difference the Spirit makes, and it is the answer to everyone who has tried to produce a settled heart by resolving to have one.

verseByVerse.quote: My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places. And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low. Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places."

Three phrases for the same thing, and every one of them is domestic. Not a fortified city, not a defensible position — a habitation, dwellings, and resting places.

After thirty-two chapters of walls, treaties, siegeworks, reservoirs and cavalry, what God finally gives his people is somewhere to live and the ability to sleep in it.

"And it will hail when the forest falls down, and the city will be utterly laid low."

The hail and the falling forest are still there. Isaiah does not remove the weather from the world in order to give his people rest; the storm goes on outside the secure dwellings, which is the same arrangement as 25:4, where God was the wall rather than the absence of the wind.

"Happy are you who sow beside all waters, who let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free."

And the last verse of the chapter is a farm at peace, described by two details a farmer would notice.

Sow beside all waters — not carefully, in the one safe irrigated corner, but everywhere there is water, which is what a man does when he is not expecting anyone to come and take the crop.

And let the feet of the ox and the donkey range free — the working animals turned loose to wander. In an unsafe country you keep your livestock penned and watched. Letting them out is the most ordinary possible sign that the danger is over.

The chapter that began with a righteous king ends with an untethered donkey wandering across a field somebody sowed without anxiety. That is what the reign in verse 1 is for, and it is a better picture of salvation than most grand ones.

32.theology:
Each one a shelter. The subject of verse 2 is the surprise: it is not the king who is the hiding place from the wind and the shade of a great rock, but each person under his rule. Good government here does not merely protect people; it turns them into shelters for one another. And every image is functional rather than decorative — things you get behind, drink, or sit under, not things you admire.

Complacency, and a season. The women of vv. 9-14 are not accused of cruelty or excess. The word used twice means secure and untroubled: the condition of people comfortable long enough to forget what the comfort rests on. And the warning is dismantled not by an army but by a failed harvest in little more than a year — close enough to check, far enough off to ignore. Complacency is rarely argued out of anyone; it is taken out by a season that fails to do what seasons have always done.

Until the Spirit. Verse 15 turns on one small word. Until says the desolation has a terminus — and that nothing before that point will work. Five chapters of alliances, competent crisis management and surveyed walls have produced nothing; what changes the situation is the Spirit poured out from on high, and Joel, Ezekiel and Acts 2 all stand downstream of it. Then verse 17 gives the order: righteousness produces peace, and peace produces quietness and trust — the very two words God offered in 30:15 and Judah refused. What could not be adopted as a policy turns out to be available as a fruit.

33.subtitle: The LORD Is Our King
33.intro: Overview. Chapter 33 is the last of the woes and serves as a hinge between judgment and hope. It opens with a woe against an unnamed destroyer (Assyria is in view) and moves through prayer, vision, and promise to one of the richest descriptions of God as king in all of Isaiah. The final verses paint a picture of the Jerusalem to come — a city whose inhabitants will never say they are sick, whose sins are forgiven.

keyVerse.quote: “For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us.”
keyVerse.note: The threefold office — judge, lawgiver, king — corresponds to the three branches of human governance, but is claimed entirely by God. This is not theocratic politics but eschatological vision: the world as it will be when every human delegation of authority returns to its source. 1 Timothy 6:15 picks up the king language for Christ; James 4:12 the lawgiver-judge.

33.reflection: The one who sees the king in his beauty is described ethically — not by spiritual intensity but by integrity in money, speech, and violence. The vision of God and the ethics of daily life are connected directly. Which of those three areas — money, speech, violence (including contempt) — most needs attention in your own life right now?
