verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Be Our Arm Every Morning
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last woe falls on a destroyer who has not himself been destroyed — when you have finished destroying, you will be destroyed (v. 1). The community answers immediately with prayer: O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in time of trouble (v. 2). Verses 5 and 6 name the stability of the times, and call the fear of the LORD Zion's treasure. Verses 7 to 9 describe the collapse: envoys weeping in the street, highways deserted, covenants broken, and Lebanon, Sharon and Bashan all withering. Verses 10 to 13 have God rising with a threefold now.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 2 is the model prayer of this section of the book, and its middle clause is the best thing in it: be our arm every morning. Not once, and not for the crisis only. Strength is asked for daily, on the assumption that yesterday's supply does not carry over — which is the same arrangement as manna, and as give us this day our daily bread.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 names one detail that dates any collapse: covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man. When agreements stop meaning anything, roads empty, because travel depends on treaties being kept by people you will never meet. Isaiah measures a society's failure by whether anyone is using the highways.

verseByVerse.quote: Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you. O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble. At the tumultuous noise peoples flee; when you lift yourself up, nations are scattered, and your spoil is gathered as the caterpillar gathers; as locusts leap, it is leapt upon. The LORD is exalted, for he dwells on high; he will fill Zion with justice and righteousness, and he will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Ah, you destroyer, who yourself have not been destroyed, you traitor, whom none has betrayed! When you have ceased to destroy, you will be destroyed; and when you have finished betraying, they will betray you."

The last woe of the series, and it is addressed to Assyria without naming her. The opening line puts a finger on the anomaly: here is a destroyer who has not been destroyed, and a betrayer nobody has yet betrayed. That is the thing that makes the wicked look invincible — not that they cannot fall, but that they have not.

Isaiah's answer is about timing rather than possibility. When you have ceased, when you have finished — the reckoning is not cancelled, it is queued.

"O LORD, be gracious to us; we wait for you. Be our arm every morning, our salvation in the time of trouble."

And the community's response to the woe is not a military plan but a prayer, which is what everything since chapter 28 has been asking for.

The middle clause is the best thing in the chapter. Be our arm every morning. Not once, and not only for the emergency — every morning, on the assumption that yesterday's strength has been used up and does not carry over.

That is the manna arrangement: gathered daily, no storing, and it went bad if you tried. It is also what Jesus taught people to ask for — give us this day our daily bread — and the reason for the arrangement is not stinginess. Daily supply keeps a person coming back, which is the whole point of the relationship.

"He will be the stability of your times, abundance of salvation, wisdom, and knowledge; the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure."

Two phrases to keep. The stability of your times — not the removal of instability but something steady inside it. And the fear of the LORD is Zion's treasure: after thirty-three chapters of treasuries emptied to buy alliances, the actual asset is named, and it is not in a vault.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly. The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man. The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. "Now I will arise," says the LORD, "now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted. You conceive chaff; you give birth to stubble; your breath is a fire that will consume you. And the peoples will be as if burned to lime, like thorns cut down, that are burned in the fire." Hear, you who are far off, what I have done; and you who are near, acknowledge my might.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, their heroes cry in the streets; the envoys of peace weep bitterly."

The diplomats are crying in public. That is a specific and terrible detail: the men whose entire profession is composure, whose job was to negotiate the treaties Judah had staked everything on, are weeping in the street where anyone can see.

"The highways lie waste; the traveler ceases. Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man."

And here is how Isaiah measures a collapse. Notice that it is not by casualties.

The highways lie waste and nobody is travelling. Roads empty when agreements stop being kept, because every journey depends on treaties honoured by people you will never meet — safe passage, tolls, borders. When covenants are broken, the practical result is that no one goes anywhere.

And the last phrase names the bottom of it: there is no regard for man. Not for this man or that class of man. For man.

"The land mourns and languishes; Lebanon is confounded and withers away; Sharon is like a desert, and Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves."

Then the four best places in the region, named one after another. Lebanon with its cedars, Sharon the coastal plain, Bashan the cattle country, Carmel the fertile headland — the four things anybody would list if asked what was beautiful about that country.

All four go. Isaiah does not describe general desolation; he takes the reader on a tour of specific loveliness and shows it withering.

"'Now I will arise,' says the LORD, 'now I will lift myself up; now I will be exalted.'"

And then, into that, God speaks — and says now three times.

Everything in the chapter so far has been about waiting: waiting for the destroyer to be destroyed, waiting on God every morning, envoys weeping while nothing happens. The threefold now is the end of the waiting, and the three verbs are all of a man getting to his feet.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–16 — Who Can Dwell with the Consuming Fire?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sinners in Zion are afraid and trembling seizes the godless, and they ask the sharpest question in the book: who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings? (v. 14). Verse 15 answers with a portrait rather than a doctrine — he who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppression, who shakes his hands free of a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil. Verse 16 gives him a height for a dwelling, a rock fortress, and bread and water that will not fail.
verseByVerse.theology: The question is asked by people inside Jerusalem, not by pagans, and it is the right question. The fire is not hell here — it is God's own presence, which is exactly what the city had assumed was a guarantee of safety. Living next door to the consuming fire is only good news for a particular kind of person, and verse 15 describes him.
verseByVerse.examples: Every item in the answer is concrete and most involve refusing money. Shaking the hands free of a bribe is a physical gesture; stopping the ears from hearing of bloodshed means declining to be in the room where such things are arranged. This is not a portrait of religious attainment but of a man whose integrity costs him income — and the reward is bread and water that will not run out.

verseByVerse.quote: The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: "Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?" He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppressions, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil, he will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The sinners in Zion are afraid; trembling has seized the godless: 'Who among us can dwell with the consuming fire? Who among us can dwell with everlasting burnings?'"

This is the sharpest question in the book, and everything depends on noticing who asks it and what the fire is.

The people asking are in Zion. They are not pagans; they are inside the city, inside the covenant, attending the festivals of chapter 29. And the fire is not hell. Verse 14 comes immediately after God arises in verse 10, and it is his presence they are looking at. The consuming fire is God himself, in the middle of the city, permanently.

That is the terror, and it is the exact reversal of everything Jerusalem assumed. They had treated God's presence in Zion as their guarantee of safety. Isaiah's point is that living next door to a consuming fire is only good news for one kind of person, and the question is whether they are that kind.

"He who walks righteously and speaks uprightly, who despises the gain of oppression, who shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe, who stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed and shuts his eyes from looking on evil."

And the answer is a portrait rather than a doctrine, and every line of it is concrete. Notice how much of it is about money.

Despises the gain of oppression — not merely refuses it: finds it contemptible, which is a different relationship to profit. Shakes his hands, lest they hold a bribe is a physical gesture, a man opening his fingers and shaking them out, and it implies a bribe was there to be taken.

Stops his ears from hearing of bloodshed means declining to be in the room where such things are planned, which usually costs a man his place in the room. And shuts his eyes from looking on evil is the refusal to be a spectator.

This is not a picture of religious attainment. It is a man whose integrity has a price and who has been paying it — and it is the answer to how anyone lives beside the consuming fire.

"He will dwell on the heights; his place of defense will be the fortresses of rocks; his bread will be given him; his water will be sure."

And the reward is not riches. It is a high place, a rock, and a supply of bread and water that does not fail. The man who let the bribes go gets the two things money was supposed to guarantee, from somebody else's hand.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–24 — The King in His Beauty
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar (v. 17). Verses 18 and 19 have the terror of the occupation become a memory — where is the one who counted, who weighed the tribute, who counted the towers? Verse 20 shows Zion as a tent whose stakes will never be pulled up. Verse 21 has broad rivers with no enemy galley on them. Verse 22 states why: the LORD is our judge, the LORD is our lawgiver, the LORD is our king; he will save us. And verse 24 ends the chapter with nobody in the city saying I am sick, because the people are forgiven their iniquity.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 22 gives God three offices that Judah had spent the book trying to fill with men: judge, lawgiver, king. Every failure in chapters 1 to 33 has been a failure in one of those three — corrupt courts, legislators drafting oppression, kings buying protection. Here all three are the same person, and the verse ends with the consequence rather than a fourth title: he will save us.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends with the two things wrong with a human being taken away in one sentence, and in a revealing order. No inhabitant will say I am sick — and the reason given is that the people are forgiven their iniquity. The sickness is dealt with by the pardon, which is the order the whole Bible keeps: the body follows the guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar. Your heart will muse on the terror: "Where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?" You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand. Behold Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be plucked up, nor will any of its cords be broken.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty; they will see a land that stretches afar."

After the fire and the trembling, this — and it is the goal of the whole chapter and arguably of the whole book.

Not you will be safe, and not the enemy will be gone, though both are coming. Your eyes will behold the king in his beauty. The reward at the end of the road is a sight, and it is a person.

Hold that against the previous verses. The man of verse 15 shut his eyes from looking on evil. Here his eyes are opened onto the king. Something was given up in order to look at something else, and the exchange is now complete.

And a land that stretches afar — the horizon back, after a siege in which the whole world had shrunk to the inside of a wall.

"Your heart will muse on the terror: 'Where is he who counted, where is he who weighed the tribute? Where is he who counted the towers?'"

Three questions about three officials, and the whole apparatus of occupation is in them. The man who counted the population for the levy. The man who weighed out the tribute payments. The man who counted the towers — the surveyor working out where the walls were weak.

These are the faces of foreign domination: not soldiers, but administrators with lists. And the promise is that one day the heart will muse on all this — turn it over as a memory, from a distance, and be unable to find the men.

"You will see no more the insolent people, the people of an obscure speech that you cannot comprehend, stammering in a tongue that you cannot understand."

The foreign language of 28:11 — the judgment on people who mocked plain teaching as baby talk — is finally gone from the streets.

"Behold Zion, the city of our appointed feasts! Your eyes will see Jerusalem, an untroubled habitation, an immovable tent, whose stakes will never be plucked up."

And the city is described as a tent that never moves. It is a deliberate contradiction: tents are the most temporary structures there are, and this one has stakes that are never pulled. Whatever permanence God gives does not have to be made of stone.

verseByVerse.quote: But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass. For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us. Your cords hang loose; they cannot hold the mast firm in its place or keep the sail spread out. Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey. And no inhabitant will say, "I am sick"; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But there the LORD in majesty will be for us a place of broad rivers and streams, where no galley with oars can go, nor majestic ship can pass."

Jerusalem's great weakness was that it had no river. Nineveh had the Tigris, Babylon the Euphrates, Thebes the Nile — and a river meant water, trade and defence. Zion had a spring and a tunnel.

Isaiah says God himself will be its broad rivers — with one qualification that turns the picture inside out. No galley with oars can go on them. The advantage of a river is that ships can come up it, and the danger of a river is exactly the same thing. This one has all the benefit and none of the exposure.

"For the LORD is our judge; the LORD is our lawgiver; the LORD is our king; he will save us."

Three offices in one line, and every one has been a scene of failure in this book.

The judge — and the courts of chapter 1 acquitted the guilty for a bribe and never heard the widow. The lawgiver — and the legislators of chapter 10 drafted oppression with the paperwork in order. The king — and Ahaz emptied the temple to buy Assyria while refusing a sign from God.

Judah spent thirty-three chapters trying to fill these three offices with men and failing in every one. Here they are all held by the same person, and the sentence does not end with a fourth title. It ends with a consequence: he will save us.

"Then prey and spoil in abundance will be divided; even the lame will take the prey."

A detail worth pausing on. When the plunder is shared out, even the lame get a share — the people who could not have fought and could not have chased anything down. The victory belongs to those who contributed nothing to it, which is how every victory in this book works.

"And no inhabitant will say, 'I am sick'; the people who dwell there will be forgiven their iniquity."

The last verse takes away the two things wrong with a human being, and the order is the important part.

Nobody says I am sick — and the reason given is not medical. It is that the people are forgiven their iniquity. The sickness goes because the guilt goes, which is the order Scripture keeps: the body follows the pardon, and not the other way round.

The chapter that began with a destroyer still standing ends with a city where nobody is ill and nobody is guilty, and the two facts are one sentence.

33.theology:
Be our arm every morning. The community answers the last woe with prayer rather than policy, and the middle clause of verse 2 is the best thing in the chapter: strength asked for every morning, on the assumption that yesterday’s supply has been used and does not carry over. That is the manna arrangement, and it is what Jesus taught people to ask for. The daily terms are not stinginess; they keep a person coming back.

Who can dwell with the consuming fire? The question is asked by people in Zion, not by pagans, and the fire is not hell — it is God’s own presence, which the city had assumed was its guarantee of safety. Living next door to a consuming fire is good news only for a particular kind of person, and verse 15 draws him: concrete, and mostly about money. He despises the gain of oppression rather than merely declining it; he shakes his hands out lest they hold a bribe; he refuses to be in the room where bloodshed is discussed. Not religious attainment — integrity that costs income.

Three offices, one holder. Verse 22 names God judge, lawgiver and king — the three roles this book has watched fail one after another: courts that acquitted for a bribe, legislators who drafted oppression, a king who emptied the temple to buy Assyria. All three are now held by the same person, and the verse ends not with a fourth title but with a consequence: he will save us. And the last verse removes sickness and guilt in one sentence, in that order — the body follows the pardon.

34.subtitle: Judgment on the Nations
34.intro: Overview. Chapter 34 is one of the most severe judgment passages in Isaiah, serving as the dark side of the diptych completed by chapter 35. The nations are summoned to hear their sentence; Edom is the representative case — a wasteland of burning pitch and thorns, inhabited by chaos creatures. The desolation is total and permanent. The vision is eschatological in scope: it is what the end of human rebellion looks like before the new creation blooms in the next chapter.

keyVerse.quote: “Seek and read from the book of the LORD: not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them.”
keyVerse.note: Even the desolation is governed by a book — by God’s word precisely applied. This is not chaos but ordered judgment. The same God who speaks creation into existence speaks desolation into a place that has refused him. The book-of-the-LORD motif connects to Isaiah 8:16–20 and ultimately to the Book of Life in Revelation.

34.reflection: Chapter 34 is difficult to read — the severity is comprehensive and without relief until chapter 35. But Isaiah places it immediately before the greatest vision of healing and return in the book. The comfort of chapter 35 lands differently if you have stood in the desolation of chapter 34 first. What aspects of the Bible’s severity do you tend to skip past? What does reading them in full do to your understanding of what grace actually costs?

Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it.<sup>2</sup>For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter.<sup>3</sup>Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood.<sup>4</sup>All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches.<sup>14</sup>And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place.<sup>15</sup>There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate.<sup>16</sup>Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Skies Rolled Up Like a Scroll
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The summons is universal — nations, peoples, the earth and all that fills it (v. 1). God's anger is against all the nations and all their host (v. 2), and verse 3 does not spare the reader the smell of it. Then verse 4 takes the judgment off the ground entirely: all the host of heaven rots away, the skies roll up like a scroll, and the stars fall as leaves fall off a vine or a fig tree. Verses 5 to 8 bring the sword down on Edom in the language of sacrifice, and name the occasion: a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 4 is not an astronomical forecast. Isaiah reaches for the only vocabulary adequate to describe the unmaking of an order that has been turned against its maker — and the images are domestic rather than cosmic: a scroll being rolled up when the reading is finished, and leaves coming off a tree in autumn. Both describe something ending on schedule rather than breaking down.
verseByVerse.examples: John takes this verse almost whole at the opening of the sixth seal: the sky vanished like a scroll being rolled up, and the stars fell as a fig tree drops its winter fruit (Rev. 6:13-14). When the New Testament needs language for the last day, it keeps reaching into this chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it. For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter. Their slain shall be cast out, and the stench of their corpses shall rise; the mountains shall flow with their blood. All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from the fig tree.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Draw near, O nations, to hear, and give attention, O peoples! Let the earth hear, and all that fills it; the world, and all that comes from it."

The widest summons in the book so far. Not a nation named and addressed, as in chapters 13 to 23, but everybody — and then the earth itself and everything in it, which is the audience called as witness back in 1:2.

"For the LORD is enraged against all the nations, and furious against all their host; he has devoted them to destruction, has given them over for slaughter."

Verse 3 then describes the aftermath without flinching: bodies unburied, the stench going up, the mountains flowing with blood. Scripture does not present judgment as clean, and a reader who wants it sanitised will have to look somewhere other than the prophets.

"All the host of heaven shall rot away, and the skies roll up like a scroll. All their host shall fall, as leaves fall from the vine, like leaves falling from a fig tree."

And then the judgment leaves the ground. This is the verse the chapter is remembered for, and the striking thing about it is how domestic the images are.

The sky is rolled up like a scroll. That is what you do at the end of a reading: the text has been read, the business is finished, and the scroll goes back on the shelf. It is not a description of something breaking. It is a description of something being put away because it is done.

And the stars come down the way leaves fall from a vine or a fig tree. Anyone who has watched a fig in autumn knows how that happens: not violently, but suddenly and all at once, and after that the branches are bare.

Isaiah is not forecasting astronomy. He is reaching for the only language adequate to say that the created order — which has been enlisted against its maker — can be taken down as easily as it was put up, and on the same authority.

John saw it and used the words. At the opening of the sixth seal the sky vanished like a scroll that is being rolled up, and the stars fell to earth as a fig tree sheds its winter fruit when shaken by a gale (Rev. 6:13-14). When the New Testament needs vocabulary for the last day, it comes here to get it.

verseByVerse.quote: For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction. The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood; it is gorged with fat, with the blood of lambs and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of rams. For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom. Wild oxen shall fall with them, and young steers with the mighty bulls. Their land shall drink its fill of blood, and their soil shall be gorged with fat. For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For my sword has drunk its fill in the heavens; behold, it descends for judgment upon Edom, upon the people I have devoted to destruction."

Out of all the nations summoned in verse 1, one is named — and the choice is not arbitrary. Edom was Esau's people: Israel's nearest relative, the brother nation, and across the Old Testament the standing example of family hostility that never healed. When Jerusalem finally fell, Edom stood and watched and cheered.

So Edom functions here the way Babylon does in chapter 13: a real country, and also the representative of every nation that sets itself against God and against his people.

"The LORD has a sword; it is sated with blood... For the LORD has a sacrifice in Bozrah, a great slaughter in the land of Edom."

The vocabulary that follows is sacrificial rather than military — lambs and goats, rams' kidneys, a sacrifice at Bozrah. Isaiah describes the judgment of a nation in the language of the altar, which puts it in a category the reader already understands: this is not an atrocity but an offering, made by God, at a place and time he appointed.

"For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion."

And here is the reason, stated plainly: for the cause of Zion.

The judgment is not free-floating anger. It is the settlement of a case — a recompense owed to people who were wronged and could do nothing about it. Everything Edom did while Jerusalem burned was recorded, and this verse is the court date.

Hold on to that if you have been on the wrong end of something that was never put right. There is a year of recompense, and it has been entered in a diary that is not ours.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Edom's streams become pitch and its soil sulphur, burning night and day with smoke going up for ever (vv. 9-10). The land is handed over to birds and animals: hawk and porcupine, owl and raven, jackals and ostriches, wild goats calling to one another, and the night bird settling to find herself a resting place (vv. 11-15). God stretches over it the line of confusion and the plumb line of emptiness (v. 11), and its nobles are called No Kingdom There (v. 12). Verses 16 and 17 send the reader to look it up: seek and read from the book of the LORD — not one of these creatures will be missing, none will lack her mate, because his mouth commanded it and his Spirit gathered them.
verseByVerse.theology: The two tools in verse 11 are the surveyor's line and plumb — the instruments used to lay out a building — and the two words attached to them are tohu and bohu, the formless and void of Genesis 1:2. God measures Edom carefully in order to un-create it. The precision is the frightening part.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 16-17 do something unusual: they tell the reader to go and check. Seek and read from the book of the LORD. The claim being tested is a small one — that every creature listed will be there and none will be without its mate — and it is offered as verifiable, because a God whose word covers the nesting habits of desert birds is a God whose word covers everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch. Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever. From generation to generation it shall lie waste; none shall pass through it forever and ever. But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness. Its nobles—there is no one there to call it a kingdom, and all its princes shall be nothing. Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches. And wild animals shall meet with hyenas; the wild goat shall cry to his fellow; indeed, there the night bird settles and finds for herself a resting place. There the owl nests and lays and hatches and gathers her young in her shadow; indeed, there the hawks are gathered, each one with her mate.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And the streams of Edom shall be turned into pitch, and her soil into sulfur; her land shall become burning pitch. Night and day it shall not be quenched; its smoke shall go up forever."

The picture is Sodom, and every reader would have known it: sulphur, burning, smoke going up from a plain. Isaiah is saying that what happened to those cities in one morning is what happens to Edom permanently.

"But the hawk and the porcupine shall possess it, the owl and the raven shall dwell in it. He shall stretch the line of confusion over it, and the plumb line of emptiness."

And here is the most chilling sentence in the chapter, and it needs its Hebrew to land. The two tools named are a surveyor's: the line and the plumb line, the instruments a builder uses to lay out a wall true and square.

And the two things being measured out are tohu and bohu — the formless and void of the second verse of the Bible, the condition of things before God said let there be light.

So God comes to Edom with building tools and carefully, accurately, measures out chaos. It is de-creation performed with precision, which is far more frightening than destruction performed in a rage. Nothing here is out of control.

"They shall name it No Kingdom There, and all its princes shall be nothing."

The nobility of a nation reduced to a place-name that says nobody rules here.

"Thorns shall grow over its strongholds, nettles and thistles in its fortresses. It shall be the haunt of jackals, an abode for ostriches."

Then the animals arrive, and Isaiah names them at length: hawk, porcupine, owl, raven, jackals, ostriches, wild goats calling to one another, and the night bird settling to find herself a resting place.

That last detail is the quiet one. The bird is not scavenging in a ruin — she is settling, choosing a spot, making a home. What was a kingdom has become somewhere comfortable for owls, and they have no idea anything was ever there.

verseByVerse.quote: Seek and read from the book of the LORD: Not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate. For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them. He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with the line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Seek and read from the book of the LORD: not one of these shall be missing; none shall be without her mate."

The chapter ends with an instruction that is unlike anything else in it: go and look it up.

Isaiah has just listed a dozen creatures that will inhabit the ruins of Edom, and he now invites the reader to check the record and see whether a single one of them turns out to be absent. It is a small and testable claim, deliberately so.

"For the mouth of the LORD has commanded, and his Spirit has gathered them."

And here is why the small claim matters. If God's word reaches to the nesting arrangements of desert birds — which owl, which mate, which ruin — then there is no scale at which it stops applying.

The argument runs from the trivial to the enormous, and it runs that way on purpose. A reader can be told that God rules history and remain unconvinced, because history is too large to check. He is told instead that not one screech owl will be missing her mate, and that is the kind of thing a person could in principle go and verify.

"He has cast the lot for them; his hand has portioned it out to them with a line; they shall possess it forever; from generation to generation they shall dwell in it."

The last verse uses the vocabulary of the conquest. When Israel entered the land it was divided by lot and measured out with a line, tribe by tribe, as an inheritance to be held from generation to generation.

Isaiah applies every one of those words to the animals in Edom. God casts lots for the jackals and portions out the ruins to the ostriches with a measuring line, and they hold it as a permanent inheritance.

It is the bleakest possible ending, and it is also strangely tender. The same care God took over the boundaries of Judah's tribes he takes over the nesting territory of birds in a wasteland nobody will ever visit — because nothing at all is beneath his attention, and everything he says is kept.

34.theology:
The sky put away. Verse 4 is not an astronomical forecast, and its images are domestic rather than cosmic. A scroll is rolled up when the reading is finished — not broken, but put away because it is done — and leaves come off a fig tree suddenly and all at once. Isaiah is saying that a created order enlisted against its maker can be taken down as easily as it was put up, and on the same authority. John takes the verse almost whole for the sixth seal (Rev. 6:13-14).

De-creation done with a plumb line. The two tools in verse 11 are a surveyor’s, and the two things measured out with them are tohu and bohu — the formless and void of Genesis 1:2. God comes to Edom with building instruments and carefully, accurately lays out chaos. Precision is the frightening part: nothing here is done in a rage or out of control. And Edom is chosen because it was Esau’s people, the brother nation that stood and watched while Jerusalem burned — a real country standing for every nation set against God.

Go and check. Verses 16-17 end the chapter with an instruction unlike anything else in it: seek and read from the book of the LORD, and see whether one of these creatures is missing or without its mate. The argument deliberately runs from the trivial to the enormous. History is too large to verify; a screech owl’s mate is not. And the closing verse gives the animals their ruins by lot and line — the conquest vocabulary for an inheritance held from generation to generation. The care God took over tribal boundaries he takes over nesting territory in a wasteland nobody will visit.

35.subtitle: The Highway of Holiness
35.intro: Overview. Chapter 35 is among the most luminous passages in all of Scripture — the other half of the diptych with chapter 34, and the first foretaste of the great vision of restoration in chapters 40–66. The wilderness blooms; the blind see, the deaf hear, the lame leap, the mute sing; a highway appears in the desert called the Way of Holiness; and the ransomed return with everlasting joy. Jesus reads from this chapter to answer John the Baptist’s question about whether he is the one who was to come (Matt. 11:5).

keyVerse.quote: “And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it… the redeemed shall walk there.”
keyVerse.note: The Way of Holiness is the image John picks up for the New Jerusalem: nothing unclean will enter it (Rev. 21:27). But Isaiah adds what John implies: it is not the pure who travel the road — it is the redeemed, the ransomed, even the simple. Holiness here is not the qualification for the road but the character of the road itself. You travel it because you have been ransomed, not because you are already holy.

35.theology:
Chapter 34 from the other side. The two chapters are one landscape photographed from opposite directions, and the vocabulary is matched item for item: streams turned to pitch, and burning sand turned to a pool; the haunt of jackals, and grass where the jackals lie down. And the generosity is pointed — the glory of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon (the three places that withered at 33:9) is not restored to them but given to the desert. The place with nothing receives the beauty of the places that had everything.

Comfort delivered by hand. The instruction in verses 3-4 is not be strong spoken to the weak; it is given to whoever is standing near them. Strengthen the weak hands; say to the anxious heart. And what they are told to say is not you will manage but behold, your God will come — the ground of the courage is an arrival rather than a resource. Verses 5-6 are the list Jesus sent back to John the Baptist in prison, answering a question about his identity by reporting that this chapter had begun (Matt. 11:4-5).

A road fools cannot wander off. The Way of Holiness sounds like a route for the qualified, and its specification says the opposite: even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. No navigational skill, no discernment about turnings, no danger of missing a sign. Everything this book has said about Israel is that they get lost — so God does not raise the entry requirements, he builds a road they cannot wander off. And the first half of Isaiah ends in a chase: sorrow and sighing flee, joy and gladness overtake. The pursuer has become the pursued.
35.reflection: Jesus chose Isaiah 35 to answer the question “are you the one who is to come?” His answer was not a theological argument but a list of healings: look at what is happening. Where in your life have you seen glimpses of chapter 35 breaking in — wilderness blooming, weakness strengthened, joy returning where sorrow was? And what in your life still feels like chapter 34, waiting for the highway to appear?
35.text: <sup>1</sup>The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus;<sup>2</sup>it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God.<sup>3</sup>Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees.<sup>4</sup>Say to those who have an anxious heart, "Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you."<sup>5</sup>Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped;<sup>6</sup>then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert;<sup>7</sup>the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes.<sup>8</sup>And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray.<sup>9</sup>No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there.<sup>10</sup>And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Desert Puts on Sharon
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After a chapter of pitch and sulphur, the wilderness is glad and the desert blossoms like a crocus (v. 1). Verse 2 gives the barren country the glory of Lebanon and the majesty of Carmel and Sharon — the three most fertile and famous landscapes in the land, handed to the place that had none of them. Verses 3 and 4 turn to people: strengthen the weak hands, make firm the feeble knees, say to those with an anxious heart, be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come. Verses 5 and 6 open blind eyes and deaf ears and set the lame man leaping and the mute tongue singing. Verse 7 turns burning sand into a pool and thirsty ground into springs.
verseByVerse.theology: The chapter is chapter 34 photographed from the other side. There the streams became pitch; here the burning sand becomes a pool. There the haunt of jackals; here grass and reeds and rushes where the jackals lay down. Isaiah wrote them adjacent so that the same reader would meet both, and the vocabulary is deliberately matched.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 5 and 6 are the list Jesus sent back to John the Baptist in prison, when John asked whether he was the one who was to come: the blind see, the lame walk, the deaf hear (Matt. 11:4-5). He did not argue. He reported that this chapter had started happening.

verseByVerse.quote: The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon. They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God. Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who have an anxious heart, "Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The wilderness and the dry land shall be glad; the desert shall rejoice and blossom like the crocus; it shall blossom abundantly and rejoice with joy and singing."

Read this immediately after chapter 34, because Isaiah put them side by side on purpose. There the streams turned to pitch and the soil to sulphur; here the desert blossoms. There the land became a haunt of jackals; here it sings.

The two chapters are the same landscape photographed from opposite sides, and the vocabulary is matched item for item so that nobody can miss the correspondence.

"The glory of Lebanon shall be given to it, the majesty of Carmel and Sharon."

And now the generosity of it. Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon were the three most famously beautiful places in the region — the cedar forests, the wooded headland, the flowering coastal plain. They are the exact three that withered in 33:9.

And they are not restored to themselves. Their glory is given to the desert. The place with nothing gets the beauty of the places that had everything, which is how grace works everywhere in this book.

"They shall see the glory of the LORD, the majesty of our God."

"Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees. Say to those who have an anxious heart, 'Be strong; fear not! Behold, your God will come with vengeance, with the recompense of God. He will come and save you.'"

The scene changes from geography to people, and the three descriptions are of exhaustion rather than wickedness: hands that have gone weak, knees that will not hold, a heart that is anxious — literally a hurried heart, racing.

Note who is given the instruction. It is not be strong addressed to the weak; it is addressed to whoever is standing near them. Strengthen the weak hands. Say to the anxious heart. The comfort in this verse is delivered by hand, through other people, and it is issued as a command to the ones who are not currently frightened.

And the content they are told to say is not you will manage. It is behold, your God will come. The ground of the courage is an arrival, not a resource.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy. For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert; the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water; in the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf unstopped; then shall the lame man leap like a deer, and the tongue of the mute sing for joy."

Four disabilities, and the reversals are not modest. The lame man does not walk — he leaps like a deer. The mute does not merely speak — his tongue sings. God does not restore people to adequate function; he overshoots.

Centuries later John the Baptist, in prison and no longer sure, sent messengers to ask Jesus whether he was the one who was to come or whether they should look for somebody else.

Jesus did not argue. He said: "Go and tell John what you hear and see: the blind receive their sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear" (Matt. 11:4-5). He answered a question about his identity by listing this chapter and letting John do the arithmetic.

Note also which of these the Gospels record most often. The blind receiving sight is the commonest miracle in the ministry of Jesus — and it is the first item on Isaiah's list, and the thing chapter 6 said had been taken away from the nation.

"For waters break forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert; the burning sand shall become a pool, and the thirsty ground springs of water."

Then the water, and the phrase to catch is the burning sand shall become a pool. The Hebrew word can mean the shimmering mirage that appears over hot ground — the thing a thirsty traveller sees and walks toward and never reaches.

Isaiah says the mirage will become an actual pool. What had been a cruel illusion turns out to be a promise arriving late, which is a fair description of a great deal that God does with human longing.

"In the haunt of jackals, where they lie down, the grass shall become reeds and rushes."

And the jackals from 34:13 are named one last time, lying down where they always did — except that the ground under them has turned into a marsh.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Road for People Who Get Lost
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A highway runs through the transformed country and is given a name: the Way of Holiness (v. 8). The unclean will not travel it; no lion or ravenous beast will be found on it (v. 9); and the redeemed walk there. Verse 10 sends the ransomed of the LORD home to Zion with singing, everlasting joy on their heads, and gladness overtaking them while sorrow and sighing flee away.
verseByVerse.theology: The most surprising clause in the passage is that the simple will not go astray on it. This road is not built for experts. It requires no navigational skill, no special competence, no discernment about which turning to take — and that is the point, because the people it is for have a long record of getting lost. Holiness here is a road rather than an achievement, and it is designed so that a fool walking on it arrives.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 10 is the last word of the first half of the book, and its last image is a chase. Sorrow and sighing flee away, and joy and gladness overtake — the pursuer becomes the pursued. John hears the same promise at the end of Scripture, where God wipes away every tear and mourning is no more (Rev. 21:4).

verseByVerse.quote: And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray. No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there. And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And a highway shall be there, and it shall be called the Way of Holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it. It shall belong to those who walk on the way; even if they are fools, they shall not go astray."

Here is the first full appearance of the image that will dominate the second half of the book — a road through the wilderness — and chapter 40 will put a construction crew on it and send John the Baptist to build it.

What this chapter adds is the road's name and its specification.

The name is the Way of Holiness, and that would ordinarily suggest a route for the qualified. The specification says the opposite: even if they are fools, they shall not go astray.

Sit with that, because it is the most surprising clause in the passage. This road requires no navigational competence. There is no skill in reading it, no discernment needed about which turning to take, no danger of missing a sign. It is built so that a simple person, walking, arrives — which is a strange design brief for a highway called Holiness, and exactly the right one for the people it was built for.

Everything this book has said about Israel is that they get lost. They could not tell good from evil, could not read a sealed book, could not see or hear. So God does not raise the entry requirements. He builds a road they cannot wander off.

"No lion shall be there, nor shall any ravenous beast come up on it; they shall not be found there, but the redeemed shall walk there."

And the second specification is safety. The desert road's real danger was predators; this one has none. Not driven off — not found there.

"And the ransomed of the LORD shall return and come to Zion with singing; everlasting joy shall be upon their heads; they shall obtain gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away."

The last verse of the first half of Isaiah, and it ends in a chase.

Look at the two verbs. Joy and gladness overtake them — the word for running someone down and catching them. And sorrow and sighing flee away.

For thirty-five chapters sorrow has been the pursuer. It has chased this nation through vineyards and sieges, through drunk priests and empty highways and a city sitting in the dust. Here the direction reverses: grief is running, and joy is the thing gaining on them.

And it is everlasting joy on their heads, which is the last thing anyone in this book has worn on his head. Chapter 3 stripped the finery; chapter 28 had a fading garland on a drunkard. This crown does not wilt.

The book will pick this up again at the very end, where God wipes away tears from all faces (25:8) and John hears it once more — no more mourning, nor crying, nor pain, for the former things have passed away.

36.subtitle: Sennacherib’s Threat
36.intro: Overview. Chapters 36–39 form a historical interlude (nearly identical to 2 Kings 18–20) that shows the principles of chapters 1–35 enacted in real time. Hezekiah’s reign provides the pivot between the Assyrian threat (chs. 36–37) and the Babylonian shadow (chs. 38–39). Chapter 36 sets up the crisis: the Rabshakeh, Assyria’s chief of staff, stands before Jerusalem and delivers a masterpiece of psychological warfare — calculated to destroy faith in God and king alike.

keyVerse.quote: “Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, ‘The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.’”
keyVerse.note: The Rabshakeh knows what he is attacking: not Egypt as a military ally, but trust in the LORD. He knows this is the specific ground of Jerusalem’s resistance. His entire speech is designed to make that trust seem irrational. This is the structure of every temptation that targets faith: it does not ask you to deny God exists; it asks you to stop trusting him in this specific situation.

36.reflection: The people on the wall heard everything and said nothing. Hezekiah had commanded silence, and they obeyed. Sometimes the right response to a sophisticated attack on faith is not a theological rebuttal but silence, followed by going to God in prayer. When was the last time you faced something that seemed to have a logical argument against trusting God — and what did you do with it?

And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.<sup>3</sup>And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.<sup>4</sup>And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours?<sup>5</sup>Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me?<sup>6</sup>Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him.<sup>7</sup>But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar"?<sup>8</sup>Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them.<sup>9</sup>How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen?<sup>10</sup>Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"<sup>11</sup>Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall."<sup>12</sup>But the Rabshakeh said, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?"<sup>13</sup>Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!<sup>14</sup>Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you.<sup>15</sup>Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, "The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria."<sup>16</sup>Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern,<sup>17</sup>until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.<sup>18</sup>Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us." Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?<sup>19</sup>Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?<sup>20</sup>Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'"<sup>21</sup>But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him."<sup>22</sup>Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–22 — The Same Patch of Ground
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sennacherib has taken every fortified city in Judah, and sends his field commander with a large army to Jerusalem (vv. 1-2). The speech that follows is the most sophisticated piece of hostile rhetoric in the Old Testament. He dismantles the Egyptian alliance as a broken reed that pierces the hand of anyone leaning on it (vv. 4-6); claims that Hezekiah's religious reforms offended the very God he trusts (v. 7); offers two thousand horses if Judah can find riders for them (v. 8); and claims the LORD himself sent him (v. 10). When the envoys ask him to speak Aramaic so the men on the wall cannot follow, he switches deliberately to Hebrew and addresses them directly (vv. 11-12). Verses 13 to 20 offer surrender on terms borrowed from Israel's own hope and then put the LORD on a list with the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim. Verses 21 and 22 end with three men in torn clothes and a city that said nothing.
verseByVerse.theology: The frightening thing about the speech is how much of it is true. Egypt is a broken reed — Isaiah said so in chapters 30 and 31. No nation's god has delivered it from Assyria; the record is accurate. The Rabshakeh has read the situation correctly and quotes God's own prophet back at Jerusalem, and the one thing he gets wrong is the only thing that matters.
verseByVerse.examples: The last verse is the most disciplined moment in the book: they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, 'Do not answer him.' A city under threat, listening to its own faith mocked in its own language, and instructed not to reply. There are arguments that are not to be won but taken somewhere else, which is exactly what Hezekiah does in the next chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them. And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem, with a great army. And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field. And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In the fourteenth year of King Hezekiah, Sennacherib king of Assyria came up against all the fortified cities of Judah and took them."

The book changes gear here. Chapters 36 to 39 are prose narrative, dropped between the two halves of Isaiah, and they exist because everything argued from chapter 7 onwards is about to be tested in a single afternoon.

And the situation is desperate. All the fortified cities have fallen; Assyrian records boast of forty-six walled towns taken in this campaign. Everything is gone except the capital.

"And the king of Assyria sent the Rabshakeh from Lachish to King Hezekiah at Jerusalem, with a great army. And he stood by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field."

Now read that last sentence very slowly, because Isaiah has been waiting twenty-nine chapters to write it.

At 7:3, God told Isaiah: Go out to meet Ahaz, you and Shear-jashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer's Field.

The same conduit. The same pool. The same road. The same patch of ground outside the wall.

There, a king of Judah was offered a sign from God as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven, and refused it, and bought Assyrian protection with temple silver. Here, at that exact spot, Assyria has arrived to collect — and a different king of Judah is about to do something different with what he is handed.

Isaiah built his book around that address, and this is the verse that closes the circuit.

"And there came out to him Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder."

Two of those names are from chapter 22. Shebna, who was cutting himself a grand tomb while the city was threatened, has been demoted from steward to secretary; Eliakim, on whom God said he would hang the key of the house of David, is now over the household. The prophecy has already happened, and the three men walking out to meet the Assyrian are the proof.

verseByVerse.quote: And the Rabshakeh said to them, "Say to Hezekiah, 'Thus says the great king, the king of Assyria: On what do you rest this trust of yours? Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war? In whom do you now trust, that you have rebelled against me? Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it. Such is Pharaoh king of Egypt to all who trust in him. But if you say to me, "We trust in the LORD our God," is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed, saying to Judah and to Jerusalem, "You shall worship before this altar"? Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them. How then can you repulse a single captain among the least of my master's servants, when you trust in Egypt for chariots and for horsemen? Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, "Go up against this land and destroy it."'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"On what do you rest this trust of yours?"

The speech begins with the right question, and it is the question the whole book has been asking Judah. The Rabshakeh is a better theologian than most of Jerusalem's officials, and that is what makes him dangerous.

"Do you think that mere words are strategy and power for war?"

A cutting line, aimed precisely at a nation whose defence consists of a prophet's sentences.

"Behold, you are trusting in Egypt, that broken reed of a staff, which will pierce the hand of any man who leans on it."

And here is the frightening part of this speech: he is right. A river reed looks like a walking stick and will take no weight; put your hand on it and it splinters and goes into your palm.

That is exactly what Isaiah has been saying for six chapters. Egypt is Rahab who sits still (30:7); the Egyptians are man and not God (31:3). The Assyrian is quoting the substance of God's own prophet back at God's own city, and the argument is sound.

"But if you say to me, 'We trust in the LORD our God,' is it not he whose high places and altars Hezekiah has removed?"

The second move is cleverer and entirely false. Hezekiah had torn down the local shrines in a religious reform — the most obedient thing he ever did — and the Rabshakeh presents it as an offence against the God being trusted.

It is the standing tactic of the accuser: take the thing done in obedience and produce it as evidence of guilt.

"Come now, make a wager with my master the king of Assyria: I will give you two thousand horses, if you are able on your part to set riders on them."

The insult is beautifully judged. He offers to supply the cavalry if Judah can find two thousand men who know how to ride, which everyone present knows they cannot.

"Moreover, is it without the LORD that I have come up against this land to destroy it? The LORD said to me, 'Go up against this land and destroy it.'"

And the last move is the boldest: a claim to divine authorisation. He says God sent him.

What makes this so unsettling is that in a sense God had. Chapter 10 called Assyria the rod of his anger, sent against a godless nation. The Rabshakeh has stumbled onto something true and is using it as a weapon, and the one thing he does not know is what chapter 10 said next about the axe that boasts against the man who swings it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, "Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall." But the Rabshakeh said, "Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?" Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: "Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria! Thus says the king: 'Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, "The LORD will surely deliver us. This city will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria." Do not listen to Hezekiah. For thus says the king of Assyria: Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern, until I come and take you away to a land like your own land, a land of grain and wine, a land of bread and vineyards.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Eliakim, Shebna, and Joah said to the Rabshakeh, 'Please speak to your servants in Aramaic, for we understand it. Do not speak to us in the language of Judah within the hearing of the people who are on the wall.'"

The officials make a diplomatic request, and their reason is transparent: there are soldiers and civilians on the wall listening, and morale is the only asset the city has left.

Aramaic was the diplomatic language of the region. They are asking him to keep this between professionals.

"But the Rabshakeh said, 'Has my master sent me to speak these words to your master and to you, and not to the men sitting on the wall, who are doomed with you to eat their own dung and drink their own urine?'"

He refuses, and he tells them why: the men on the wall are exactly who he came to talk to. He has not come to negotiate with the government; he has come to detach the population from it.

And then the brutal detail about siege conditions, said in the hearing of the people it describes.

"Then the Rabshakeh stood and called out in a loud voice in the language of Judah: 'Hear the words of the great king, the king of Assyria!'"

So he switches to Hebrew and raises his voice. Isaiah records this deliberately: an Assyrian officer, fluent in the language of Judah, standing where a prophet once stood, and shouting theology at a wall.

"Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, for he will not be able to deliver you. Do not let Hezekiah make you trust in the LORD by saying, 'The LORD will surely deliver us.'"

Note precisely what he attacks. Not the existence of God — he has already claimed God sent him. He attacks trust, by name, twice, and the mechanism is to drive a wedge between the people and the man telling them to trust.

"Make your peace with me and come out to me. Then each one of you will eat of his own vine, and each one of his own fig tree, and each one of you will drink the water of his own cistern."

And then the offer, and it is the cruellest thing in the speech, because it is quoted from the Bible. Every man under his own vine and his own fig tree is the standard picture of covenant peace.

He is offering Israel's own hope, on Assyria's terms, in exchange for surrender — and the small print is in the next verse: until I come and take you away to a land like your own. Deportation, described as an estate agent describes a house.

verseByVerse.quote: Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, "The LORD will deliver us." Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria? Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand? Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?'" But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, "Do not answer him." Then Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and Joah the son of Asaph, the recorder, came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Beware lest Hezekiah mislead you by saying, 'The LORD will deliver us.' Has any of the gods of the nations delivered his land out of the hand of the king of Assyria?"

Now the argument from evidence, and it is the strongest thing he has said.

"Where are the gods of Hamath and Arpad? Where are the gods of Sepharvaim? Have they delivered Samaria out of my hand?"

He names cities and asks where their gods are, and every answer is the same: gone. His record is unbroken and entirely factual. Nobody's god has stopped Assyria.

And then the sentence that puts his foot through the floor.

"Who among all the gods of these lands have delivered their lands out of my hand, that the LORD should deliver Jerusalem out of my hand?"

He has put the LORD on the list.

Everything up to this point was accurate: Egypt is a reed, the record is unbroken, the situation is hopeless. The one error in the entire speech is the category — he has filed the God of Israel among the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim, which is the mistake chapter 10 said he would make and be judged for.

It is also the mistake the whole first half of this book has been written to prevent. Chapter 40 will spend thirty-one verses on it: to whom then will you compare me? The Rabshakeh has just answered that question out loud, in Hebrew, at the top of his voice, and he has answered it wrong.

"But they were silent and answered him not a word, for the king's command was, 'Do not answer him.'"

And here is the most disciplined moment in the book. A city listening to its faith ridiculed in its own language, by a man who has most of the facts on his side — and the order is to say nothing.

That is not weakness and it is not indifference. There are arguments that cannot be won on the ground they are offered on, and the right response is to take them somewhere else. The next chapter shows exactly where Hezekiah took this one.

"Then Eliakim... and Shebna... and Joah... came to Hezekiah with their clothes torn, and told him the words of the Rabshakeh."

36.theology:
The same patch of ground. The Rabshakeh stands by the conduit of the upper pool on the highway to the Washer’s Field (v. 2) — word for word the spot where Isaiah met Ahaz at 7:3. Two kings of Judah, one address, two answers: Ahaz refused a sign as deep as Sheol and bought Assyria with temple silver; Hezekiah takes what he is handed into the house of the LORD. Isaiah built his book around that piece of ground, and this verse closes the circuit. The three officials who walk out are the men of chapter 22, with Shebna demoted and Eliakim over the household exactly as promised.

A speech that is mostly true. What makes the Rabshakeh dangerous is his accuracy. Egypt is a broken reed that pierces the hand — Isaiah said so in chapters 30 and 31. No nation’s god has stopped Assyria; the record is unbroken and factual. He even claims God sent him, and in a sense chapter 10 said he did. His cleverest move is to take Hezekiah’s religious reform — the most obedient act of his reign — and present it as an offence against the God being trusted, which is the standing tactic of the accuser.

The one error, and the silence. Everything holds until he asks how the LORD should deliver Jerusalem when the gods of Hamath and Sepharvaim could not. He has put the LORD on the list — the category mistake chapter 10 said he would be judged for, and the exact question chapter 40 will spend thirty-one verses answering. And the reply is the most disciplined moment in the book: they were silent and answered him not a word. Some arguments cannot be won on the ground they are offered on, and the right move is to take them somewhere else.

37.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Prayer and the Angel
37.intro: Overview. Chapter 37 is the climax of the Assyrian crisis — one of the greatest answered-prayer narratives in the Bible. Hezekiah receives the threatening letter, spreads it before the LORD in the temple, and prays. Isaiah delivers the divine response: Sennacherib’s arrogance will be answered, and Jerusalem will not fall. That night, 185,000 Assyrian soldiers die. Sennacherib returns to Nineveh and is killed by his own sons. Every element of the Rabshakeh’s mockery is precisely reversed.

keyVerse.quote: “So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.”
keyVerse.note: The missional motive for answered prayer runs all the way from here to the Lord’s Prayer: “hallowed be your name.” Hezekiah does not pray primarily for his own comfort or survival but for the display of God’s uniqueness among the nations. The request is aligned with God’s own purposes, which is why it is answered so spectacularly.

37.reflection: Hezekiah spread the threatening letter before the LORD. He didn’t summarize it, argue with it, or strategize around it — he laid it in front of God. This is one of the most practical models of prayer in the Bible: bring the actual problem, in its full severity, and lay it before the one who made heaven and earth. What letter do you need to spread before the LORD right now?
37.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD.<sup>2</sup>And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz.<sup>3</sup>They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, 'This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth.<sup>4</sup>It may be that the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.'"<sup>5</sup>When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah,<sup>6</sup>Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the young men of the king of Assyria have reviled me.<sup>7</sup>Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"<sup>8</sup>The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish.<sup>9</sup>Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "He has set out to fight against you." And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying,<sup>10</sup>"Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria.<sup>11</sup>Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered?<sup>12</sup>Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar?<sup>13</sup>Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'"<sup>14</sup>Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD:<sup>16</sup>"O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth.<sup>17</sup>Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God.<sup>18</sup>Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands,<sup>19</sup>and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed.<sup>20</sup>So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."<sup>21</sup>Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria,<sup>22</sup>this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "'She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem.<sup>23</sup>"'Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!<sup>24</sup>By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon, to cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses, to come to its remotest height, its most fruitful forest.<sup>25</sup>I dug wells and drank waters, to dry up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.<sup>26</sup>"'Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should make fortified cities crash into heaps of ruins,<sup>27</sup>while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown.<sup>28</sup>"'I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me.<sup>29</sup>Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come to my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.'<sup>30</sup>"And this shall be the sign for you: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that. Then in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit.<sup>31</sup>And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward.<sup>32</sup>For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors.
