The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this.<sup>33</sup>"Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it.<sup>34</sup>By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD.<sup>35</sup>For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David."<sup>36</sup>And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies.<sup>37</sup>Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh.<sup>38</sup>And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword. And after they escaped into the land of Ararat, Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–20 — He Spread It Before the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah tears his clothes, puts on sackcloth and goes into the house of the LORD (v. 1). He sends to Isaiah with an image of total exhaustion — children have come to the point of birth and there is no strength to bring them forth (v. 3) — and Isaiah answers at once: do not be afraid; I will put a spirit in him and he will hear a rumour and go home and fall by the sword in his own land (vv. 6-7). Then a second letter arrives, sharper than the first (vv. 9-13). And verse 14 is the hinge of the chapter and arguably of the book: Hezekiah received the letter and read it; and he went up to the house of the LORD and spread it before the LORD. His prayer follows in verses 16 to 20.
verseByVerse.theology: The prayer is a model, and its shape is the thing to learn. It opens with four lines of theology before it makes a single request — enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms, you have made heaven and earth — and when the petition comes it is not save us because we deserve it but save us, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD. The ground of the request is God's reputation, not Judah's need.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 is the answer to the silence of 36:21. Told not to reply to the Rabshakeh, Hezekiah takes the letter itself — the physical document, with the insults in it — carries it up the hill and unrolls it in front of God. He does not summarise it or soften it. He puts the thing where it can be read.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD. And he sent Eliakim, who was over the household, and Shebna the secretary, and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah the son of Amoz. They said to him, "Thus says Hezekiah, 'This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth. It may be that the LORD your God will hear the words of the Rabshakeh, whom his master the king of Assyria has sent to mock the living God, and will rebuke the words that the LORD your God has heard; therefore lift up your prayer for the remnant that is left.'" When the servants of King Hezekiah came to Isaiah, Isaiah said to them, "Say to your master, 'Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the young men of the king of Assyria have reviled me. Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As soon as King Hezekiah heard it, he tore his clothes and covered himself with sackcloth and went into the house of the LORD."

The contrast with chapter 7 could not be sharper and Isaiah does not point it out, because he does not need to. Ahaz, faced with a smaller threat at the same spot, went to inspect the water supply and sent to Assyria. Hezekiah, faced with Assyria itself, goes into the temple.

"And he sent Eliakim... and the senior priests, covered with sackcloth, to the prophet Isaiah."

The second thing he does is send for the prophet. Ahaz had a prophet come to him unasked, and refused what he offered.

"They said to him, 'Thus says Hezekiah: This day is a day of distress, of rebuke, and of disgrace; children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring them forth.'"

And here is the message, in one of the most exact images of helplessness in Scripture. A labour that has reached full term and stopped. The child is there, the moment has come, and the strength required is not there.

Anyone who has been at the end of their resources with the thing still unfinished knows that picture. It is not despair — despair has given up. This is the specific misery of having got all the way to the last stage and having nothing left for it.

"Isaiah said to them: 'Say to your master, Thus says the LORD: Do not be afraid because of the words that you have heard, with which the servants of the king of Assyria have reviled me.'"

The reply comes immediately, and note whose insult God says it was. Not the words with which they reviled you. With which they have reviled me.

God takes the mockery personally and takes it off Hezekiah, which is the first relief in the chapter and a considerable one.

"'Behold, I will put a spirit in him, so that he shall hear a rumor and return to his own land, and I will make him fall by the sword in his own land.'"

And the whole deliverance is announced in advance, in one sentence, before anything has happened. A rumour, a withdrawal, and a death at home — and every part of it comes true by the end of the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: The Rabshakeh returned, and found the king of Assyria fighting against Libnah, for he had heard that the king had left Lachish. Now the king heard concerning Tirhakah king of Cush, "He has set out to fight against you." And when he heard it, he sent messengers to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus shall you speak to Hezekiah king of Judah: 'Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria. Behold, you have heard what the kings of Assyria have done to all lands, devoting them to destruction. And shall you be delivered? Have the gods of the nations delivered them, the nations that my fathers destroyed, Gozan, Haran, Rezeph, and the people of Eden who were in Telassar? Where is the king of Hamath, the king of Arpad, the king of the city of Sepharvaim, the king of Hena, or the king of Ivvah?'" Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD. And Hezekiah prayed to the LORD: "O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made the heavens and the earth. Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God. Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands, and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone. Therefore they were destroyed. So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the king of Assyria heard that the king of Cush had set out to fight against him, he sent messengers to Hezekiah."

The rumour of verse 7 arrives on schedule — an Egyptian-Cushite army on the move — and Sennacherib's response is to send a letter rather than break off. It is more threatening than the first speech, because it is written and it is personal.

"Do not let your God in whom you trust deceive you by promising that Jerusalem will not be given into the hand of the king of Assyria."

The letter goes further than the Rabshakeh did. He said Hezekiah was deceiving the people; the letter says God is deceiving Hezekiah.

"Hezekiah received the letter from the hand of the messengers, and read it; and Hezekiah went up to the house of the LORD, and spread it before the LORD."

Here is the hinge of the chapter and one of the great moments in the Old Testament, and it is done without a word being said.

He takes the document itself — the actual sheet, with the blasphemy on it — carries it up the hill, and opens it out flat in front of God.

He does not summarise it. He does not soften the parts about God being a liar. He does not compose a reply. He puts the thing where it can be read, and steps back.

In chapter 36 the order was do not answer him, and the city obeyed and said nothing. This is what the silence was for. Some accusations should not be argued with on the terms they are offered; they should be carried somewhere and laid out.

And it is a model for anyone holding a letter, a diagnosis, a message they cannot answer. Take it to the one it is really about, unedited, and spread it out.

"O LORD of hosts, God of Israel, enthroned above the cherubim, you are the God, you alone, of all the kingdoms of the earth; you have made heaven and earth."

Then the prayer, and its shape is the lesson. Four clauses of theology before a single request: who God is, where he sits, how far his jurisdiction runs, what he made.

"Incline your ear, O LORD, and hear; open your eyes, O LORD, and see; and hear all the words of Sennacherib, which he has sent to mock the living God."

"Truly, O LORD, the kings of Assyria have laid waste all the nations and their lands, and have cast their gods into the fire. For they were no gods, but the work of men's hands, wood and stone."

He concedes the Assyrian's evidence entirely. The other gods did fall, and Hezekiah says why: they were no gods. The Rabshakeh's argument is not disputed, it is reclassified.

"So now, O LORD our God, save us from his hand, that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD."

And the petition, when it finally comes, is not grounded in Judah's need or merit. It is grounded in what the outcome will teach the watching world about God, which is the safest ground any prayer can stand on.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–38 — By the Way He Came
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah's answer is a taunt-song, the form Assyria used on everybody else, turned back on her: the virgin daughter of Zion despises you and wags her head behind you (v. 22). Verse 23 asks the real question — whom have you mocked, and against whom have you raised your voice? Verses 24 and 25 quote the boast; verses 26 and 27 answer that God planned it long ago and Assyria was only carrying it out. Verse 29 puts a hook in his nose and turns him back by the way he came. Verses 30 to 32 give Hezekiah a sign that is agricultural, and verses 36 to 38 record the outcome in three sentences.
verseByVerse.theology: Verses 26-27 are the theological centre and the direct answer to the boast of chapter 36. Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? Assyria thought it was writing history and was executing a script — which is the same point as the axe that cannot boast against the man who swings it (10:15), now delivered to the axe's face.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign in verses 30-32 is remarkable for what it is not. It is not a display of power but a farming calendar: this year eat what grows of itself, next year what springs from that, and in the third year sow and reap and plant vineyards. God's sign that the crisis is over is two years of ordinary agriculture — the resumption of normal life, which is what deliverance actually looks like from inside a household.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah the son of Amoz sent to Hezekiah, saying, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel: Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him: "'She despises you, she scorns you— the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you— the daughter of Jerusalem. "'Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel! By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon, to cut down its tallest cedars, its choicest cypresses, to come to its remotest height, its most fruitful forest. I dug wells and drank waters, to dry up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt. "'Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should make fortified cities crash into heaps of ruins, while their inhabitants, shorn of strength, are dismayed and confounded, and have become like plants of the field and like tender grass, like grass on the housetops, blighted before it is grown. "'I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come to my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Because you have prayed to me concerning Sennacherib king of Assyria, this is the word that the LORD has spoken concerning him."

Because you have prayed. The chapter attributes what follows to a man with a letter on the floor of a temple.

"She despises you, she scorns you — the virgin daughter of Zion; she wags her head behind you — the daughter of Jerusalem."

The answer is a taunt-song, which is the literary form Assyria used on everyone it conquered. God turns it back, and the figure he chooses is deliberately humiliating: not an army but a young girl, standing behind a retreating emperor, shaking her head at him.

"Whom have you mocked and reviled? Against whom have you raised your voice and lifted your eyes to the heights? Against the Holy One of Israel!"

And here is the question the whole confrontation turns on. Not what have you done but whom have you done it to — which is the one thing the Rabshakeh never established before he started talking.

"By your servants you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, 'With my many chariots I have gone up the heights of the mountains... I dug wells and drank waters, and I dried up with the sole of my foot all the streams of Egypt.'"

The boast is quoted, and the last clause is the emperor at his most absurd: he dried up the rivers of Egypt with the sole of his foot, by walking through them.

"Have you not heard that I determined it long ago? I planned from days of old what now I bring to pass, that you should make fortified cities crash into heaps of ruins."

And here is the answer, and it is the theological centre of the chapter.

Assyria believed she was writing history. God says she was performing a script settled long ago — and every conquest she took credit for was an item on somebody else's list. It is chapter 10's axe again, delivered this time to the axe's face.

"I know your sitting down and your going out and coming in, and your raging against me. Because you have raged against me and your complacency has come to my ears, I will put my hook in your nose and my bit in your mouth, and I will turn you back on the way by which you came."

The image is from the Assyrian reliefs themselves: prisoners of war led away with hooks through their lips. God takes the empire's own trademark cruelty and applies it to the empire, and the destination is not a prison. It is home — back on the way by which you came, the same road, in reverse.

verseByVerse.quote: "And this shall be the sign for you: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that. Then in the third year sow and reap, and plant vineyards, and eat their fruit. And the surviving remnant of the house of Judah shall again take root downward and bear fruit upward. For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. "Therefore thus says the LORD concerning the king of Assyria: He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there or come before it with a shield or cast up a siege mound against it. By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD. For I will defend this city to save it, for my own sake and for the sake of my servant David." And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down 185,000 in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies. Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh. And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword. And after they escaped into the land of Ararat, Esarhaddon his son reigned in his place.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And this shall be the sign for you: this year you shall eat what grows of itself, and in the second year what springs from that. Then in the third year sow and reap, plant vineyards and eat their fruit."

The sign given to Hezekiah is a farming calendar, which is not what anyone would have asked for and is exactly right.

The first two years there will be no sowing — an occupied country cannot plant — so they will eat volunteer growth, whatever comes up on its own. And in the third year: sow, reap, plant vineyards, eat the fruit.

That is the sign. Not fire from heaven — two years of scavenging and then a normal harvest. Planting a vineyard is the most confident act in agriculture, because vines take years to bear and nobody plants them expecting to leave.

God's proof that the crisis is over is that ordinary life resumes, which is what deliverance actually looks like from inside a household.

"For out of Jerusalem shall go a remnant, and out of Mount Zion a band of survivors. The zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this."

And the guarantee is the same sentence that closed the promise of the child in 9:7: the zeal of the LORD of hosts will do this. Not Hezekiah's faith, not the walls, not the Egyptian army marching up from the south. His zeal.

"He shall not come into this city or shoot an arrow there... By the way that he came, by the same he shall return, and he shall not come into this city, declares the LORD."

Not one arrow. The most powerful army in the world, camped outside, and the promise is that it will not loose a single shot into the city.

"And the angel of the LORD went out and struck down a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. And when people arose early in the morning, behold, these were all dead bodies."

The whole deliverance is reported in two sentences, and there is no battle in them. Judah does not appear. No Judean sword is mentioned, because none was drawn — exactly as 31:8 promised: the Assyrian shall fall by a sword, not of man.

And the timing is the sentence from 17:14: at evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more. Written years earlier, and here it is, with the phrase when people arose early in the morning doing the work.

"Then Sennacherib king of Assyria departed and returned home and lived at Nineveh. And as he was worshiping in the house of Nisroch his god, Adrammelech and Sharezer, his sons, struck him down with the sword."

The last verse completes the word given back in verse 7, item by item: a rumour, a return, and a death by the sword in his own land.

And the place is the sharpest detail in the chapter. The man who asked what god had ever delivered anybody was killed by his own sons while praying in the temple of his own god — and the God he had put on a list with Hamath and Sepharvaim never sent a soldier. Only an angel, once, at night.

37.theology:
He spread it before the LORD. Verse 14 is the hinge, and it is done without a word. Hezekiah takes the actual letter — the sheet with the blasphemy on it — carries it up the hill and opens it out flat in front of God. He does not summarise it, soften the part about God being a liar, or compose a reply. In chapter 36 the order was do not answer him; this is what the silence was for. Some accusations should not be argued with on the terms they are offered, but carried somewhere and laid out.

The shape of the prayer. Four clauses of theology before a single request — enthroned above the cherubim, you alone are God of all the kingdoms, you made heaven and earth. Hezekiah then concedes the Assyrian’s evidence entirely: the other gods did fall, for they were no gods but the work of men’s hands. The argument is not disputed, it is reclassified. And the petition is grounded not in Judah’s need or merit but in what the outcome will teach the watching world — that all the kingdoms of the earth may know that you alone are the LORD.

Three earlier promises land here. 31:8 said Assyria would fall by a sword, not of man, and no Judean sword is mentioned because none was drawn. 17:14 said at evening time, behold, terror! Before morning, they are no more, and the narrative reports it with when people arose early in the morning. And 7:3 put a king of Judah at the same conduit where 36:2 put the Rabshakeh. The sign given meanwhile is a farming calendar rather than a display of power — two years of volunteer growth, then sowing and planting vineyards, which nobody does unless he expects to stay.

38.subtitle: Hezekiah’s Illness and Recovery
38.intro: Overview. Chapter 38 begins the Babylonian shadow that will darken the second movement of Isaiah. Hezekiah falls ill and is told he will die. He prays; God gives him fifteen more years. The sundial goes back ten steps as a sign. Hezekiah writes a song of thanksgiving (vv. 9–20) that is one of the most honest accounts of the experience of near-death in the Bible — moving from lament to praise by way of a genuine wrestling with what had seemed certain.

keyVerse.quote: “It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.”
keyVerse.note: The theological logic of suffering-for-welfare is the logic of the cross: the deepest bitterness becomes the vehicle of the deepest love. Hezekiah does not explain how this works; he simply reports that it was so. The forgiveness placed at the center — not healing, not the sundial miracle, but “you have cast all my sins behind your back” — suggests that what he most needed was not years but pardon.

38.reflection: Hezekiah’s prayer was heard, his life was extended, and then — in chapter 39 — he will make the worst decision of his reign. The fifteen years included the birth of Manasseh (2 Kings 21:1), Judah’s most wicked king. God’s answer to prayer is not a guarantee of what we will do with the gift. How does that complicate your understanding of answered prayer? And what does “casting sins behind the back” mean for what you are carrying right now?
38.text: <sup>1</sup>In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, "Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover."<sup>2</sup>Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD,<sup>3</sup>and said, "Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly.<sup>4</sup>Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah:<sup>5</sup>"Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.<sup>6</sup>I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and will defend this city.<sup>7</sup>"This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he has promised:<sup>8</sup>Behold, I will make the shadow cast by the declining sun on the dial of Ahaz turn back ten steps." So the sun turned back on the dial the ten steps by which it had declined.<sup>9</sup>A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness:<sup>10</sup>I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years.<sup>11</sup>I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world.<sup>12</sup>My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom; from day to night you bring me to an end;<sup>13</sup>I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones; from day to night you bring me to an end.<sup>14</sup>Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety!<sup>15</sup>What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul.<sup>16</sup>O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live!<sup>17</sup>Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back.<sup>18</sup>For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness.<sup>19</sup>The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day; the father makes known to the children your faithfulness.<sup>20</sup>The LORD will save me, and we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD.<sup>21</sup>Now Isaiah had said, "Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover."<sup>22</sup>Hezekiah also had said, "What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?"

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah brings the king a message with no comfort in it: set your house in order, for you shall die and not live (v. 1). Hezekiah turns his face to the wall, prays, and weeps bitterly (vv. 2-3). Before Isaiah is out of the palace the word comes back — I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears; behold, I will add fifteen years to your life (v. 5) — with the deliverance of the city attached to it (v. 6). The sign is the shadow on the steps of Ahaz going back ten steps (vv. 7-8).
verseByVerse.theology: Notice what the prayer is: not resignation but protest. Hezekiah does not accept the verdict quietly; he weeps bitterly and argues from his record. Scripture contains a good deal of this kind of praying and does not disapprove of it, and the answer here comes so fast that Isaiah has to be sent back before he can leave the middle court.
verseByVerse.examples: The sign is chosen with some irony. The shadow moves back on the steps of Ahaz — the stairway built by the king who, at the same city, was offered any sign he liked from Sheol to heaven and refused it (7:11-12). What Ahaz would not ask for, his son is given on a structure bearing his father's name.

verseByVerse.quote: In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, "Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover." Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD, and said, "Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight." And Hezekiah wept bitterly. Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah: "Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life. I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and will defend this city. "This shall be the sign to you from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he has promised: Behold, I will make the shadow cast by the declining sun on the dial of Ahaz turn back ten steps." So the sun turned back on the dial the ten steps by which it had declined.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"In those days Hezekiah became sick and was at the point of death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said to him, 'Thus says the LORD: Set your house in order, for you shall die, you shall not recover.'"

The message has no comfort in it whatever. Not you are seriously ill. Set your house in order — the instruction given to a man with days rather than years.

"Then Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and prayed to the LORD."

The detail is exact and human. He turns to the wall, which is what a person does when he does not want to be watched, and it is where this prayer happens: not in the temple, as in the previous chapter, but with his face six inches from plaster.

"'Please, O LORD, remember how I have walked before you in faithfulness and with a whole heart, and have done what is good in your sight.' And Hezekiah wept bitterly."

The prayer is a protest and Scripture does not apologise for it. He does not accept the verdict; he argues, from his record, and then cries.

Modern readers sometimes find that unspiritual. The Bible does not: it is full of people arguing with God about a decision, and it records God's response to this one in the next verse.

"Then the word of the LORD came to Isaiah: 'Go and say to Hezekiah, Thus says the LORD, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Behold, I will add fifteen years to your life.'"

The answer comes so fast that Isaiah is sent back before he can leave the building — the parallel account has him not yet out of the middle court.

And note the two verbs: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. The tears are mentioned separately, as a second thing God noticed. There was information in the crying that was not in the words.

"'And I will deliver you and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria, and will defend this city.'"

"'This shall be the sign to you from the LORD: behold, I will make the shadow cast by the declining sun on the dial of Ahaz turn back ten steps.'"

And the sign is a shadow going backwards up a staircase — and it is set on the steps of Ahaz.

Ahaz is the king who stood at the conduit and was offered any sign at all, as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven, and said he would not ask (7:11-12). His son is given a sign he did not request, on a structure his father built, in the one currency Ahaz refused.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–22 — I Walked Slowly All My Years
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Hezekiah's own writing after the recovery, and it is unusually honest about what facing death felt like. He thought he was going through the gates of Sheol — consigned for the rest of his years, never seeing the LORD in the land of the living again (vv. 10-11). His life was pulled down like a shepherd's tent and cut off like a weaver rolling up his cloth (v. 12). He moaned like a dove and his eyes were weary with looking upward (v. 14). Then the turn in verse 17 — it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness — and God casting his sins behind his back. Verses 18 to 20 end with the living praising God, and a father telling children about his faithfulness.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 15 contains one of the most striking things a healed man ever said: I shall walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul. He does not describe himself as restored to his old pace. Something has changed in the way he moves, permanently, and he offers it as gain rather than damage.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 17 is the retrospect the whole song exists for: it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness — a judgment he could not have made at the time, and would have found intolerable if anyone had made it for him. The pardon in the same verse is the best image in it: God casts all his sins behind his back, which is the one place he does not look.

verseByVerse.quote: A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness: I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years. I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world. My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom; from day to night you bring me to an end; I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones; from day to night you bring me to an end. Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward. O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety!
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, after he had been sick and had recovered from his sickness."

What follows is Hezekiah's own composition, written afterwards, and its value is that it does not tidy up what the experience was like.

"I said, In the middle of my days I must depart; I am consigned to the gates of Sheol for the rest of my years."

In the middle of my days. He was about thirty-nine. That is a particular grief and it has its own shape: not the end of a long life but the interruption of one, with the second half simply cancelled.

"I said, I shall not see the LORD, the LORD in the land of the living; I shall look on man no more among the inhabitants of the world."

Two losses, and he names God first. What he expects to lose is the seeing — and then, second, human company. That order tells you a great deal about the man.

"My dwelling is plucked up and removed from me like a shepherd's tent; like a weaver I have rolled up my life; he cuts me off from the loom."

Two images, and both are of something being taken down before it looks finished.

A shepherd's tent is pulled up in the morning — pegs out, poles down, gone in minutes, and there is no sign anyone lived there. And a weaver rolls his cloth as he works, so the finished part is wound out of sight; then somebody cuts the thread at the loom, and whatever was going to be woven is simply not going to exist.

Anyone facing an early death recognises both: the speed, and the unfinishedness.

"I calmed myself until morning; like a lion he breaks all my bones... Like a swallow or a crane I chirp; I moan like a dove. My eyes are weary with looking upward."

And here is the sound of it. Not eloquence — bird noises. Chirping, moaning: the small, involuntary sounds a person makes when there are no sentences left.

My eyes are weary with looking upward. He has been praying so long that the act of looking up has become physically tiring. That is one of the truest lines in Scripture about protracted prayer.

"O Lord, I am oppressed; be my pledge of safety!"

verseByVerse.quote: What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul. O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live! Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back. For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day; the father makes known to the children your faithfulness. The LORD will save me, and we will play my music on stringed instruments all the days of our lives, at the house of the LORD. Now Isaiah had said, "Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover." Hezekiah also had said, "What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"What shall I say? For he has spoken to me, and he himself has done it. I shall walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul."

Here is one of the most remarkable things a healed man ever said, and it is easy to read past.

He has his fifteen years. And what he says about them is that he will walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul.

He does not describe himself as restored to what he was. Something in the way he moves through life has changed permanently — a man who has been that close does not walk at the old pace — and he offers it not as damage but as the settled result. The experience did not simply end when the illness did.

"O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these is the life of my spirit. Oh restore me to health and make me live!"

"Behold, it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness; but in love you have delivered my life from the pit of destruction, for you have cast all my sins behind your back."

And there is the retrospect the whole song was written for.

It was for my welfare that I had great bitterness. That is a verdict he could only reach afterwards, and it would have been intolerable from anybody else at the time. Nobody should say this sentence to a suffering person; it belongs in the mouth of the person who suffered, looking back, and nowhere else.

Then the pardon, and it is the best image in the song. God casts his sins behind his back — the one direction in which a person does not look. Not forgiven and filed; put where they cannot be seen from the throne.

"For Sheol does not thank you; death does not praise you; those who go down to the pit do not hope for your faithfulness. The living, the living, he thanks you, as I do this day."

Hezekiah's theology of death is limited — the fuller answer is at 26:19, where the dead live and their bodies rise, and it will not be complete until an empty tomb outside this same city. What he has is the strong Old Testament conviction that praise belongs to the living, and he doubles the word: the living, the living.

"The father makes known to the children your faithfulness."

And the point of the extra years is named. Not achievement, not more reign — telling children what God is like. It is the last thing the song says about the fifteen years, and it is the best use anyone has found for extra time.

"Now Isaiah had said, 'Let them take a cake of figs and apply it to the boil, that he may recover.'"

The last detail is a poultice, and it is left in deliberately. God adds fifteen years by sovereign decree and the prophet sends for a fig plaster, and the narrative sees no tension between them at all.

38.theology:
Prayer as protest. Hezekiah does not receive the death sentence quietly. He turns his face to the wall, argues from his record and weeps bitterly — and Scripture reports the answer coming back before Isaiah can leave the building. Note the two verbs God uses: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. The tears are named separately, as a second thing noticed. There was information in the crying that was not in the words.

The steps of Ahaz. The sign is a shadow travelling backwards up a staircase, and the staircase is named for the king who was offered any sign he liked — as deep as Sheol or as high as heaven — and refused to ask (7:11-12). What the father would not request, the son is given, on a structure bearing the father’s name.

Two verses to keep from the song. First, verse 15: I shall walk slowly all my years because of the bitterness of my soul. He is not restored to his old pace, and he reports the change as a settled result rather than as damage. Second, verse 17: it was for my welfare that I had great bitterness — a verdict reachable only afterwards, and intolerable in anyone else’s mouth. It belongs to the person who suffered, looking back, and nowhere else. The pardon beside it is the finest image in the song: God casts his sins behind his back, the one direction in which he does not look. And the song ends by naming what the extra years are for — a father making God’s faithfulness known to his children.

39.subtitle: The Shadow of Babylon
39.intro: Overview. Chapter 39 is brief and devastating. Babylon’s king sends envoys to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery, and Hezekiah, in a moment of pride, shows them everything — every treasure of his palace, every weapon in his armory. Isaiah pronounces the consequence: all of this will be carried to Babylon; your own sons will be eunuchs in the king’s palace. Hezekiah’s response — “there will be peace and security in my days” — is one of the saddest lines in the whole book. The chapter pivots the entire book from Assyrian crisis to Babylonian captivity.

keyVerse.quote: “Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, ‘The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.’ For he thought, ‘There will be peace and security in my days.’”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with chapter 37’s prayer is stark. There, Hezekiah interceded for others and future generations; here, he accepts judgment on his descendants with private relief. The chapter stands as a warning about the way personal comfort can corrupt what began as genuine faith. Hezekiah did not lose his faith; he privatized it.

39.reflection: Hezekiah showed the Babylonians everything. Pride after a great deliverance is one of the most common patterns in the spiritual life — the recovery that becomes an occasion for display rather than gratitude. What has God delivered you from that you are now tempted to exhibit for your own credit? And whose future are you shaping by choices you’re making today?
39.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered.<sup>2</sup>And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them.<sup>3</sup>Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said, "They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon."<sup>4</sup>He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."<sup>5</sup>Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD of hosts:<sup>6</sup>Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.<sup>7</sup>And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon."<sup>8</sup>Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "There will be peace and security in my days."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The Door That Was Left Open
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Merodach-baladan of Babylon sends letters and a present to congratulate Hezekiah on his recovery (v. 1). Hezekiah is glad, and shows the envoys his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armoury and everything in his storehouses — there was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them (v. 2). Isaiah asks two questions: what did these men say, and what did they see? The answers are 'they came from Babylon' and 'everything' (vv. 3-4). The oracle follows: all of it will be carried to Babylon, and some of your own sons will be eunuchs in that palace (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Babylon was a minor power at this date and Assyria was the enemy; the visit looked like a diplomatic opportunity and was in fact the test. Hezekiah, who took Sennacherib's letter into the temple two chapters ago, takes this delegation on a tour and never once asks God about it. The man who prayed brilliantly under threat did not think to pray under flattery.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is the most uncomfortable line in the chapter: the word of the LORD that you have spoken is good... there will be peace and security in my days. He accepts a sentence on his grandchildren because it will not fall in his lifetime. It is not defiance; it is relief — which is worse, and which is why the chapter ends the first half of the book here rather than on the deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered. And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly. And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them. Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, "What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?" Hezekiah said, "They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon." He said, "What have they seen in your house?" Hezekiah answered, "They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"At that time Merodach-baladan the son of Baladan, king of Babylon, sent envoys with letters and a present to Hezekiah, for he heard that he had been sick and had recovered."

Set the scene properly, because the timing is everything. Assyria has just been broken outside the walls. Hezekiah has been raised from his deathbed. And now a delegation arrives from Babylon — at this date a second-rank power with its own reasons for wanting allies against Assyria — carrying letters and a gift and congratulations.

It looks like a diplomatic opportunity. It is the test, and it comes immediately after the two greatest deliverances of his life, which is generally when tests come.

"And Hezekiah welcomed them gladly."

The parallel account adds the detail this one implies: he was glad. Somebody had noticed him. The most powerful empire in the world had been mocking this city a few months earlier, and here is a foreign king sending presents.

"And he showed them his treasure house, the silver, the gold, the spices, the precious oil, his whole armory, all that was found in his storehouses."

And so the tour begins, and Isaiah lists the stops the way an inventory is read out. The treasury. The silver. The gold. The spices. The oil. The armoury — which is to say, his military capacity, shown to a foreign power.

"There was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them."

The sentence is written to be conclusive. Nothing. Not one room kept back.

Note what is not recorded anywhere in these four verses. He does not send for Isaiah. He does not go up to the house of the LORD. Two chapters ago he received a hostile letter and carried it straight up the hill and spread it out; here he receives a friendly one and handles it entirely by himself.

"Then Isaiah the prophet came to King Hezekiah, and said to him, 'What did these men say? And from where did they come to you?'"

The prophet arrives unsummoned, which is itself the comment.

"Hezekiah said, 'They have come to me from a far country, from Babylon.' He said, 'What have they seen in your house?' Hezekiah answered, 'They have seen all that is in my house. There is nothing in my storehouses that I did not show them.'"

Isaiah's second question is the one that matters, and it is beautifully clinical. Not what did you say but what did they see.

And Hezekiah answers it fully and without embarrassment. He does not appear to know anything is wrong. That is the most sobering thing in the chapter.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, "Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD. And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon." Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, "The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good." For he thought, "There will be peace and security in my days."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, 'Hear the word of the LORD of hosts: Behold, the days are coming, when all that is in your house, and that which your fathers have stored up till this day, shall be carried to Babylon. Nothing shall be left, says the LORD.'"

The judgment is shaped exactly to the act, which is how judgment usually works in this book. He showed them everything; everything will go. He left nothing unshown; nothing shall be left.

And the destination is the point. Not Assyria — the enemy that has just been broken — but Babylon, the friendly delegation with the presents. The men admiring the silver were the advance party.

"'And some of your own sons, who will come from you, whom you will father, shall be taken away, and they shall be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.'"

Then the second half, and it is far worse. Not only the treasure but the sons — and not as princes but as eunuchs, castrated palace servants in a foreign court. A man who has just been given fifteen extra years is told what will happen to the children born in them.

"Then Hezekiah said to Isaiah, 'The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.' For he thought, 'There will be peace and security in my days.'"

And here is the last sentence of the first half of Isaiah, and it is the most uncomfortable line in the book.

Read the first half on its own and it sounds like piety: the word of the LORD that you have spoken is good. Submissive, even admirable.

Then the narrator tells us what he was thinking, and it is not defiance. It is relief. There will be peace in my days — and the days in question are the fifteen he was given as a gift when he wept at the wall.

That is what makes it so quietly appalling. He is not raging against the sentence. He is comfortable with it, because the cost falls on people he will not meet. A man who begged for his own life accepts the mutilation of his grandsons as good news, on the grounds of timing.

Isaiah ends the first half of his book here, and the placement is deliberate. Not on the angel and the hundred and eighty-five thousand; not on the shadow going back up the steps. On a good king, at the end of a good life, discovering that his real horizon was his own lifetime.

And that is why chapter 40 has to say what it says. Everything from here on is written to people in the Babylon this chapter opened the door to — and the first word spoken to them, after this, is comfort.

39.theology:
The test after the deliverance. The Babylonian delegation arrives immediately after the two greatest rescues of Hezekiah’s life — the Assyrian broken outside the walls and his own recovery from a deathbed — which is generally when tests come. And it does not arrive as a threat but as flattery: letters, a present, congratulations from a foreign king to a man whose city had been mocked a few months earlier.

The prayer he did not make. Two chapters ago Hezekiah received a hostile letter and carried it up the hill and spread it before the LORD. Here he receives a friendly one and handles the whole matter himself: no prophet sent for, no visit to the temple, and a complete tour — there was nothing in his house or in all his realm that Hezekiah did not show them. The man who prayed brilliantly under threat did not think to pray under admiration. And Isaiah’s second question is the clinical one: not what did you say, but what did they see.

Peace in my days. The last sentence of the first half of the book is the most uncomfortable in it. The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good sounds like submission until the narrator supplies the thought behind it: there will be peace and security in my days. Not defiance — relief. A man who wept for his own life accepts the mutilation of his grandsons as good news on the grounds of timing. Isaiah ends here rather than on the angel or the shadow, because everything after this is written to people already in the Babylon this chapter opened the door to — and the first word spoken to them is comfort.

40.subtitle: Comfort, Comfort My People
40.intro:
Overview. Chapter 40 is the great turn of the book. After thirty-nine chapters of indictment and the shadow of Babylon, God commissions a company of heralds with one word said twice — comfort — and three announcements: the sentence is served, the iniquity is pardoned, the debt is settled in full. Then a voice is sent into the wilderness to build a road, because God is coming in person, and the glory that arrives on it will be seen by all flesh at once.

The middle of the chapter resets the scale for people whose whole horizon had become an empire: oceans measured in a cupped hand, the nations weighed and found to be dust on a balance, idols that have to be kept from falling over, and stars that answer a roll call by name. The last five verses bring all of it down onto one complaint — my way is hidden from the LORD — and answer it not with sympathy but with God himself: the everlasting God does not faint or grow weary, and those who wait for him exchange their spent strength for his. All four Gospels quote verse 3 of John the Baptist, and Peter grounds Christian assurance on verse 8.

keyVerse.quote: “But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.”
keyVerse.note: The word wait (qavah) means to bind together, to strain toward — it is not passive waiting but directed, tethered hoping. The renewal is not a restoration of natural energy but a supernatural infusion. R.C. Sproul called this the great promise of the second section of Isaiah: what human strength cannot sustain, divine grace can renew.

40.theology:
The incomparability of God. Everything in chapters 40 to 55 rests on the claim made here: the God who speaks is not the largest item in a list of powerful things but the ground of everything that exists. Later theology calls this aseity — God’s existence from himself, depending on nothing and taught by nobody — and verses 13 and 14 state it as bluntly as Scripture ever does. The pastoral force is exact: only an infinite God can offer an infinite comfort, so the tenderness of verses 1 and 2 and the cosmic scale of verses 12 to 26 are not two subjects but one argument.

The road built for the LORD. Verse 3 prepares a way for Yahweh, and all four Gospels assign that road-building to John the Baptist, whose road was walked by Jesus of Nazareth (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6; John 1:23). The New Testament does not argue the identification; it assumes it. Verse 5 promises that the glory of the LORD will be revealed to all flesh, and John reports the sighting: we have seen his glory (John 1:14).

Grace to the empty-handed. The chapter’s last movement is the whole economy of grace in miniature. Human strength is measured at its peak and found to fail (v. 30); the strength that does not fail is given to the faint and to the man with no might at all (v. 29); and the verb for renewing it in verse 31 means to exchange. Nothing is topped up. The spent thing is handed over and something else is received in its place, which is how every other gift of God has ever worked.
40.reflection: The chapter begins with double comfort for people who feel their sin has been answered double. It ends with renewal for people who have grown weary waiting. Which of those two do you need most right now — the assurance of pardon, or the renewal of strength? And what does “waiting for the LORD” actually look like in the specific weariness you are carrying this week?
40.text: <sup>1</sup>Comfort, comfort my people, says your God.<sup>2</sup>Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.<sup>3</sup>A voice cries: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.<sup>4</sup>Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain.<sup>5</sup>And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."<sup>6</sup>A voice says, "Cry!" And I said, "What shall I cry?" All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field.<sup>7</sup>The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.<sup>8</sup>The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.<sup>9</sup>Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, "Behold your God!"<sup>10</sup>Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.<sup>11</sup>He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.<sup>12</sup>Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?<sup>13</sup>Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel?<sup>14</sup>Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?<sup>15</sup>Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust.<sup>16</sup>Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering.<sup>17</sup>All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.<sup>18</sup>To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?<sup>19</sup>An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains.<sup>20</sup>He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.<sup>21</sup>Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth?<sup>22</sup>It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in;<sup>23</sup>who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness.<sup>24</sup>Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble.<sup>25</sup>To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One.<sup>26</sup>Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing.<sup>27</sup>Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, "My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God"?<sup>28</sup>Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.<sup>29</sup>He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength.<sup>30</sup>Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted;<sup>31</sup>but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–11 — Comfort, and the Road for God to Come On
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half of Isaiah opens, and after thirty-nine chapters of indictment the first word is comfort, spoken twice. Verses 1 and 2 announce a sentence served, a pardon granted and a debt settled. Verses 3 to 5 send a voice into the wilderness to build a road, because God is coming in person and the glory that arrives will be seen by all flesh at once. Verses 6 to 8 measure that promise against human frailty — all flesh is grass, and the only thing that outlasts the withering is the word of God. Verses 9 to 11 put a herald on a mountain with two pictures of the God she announces: a warrior whose arm rules, and a shepherd carrying lambs.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort of this chapter is not encouragement; it is the announcement of an accomplished settlement, which is why it can be commanded rather than merely hoped. And the road in verse 3 is built for the LORD himself. When all four Gospels apply that verse to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus of Nazareth, they are not borrowing a convenient phrase — they are identifying the one whose road it was. The two images of verses 10 and 11 are not in tension: omnipotence in the service of tenderness is what the arm of God is for.
verseByVerse.examples: John the Baptist, asked directly who he was, answered by quoting verse 3 — I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness (John 1:23). Peter grounds Christian assurance on verse 8 and then names the abiding word: it is the good news that was preached to you (1 Pet. 1:24-25). And the herald's message in verse 9 is still the shortest summary of Christian proclamation available: Behold your God.

verseByVerse.quote: Comfort, comfort my people, says your God. Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and cry to her that her warfare is ended, that her iniquity is pardoned, that she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Comfort, comfort my people, says your God."

Thirty-nine chapters of indictment stop here. The last thing said before this was that everything in Hezekiah's house would be carried to Babylon, and the first word after it is comfort, said twice. In Hebrew the imperative is plural — God is not speaking to one prophet but commissioning a company of heralds, and the doubling is how the language shouts.

Then two possessives that have been missing for a long time. My people. Your God. Through the first half of the book they have mostly been "this people," which is what you call a nation you are addressing at arm's length. The relationship is being spoken back into place before anything is explained.

"Speak tenderly to Jerusalem." The Hebrew is dabberu al-lev — speak to the heart of Jerusalem — and it is not a general instruction to be gentle. It is the idiom for courtship. It is what Shechem does when he loves Dinah, what Boaz does when Ruth is frightened, what God says he will do when he takes his unfaithful wife into the wilderness to win her back (Hos. 2:14). God is not merely informing his people that the punishment is over. He is wooing them.

Three things are then cried over the city. Her warfare is ended — the word is the one used for compulsory military service, a term of hard duty with a fixed end. Her iniquity is pardoned. And she has received from the LORD's hand double for all her sins.

That last phrase troubles readers, and it should not. It does not mean God overcharged her. The word means the matching half of something folded over — the second panel that exactly answers the first — so the sense is that the sentence has been served in full, right to the last day of it, with nothing outstanding. Nothing is still owing. There is no residue to be collected later.

Which is why comfort can be commanded here rather than merely offered. Christian comfort has never been a mood worked up in the face of trouble; it is the proper response to a settled account. If the debt is paid, cheer is not optimism but accuracy — and the double that fell on the head of the servant in chapter 53 is what makes the arithmetic work.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice cries: "In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God. Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain. And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A voice cries: 'In the wilderness prepare the way of the LORD; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.'"

The picture is a road gang. When an eastern king travelled, men went ahead of him to make the route passable — filling holes, cutting through spurs, levelling the surface — because the road had to be ready before the king would come. Isaiah takes that ordinary piece of imperial logistics and puts it in the desert between Babylon and home, and the king being announced is God.

"Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill be made low; the uneven ground shall become level, and the rough places a plain." Nothing is left in the way. Not the mountains, which is to say not the obstacles that cannot ordinarily be moved.

Then verse 5, which is the point of the roadworks: "And the glory of the LORD shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together, for the mouth of the LORD has spoken." Not a rumour of God, and not a report brought back by specialists. The glory itself, in the open, seen by everybody at once.

Now hold that against the Gospels, because all four of them quote this verse, and they quote it about one man. Matthew, Mark and Luke apply it to John the Baptist (Matt. 3:3; Mark 1:3; Luke 3:4-6), and when the delegation from Jerusalem asked John directly who he was, he refused every title they offered him and answered with this verse: "I am the voice of one crying out in the wilderness, 'Make straight the way of the Lord'" (John 1:23).

Follow what that does. Isaiah says the road is being built for the LORD — the covenant name, the God whose glory fills the earth. John built his road, and then Jesus of Nazareth walked up it. The Gospel writers do not argue this; they simply take a sentence about the coming of God and hand it to a carpenter's son, and expect the reader to notice.

And what the road-builders were told to expect, John saw. "We have seen his glory, glory as of the only Son from the Father" (John 1:14). The valleys had been filled and the mountains taken down, and what came along the finished road was a man they could touch.

verseByVerse.quote: A voice says, "Cry!" And I said, "What shall I cry?" All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A voice says, 'Cry!' And I said, 'What shall I cry?'"

The herald is willing and does not know what the message is. The answer he gets is not the one he expects: before the comfort can be preached, something has to be said about the people being comforted.

"All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD blows on it; surely the people are grass."

The image is exact, and anyone who has lived in that country knows it. After the rains the hills go green and the wildflowers come, and it is genuinely lovely, and then the east wind arrives off the desert — the sirocco, hot and dry — and in a day or two the whole hillside is brown. Not weeks. Days.

And Isaiah does not say all flesh is weak. He says all flesh is grass, and specifies that what goes first is the beauty. Not the ugliness of human life but its loveliness: strength, looks, competence, the years when everything works. Read the obituaries of the people who ran the world eighty years ago. Look up the books everyone was required to have an opinion about in the decade you were born. The withering is not a threat hanging over human glory. It is the ordinary weather of it.

And notice who does the withering. Not time, not bad luck, not the market. "The breath of the LORD blows on it." The same breath that gave the grass its life takes it, on a schedule that belongs to God and not to us — which is a harder thought than mortality in the abstract, and a better one, because a wind that is God's breath is not a random wind.

verseByVerse.quote: The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God will stand forever."

The whole architecture of the chapter rests on this one sentence. Two clauses of the verse repeat what has just been said, so the third lands with everything behind it: one thing in the picture is not grass.

Take the comfort of verses 1 and 2 and ask what it is standing on. If the pardon were built on national recovery, or on a change of imperial policy, or on the exiles finding new resolve, then it would be grass and it would go the way of grass — beautiful for a season and brown by summer. It is built on something God said. And what God has said outlasts the people he said it to, the empire that overheard it, and the language it was first spoken in.

That is a specific kind of security, and its precise shape matters. It is not the promise that the believer will feel certain. Feelings are grass; they were in the list. It is the promise that the thing believed does not depend on the believer to hold it up.

Peter takes these two verses to Christians scattered across five provinces and under real pressure, quotes them in full, and then does something remarkable: "And this word is the good news that was preached to you" (1 Pet. 1:24-25). The abiding, unwithering, imperishable word is not left as an abstraction hovering over history. Peter puts his finger on it and says: you have already heard it. It was the gospel, in a room, out of somebody's mouth, and it is the one thing in your life that is not grass.

verseByVerse.quote: Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, "Behold your God!" Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him. He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go on up to a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news; lift up your voice with strength, O Jerusalem, herald of good news; lift it up, fear not; say to the cities of Judah, 'Behold your God!'"

The city that has spent thirty-nine chapters being preached at is handed the microphone. Zion is now the herald, sent up a hill so the sound will carry, told twice to lift her voice and once not to be afraid — which suggests that the natural instinct of a recently disgraced people with good news is to say it quietly.

And the message she is given is two words long. Not behold your deliverance, or behold your restored fortunes, though both are coming. Behold your God. Everything the exiles wanted was downstream of that, and Isaiah will not let the gift be announced ahead of the giver.

Then, in two verses, two pictures of the God being pointed at, and they do not sit together comfortably.

"Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and his arm rules for him; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him." That is a conqueror coming home — the arm that does the ruling, the spoils carried in front of the column. It is the image that terrifies the enemies of God, and it is meant to.

"He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom, and gently lead those that are with young." Same God, next sentence. The arm that rules for him in verse 10 is the arm the lambs are carried in in verse 11.

Notice the last clause especially, because it is the most practical thing in the chapter. Gently lead those that are with young. A flock moves at the speed of its slowest member, and a shepherd who drives it at the pace of the strongest will kill the pregnant ewes. Jacob knew it and said so to Esau: if the flocks are driven hard for one day, all of them will die (Gen. 33:13-14). God sets the pace of his people by the weakest one in it.

Two images and one God. The arm that will not be resisted is the arm that carries lambs; the might that comes with recompense is the tenderness that slows down for a pregnant animal. There is no tension in it and never was. This is what omnipotence looks like when it belongs to a shepherd, and it is the same one who said, centuries later, that he was the good shepherd and would lay down his life for the sheep.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–26 — To Whom Then Will You Compare Me?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The middle movement resets the scale for people whose whole horizon had become Babylon. Verses 12 to 14 ask who measured the oceans in a cupped hand and who taught God anything. Verses 15 to 17 weigh the nations and find them a drop and a speck of dust. Verses 18 to 20 turn to the alternative and follow an idol from the timber yard to the workshop, ending on the specification that matters most to its owner: that it will not fall over. Verses 21 to 24 have God stretching the sky like a tent and blowing on princes until they go like stubble. Verses 25 and 26 close the movement by summoning the stars and finding all of them present.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the doctrine later theology calls aseity — that God exists of himself, depending on nothing, taught by nobody. The polemic is precise rather than sneering: the nations and their gods are not God's rivals but his creation, and an idol is a category mistake before it is a sin. Verse 17 uses the word for the formless void of Genesis 1:2 of the nations, which is the point exactly — apart from God nothing has standing of its own.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul quotes verse 13 twice, at Romans 11:34 and 1 Corinthians 2:16, both times to stop an argument in front of the unsearchable wisdom of God. And the idol of verses 19 and 20 has never gone out of production. Every age builds something impressive with real skill, gives it the weight of its trust, and then has to take steps to stop it toppling over.

verseByVerse.quote: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance? Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand and marked off the heavens with a span, enclosed the dust of the earth in a measure and weighed the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance?"

Four measurements, and the units are the point. The hollow of the hand is the cupped palm — every ocean on earth held the way you would hold a mouthful of water. A span is the distance from thumb-tip to little finger on a spread hand, about nine inches, and it is being used to measure the sky. The dust of the earth goes into a grain scoop. The mountains go on the kitchen scales.

These are not images of a very large God. They are images of a God who is not on the same scale at all — who handles the whole created order with the casual gestures of a merchant checking a quantity.

"Who has measured the Spirit of the LORD, or what man shows him his counsel? Whom did he consult, and who made him understand? Who taught him the path of justice, and taught him knowledge, and showed him the way of understanding?"

The questions turn from power to wisdom, and every one of them expects the answer nobody. God has never taken advice. He has never had a teacher, never revised a position in the light of better information, never been shown something he had not considered. Paul quotes verse 13 twice — at the end of eleven chapters of argument in Romans (11:34), and again in 1 Corinthians (2:16) — both times at the moment where the right response to God is to stop talking.

To an exile this is intensely practical. Babylon was full of professional advisers — astrologers, diviners, wise men whose whole trade was telling a king what was coming. The God directing the history that had swept them into that city had not consulted any of them, and did not need to.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales; behold, he takes up the coastlands like fine dust. Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering. All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are accounted as the dust on the scales."

Watch how precisely that is chosen. Not a bucket — a drop from a bucket: the single bead of water that hangs on the rim and falls when you lift it, which nobody notices and nobody counts. Not a load of dust — the dust that has settled on the pan of a balance and is not enough to move the needle.

"Lebanon would not suffice for fuel, nor are its beasts enough for a burnt offering." Lebanon meant the great cedar forests, the timber kings sent for when they wanted a temple or a palace. Isaiah says: burn the whole forest, put every animal in it on the altar, and you still have not made an offering big enough to be adequate to this God.

"All the nations are as nothing before him, they are accounted by him as less than nothing and emptiness." The last word is tohu — the same word used of the formless void in the second verse of the Bible, before anything had been shaped.

Remember who is being told this and where they are standing. These are people living inside the Babylonian empire, for whom Babylon is not one nation among several but the entire horizon: its army, its gods, its processions, its buildings, the sheer daily weight of it. Isaiah is not insulting them and he is not exaggerating for effect. He is resetting the scale, because a captive's real problem is usually not that he has too high a view of God but that he has an accurate view of his captor and no idea what to set beside it.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him? An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains. He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skillful craftsman to set up an idol that will not move.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?"
