The question is not rhetorical padding; it is the hinge of chapters 40 to 48, and Isaiah will keep asking it. Having described a God who measures oceans in his palm, he now turns and looks at the competition.

"An idol! A craftsman casts it, and a goldsmith overlays it with gold and casts for it silver chains." The sequence is followed like a work order. Somebody founds it, somebody gilds it, somebody chains it — and then verse 20 goes down the market to the customer who cannot afford that: "He who is too impoverished for an offering chooses wood that will not rot; he seeks out a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not move."

Read the last clause again, because it is the sharpest sentence in the passage. After the timber selection and the hiring of a specialist, the specification that matters — the thing the whole investment is for — is that the finished god will stay upright. That is the ambition. Not that it will act, or hear, or save. That it will not fall over.

Two verses ago the nations were dust on a balance. Here the gods of those nations are objects that have to be steadied. They are not God's rivals. They are his furniture.

And the error Isaiah is exposing is a category mistake before it is a wickedness: treating a made thing as though it were the Maker. That reaches a good deal further than carved wood. Anything that gets a person's ultimate trust while remaining something he himself built — a portfolio, a reputation, a marriage, a body, a career, a church building — will need propping up, and the propping is the tell. Ask what in your life you spend most effort keeping upright. Whatever that is, you are its shipwright and not the other way round.

verseByVerse.quote: Do you not know? Do you not hear? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth? It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Have you not known? Have you not heard? Has it not been told you from the beginning? Have you not understood from the foundations of the earth?"

Four questions, and not one of them offers new information. Isaiah is not introducing a doctrine; he is charging his hearers with forgetting something that has been in plain view since the world began. That is the same argument Paul makes about the whole human race — what can be known about God is evident, and the problem is suppression rather than shortage (Rom. 1:18-20). Nobody in this chapter is short of evidence. They are short of attention.

"It is he who sits above the circle of the earth, and its inhabitants are like grasshoppers; who stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them like a tent to dwell in."

The tent is the striking picture, and it is domestic. Anyone in that world had watched one go up: the cloth shaken out, hauled over the poles, the guys pegged into the ground, and a household living underneath it by evening. Isaiah says that is what God did with the sky. One unhurried gesture, performed at the beginning, and every human being who has ever lived has lived inside it.

And grasshoppers is not contempt. Isaiah has just called the nations dust on a balance; if he wanted to insult us he had better material. It is scale. An insect on the floor of a very large tent is not worthless — it is alive, it is fed, it is provided for — it is simply very small in a very big room. The verse is not asking the reader to despise himself. It is asking him to stop imagining that the room is the size of his own concerns.

He sits above the circle of the earth. Not perched on it, not managing it from within it, not one of the forces operating inside the system — above it, seated, which is the posture of a king who is not worried.

verseByVerse.quote: who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness. Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who brings princes to nothing, and makes the rulers of the earth as emptiness."

Isaiah now applies the scale to the one thing an exile could not stop thinking about: power. Not power in general — princes, rulers of the earth, named individuals with armies and treasuries and the ability to decide where a family would live and whether it would live.

"Scarcely are they planted, scarcely sown, scarcely has their stem taken root in the earth, when he blows on them, and they wither, and the tempest carries them off like stubble."

Three times scarcely, hammered. The dynasties that seemed permanent are seedlings that have not got their roots down yet. And read what God actually does to them: he does not send an army, or raise up a rival, or uproot them. He blows on them. The gesture is the smallest one in the chapter.

It is also the same gesture as verse 7, where the breath of the LORD blows on the grass. Isaiah has now used one image twice, deliberately: what happens to a wildflower in the sirocco is what happens to an empire. The difference between them is size, not kind — both are vegetation, both are seasonal, and both go down before the same breath.

Nebuchadnezzar was the most powerful man alive when these words were being read by people he had deported. There is a photograph of that empire in the British Museum and nothing else left of it. That is not a comfort about politics being unimportant; the exiles' suffering under it was real and God takes a whole book to say so. It is a comfort about proportion. A believer who is frightened of a government is frightened of stubble in a wind — and the wind belongs to his Father.

verseByVerse.quote: To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him? says the Holy One. Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"'To whom then will you compare me, that I should be like him?' says the Holy One."

The question comes back, and this time God asks it himself, in his own voice, using the title that has run through the whole book: the Holy One. The claim inside the question is not that God wins the comparison. It is that there is no category to run the comparison in. He is not the best of a kind; there is no kind.

"Lift up your eyes on high and see: who created these? He who brings out their host by number, calling them all by name; by the greatness of his might and because he is strong in power, not one is missing."

Consider who is being addressed. Babylon was the great civilisation of the night sky. Its astronomers kept star records over centuries, its priests read the heavens for omens, and its gods were largely the lights themselves. To an exile, looking up meant looking at the religion of the people who owned him.

Isaiah tells him to look up anyway, and then reframes everything he sees. The lights are not gods and not fates. They are a host — an army — and God brings them out the way a commander parades a regiment, by number, calling each one by its name. The Babylonians catalogued the stars. God named them, and they answer to him.

"Not one is missing." He takes the roll every night and the roll is always complete. Hold that phrase, because the next verse is about people who believe God has lost track of them.

He brings them out by number and calls them all by name, and he has never once been short. The furnaces of a hundred billion suns are on parade, each of them known by a name he gave it, and the whole procession is no strain to him at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 27–31 — Waiting, and the Exchange of Strength
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter comes to ground on a complaint. In verse 27 the people say their way is hidden from the LORD and their case ignored — not that God does not exist, but that he has stopped noticing. Verse 28 answers with theology rather than sympathy, and picks precisely the attribute the complaint needs: the everlasting God does not faint or grow weary. Verses 29 and 30 set the strongest human beings against that and watch them fall exhausted. Verse 31 gives the promise the whole chapter has been building toward, and puts its three verbs in an order nobody expects.
verseByVerse.theology: The answer to feeling forgotten is not a better feeling but a larger God, and the text takes that route deliberately: verse 28 does not tell them they are wrong to feel it, it tells them who it is they think has forgotten them. The verb in verse 31 for renewing strength is the ordinary word for exchanging one thing for another. The promise is not that the faithful will stop running out. It is that there is a place to trade what has run out for what has not.
verseByVerse.examples: The order of verse 31 runs backwards from every instinct — mount up, then run, then walk — as though the plodding faithfulness of an ordinary week were the hardest thing to sustain and the last thing worth promising. Most Christian lives are lived in the third clause, and it is the one the verse ends on.

verseByVerse.quote: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, "My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God"? Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, 'My way is hidden from the LORD, and my right is disregarded by my God'?"

This is the sentence the whole chapter has been walking toward, and notice what kind of complaint it is. It is not unbelief. Nobody here is saying there is no God, or that he is powerless, or that the exile was undeserved. They are saying two much more ordinary things: he cannot see where I am, and he is not doing anything about what has been done to me. My way. My right. It is the believer's complaint, and the possessives are the ache in it.

Anyone who has prayed for years about the same thing knows the exact temperature of that verse. Not rebellion — attrition. The doctrine is all still in place and the sense that any of it applies to you personally has quietly drained away.

"Have you not known? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He does not faint or grow weary; his understanding is unsearchable."

God does not answer the feeling. He answers with himself, and the choice of attributes is not random. To people who feel overlooked he says: his understanding is unsearchable — there is no corner of your situation he has not thought all the way through. To people worn out with waiting he says: he does not faint or grow weary — the very thing that has happened to you has never once happened to him.

That is not evasion. It is the only real cure. A believer who feels forgotten does not need to be told his feelings are wrong; he needs a bigger God than the one he has been carrying around, because the small god of his imagination genuinely could lose track of him. The everlasting God, who has just been shown taking roll call of the stars, could not.

verseByVerse.quote: He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength. Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He gives power to the faint, and to him who has no might he increases strength."

Notice the two categories God works with, because neither is the one we would choose. Not the promising and the committed. The faint — people already running on empty — and the man with no might at all, which is not a low reading but a nil one. This is where the enormous theology of the last twenty verses has been going. The God who does not grow weary distributes strength, and he distributes it downward, to the people who have none.

"Even youths shall faint and be weary, and young men shall fall exhausted."

Isaiah takes the best specimen available and puts him on the ground. Young men at the absolute peak — the ones who do not get tired, who can go all day, whose bodies have not yet started sending the bills — shall fall exhausted. The verb is the one for stumbling: not a graceful decline but a man whose legs go.

He is not being gloomy. He is closing an exit. As long as the reader believes there is some level of human vigour that would be sufficient, he will keep trying to reach it and keep half-praying about the shortfall. Isaiah takes the highest human number available, shows it failing, and leaves only one place for the strength to come from.

Which is a strange kind of relief. Most of the exhaustion Christians carry is not from serving God; it is from the effort of appearing to have enough. Verse 30 says the strongest man you know does not have enough either, and it says it so that verse 31 has somewhere to land.

verseByVerse.quote: but they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But they who wait for the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings like eagles; they shall run and not be weary; they shall walk and not faint."

Both verbs repay attention. Wait is qavah, and the root has to do with twisting strands together into a cord — waiting under tension, pulled toward something, the very opposite of passive. Nobody in this verse is sitting still. And renew is the ordinary word for exchange, the one you would use for swapping a worn-out coat for a new one. The promise is not that strength gets topped up from a reserve. It is that there is a counter where the spent thing can be handed in and something else received across it.

That distinction decides how a person prays on a bad week. Topping up asks God to make a depleted resource go further, which keeps the depleted resource at the centre. Exchange brings the emptiness itself and hands it over. The first is a request for endurance; the second is closer to what the whole Bible means by faith.

Then three clauses, and their order is wrong on purpose. Mount up, run, walk. Every instinct in a writer builds the other way — walking, then running, then flight, with the eagles at the summit — and Isaiah puts the eagles first and finishes with walking.

He is not describing a crescendo. He is describing a life. There are days that feel like flight, and they are rare and they are gifts. There are seasons of running, of real effort with visible progress. And then there is most of a Christian life, which is walking: the same obedience, the same prayers, the same marriage, the same job, the same body, on an ordinary Tuesday, with nothing whatever to show anybody. That is the hardest of the three to sustain, and it is the one the verse ends on. To walk and not faint is the last promise and the greatest.

So the chapter that opened with a company of heralds told to comfort a beaten people comes to rest here. He does not faint. He does not grow weary. He gives power to the faint, and he never runs low himself, because what he hands out is not a portion of a supply but an overflow of who he is. Grass withers and princes go like stubble and the stars answer to the names he gave them, and the everlasting God stoops to the ones with no might left and trades them his own strength for their emptiness.

41.subtitle: Fear Not, I Am with You
41.intro: Overview. Chapter 41 opens the great courtroom sequence of Isaiah 40–48, in which God puts the nations and their gods on trial. The charge: who can declare what is coming? Who has roused the conqueror from the east (Cyrus, though unnamed until chapter 44)? The answer is God alone. Against the silence of the idols — “they are all a delusion” — God speaks the most repeated promise in all of Isaiah: Fear not, I am with you.

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.”
keyVerse.note: The command “fear not” appears more often in Isaiah 40–55 than anywhere else in the Bible. It is not a rebuke of honest fear but a reorientation: you are looking at the wrong thing. The antidote to fear is not courage but the presence of God — I am with you is the reason, not an afterthought.

41.reflection: God says “fear not” immediately after describing himself as the one who roused a conqueror to destabilize the world. The same God who orchestrates the turbulence is the one who says “I am with you.” What would it change about your current fears if you believed that the same God who governs what frightens you is personally committed to upholding you?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Court Is Called to Order
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God convenes a hearing and summons the coastlands to it (v. 1), then opens with a question rather than a charge: who stirred up the conqueror from the east, whom victory meets at every step (vv. 2-3)? He answers it himself in verse 4 — I, the LORD, the first, and with the last. Verses 5-7 show what the nations do with the evidence. They see, they tremble, and they go to the workshop: craftsman encouraging goldsmith, hammer encouraging anvil, and a new god nailed down at the end of verse 7 so that it cannot topple over.
verseByVerse.theology: The courtroom question in this chapter is never whether history is turbulent. Both sides agree that it is. The question is who is causing it, and the trial turns on one piece of evidence only: whether anyone announced it in advance. That is the credential God stakes his case on from here to chapter 48.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 7 is the sharpest picture of religion in the book: men steadying each other, then steadying their god with nails. Three verses later the LORD says the opposite sentence to his people — I will uphold you. The two religions in this chapter are distinguished by which way the holding runs.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me in silence, O coastlands; let the peoples renew their strength; let them approach, then let them speak; let us together draw near for judgment. Who stirred up one from the east whom victory meets at every step? He gives up nations before him, so that he tramples kings underfoot; he makes them like dust with his sword, like driven stubble with his bow. He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trod. Who has performed and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he. The coastlands have seen and are afraid; the ends of the earth tremble; they have drawn near and come. Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, "Be strong!" The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer him who strikes the anvil, saying of the soldering, "It is good"; and they strengthen it with nails so that it cannot be moved.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me in silence, O coastlands; let the peoples renew their strength; let them approach, then let them speak; let us together draw near for judgment."

A court is convened, and the summons goes out to the coastlands — the far edge of the known world, the places at the end of every shipping lane. Everyone is called, and the first instruction is silence.

Then a small phrase that anyone who has just read chapter 40 will catch: let the peoples renew their strength. That is the promise of 40:31, offered here to the other side. Bring whatever strength you can raise; the court will wait while you gather it.

"Who stirred up one from the east whom victory meets at every step? He gives up nations before him, so that he tramples kings underfoot... He pursues them and passes on safely, by paths his feet have not trod."

The evidence entered is a man on a horse. He is Cyrus of Persia, though Isaiah keeps the name back for three more chapters, and the description is of a campaign that never stalls: kings underfoot, armies turned to dust and driven stubble, and a general moving so fast through country he has never seen that his feet hardly seem to touch it.

"Who has performed and done this, calling the generations from the beginning? I, the LORD, the first, and with the last; I am he."

He answers his own question, and the title he gives himself is the whole argument in four words. He was there before the first generation was called and he will be there when the last one is finished — the one who opened the file and will close it. John hears the same voice give the same title on Patmos, and it belongs to the risen Christ (Rev. 1:17).

"The coastlands have seen and are afraid... Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, 'Be strong!' The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith... and they strengthen it with nails so that it cannot be moved."

Here is what the nations do with the evidence. They see it, they tremble, and then they go down to the workshop. It is an exact picture of frightened religion: men slapping each other on the back, the metalworker telling the goldsmith the soldering has come out well, everybody busy and encouraging.

Read the last clause slowly. They strengthen it with nails so that it cannot be moved. The god is finished by being fastened down, because otherwise it falls over. Keep that nail in mind for four more verses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–20 — Fear Not, I Am with You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The address turns, and everything hardens into promise. Israel is named servant, chosen, offspring of Abraham my friend (v. 8), taken from the ends of the earth and not cast off (v. 9); then the most quoted sentence in the book, fear not, for I am with you, with its three verbs of strengthening, helping and upholding (v. 10). Enemies who look permanent will be looked for and not found (vv. 11-12). God holds the right hand he has just promised to uphold (v. 13). The worm Jacob is given teeth and becomes a threshing sledge (vv. 14-16). And the section closes with water on bare hilltops and seven kinds of tree planted in a desert (vv. 17-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The grounds offered for courage are not circumstantial. Nothing in verse 10 says the enemy is weaker than he looks or the exile shorter than it feels. The reasons given are two statements about God — I am with you, I am your God — and the commands rest on them entirely. Fear is treated here as a problem of attention rather than of nerve.
verseByVerse.examples: Redeemer (v. 14) is a family word, not a religious one: the go'el was the nearest relative, the man legally obliged to pay off your debt, buy back the land you had lost and stand up for you in court. Boaz does it for Ruth. God takes the family obligation on himself, and the same title is the one Job reached for when he had nothing else left.

verseByVerse.quote: But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend; you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, "You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off"; fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But you, Israel, my servant, Jacob, whom I have chosen, the offspring of Abraham, my friend; you whom I took from the ends of the earth, and called from its farthest corners, saying to you, 'You are my servant, I have chosen you and not cast you off'."

The address turns, and the turn is audible: but you. Three names are laid down in a row, and none of them is achievement. Servant is a job God assigned. Chosen is something done to a person, not by him. And Abraham is called my friend — a staggering word to use of a man, kept and repeated by Israel long afterwards (2 Chron. 20:7), and picked up by James when he wants to say what faith finally amounts to (James 2:23).

Look at which fear verse 9 answers. It is not will I be rescued. It is have I been dropped. People in exile do not usually doubt that God is strong; they doubt that they are still his. So the sentence God puts in their mouths ends: I have chosen you and not cast you off.

"Fear not, for I am with you; be not dismayed, for I am your God; I will strengthen you, I will help you, I will uphold you with my righteous right hand."

Two commands, each with its reason attached, and then three promises. What is remarkable is that neither reason has anything to do with the situation. Nothing here says the Babylonian empire is weaker than it looks or the exile shorter than it feels. The reasons are two facts about God: I am with you, I am your God.

Try the test on yourself. Name the thing you are afraid of, then finish this sentence: my fear would lift if ______. The honest answer is nearly always a change in circumstances — the scan comes back clear, the money arrives, the person relents. This verse offers something else instead, and it is offered as sufficient.

The three verbs move outward: strengthen (something put into you), help (something done alongside you), uphold (something that carries you when the first two have run out). And the hand is not merely strong. It is righteous — a grip that will not let go and also will not do anything shabby to keep hold of you.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish. You shall seek those who contend with you, but you shall not find them; those who war against you shall be as nothing at all. For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, "Fear not, I am the one who helps you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, all who are incensed against you shall be put to shame and confounded; those who strive against you shall be as nothing and shall perish. You shall seek those who contend with you, but you shall not find them; those who war against you shall be as nothing at all."

The promise in verse 12 is stranger than it first sounds. It is not that the enemy will be defeated in front of you. It is that one day you will go looking for him and be unable to find him.

Anyone who has been afraid of a person for years knows how much room that person occupies. He is in the diary, in the stomach, in the last thought before sleep. Isaiah says there is coming a time when the search party goes out for that figure and comes back empty. Not smaller. Not manageable. Gone.

This is not a promise that the pressure lifts by Thursday, and Israel's own history is the proof: Babylon did not evaporate the year after this was written. It is a statement about the end of the account. Paul says the same thing in his own vocabulary when he names the last enemy to be destroyed and does not pretend it has been destroyed yet (1 Cor. 15:26).

"For I, the LORD your God, hold your right hand; it is I who say to you, 'Fear not, I am the one who helps you.'"

Now the nail from verse 7 comes back. There, men held their god upright so that it would not fall. Here, God holds the man.

The picture is a hand taken at a kerb. A small child crossing a road does grip back, and the grip is real, and it is not what keeps him safe — what keeps him safe is that the hand around his is not going to open. Everything in this chapter that looks like religion is a question of which hand is doing the holding.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel. Behold, I make of you a threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth; you shall thresh the mountains and crush them, and you shall make the hills like chaff; you shall winnow them, and the wind shall carry them away, and the tempest shall scatter them. And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Fear not, you worm Jacob, you men of Israel! I am the one who helps you, declares the LORD; your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel."

The tenderest promise in the chapter is fastened to the most humiliating name in it. A worm is what is underfoot: no defence, no speed, no dignity, something a man steps on without breaking stride. God does not flatter his people out of their fear. He agrees with their estimate of themselves and then tells them not to be afraid anyway, which is a far better comfort than being told they were stronger than they thought.

The name also has a future. When the psalmist reaches the bottom of his abandonment he says I am a worm and not a man (Ps. 22:6) — the psalm that begins with the cry Jesus made from the cross. The name God speaks over Jacob here is one the Son of God took to himself, in public, under nails of another kind.

Then a word that will dominate the rest of Isaiah: Redeemer. It is not a religious term but a family one. The redeemer was the nearest relative, the man legally obliged to buy back the land you had lost, pay the debt you could not pay, and stand up for you when nobody else would. Boaz is one for Ruth. God tells a worm that the Holy One of Israel has taken that place in the family.

"Behold, I make of you a threshing sledge, new, sharp, and having teeth; you shall thresh the mountains and crush them... And you shall rejoice in the LORD; in the Holy One of Israel you shall glory."

A threshing sledge was a heavy board studded with stone or iron teeth, dragged over cut grain until the husks broke off. So the worm gets teeth. What was trodden on does the threshing, and the mountains — every immovable obstacle in the book so far — go through it like chaff and blow away.

The Holy One of Israel is the title Isaiah heard shouted in the temple when he thought it would kill him. That holiness owed this people nothing and could have stayed at an infinite distance. Instead it came near, took the family name of Redeemer, and accepted the obligations that go with it. Holiness did not have to stoop to kinship; it stooped.

verseByVerse.quote: When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them. I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys. I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water. I will put in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane and the pine together, that they may see and know, may consider and understand together, that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"When the poor and needy seek water, and there is none, and their tongue is parched with thirst, I the LORD will answer them; I the God of Israel will not forsake them."

The scene shrinks from empires to a dry mouth. This is thirst at the stage where speech has begun to fail, and the answer is given in two clauses that do not quite match: they seek water, and God says he will answer them. The promise attaches to the people before it attaches to the supply.

"I will open rivers on the bare heights, and fountains in the midst of the valleys. I will make the wilderness a pool of water, and the dry land springs of water."

Rivers on the bare heights is deliberately the wrong place for water. Hilltops are where water runs off; springs belong in valleys. God names the ridgelines first, as though to say that the shortage was never about geography.

"I will put in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the olive. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane and the pine together."

Seven trees, planted in a desert, and not one of them is a survival crop. Cedar is timber for temples, myrtle is scent, olive is oil and light and food. A thirsty man asked for a cup and is given a forest with shade in it. God's answers in this book habitually overrun the request.

"...that they may see and know, may consider and understand together, that the hand of the LORD has done this, the Holy One of Israel has created it."

Verse 20 gives the reason for all of it, and the reason is attribution. Four verbs of noticing are stacked up — see, know, consider, understand — because a gift can be received and the giver still missed. The desert is watered so that somebody will say who did it.

Centuries later a man stood up at a festival where water was being poured out in the temple and said, if anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink (John 7:37). The last page of Scripture keeps both halves of this passage: no more thirst, and the Lamb himself leading them to springs of living water (Rev. 7:16-17).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — The Silence in the Dock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hearing resumes and the idols are called to give evidence (v. 21). The tests are simple: account for the past, or announce the future (v. 22); failing that, do something — do good, or do harm, anything at all that would prove you are there (v. 23). The verdict is returned in verse 24 before any answer comes, because no answer comes. God then produces his own exhibit: the man stirred up from the north, announced beforehand by nobody but the LORD (vv. 25-27), and the courtroom is empty of counsel (v. 28). Verse 29 closes the file: a delusion, nothing, empty wind.
verseByVerse.theology: An idol is not exposed by argument here but by silence. The gods of the nations are not refuted; they are asked a question and nothing happens, and the nothing is the whole case. Isaiah's verdict is not that they are weak but that they are not there.

verseByVerse.quote: Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, that we may know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come. Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be dismayed and terrified. Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Set forth your case, says the LORD; bring your proofs, says the King of Jacob. Let them bring them, and tell us what is to happen. Tell us the former things, what they are, that we may consider them, that we may know their outcome; or declare to us the things to come."

The hearing resumes and the gods of the nations are called to the stand. The examination is fair and the questions are open: explain the past, or announce the future. Either will do.

"Tell us what is to come hereafter, that we may know that you are gods; do good, or do harm, that we may be dismayed and terrified."

When nothing comes, the bar drops until it is lying on the floor. Do good, or do harm. Do anything. Frighten us, if that is all you have. God is no longer asking these gods to be good; he is asking them to be present.

The room stays quiet, and the silence is the entire case. Isaiah never argues that the idols are weaker than the LORD. His claim is more devastating and much simpler: there is nobody in there.

"Behold, you are nothing, and your work is less than nothing; an abomination is he who chooses you."

Note the arithmetic. Nothing would be bad enough. Less than nothing means the account goes negative — the thing does not merely fail to help, it takes. Whatever is served in place of God charges a fee for services it never renders.

There is a test here that can be run this week. Take the thing your peace actually depends on, and put it under Isaiah's two questions: can it tell you one true thing about tomorrow, and can it do one thing about tomorrow? A career, a portfolio, a diagnosis that has not come back yet, a person's approval — all of them fail both questions, and all of them are still being consulted daily by somebody.

verseByVerse.quote: I stirred up one from the north, and he has come, from the rising of the sun, and he shall call upon my name; he shall trample on rulers as on mortar, as the potter treads clay. Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know, and beforehand, that we might say, "He is right"? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed, none who heard your words. I was the first to say to Zion, "Behold, here they are!" and I give to Jerusalem a herald of good news. But when I look, there is no one; among these there is no counselor who, when I ask, gives an answer. Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I stirred up one from the north, and he has come, from the rising of the sun, and he shall call upon my name; he shall trample on rulers as on mortar, as the potter treads clay."

North and east in the same sentence is not a slip. Cyrus came out of Persia, which is east of Babylon, but the armies that took the city came down on it from the north, because that is the way the road runs. Isaiah is describing a campaign, not drawing a compass.

The verb is the same one from verse 2, and it is the point of the chapter: I stirred him up. The most powerful man in the world of the sixth century is introduced as something God set in motion, and the treading of rulers like clay under a potter's feet is work God assigns.

"Who declared it from the beginning, that we might know... 'He is right'? There was none who declared it, none who proclaimed, none who heard your words."

Three times, no one. No other voice in the ancient world put this on record beforehand. That is the evidence the whole trial has been driving at, and it is the reason these chapters keep insisting on prediction: anyone can explain a thing once it has happened.

"I was the first to say to Zion, 'Behold, here they are!' and I give to Jerusalem a herald of good news."

A runner appears in the middle of a courtroom. The word for what he carries is the Old Testament's word for gospel, already used of the messenger climbing the mountain in 40:9, and Isaiah will send him over the hills again with beautiful feet at 52:7 — where Paul finds him and puts him at the centre of Christian preaching (Rom. 10:15).

"But when I look, there is no one; among these there is no counselor... Behold, they are all a delusion; their works are nothing; their metal images are empty wind."

The case closes with an empty bench. Nobody rises to advise, nobody rises to answer, and the verdict on everything the nations were nailing down in verse 7 is three words long: empty wind.

One voice has been speaking in this room from the beginning, and it is the only one that ever was. He called the generations before there was anyone to hear him, he moved an emperor across a continent without consulting him, and he stooped to a worm and called himself its kinsman. The court adjourns with the LORD still on his feet, and the whole earth has nothing to say back to him.

41.theology:
The credential God stakes everything on. Chapters 41–48 are a trial, and the LORD chooses the ground he will be judged on: not power, which the nations could claim too, but prediction. Tell us the former things, or declare to us the things to come. He names a conqueror before that conqueror is born, and points to the record afterwards. It is the same logic Jesus uses in the upper room — I have told you before it takes place, so that when it does take place you may believe (John 14:29). God secures faith by putting his word on record in advance and then keeping it.

Two religions, told apart by one nail. Verse 7 is the picture of everything human religion can manage: a god assembled by committee, admired by its makers, and finally fastened down with nails so that it cannot fall over. Three verses later the LORD says I will uphold you with my righteous right hand, and at verse 13 I hold your right hand. In the workshop the worshipper steadies the god; in the covenant the God steadies the worshipper. Every idol eventually asks to be carried, and the whole difference in this chapter is which way the holding runs.

Fear not is not a rebuke. The command comes four times here, and never once with a reason drawn from the circumstances. Nothing suggests the empire is weaker than it looks. The grounds are two sentences about God — I am with you, I am your God — and three verbs, strengthen, help, uphold, that move from something put into a person to something that carries him when nothing has been put in. Courage here is not manufactured; it is a by-product of attention.

The worm and the Redeemer. God calls Jacob a worm and then, in the same breath, calls himself its go’el, the kinsman legally bound to buy back the family land and pay the family debt. Holiness that owed this people nothing took a family obligation on itself. And the name went further than Jacob: the psalm that begins my God, my God, why have you forsaken me has a man saying I am a worm and not a man (Ps. 22:1, 6). The Redeemer of Isaiah 41 took the name of the redeemed.

42.subtitle: The First Servant Song
42.intro:
Overview. Chapter 42 opens with the first of the four Servant Songs (vv. 1-9). God introduces someone he upholds, has chosen and delights in, puts his Spirit on him, and sends him to bring justice to the nations — by a method nobody expects, since he will not raise his voice in the street, will not snap a bruised reed, and will not pinch out a wick that has stopped giving light. He is made a covenant in person and a light for the nations, with three tasks: open blind eyes, bring prisoners out, carry light into the dark.

The world answers with a new song from every corner of the map, and God explains his own long silence as restraint rather than absence, in the startling image of a woman holding her breath in labour. Then the chapter turns and asks who is blind but the LORD’s servant — and means Israel. The nation commissioned to open eyes cannot see; the fire of judgment burns around a man who does not notice. That gap between the servant of verse 1 and the servant of verse 19 is the problem the rest of the book exists to solve. Matthew quotes vv. 1-4 in full of Jesus (Matt. 12:18-21), and the words of verse 1 were spoken over him at his baptism.

keyVerse.quote: “Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.”
keyVerse.note: The divine introduction of the Servant is the same language used at Jesus’ baptism (Matt. 3:17). The Spirit on the Servant and the justice for the nations are both explicitly taken up in Jesus’ ministry: Luke 4:18 (Spirit upon me) and the Gentile mission of Acts. The Servant Song is not merely predictive but constructive — it defines what the mission will look like before it happens.

42.reflection: The Servant brings justice without a raised voice, without breaking what is already bruised. This describes both Jesus’ method and the method he calls his followers to. Where in your life are you trying to bring about what is right through pressure, volume, or force — rather than the Servant’s patient, gentle faithfulness?
42.text: <sup>1</sup>Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.<sup>2</sup>He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street;<sup>3</sup>a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God introduces someone. Verses 1 and 2 give the credentials — upheld, chosen, delighted in, Spirit-endowed — and then the method, which is silence: no shouting, nothing raised in the street. Verses 3 and 4 promise that he will not discard damaged people and will not himself be damaged in the work. Verses 5 to 7 have the Creator commission him as a covenant for the people and a light for the nations, with three concrete tasks: open blind eyes, bring prisoners out, bring light into dark places. Verses 8 and 9 close the song with God refusing to share his glory with any other, and announcing new things before they happen.
verseByVerse.theology: The song sets out a Messiah whose power is not coercive. Justice will be established in the earth — the word is repeated three times — but by a man who does not raise his voice. Verse 8 sharpens the christology without arguing it: God will not give his glory to another, and in the same breath he gives this servant his Spirit, his commission and the salvation of the nations. The servant is evidently not an 'other'.
verseByVerse.examples: Matthew quotes verses 1 to 4 in full — his longest quotation of the Old Testament — to explain why Jesus healed crowds and then told them not to make him known (Matt. 12:18-21). The words of verse 1 were spoken over Jesus at his baptism (Matt. 3:17), and verse 7's three tasks are the shape of his public ministry. The bruised reed and the smouldering wick have comforted more frightened Christians than almost any other line in the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold my servant, whom I uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth justice to the nations."

God introduces somebody, and the introduction is all affection before it is any description of the work. Whom I uphold — the hand is under him. My chosen — the selection is God's and it is settled. In whom my soul delights, which is not the language of an employer about a competent worker but of a father about a son.

Stand at the Jordan seven centuries later and listen to what the voice from heaven actually says: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased" (Matt. 3:17). It is this verse, spoken out loud, over a man standing in a river. Before Jesus has preached a sermon or healed anybody, before there is a single thing on the record to be pleased about, the Father says over him the sentence Isaiah wrote down — and then the Spirit descends, exactly as the second half of the verse specifies.

Notice how much of God is in this one line. A Father who delights, a Spirit who is placed, and a servant who is sent. The Old Testament does not have the vocabulary the church would later need, and it does not need it here; it simply describes the scene, and the scene has three in it.

"He will bring forth justice to the nations." The word is mishpat, and it runs three times through the first four verses. It does not mean punishment. It means the setting right of things — the whole created order put back in good order, the crooked made straight, everything at last as it should be. And its reach is stated in the opening sentence: not Israel, the nations. The universality is not a late development in the servant's mission. It is in the first verse of the first song.

verseByVerse.quote: He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He will not cry aloud or lift up his voice, or make it heard in the street."

Here is the surprise of the song, and it is easy to read past. Every other programme for setting the world right runs on volume. It needs a platform, a crowd, a slogan and an enemy; it wins by being louder and more insistent than the alternative, and its progress can be measured by how much noise it is making. This one refuses all of it.

The picture is of a man who does not shout in the street — the street being the public square, where causes were argued and reputations made. He will bring justice to the nations without once raising his voice to do it.

Matthew noticed, and made this his explanation for something in Jesus that would otherwise look strange. Jesus heals everyone who comes, and then "ordered them not to make him known" — and Matthew writes, "This was to fulfil what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah," and quotes the whole song (Matt. 12:15-21). The reticence was not modesty and not tactics. It was the shape of the mission, written down centuries in advance.

There is a test in this for anyone who wants to see something put right. The instinct is always toward pressure — a louder argument, a sharper post, a confrontation that finally settles it. The servant's method is the exact opposite, and it worked; nothing has changed the world as much and almost nothing has been quieter at the start of it.

verseByVerse.quote: a bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice. He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth; and the coastlands wait for his law.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A bruised reed he will not break, and a faintly burning wick he will not quench; he will faithfully bring forth justice."

Both pictures are of things you throw away. A reed is a hollow marsh cane; a shepherd cuts one to make a pipe, and once it is bent or split it will not sound a note, so he snaps it, drops it in the water and cuts another — there is a whole riverbank of them. A wick is a twist of flax in an oil lamp; when it has burned down it stops giving light and starts giving smoke, and you pinch it out and put a new one in. Neither act is cruel. Both are simply what a sensible person does with something that no longer works.

The servant will not do it. And the two objects are chosen with terrible accuracy, because they are exactly what damaged people are like: not dead, but not functioning — still technically alight, still technically a reed, producing smoke and no note at all. It is one thing to believe God is patient with sinners. It is a harder thing to believe he has any use for someone who has stopped working.

Now verse 4, and here is what the English cannot show. "He will not grow faint or be discouraged till he has established justice in the earth." The two words are the same two words. The reed is ratsuts, crushed; the wick is kehah, faint. And the servant will not be yikheh and will not be yaruts — he will not grow faint, he will not be crushed.

Isaiah has written the sentence so that the servant and the people he rescues are described in one vocabulary. He will not break the crushed, and he will not be crushed. He will not quench the faint, and he will not grow faint. Whatever it costs to carry the smouldering and the splintered, he does not himself become smouldering and splintered under the weight of them.

Which is precisely the fear of anyone who has ever been the difficult person in somebody's life — that patience is a finite resource and you are drawing it down, and that one day the person carrying you will reach the end of it and be right to. The verse says the supply does not run out and the carrier does not wear through. And the coastlands wait for his teaching: the far edge of the world is standing on tiptoe for a man whose defining characteristic is that he will not discard the useless.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says God, the LORD, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and what comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it and spirit to those who walk in it: "I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness; I will take you by the hand and keep you; I will give you as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations,
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says God, the LORD, who created the heavens and stretched them out, who spread out the earth and what comes from it, who gives breath to the people on it and spirit to those who walk in it."

Before the commission is handed over, the one handing it over is identified at full length, and the credentials are cosmic: he made the sky, he laid out the ground, and every person walking about on it is breathing air he supplied. A commission is only as good as the authority behind it, and Isaiah spends an entire verse establishing the authority before a single word of the job is given.

"I am the LORD; I have called you in righteousness; I will take you by the hand and keep you; I will give you as a covenant for the people, a light for the nations."

The hand is the first thing. The same God who spread out the earth takes hold of one man's hand — the gesture is domestic, almost parental, and it is set immediately beside the making of the heavens.

Then two titles, and the first should stop the reader. The servant is not given the covenant, or sent to explain the covenant, or appointed a minister of it. He is the covenant — the entire relationship between God and his people existing as a person rather than as a document. Everything a covenant does, he does, because he is it. Centuries later a man would hold up a cup at a supper table and say that the new covenant was in his blood, and nobody at that table would have found the grammar surprising if they had known this verse.

And the second title reaches straight past Israel: a light for the nations. That is the sentence an old man will sing over a six-week-old baby in the temple courts — a light for revelation to the Gentiles (Luke 2:32) — and the one Paul and Barnabas will quote when a synagogue turns them out and they go to the Gentiles instead (Acts 13:47).

verseByVerse.quote: to open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To open the eyes that are blind, to bring out the prisoners from the dungeon, from the prison those who sit in darkness."

The job description, and all three items are concrete. Not principles — sight, freedom, light.

Read the Gospels with those three in your hand and the ministry of Jesus stops looking like an assortment of kindnesses and starts looking like a man working through a list. He opened literal eyes, more often than he did anything else, and he opened others that had never been shut. He let prisoners go, and told a synagogue in Nazareth that this was what he had come to do, reading the parallel passage from chapter 61 and sitting down with every eye on him to say the Scripture had been fulfilled that day in their hearing (Luke 4:18-21).

The dungeon is worth a moment. The word is the pit-prison, a hole with the door overhead, where a man is not being punished for a term but simply kept — no daylight, no timetable, no reason to expect the door to open today rather than any other day. That is Isaiah's picture of what the servant walks into. Not a courtroom where a fine is paid but a hole where somebody is sitting because nobody has ever come.

And the last phrase names the posture: those who sit in darkness. Not those who fight it, or search it, or cry out in it. Sit. It is what people do when they have stopped expecting the situation to change, and it is exactly where the light was sent.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols. Behold, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I am the LORD; that is my name; my glory I give to no other, nor my praise to carved idols."

The song ends where the whole of chapters 40 to 48 stands: God will not share. Not a sliver of glory goes anywhere else, and the alternative claimants are named — carved idols, the manufactured gods of chapter 40 who had to be kept from falling over.

Now set that sentence beside the seven verses in front of it. God has put his Spirit on this servant, called him in righteousness, taken him by the hand, made him the covenant in person, given him the light of the nations, the opening of blind eyes and the justice of the earth. If God gives his glory to no other, and has given all of that to the servant, then the servant is not in the category of "other."

Isaiah does not argue it. He puts verse 8 immediately after verses 1 to 7 and leaves the two standing next to each other, which is how the Old Testament usually does its deepest work — not by stating a doctrine but by laying two things down and declining to separate them.

"Behold, the former things have come to pass, and new things I now declare; before they spring forth I tell you of them."

This is the standing argument of these chapters for who is God: the ability to say what will happen before it happens. The idols of Babylon were explained by their priests after the event, which any of us could manage. The LORD announces beforehand and then brings it about, and he offers the record of the former things as evidence for the new ones.

And notice the gardening word — before they spring forth, as of a shoot breaking the surface of the soil. The new thing is already germinating underground while the announcement is being made. By the time anybody sees it, it will have been growing for a long time.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — A New Song, and the God Who Has Kept Quiet
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The response to the song is music. Verses 10 to 12 call for a new song from the ends of the earth — sea, coastlands, desert, the villages of Kedar, the rock of Sela — the whole map singing. Then verses 13 and 14 give two pictures of God that are almost impossible to hold together: a soldier roaring into battle, and a woman in labour who has held her breath as long as she can. Verses 15 to 17 have him levelling the landscape to bring blind people home by a road they do not know, while those who trust carved images are turned back in shame.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 is the most important verse in the section, because it answers the question the exiles were actually asking. God's long silence is not indifference and not absence: 'For a long time I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself.' The stillness was self-restraint, and restraint has an end. The two images belong together — a warrior's cry and a woman's cry are both the sound of something held back finally being released.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who has waited years for God to act on something has felt the silence of verse 14 from the inside and drawn the natural conclusion from it. This verse denies the conclusion without denying the experience. And the promise of verse 16 is exact about how the leading works: the blind are led 'in a way that they do not know', which is the only way anyone has ever been led by God.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise from the end of the earth, you who go down to the sea, and all that fills it, the coastlands and their inhabitants. Let the desert and its cities lift up their voice, the villages that Kedar inhabits; let the habitants of Sela sing for joy, let them shout from the top of the mountains. Let them give glory to the LORD, and declare his praise in the coastlands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Sing to the LORD a new song, his praise from the end of the earth."

The song about the servant is answered by a song from the world, and the geography is the whole point. The sea and everything in it. The coastlands and their inhabitants — the far edge of the known map. The desert and its towns. Kedar, which meant the black goat-hair tents of the Arab nomads out on the steppe. Sela, the rock city in Edom, in old enemy territory. And then the tops of the mountains, where people shout because sound carries.

Isaiah is listing places that had no share in Israel's worship and no reason on earth to join it, and he puts a hymn in every one of them. The mission announced in verse 6 has already produced its result inside the poetry: the light went to the nations, and the nations sang back.

A new song, specifically — not the old song sung louder. In Scripture the new song is always the song of people who have just seen God do something. It appears when the sea is crossed and when the exile ends, and finally around the throne, where the new song is sung to a Lamb who was slain and ransomed people for God from every tribe and language and people and nation (Rev. 5:9). Isaiah 42:10 and Revelation 5:9 are the same music heard from different distances.

"Let them give glory to the LORD, and declare his praise in the coastlands." Praise turns outward here without being instructed to. The redeemed do not sing privately; the song itself carries the report to people who have not heard it, which is why worship and mission have never really been two separate departments of the church's life.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD goes out like a mighty man, like a man of war he stirs up his zeal; he cries out, he shouts aloud, he shows himself mighty against his foes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD goes out like a mighty man, like a man of war he stirs up his zeal; he cries out, he shouts aloud, he shows himself mighty against his foes."

Notice what has just happened to the volume. Eleven verses ago the servant would not raise his voice or let it be heard in the street. Now God himself is shouting, and the word is the battle cry — the noise a line of men makes going forward.

The two are not in contradiction, and Isaiah has put them close together so that they will be read as one thing. The quietness of the servant was never weakness in God, and it was never all there is of God. It was a chosen method for a particular work. The same God who will not snap a bruised reed goes out like a soldier against what is destroying the people the reed belongs to.

Any parent understands the pairing without needing it explained. The gentleness shown to a frightened child and the ferocity shown to whatever frightened him are not two temperaments. They are one love, meeting two different objects.

And it is his zeal that is stirred up — the word for jealous, burning commitment, the heat a person feels about something that belongs to them. God is not described here as reluctantly discharging a duty of justice. He is described as angry.

verseByVerse.quote: For a long time I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself; now I will cry out like a woman in labor; I will gasp and pant.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For a long time I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself; now I will cry out like a woman in labor; I will gasp and pant."

This is one of the most astonishing sentences in the Old Testament, and it exists to answer the question the exiles were actually asking. Not is God able? They knew he was able. The question was: where has he been?

God answers it himself, in the first person, and the answer is not I was not there or I did not see. It is I held my peace. I kept still. I restrained myself. The silence that felt from underneath like absence was self-control — a decision, held at cost, for reasons that belonged to God and were never explained to the people doing the waiting.

Then he reaches for the one experience that combines a long enforced silence with an irresistible release, and it is not a military image at all. It is a woman in labour: the panting, the crying out, the point past which nothing can be held in any longer. The Lord of hosts describes himself as a woman giving birth, and does not soften it or explain it away.

If you have prayed about the same thing for years and heard nothing back, this verse is God's own account of what that silence was. It was not neglect and it was not the absence of a case; it was restraint. And restraint, by its nature, is pressure held back rather than pressure that does not exist, which means it has an end built into it. What comes out at the end of it is not an explanation. It is a birth — something alive that was not there before, and that could not have arrived any sooner.

verseByVerse.quote: I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their vegetation; I will turn the rivers into islands, and dry up the pools. And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them. I will turn the darkness before them into light, the rough places into level ground. These are the things I do, and I do not forsake them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will lay waste mountains and hills, and dry up all their vegetation; I will turn the rivers into islands, and dry up the pools."

The landscape is dismantled, and for a verse it reads like sheer destruction. Then the reason arrives, and it changes the colour of everything before it: the ground is being cleared for people who cannot see where they are going.

"And I will lead the blind in a way that they do not know, in paths that they have not known I will guide them. I will turn the darkness before them into light, the rough places into level ground."

Two things there deserve slowing down. The first is who is being led. In this chapter the blind are not a polite metaphor for outsiders — verse 19 is three verses away and will say plainly that the blind man is God's own servant. These are his people; their blindness is their own fault; and he flattens mountains for them anyway.

The second is the phrase in a way that they do not know. That is not an apology for the route. It is the specification. A blind man walking a road he knows can still tell himself he is managing; on an unfamiliar road he has nothing at all except the hand he is holding. God does not usually cure the blindness first and then hand over directions. He takes the hand and starts walking, and the not-knowing is the thing that converts the walk into trust.

"These are the things I do, and I do not forsake them." A flat, unadorned promise dropped into the middle of the cosmic engineering. Mountains flattened, rivers dried up, darkness turned to light — and the sentence he wants remembered out of all of it is that he does not let go of people's hands.

verseByVerse.quote: They are turned back and utterly put to shame, who trust in carved idols, who say to metal images, "You are our gods."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They are turned back and utterly put to shame, who trust in carved idols, who say to metal images, 'You are our gods.'"

The chapter keeps its two roads clearly apart, and this verse is the other one. One set of people is being led home along a road they do not know, by a God they cannot see. The other is standing perfectly still, trusting objects they can see very well, and going backwards.

Turned back is the picture. Not struck down — reversed. They set out somewhere and end up further from it than when they started, which is the characteristic motion of trusting something that cannot move.

And the shame is not God being vindictive. Shame is what happens when a thing is finally seen for what it is, in public, by everybody including its owner. A man who has given his life to an object that cannot act does not need to be punished for it in order to be humiliated by it; he only needs to see it clearly on a day when he badly needs it to do something.

Which is why the verse is set immediately after the promise about the hand. The whole question of the chapter is not whether a person will trust — everybody trusts something — but whether the thing trusted has hands.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–25 — Who Is Blind but My Servant?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns and the turn is brutal. Verses 18 and 19 summon the deaf to hear and the blind to look, and then ask who is blind but the LORD's own servant — the nation commissioned in verse 6 to open blind eyes. Verse 20 states the failure exactly: he sees many things but does not observe, his ears are open but he does not hear. Verses 21 and 22 set God's glorious purpose in the law beside the actual condition of the people who had it — plundered, trapped in holes, with nobody saying 'Restore!' Verses 23 to 25 ask who handed Jacob over, answer that it was the LORD, and end with a man on fire who does not notice.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the theological problem the servant songs exist to solve. Israel is God's servant and Israel cannot do the work: the people appointed to open eyes are the people who cannot see. Nothing in the chapter suggests that more effort or a better generation would fix it, and verse 25 forecloses the hope that suffering itself will teach — the fire burned him and he did not take it to heart. What is needed is not a better Israel but a servant who succeeds where Israel failed.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 20 describes a condition that is not confined to ancient Judah: full access and no attention. These were people with the law, the prophets, the temple and the history, and the problem was never supply. Paul spends three chapters of Romans on exactly this and refuses to explain it away (Rom. 9-11); the honest response to verse 25 is not to identify somebody else in it.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see! Who is blind but my servant, or deaf as my messenger whom I send? Who is blind as my dedicated one, or blind as the servant of the LORD?
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear, you deaf, and look, you blind, that you may see! Who is blind but my servant, or deaf as my messenger whom I send?"

The chapter has been about a servant since its first word, and the reader has spent seventeen verses admiring him. Now the same title lands on the nation, and it lands as an accusation. Who is blind but my servant? The people commissioned in verse 6 to be a light, and in verse 7 to open blind eyes, turn out to be the blind man in the story.

Isaiah stacks up four titles in one verse and they get worse as they go: my servant, my messenger whom I send, the one at peace with me, the servant of the LORD. Every one of them is an honour, and every one of them is being used as an indictment. The closer the relationship, the worse the blindness looks.

This is the hinge of the entire servant material, and Isaiah has arranged the chapter so that the gap cannot be missed. One servant will not break a bruised reed and will not himself be crushed. The other servant cannot see, cannot hear, and has to be led home along a road he does not know. They cannot be the same servant — and by chapter 53 it will be perfectly clear that one of them is dying for the other.

verseByVerse.quote: He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He sees many things, but does not observe them; his ears are open, but he does not hear."

A precise and uncomfortable diagnosis, because it is not ignorance. The eyes work. The ears are open — the Hebrew has them wide open, which makes it worse. The information is arriving in full and nothing whatever is being done with it.

These were people with the law, the prophets, the temple, the priesthood and the exodus in living memory. The problem was never the supply of revelation. It was attention. And the two halves of the verse are careful: he sees many things. He is not uninformed. He could pass an examination on the covenant. He simply does not observe — does not keep, does not guard, does not do anything with what he has plainly seen.

There is no comfort available in treating this as an ancient problem. A person can read this chapter, follow the argument, notice the Hebrew in verse 4, be genuinely moved by the bruised reed, and put the book down entirely unchanged by any of it. Seeing many things and observing none of them is the standard condition of a well-taught believer, and it is the specific danger of reading a lot of good material.

So the question the verse puts is not whether you have heard enough. It is what happened to the last thing you heard — the particular thing, six months ago, that you knew at the time was for you.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious. But this is a people plundered and looted; they are all of them trapped in holes and hidden in prisons; they have become plunder with none to rescue, spoil with none to say, "Restore!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The LORD was pleased, for his righteousness' sake, to magnify his law and make it glorious."

Verse 21 is the intention, and it is entirely positive. God gave the law to display his own righteousness, and he meant it to be magnificent — a whole nation living visibly well in front of a watching world, so that anyone could look at Israel and work out what God was like.

"But this is a people plundered and looted; they are all of them trapped in holes and hidden in prisons; they have become plunder with none to rescue, spoil with none to say, 'Restore!'"

And there is what actually happened, laid immediately beside it without a word of transition. Plundered. Looted. Trapped in holes — hiding down cisterns and caves while soldiers went through the villages. Prisoners with nobody to bail them out. And the last detail is the loneliest in the chapter: not one voice anywhere in the world saying give it back.

The measure of Israel's failure is the distance between those two verses. Not a standard fallen short of by a percentage, but a total inversion: the people who were to be the glory of the law are the people being carried off in pieces by their neighbours. Isaiah puts the intention and the outcome in adjacent sentences because the size of the gap is itself the argument.

It also explains why the answer, when it comes, cannot be more law. The law was glorious, the law was given, and this is the result. Something else has to happen — which is what the servant is for, and why chapter 53 will speak of iniquity being laid on somebody rather than being met by better behaviour.

verseByVerse.quote: Who among you will give ear to this, will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave up Jacob to the looter, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned, in whose ways they would not walk, and whose law they would not obey? So he poured on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Who among you will give ear to this, will attend and listen for the time to come? Who gave up Jacob to the looter, and Israel to the plunderers? Was it not the LORD, against whom we have sinned, in whose ways they would not walk, and whose law they would not obey?"

Isaiah asks who did this to Israel, and the answer is not Assyria, and not Babylon, and not bad luck. It was the LORD. The armies were real, their cruelty was real, and they will answer for it in due course — and behind all of it stood God, handing his own people over.

That is a hard thing to say, and notice that Isaiah says it in the first person plural: against whom we have sinned. He does not stand outside the sentence he is pronouncing. It is the same instinct as chapter 6, where he confessed unclean lips and then immediately added that he lived in the middle of a people of unclean lips.

"So he poured on him the heat of his anger and the might of battle; it set him on fire all around, but he did not understand; it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart."

The chapter ends on a picture that is hard to shake off: a man standing inside a fire that is burning all around him, and not noticing. Not defying it, not enduring it heroically — failing to register it. The judgment fell, the cities went, the people were carried away, and the thing it had been sent to teach was not learned.

Which closes the last comfortable option. If revelation did not open their eyes and catastrophe did not open their eyes, then nothing available anywhere in the human situation is going to. The chapter that began by introducing a servant who opens blind eyes ends with a people still blind and now burned as well, and the only door left in the room is the one the servant came through.

42.theology:
Two servants, and why there must be. The chapter names a servant who will not fail and a servant who cannot see, and it does so deliberately. Israel is God’s servant (v. 19) and Israel is the blind man in the story; the one appointed to open eyes has none of his own. Nothing in the chapter suggests that more effort or a better generation would close the gap, and verse 25 shuts the last door by showing that suffering itself does not teach. What is required is not a reformed Israel but a servant who does what Israel could not, which is where the songs are going.

Power that refuses coercion. Justice is promised three times in four verses and it is established without volume. The Hebrew of vv. 3 and 4 makes the point that translation cannot: the servant will not break the crushed reed nor quench the faint wick, and he himself will not be crushed nor grow faint. He will not become what he refuses to discard. Matthew reads this as the explanation of Jesus’ deliberate obscurity (Matt. 12:15-21).

The silence of God. Verse 14 is the Old Testament’s own account of divine delay: I have held my peace; I have kept still and restrained myself. The silence was neither absence nor indifference but self-restraint, and restraint by its nature has an end. What ends it is described not as a verdict but as a birth.

43.subtitle: I Have Called You by Name
43.intro: Overview. Chapter 43 is one of the most personally intimate chapters in Isaiah. After the cosmic sweep of chapters 40–42, God addresses Israel with singular directness: you are mine. The chapter contains the extraordinary promise that when they pass through waters and fire, God will be with them — and then the declaration that Israel is his witness, the one group in all the world called to testify that he alone is God.

keyVerse.quote: “Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.”
keyVerse.note: Three ground-level declarations: redeemed, named, owned. Each one is a complete answer to a different fear — the fear of condemnation (redeemed), the fear of anonymity (named), the fear of abandonment (mine). The chapter builds everything else on these three. Knowing you are named and owned is the prerequisite for walking through waters and fire without being overwhelmed.

43.reflection: God says “I am doing a new thing; do you not perceive it?” The question implies that the new thing is already present but not yet seen. Where might God be doing something new in your situation that you are too focused on the wilderness to perceive? What would it take to look up from the desert and see the river he is making there?
