I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you.<sup>4</sup>Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life.<sup>5</sup>Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you.<sup>6</sup>I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth,<sup>7</sup>everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made."<sup>8</sup>Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears!<sup>9</sup>All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right, and let them hear and say, It is true.<sup>10</sup>"You are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me.<sup>11</sup>I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior.<sup>12</sup>I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you; and you are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and I am God.<sup>13</sup>Also henceforth I am he; there is none who can deliver from my hand; I work, and who can turn it back?"<sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice.<sup>15</sup>I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King."<sup>16</sup>Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters,<sup>17</sup>who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick:<sup>18</sup>"Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old.<sup>19</sup>Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert.<sup>20</sup>The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people,<sup>21</sup>the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise.<sup>22</sup>"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!<sup>23</sup>You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense.<sup>24</sup>You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities.<sup>25</sup>"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins.<sup>26</sup>Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right.<sup>27</sup>Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me.<sup>28</sup>Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens on a hinge: But now (v. 1), spoken directly after chapter 42 ended with Jacob handed over to the spoiler. Four things are said before anything is asked — created, formed, redeemed, called by name — and then the sentence the chapter is built on: you are mine. Verse 2 sends the people through water and fire rather than round them. Verses 3-4 name a price, Egypt and Cush and Seba, and the reason for it: you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you. Verses 5-7 call the four points of the compass to give back the scattered, sons and daughters alike, everyone called by God's name and created for his glory.
verseByVerse.theology: The promise of verse 2 is precisely worded and the wording matters. It does not say there will be no rivers and no fire, and it does not say they will be diverted. It says they will not overwhelm and will not consume, and the reason given is a person rather than a technique: I will be with you.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is the one place in the book where the tenderness has no argument attached to it. Precious, honored, loved — three words about a nation that has just been described as plundered and imprisoned, with no explanation offered except that God feels this way about them.

verseByVerse.quote: But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: "Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine. When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But now thus says the LORD, he who created you, O Jacob, he who formed you, O Israel: 'Fear not, for I have redeemed you; I have called you by name, you are mine.'"

Two words carry this chapter, and they are the first two. Chapter 42 finished with Israel robbed, trapped in holes, given up to the spoiler, and nobody saying restore. But now. There is no repentance recorded in between. The change of tone is entirely God's doing.

Then four statements, none of which the people did anything to earn. Created and formed are potter's words, used of a nation as though it were a body being shaped. Redeemed is the family word from 41:14 — the kinsman who pays what you cannot. And then two clauses that go in deeper than any of them: I have called you by name, you are mine.

A great many people can believe that God saves in general and quietly doubt that he knows which one they are. Exile is a machine for producing that fear: you become one of a column of prisoners, a number in somebody's ledger. Against that, God does not say I have saved your nation. He says I have called you by name.

"When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers, they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame shall not consume you."

Read what this verse does not say. It does not say there will be no rivers. It does not promise a bridge, a detour, or a lower water level. The preposition is through, and it is used four times.

What is promised is a limit and a companion. The water will not close over your head, the fire will not finish you, and you will not be in either of them alone. Three men found out exactly how literally God means it when they were thrown into a furnace and a fourth figure was seen walking about in there with them (Dan. 3:25).

Ask what you have actually been praying for in the hard thing you are carrying. Nearly always it is the detour. This verse offers something better and harder: not an exemption from the river, but company in it and a guarantee about the far bank.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you. Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For I am the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, your Savior. I give Egypt as your ransom, Cush and Seba in exchange for you. Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you, I give men in return for you, peoples in exchange for your life."

God begins to talk about price. Ransom and exchange are commercial words, the vocabulary of a slave market: this much handed over, that one released. And the sums named are entire countries. Egypt, Cush and Seba are the wealth of the Nile from the delta to the far south, and God speaks of them the way a man might speak of emptying his account for one person.

Then he says why, and the reason is not usefulness. Because you are precious in my eyes, and honored, and I love you. Three words about a nation last seen being plundered, and the middle one is the strangest: honored. Not pitied. Honored.

This is language that ought to be checked, because it is easily sentimentalised. It is not saying Israel deserved it; the last chapter and the end of this one both say the opposite. It is saying that worth here is conferred rather than detected. A thing is precious because somebody prices it that way, and God has set the price of this people at the wealth of three empires.

That turns out not to be the final figure. The exchange language runs on through Scripture until it arrives at a Son of Man who came to give his life as a ransom for many (Mark 10:45), and at a sentence Paul writes with this chapter's arithmetic in his head: he who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. 8:32).

Egypt, Cush and Seba were what God was prepared to spend. In the end he did not spend them. He spent his Son, and the price tells the truth about the value in a way no adjective could. Nothing in creation was ever worth that much, and it was paid anyway.

verseByVerse.quote: Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth, everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Fear not, for I am with you; I will bring your offspring from the east, and from the west I will gather you. I will say to the north, Give up, and to the south, Do not withhold; bring my sons from afar and my daughters from the end of the earth."

The four directions are addressed as though they were jailers. North and south are spoken to directly and told to hand over what they are holding: give up, do not withhold. Nobody is negotiating. The scattering was the judgment of chapter 42; the gathering is God going round the compass collecting his own.

Note that the daughters are named. In a world where a genealogy could run for pages without a woman in it, the sons come from afar and the daughters from the end of the earth, and the distance given to the daughters is the longer of the two.

"...everyone who is called by my name, whom I created for my glory, whom I formed and made."

Verse 7 gives the reason the gathering happens at all, and it is not that the exiles were homesick. It is glory. That can sound cold until you notice what it rules out: if a people exists for God's glory, then their return is as secure as his reputation, and it does not depend on their usefulness or their behaviour on the road home.

John reaches for this promise when he explains what the death of Jesus was for: not for the nation only, but to gather into one the children of God who are scattered abroad (John 11:52). The compass points are still being emptied. John's last sight of this crowd has them out of every nation and tribe and people and language, and no one has been left behind in any direction.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The court reconvenes, and the first people called are the blind who have eyes and the deaf who have ears (v. 8) — Israel, exactly as chapter 42 left them. The nations are invited to produce evidence and cannot (v. 9), so God calls his own witness: you are my witnesses, and my servant whom I have chosen (v. 10). The testimony is that there is no god before or after, and no savior besides (vv. 11-13). Then two exhibits: Babylon brought down (v. 14) and the sea opened, with chariot and horse snuffed out like a wick (vv. 16-17). And on the strength of those, the command to stop looking backwards (v. 18) and watch a new thing spring up — a road through the wilderness, rivers in the desert, jackals and ostriches honoring God, and a people formed to declare his praise (vv. 19-21).
verseByVerse.theology: The witness is not chosen for his eyesight. He is chosen because he was there. What Israel is required to testify to is not doctrine she worked out but events she lived through, and the striking clause in verse 10 is the purpose: that you may know and believe and understand. Testifying is how the witness comes to believe her own evidence.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 sits four verses after the exodus has been rehearsed, which looks like a contradiction and is not. The former things are not to be forgotten but to be demoted from ceiling to floor: what God did at the sea is the smaller thing now, and the reader who keeps staring at it will miss the river already running behind him.

verseByVerse.quote: Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears! All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things? Let them bring their witnesses to prove them right, and let them hear and say, It is true. "You are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he. Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me. I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior. I declared and saved and proclaimed, when there was no strange god among you; and you are my witnesses," declares the LORD, "and I am God. Also henceforth I am he; there is none who can deliver from my hand; I work, and who can turn it back?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Bring out the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears! All the nations gather together, and the peoples assemble. Who among them can declare this, and show us the former things?"

The courtroom of chapter 41 reopens, and the first people brought in are the blind and the deaf. That is not a description of the nations. It is what God called Israel at the end of chapter 42: his own servant, with functioning eyes and ears and nothing coming through them.

"'You are my witnesses,' declares the LORD, 'and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he.'"

Here is the surprise of the chapter. God's case against every idol in the world rests on the testimony of the blind man in the dock. He is not chosen for his eyesight. He is chosen because he was there — at the sea, in the wilderness, at Sinai — and a witness is required for what he saw, not for what he understands.

Look at the purpose clause: that you may know and believe me and understand. The testimony is for God's sake in the world and for the witness's own sake at the same time. Something happens to a person who is made to say out loud what God has done: the saying of it is part of how the believing arrives. Any Christian who has stammered out an account of his own conversion and found his own faith steadier at the end of it has met verse 10.

"I, I am the LORD, and besides me there is no savior... I work, and who can turn it back?"

Three claims stand at the centre of the testimony: none before, none after, none besides. And the last clause is the one to take to bed: I work, and who can turn it back? Not who would like to, but who can. Jesus takes this verse's job description and hands it to a room of frightened men on a hillside: you will be my witnesses, to the end of the earth (Acts 1:8).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King." Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters, who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick:
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: 'For your sake I send to Babylon and bring them all down as fugitives, even the Chaldeans, in the ships in which they rejoice. I am the LORD, your Holy One, the Creator of Israel, your King.'"

The empire's own pleasure boats become the transport for its refugees. Babylon is a river city and its ships were a matter of civic pride; God says the day is coming when the people who cheered them will be going downstream in them, running.

Three words to notice in the middle of it: for your sake. Whole imperial histories turn over, and God tells a small displaced people that the reason is them.

"Thus says the LORD, who makes a way in the sea, a path in the mighty waters, who brings forth chariot and horse, army and warrior; they lie down, they cannot rise, they are extinguished, quenched like a wick."

Then the exodus, told in six seconds. Notice the verbs applied to the greatest army of its age: they lie down, they cannot rise, they are quenched. Pharaoh's chariot corps goes out like a candle pinched between finger and thumb — no battle described, no struggle worth recording, just a small hiss and the smell of smoke.

The same God who opened that sea has just said he will open a way home from Babylon. The argument of these verses is not that God is able in principle. It is that this has already happened once, at a specific place, to a specific army, and there are people alive who tell their children about it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it? I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people, the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Remember not the former things, nor consider the things of old. Behold, I am doing a new thing; now it springs forth, do you not perceive it?"

Two verses after rehearsing the exodus, God says stop remembering. The apparent contradiction is the point of the passage. He is not asking them to forget the sea; he has just used it as evidence. He is telling them not to let the best thing God has done become the biggest thing they expect him to do.

That is a real and common danger, and it wears a devout face. A man can hold his conversion, or a rescue thirty years ago, so tightly that it functions as a ceiling: God was great, once. Isaiah says the former things are the floor.

There is a rebuke folded into do you not perceive it? The new thing is not scheduled. It is already springing up, and the reason it is unnoticed is that everyone is still facing the other way.

"I will make a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert. The wild beasts will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches, for I give water in the wilderness, rivers in the desert, to give drink to my chosen people."

The jackals and the ostriches are the creatures that inherited the ruins in chapter 34 — the standard scriptural shorthand for a place where nothing lives. Here they are not driven out. They are given a drink, and they honour the one who gives it. Even the scavengers get water in this new thing.

"...the people whom I formed for myself that they might declare my praise."

The chain closes here: formed for himself, so that praise would exist. That is what the people are for, and what the road and the rivers are for. The Lord God takes a desert nobody crosses and a nation nobody wants, and out of the two of them he makes a river, a road, and a song about himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone drops without warning. The complaint is not that the sacrifices were poor but that they were never brought (vv. 22-23); God adds that he never made worship heavy in the first place. Then the sentence turns over: you have burdened me with your sins, you have wearied me with your iniquities (v. 24). And into that, with no repentance in between, comes verse 25 — I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. The chapter then invites the accused to argue the case (v. 26), notes that the fathers and the mediators both failed (v. 27), and ends in profaned princes and reviling (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The ground of the pardon is stated and it is not repentance, merit, or even pity: for my own sake. God forgives because of who he is, which is the only foundation that cannot be undermined by the person standing on it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel! You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense. You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel! You have not brought me your sheep for burnt offerings, or honored me with your sacrifices. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense."

After all that tenderness, the bill is presented. And the charge is not that the worship was badly done. It is that it was not done: no sheep, no sacrifices, no calling on his name at all. Whatever was happening in the temple, God says he was not receiving it.

The most striking thing is what he adds in his own defence. I have not burdened you with offerings, or wearied you with frankincense. The requirements were never heavy. God answers the ancient complaint that religion is exhausting by pointing out that he did not make it so.

"You have not bought me sweet cane with money, or satisfied me with the fat of your sacrifices. But you have burdened me with your sins; you have wearied me with your iniquities."

Then the two verbs swap shoulders. They were not burdened; they were burdening. They were not wearied; they were wearying. The load was real all along and it was on the wrong back.

Set this beside 40:28, where the everlasting God does not faint or grow weary. Both are true, and the difference is what kind of weariness is meant. His strength never runs down. His heart can be worn out by the people he loves — which is not weakness but the cost of caring about them at all.

Centuries later the God who says here that he never made worship heavy stands up and says it again to a crowd of exhausted religious people: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest, for my yoke is easy and my burden is light (Matt. 11:28-30).

verseByVerse.quote: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins. Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right. Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me. Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins."

Consider where this sentence is placed. It follows three verses of indictment and there is no confession in between, no promise of improvement, nothing. God interrupts his own charge sheet to announce a pardon.

The doubled pronoun is emphatic — I, I am he — as though nobody else were in the running for the job. Blotting out is the picture of ink being sponged off a scroll while the writing is still wet enough to lift; the record is not filed away, it is removed. And I will not remember is not divine amnesia. It is a promise about what will never be raised again, the way a debt cancelled is a debt that will not be mentioned at the next meeting (Jer. 31:34; Heb. 8:12).

Then the ground of it: for my own sake. Not because they repented, not because they were worth it, not because the sins were minor. If forgiveness rested on anything in them, it could be lost by something in them. Resting on God's own name, it cannot.

"Put me in remembrance; let us argue together; set forth your case, that you may be proved right. Your first father sinned, and your mediators transgressed against me. Therefore I will profane the princes of the sanctuary, and deliver Jacob to utter destruction and Israel to reviling."

God offers them the floor, and the invitation is heavy with irony: make your case, if you have one. What follows is the answer nobody wants. The first father sinned. The mediators, the very men whose job was to stand in the gap, transgressed. There is no clean generation to appeal to and no clean priest to send in.

So the chapter that began with you are mine ends in profaned princes and reviling, and it is honest to say so. The pardon of verse 25 is announced inside a history that is still running its course; the debt is cancelled while the consequences are still being lived through.

How a holy God blots out ink for his own sake and remains just is the question this chapter raises and does not answer. The answer is given at a hill outside Jerusalem, where the record of debt that stood against us was cancelled and nailed to the cross (Col. 2:14). The blotting was never cheap. It only looked free from the side that received it.

43.theology:
Grace with no bridge in front of it. Twice this chapter puts mercy immediately after guilt with nothing in between. Chapter 42 ends with Jacob handed to the spoiler; chapter 43 opens But now. Verses 22-24 charge a people with never bringing an offering; verse 25 blots out their transgressions. In neither case is repentance recorded first. This is not a denial that repentance matters — it is a statement about what causes it: the pardon comes first and the turning follows, which is exactly Paul’s order when he says God’s kindness is meant to lead us to repentance (Rom. 2:4).

For my own sake. The stated ground of forgiveness in verse 25 is God’s own name. That is the most stable foundation there is, because nothing the forgiven person does afterwards can weaken it — a pardon granted on account of merit can be revoked when the merit fails, and a pardon granted on account of God’s character can only fail if his character does. The question the chapter leaves open is how a just God can blot ink and remain just, and the answer is not in Isaiah 43. It is at the cross, where the record of debt was cancelled by being nailed there (Col. 2:14).

Through, not around. Verse 2 is one of the most quoted sentences in the Old Testament and it promises less, and more, than it is usually made to promise. Less: no diversion, no lower water, no cooler fire. More: a limit on what the fire may do, and the presence of God inside it. The three men in Nebuchadnezzar’s furnace had the whole of verse 2 fulfilled in an afternoon — not spared the furnace, not burned in it, and not alone in it (Dan. 3:25).

Witnesses who cannot see. God stakes his case against the gods of the nations on the testimony of a servant he has just called blind and deaf (vv. 8, 10). A witness is summoned for what he saw, not for what he understands, and the purpose clause runs both ways: the testimony convinces the court and steadies the witness, that you may know and believe me. Jesus hands the same commission, in the same words, to a group of men who had understood almost nothing until the previous week (Acts 1:8).

44.subtitle: I Have Blotted Out Your Transgressions
44.intro: Overview. Chapter 44 continues the sustained anti-idol polemic of chapters 40–48, but bookends it with two of the most tender promises in Isaiah. God pours out his Spirit on the offspring of his people like water on a thirsty land; the idolater’s absurdity is exposed in devastating detail; and Cyrus is named for the first time as the agent of Israel’s release. It ends with a call to sing — because the LORD has redeemed Jacob.

keyVerse.quote: “I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you.”
keyVerse.note: The metaphor is precisely chosen: a cloud dissipates without leaving a trace. God does not file Israel’s sins for later reference; he makes them as though they had never been. The motivation for returning is not fear of punishment — the sins are gone — but gratitude: for I have redeemed you. The imperative follows the indicative.

44.reflection: The idol-maker cannot see that half the log is warming his house and the other half is being worshiped as his god. Isaiah says a “deluded heart” blocks the perception. What are the things in your life that you are using half for legitimate comfort and half as ultimate security? What would it take to see clearly enough to say “shall I fall down before a block of wood?”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The address opens with a nickname. Jeshurun, the upright one, is the affectionate name Moses used for this people (v. 2), and God uses it of a nation in exile. Verse 3 gives the chapter's first picture: water poured on thirsty land, and in the same breath the Spirit poured on the next generation, so that the children come up like willows by a stream (v. 4). Verse 5 shows the result — outsiders writing the LORD's on their own hands. Verses 6-8 then return to the courtroom: the first and the last, no god besides, and a witness box that Israel occupies (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: The last clause of verse 8 is the strongest denial in the chapter and it is put modestly: There is no Rock; I know not any. The one who knows everything there is to know reports that he has never come across another god.
verseByVerse.examples: The Spirit is promised to the offspring rather than to the generation being addressed. A people who could see no future beyond their own captivity are told that the thing God is pouring out will land on their grandchildren, which is a particular kind of comfort and a hard one to receive.

verseByVerse.quote: "But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! Thus says the LORD who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen. For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants. They shall spring up among the grass like willows by flowing streams. This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But now hear, O Jacob my servant, Israel whom I have chosen! Thus says the LORD who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you: Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen."

Jeshurun is a nickname. It means something like the upright one, and Moses used it four times in his last songs — including once, memorably, of a people who grew fat and kicked (Deut. 32:15). God is using the family pet name of a nation currently in chains for its idolatry.

"For I will pour water on the thirsty land, and streams on the dry ground; I will pour my Spirit upon your offspring, and my blessing on your descendants. They shall spring up among the grass like willows by flowing streams."

The two halves of verse 3 are one sentence, and the second explains the first. What water does to cracked ground, the Spirit does to a family. Willows are not a rugged plant; they grow where there is a great deal of water and nowhere else, so the image is of a generation whose greenness is entirely a matter of what is running past their roots.

The promise is made to the offspring, not to the men hearing it. Peter stands up in Jerusalem centuries later, says this is what was uttered through the prophet, and watches the pouring begin (Acts 2:16-17).

"This one will say, 'I am the LORD's,' another will call on the name of Jacob, and another will write on his hand, 'The LORD's,' and name himself by the name of Israel."

Verse 5 shows what happens when the water lands. People who were never born into this family start claiming it, and one of them writes the owner's name on his own hand, the way a household slave was marked. He is not embarrassed to be owned; he is signing up for it.

Five chapters later God will say that he has engraved these same people on the palms of his hands (49:16). The writing goes both ways, and his was there first.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of hosts: "I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god. Who is like me? Let him proclaim it. Let him declare and set it before me, since I appointed an ancient people. Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen. Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, the King of Israel and his Redeemer, the LORD of hosts: 'I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god.'"

Three titles are stacked before the claim: King, Redeemer, LORD of hosts. He rules them, he is the relative obliged to buy them back, and he commands the armies of heaven. Then the claim itself, which the risen Christ takes on his own lips at the beginning and the end of Revelation (Rev. 1:17; 22:13).

"Who is like me? Let him proclaim it... Let them declare what is to come, and what will happen."

The challenge is the same one from chapter 41 and the terms have not moved. Anybody may enter; the test is prediction. It is the one credential that cannot be faked after the fact.

"Fear not, nor be afraid; have I not told you from of old and declared it? And you are my witnesses! Is there a God besides me? There is no Rock; I know not any."

The last clause is the most understated sentence in the chapter. God has just claimed to be the only God there is; he could have thundered it. Instead he files the report a truthful witness would file: I know not any.

Consider who is speaking. This is the one who calls the generations from the beginning, who counts the stars and names them, and who has been present at everything that has ever happened. When he says he has not come across another God, the modesty of the phrasing is itself the argument. There is nowhere he has not looked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–20 — Half of It He Burns in the Fire
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Isaiah stops arguing and starts describing. The ironsmith hammers his god and grows faint from hunger while he does it (v. 12); the carpenter measures with line, pencil, plane and compass and shapes the block into the figure of a man (v. 13); the tree itself was planted by a man and watered by God's own rain (v. 14). Then the sentence the whole passage exists for: half of the log warms him and bakes his bread, and out of the other half he makes a god and says, deliver me (vv. 15-17). The reason nobody notices is given in verse 18 and again in verse 20: eyes that have been shut, a heart that has been deluded, and a man feeding on ashes with a lie in his right hand.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 quietly reverses the first chapter of the Bible. There, God makes man in his own image; here, man makes a god in his, with the beauty of a man, to live in a house like a lodger.
verseByVerse.examples: The satire has no punchline because it does not need one. Isaiah simply puts the two sentences the same man says on the same afternoon next to each other — Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire, and Deliver me, for you are my god — and lets the order of events do the work.

verseByVerse.quote: All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame. Who fashions a god or casts an idol that is profitable for nothing? Behold, all his companions shall be put to shame, and the craftsmen are only human. Let them all assemble, let them stand forth. They shall be terrified; they shall be put to shame together. The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint. The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame."

The court is still sitting, and the idols are allowed witnesses of their own. The trouble is that they are the same men who did the carving, and Isaiah's verdict on them is the verdict he has just passed on their gods: they neither see nor know.

"The ironsmith takes a cutting tool and works it over the coals. He fashions it with hammers and works it with his strong arm. He becomes hungry, and his strength fails; he drinks no water and is faint."

Watch the strong arm give out. The man is beating a god into shape and halfway through the job he needs his lunch. Isaiah does not comment on it; he simply lets the reader notice that the deity has to wait while its maker recovers.

"The carpenter stretches a line; he marks it out with a pencil. He shapes it with planes and marks it with a compass. He shapes it into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house."

The tools are laid out one by one — line, pencil, planes, compass — and the craftsmanship is real. Nothing here is shoddy. The finished piece is beautiful, and that is precisely the danger: the better the work, the more convincing the lie.

The last phrase turns the Bible's first chapter upside down. God made man in his own image; this man makes a god in his, with the beauty of a man, to live in a house like a lodger. Every idol ever made has been a self-portrait, which is why they never say anything their makers did not already believe.

verseByVerse.quote: He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it. Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it; he makes it an idol and falls down before it. Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, "Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!" And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, "Deliver me, for you are my god!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"He cuts down cedars, or he chooses a cypress tree or an oak and lets it grow strong among the trees of the forest. He plants a cedar and the rain nourishes it."

Isaiah goes further back than the workshop, all the way to the seedling. The man planted the tree; God sent the rain that grew it. Before a single tool is picked up, the raw material of the idol has been supplied by the God it will be used to replace.

"Then it becomes fuel for a man. He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it... Half of it he burns in the fire. Over the half he eats meat; he roasts it and is satisfied. Also he warms himself and says, 'Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!' And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it. He prays to it and says, 'Deliver me, for you are my god!'"

This is one of the great passages of satire in Scripture and there is not a joke in it. Isaiah only puts things in order: the same log, the same afternoon, the same man. He cooks his dinner over one end of it and kneels down in front of the other.

Set the two sentences side by side, because they are both quoted. Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire. And then, an hour later: Deliver me, for you are my god. The first is honest and the second is desperate, and the wood cannot tell the difference.

What makes the passage uncomfortable rather than merely funny is that the man is not stupid. He is a skilled tradesman doing careful work. Idolatry has never been a failure of intelligence.

verseByVerse.quote: They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand. No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, "Half of it I burned in the fire; I also baked bread on its coals; I roasted meat and have eaten. And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?" He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, "Is there not a lie in my right hand?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They know not, nor do they discern, for he has shut their eyes, so that they cannot see, and their hearts, so that they cannot understand."

The explanation Isaiah gives is not the one a modern reader expects. He does not say the idolater lacks education. He says the eyes have been shut — and the shutting is God's, the same judicial closing pronounced over Isaiah's own hearers in the temple (6:9-10). Persistent refusal to see eventually becomes an inability to see, and Scripture is willing to say that God himself confirms the man in what he chose.

"No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment to say, 'Half of it I burned in the fire... And shall I make the rest of it an abomination? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?'"

Verse 19 gives the exact question the man cannot ask himself. It is not complicated. He has all the information; he handled both halves of the log. What is missing is the ability to put the two facts side by side.

"He feeds on ashes; a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, 'Is there not a lie in my right hand?'"

Feeding on ashes is the picture to keep: a man sitting down to a meal of what is left when the fire has gone out, and rising from the table as hungry as he sat down.

Here is the test the passage hands over. Not do I own an idol, which everybody answers correctly. It is the question in the man's mouth that never gets asked: is there a lie in my right hand? Take the thing you are quietly counting on — the savings, the reputation, the person whose approval settles you — and ask whether you have been feeding on it, and whether it has ever once fed you back.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–28 — Blotted Out Like a Cloud, and a Pagan Called My Shepherd
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter turns home. Israel is told she will not be forgotten (v. 21), and then given the promise the chapter is remembered for: transgressions blotted out like a cloud, sins like mist, and a summons to come back on the strength of a redemption already accomplished (v. 22). Creation is called to sing about it, mountains and forest and every tree (v. 23). The closing chain of participles runs from the God who stretched out the heavens alone (v. 24), through the God who makes fools of diviners (v. 25), to the God who dries up rivers (v. 27) and names Cyrus his shepherd more than a century before the man was born (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: The order of verse 22 is the order of the gospel. The blotting out is announced in the perfect tense and the command to return follows it. Nobody here is being asked to come back in order to be forgiven; they are being asked to come back because they have been.
verseByVerse.examples: Shepherd is the royal title of David, and God hands it to a Persian who does not know him (45:4 will say so plainly). The point is not that Cyrus was secretly godly. It is that God's purposes are not restricted to the people who intend to serve them.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me. I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you. Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Remember these things, O Jacob, and Israel, for you are my servant; I formed you; you are my servant; O Israel, you will not be forgotten by me."

Servant is said twice in one verse, as though the fear he is answering is that the job has been withdrawn. Then the last clause meets the deepest fear of a small nation in a big empire: not that God is unable, but that he has moved on. You will not be forgotten by me.

"I have blotted out your transgressions like a cloud and your sins like mist; return to me, for I have redeemed you."

The image is chosen with care. A stain has to be scrubbed and often leaves a shadow. A cloud does not: the sun comes up, the mist lifts off the field, and by mid-morning there is no evidence that anything was ever there. That is what God says he has done with the record of a nation's idolatry.

Then the order of the sentence, which is the order of the whole gospel. Not return to me so that I may redeem you, but return to me, for I have redeemed you. The homecoming is not the price of the pardon. It is the response to it.

"Sing, O heavens, for the LORD has done it; shout, O depths of the earth; break forth into singing, O mountains, O forest, and every tree in it! For the LORD has redeemed Jacob, and will be glorified in Israel."

The summons goes out to the sky, the deep places, the hills — and to the forest, and to every tree in it. Nine verses ago those trees were being felled and carved into gods that could not speak. Now the timber has found its voice, and what it sings is not about itself. The LORD has redeemed Jacob; the whole creation is called in to make the noise, because there is not a mouth on earth equal to the news.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: "I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself, who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish, who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers, who says of Jerusalem, 'She shall be inhabited,' and of the cities of Judah, 'They shall be built, and I will raise up their ruins'; who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers'; who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, who formed you from the womb: 'I am the LORD, who made all things, who alone stretched out the heavens, who spread out the earth by myself.'"

A single sentence runs from here to the end of the chapter, hung on a string of clauses that all begin who. It starts at creation, with two words that will matter in a moment: alone, and by myself. Nobody assisted.

"...who frustrates the signs of liars and makes fools of diviners, who turns wise men back and makes their knowledge foolish, who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers."

Babylon was the world capital of divination, a place where the state employed men to read livers and stars for the future. God says he makes fools of them, and in the same breath says he confirms the word of his servants. Two kinds of prediction are being set side by side and only one of them ever comes true.

"...who says to the deep, 'Be dry; I will dry up your rivers'; who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'; saying of Jerusalem, 'She shall be built,' and of the temple, 'Your foundation shall be laid.'"

Then the name. Cyrus is a Persian who will not be born for well over a century, and God speaks of him the way a man speaks of an employee: he shall fulfill all my purpose. The title given him is the shocking part. Shepherd is David's word, the word for Israel's king; it is handed to a foreigner who does not know the God who is handing it (45:4).

Two consequences follow, and they are not comfortable ones. God is free to accomplish his promises through people who have no interest in him. And the empires that look like the weather in which small nations must survive are, in this book, personnel.

The heavens were stretched out by one pair of hands and the earth spread out by the same pair, with no one standing by to help. That God bends over the ruins of a provincial city and says she shall be built, and over a burnt-out temple and says your foundation shall be laid, and moves an unborn emperor into position to do it. Nothing is too large for him to hold and nothing is too small for him to bother with, and it is the same hand in both.

44.theology:
Idolatry is not a failure of intelligence. The man in verses 12-17 is a skilled tradesman: he stretches a line, works with plane and compass, and produces something beautiful. He is not a fool with a chisel. What he cannot do is put two facts side by side that he handled himself an hour apart — half the log cooked his dinner, and the other half is being asked to save him. Isaiah diagnoses the failure as a shut eye and a deluded heart (vv. 18, 20), not an uneducated one, which is why the passage transfers so easily out of the ancient workshop. The modern equivalent is not a wooden figure; it is anything that is half legitimate comfort and half ultimate security, held by somebody far too intelligent to be worshipping wood.

The image reversed. Verse 13 says the carpenter shapes the block into the figure of a man, with the beauty of a man, to dwell in a house. Genesis has God making man in his own image; here a man makes a god in his. That inversion explains why idols are so restful and so useless: a self-made god never says anything its maker did not already think, never contradicts him, and therefore can never rescue him from himself.

Blotted out like a cloud, and the order of the sentence. Verse 22 chooses its picture precisely. A stain is scrubbed and may leave a shadow; mist burns off and leaves no evidence that it was ever in the field. And the clauses run in the gospel’s order — return to me, for I have redeemed you. The pardon is announced in the perfect tense and the summons rests on it. Nobody in this chapter is asked to come home in order to be forgiven; they are asked to come home because they have been.

A pagan called my shepherd. Cyrus is named a century and a half before his birth and given David’s royal title (v. 28). Chapter 45 will add that he does not know the God who names him. Two things follow. God’s purposes are not confined to people who intend to serve them, which is the same logic Peter uses about Herod and Pilate doing whatever God’s hand had predestined to take place (Acts 4:27-28). And prophecy of this kind is the credential these chapters keep staking everything on: anyone can explain history afterwards, and only God writes the name down first.

45.subtitle: The Creator’s Sovereign Freedom
45.intro: Overview. Chapter 45 is the fullest development of the Cyrus oracle and the theological argument behind it: God is the creator of all things, including darkness and disaster, and he can therefore use whomever he chooses — even an uncircumcised Persian king — as his instrument. The chapter culminates in the most universal call to salvation in all of Isaiah: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth.”

keyVerse.quote: “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.”
keyVerse.note: Spurgeon heard this verse preached at age fifteen and was converted. He later called it the simplest and greatest verse in the Bible: nothing required of the one turning except the turn itself. The universal scope — all the ends of the earth — is not a prediction of universalism but an unlimited offer. The chapter that began with an uncircumcised Persian king ends with an uncircumcised invitation.

45.reflection: God says he is a God who hides himself — and then immediately says he did not speak in secret or in vain. The hiddenness and the revelation are both real. Where in your life does God feel hidden? And what has he already spoken clearly that you can hold onto while waiting for more light?
45.text: <sup>1</sup>Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed:<sup>2</sup>"I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron,<sup>3</sup>I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name.<sup>4</sup>For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me.<sup>5</sup>I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me,<sup>6</sup>that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other.<sup>7</sup>I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things.<sup>8</sup>"Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it.<sup>9</sup>"Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'?<sup>10</sup>Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?'"<sup>11</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: "Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands?<sup>12</sup>I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host.<sup>13</sup>I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward," says the LORD of hosts.<sup>14</sup>Thus says the LORD: "The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you; they shall come over in chains and bow down to you. They will plead with you, saying: 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.'"<sup>15</sup>Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior.<sup>16</sup>All of them are put to shame and confounded; the makers of idols go in confusion together.<sup>17</sup>But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity.<sup>18</sup>For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): "I am the LORD, and there is no other.<sup>19</sup>I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right.<sup>20</sup>"Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, you survivors of the nations! They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save.<sup>21</sup>Declare and present your case; let them take counsel together! And there is no other god besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me.<sup>22</sup>"Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other.<sup>23</sup>By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.'<sup>24</sup>"Only in the LORD, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength; to him shall come and be ashamed all who were incensed against him.<sup>25</sup>In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — My Anointed, Who Does Not Know Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks to a Persian king by name and calls him my anointed (v. 1), then promises to walk ahead of him levelling ground, breaking bronze doors and handing over the treasures of darkness (vv. 2-3). Twice, in consecutive verses, the same qualification is added: though you do not know me (vv. 4-5). The purpose is stated in two directions — for the sake of Jacob, and so that the whole world from east to west may know there is no other (vv. 4, 6). Verse 7 makes the widest claim in the chapter, light and darkness, well-being and calamity; verse 8 answers it with rain.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is not a statement that God authors moral evil; Scripture is explicit that he tempts no one. It is a refusal to divide the universe between two powers. Nothing that happens, including catastrophe, falls outside his governance, and the alternative comfort — a disaster God had nothing to do with and cannot use — is no comfort at all.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is a prayer for weather. Righteousness is to come down like rain and salvation to sprout up out of the opened ground, which is exactly the shape of what happened when heaven sent down a Son and a virgin's womb gave him back to the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed: "I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron, I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name. For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have grasped, to subdue nations before him and to loose the belts of kings, to open doors before him that gates may not be closed."

The word translated anointed is mashiach, messiah. It is the word for kings and priests set apart by oil poured over the head, and it is used here of a Persian who worships other gods. No other foreigner in Scripture is given the title.

The picture in the next phrase would have carried weight in Babylon, where a king's right to rule was expressed by taking his god by the hand in procession. Isaiah reverses the grip. Cyrus does not take hold of God; God takes hold of Cyrus, and the loosing of the belts of kings is a picture of men being disarmed before he arrives.

"I will go before you and level the exalted places, I will break in pieces the doors of bronze and cut through the bars of iron, I will give you the treasures of darkness and the hoards in secret places, that you may know that it is I, the LORD, the God of Israel, who call you by your name."

Treasures of darkness are the contents of vaults: the bullion of conquered cities, stored where no light gets in. God offers a general the wealth of the world and gives the reason in the same breath — that you may know. The plunder is meant to end in a recognition.

"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me."

Two things sit in one verse. The first is the purpose: an empire changes hands for the sake of a small captive people whose name is on no map of consequence. The second is the qualification God attaches to his own commissioning, and he will repeat it in the next verse — though you do not know me. Cyrus is not a secret believer. He is a man being used, by name, by a God he could not have identified.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me; I am the LORD, and there is no other. I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things. "Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I am the LORD, and there is no other, besides me there is no God; I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me."

The commissioning of Cyrus is not an end in itself. It is evidence, staged from one horizon to the other, so that people who never heard of Judah will hear that something was announced in advance and then happened.

"I form light and create darkness; I make well-being and create calamity; I am the LORD, who does all these things."

This is the hardest sentence in the chapter, and it must be read for what it says. It does not say God authors moral evil; the New Testament is flat that he tempts no one (James 1:13). The word rendered calamity is the ordinary word for disaster and trouble — the famine, the invasion, the loss.

What the verse refuses is a tidy universe with two managements, a good power responsible for light and a rival responsible for the dark. Isaiah will not allow it. Everything, including the day everything went wrong, is under one hand.

That sounds severe until you try the alternative. A calamity God had nothing to do with is a calamity he cannot use, cannot time, cannot end and cannot redeem. Job knew which was the better comfort when he asked whether we should receive good from God and not evil (Job 2:10), and he asked it sitting in ashes.

"Shower, O heavens, from above, and let the clouds rain down righteousness; let the earth open, that salvation and righteousness may bear fruit; let the earth cause them both to sprout; I the LORD have created it."

After the hardest verse comes the loveliest, and it is a prayer for weather. Righteousness is not to be manufactured on the ground; it is to fall out of the sky like rain, soak in, and come up green.

Heaven poured down and the earth opened, and what grew was a child. The church has prayed this verse through every Advent for centuries, and it has never once needed to change a word of it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–13 — Woe to the Pot That Argues with the Potter
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two woes answer the objection the chapter has provoked: God cannot possibly work through a pagan. The first puts the objector in a workshop, a pot among pots, asking the potter what he thinks he is making and complaining that the design has no handles (v. 9). The second puts him in a delivery room, telling a father what he may beget and a woman what she may labour to bring out (v. 10). God then answers the substance rather than only the impertinence (vv. 11-12), and returns to Cyrus: stirred up in righteousness, and he will build the city and set the exiles free without a fee (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Notice what the clay actually complains about. Not the potter's competence in general but its own shape — your work has no handles. Most quarrels with God are design complaints, filed by people about the way they were made.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause of verse 13 is easy to skim. Cyrus releases the exiles not for price or reward. The most expensive thing in the chapter is the one nobody is charged for.

verseByVerse.quote: "Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'? Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?'" Thus says the LORD, the Holy One of Israel, and the one who formed him: "Ask me of things to come; will you command me concerning my children and the work of my hands? I made the earth and created man on it; it was my hands that stretched out the heavens, and I commanded all their host. I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward," says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Woe to him who strives with him who formed him, a pot among earthen pots! Does the clay say to him who forms it, 'What are you making?' or 'Your work has no handles'?"

Somebody has objected. The chapter has just announced that God will save his people through an uncircumcised foreigner, and the objection is easy to reconstruct: that is not how this is supposed to work.

God's answer puts the objector in a pottery. He is not a critic standing outside the workshop; he is one of the pots, and the complaint he is making is a complaint about his own manufacture. Your work has no handles is the detail to keep. The pot is not disputing theology in the abstract. It is saying: I would have been made differently.

That is where most quarrels with God actually live. Not in the arguments about providence but in a settled objection to one's own design — the temperament, the family, the limitation that will not lift.

"Woe to him who says to a father, 'What are you begetting?' or to a woman, 'With what are you in labor?'"

The second woe moves from the workshop to the delivery room, and it is deliberately grotesque: a man standing over a woman in labour, demanding to know what she intends to produce. Isaiah is not saying that questions are forbidden. Chapter 40 encouraged them and this book is full of God explaining himself. He is saying that there is a way of questioning that has misunderstood who is being born.

"I have stirred him up in righteousness, and I will make all his ways level; he shall build my city and set my exiles free, not for price or reward."

The answer to the objection is simply a restatement of the plan, and the last phrase is the one to notice. Cyrus will not charge. There is no ransom to be raised, no bribe, no fee for release — the exiles go home for nothing, because the arrangement was never between them and the empire in the first place.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–25 — Turn to Me and Be Saved
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Foreigners arrive confessing that God is in Israel and nowhere else (v. 14), and the response is one of the strangest sentences in the book: truly, you are a God who hides himself (v. 15). Against that, verse 19 insists he never spoke in a corner and never told anyone to seek him in vain, and verse 18 says the earth was not made empty but made to be lived in. The nations are summoned once more (vv. 20-21), and then the chapter opens all the way out: turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth (v. 22), with an oath sworn by God on himself that every knee shall bow (v. 23) and the promise that in the LORD his people shall be justified (v. 25).
verseByVerse.theology: The hiddenness and the clarity are both true and they are not in tension. God does not explain himself on demand, and he has never left the world without a word it could act on. What he hides is his timing and his method; what he has published is his character and his summons.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 23 is the sentence God swears by himself, and Paul twice takes it out of Isaiah's mouth and puts it under the name of Jesus (Rom. 14:11; Phil. 2:10-11). The knee that Isaiah says will bow to the LORD alone bows, Paul says, to a crucified carpenter — and no apology is offered for the transfer, because none is needed.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours; they shall follow you; they shall come over in chains and bow down to you. They will plead with you, saying: 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.'" Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior. All of them are put to shame and confounded; the makers of idols go in confusion together. But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"The wealth of Egypt and the merchandise of Cush, and the Sabeans, men of stature, shall come over to you and be yours... They will plead with you, saying: 'Surely God is in you, and there is no other, no god besides him.'"

Foreigners arrive, and what they bring in the end is not tribute but a confession. The sentence they say is the sentence the whole book has been arguing for, and it comes out of the mouths of people who were not raised on it.

"Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior."

Verse 15 is one of the most surprising interruptions in Scripture. It is not the complaint of an unbeliever; it is said in the middle of worship, by people who have just watched God act. The confession of his hiddenness comes from those who have seen the most.

Anyone who has walked with God for long knows this double experience. He is not vague; he is hidden — which is a different thing. A vague God has no clear edges. A hidden God has edges you cannot see round, and the frustration of not seeing round them is the frustration of dealing with someone real.

"But Israel is saved by the LORD with everlasting salvation; you shall not be put to shame or confounded to all eternity."

Set against the hiddenness is something with no time limit on it at all. The two adverbs at the end of verse 17 are the emphasis: everlasting, and to all eternity. God may keep his methods to himself. He has not kept the outcome to himself.

verseByVerse.quote: For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): "I am the LORD, and there is no other. I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right. "Assemble yourselves and come; draw near together, you survivors of the nations! They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save. Declare and present your case; let them take counsel together! Who told this long ago? Who declared it of old? Was it not I, the LORD? And there is no other god besides me, a righteous God and a Savior; there is none besides me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For thus says the LORD, who created the heavens (he is God!), who formed the earth and made it (he established it; he did not create it empty, he formed it to be inhabited!): 'I am the LORD, and there is no other.'"

The word behind empty is the word for the formless waste of Genesis 1:2. God says that is not what he was aiming at. The planet was not made as a void with some life accidentally on it; it was made to be lived in, which means that every settled house and occupied city is nearer the purpose of creation than the ruins Isaiah's readers were looking at.

"I did not speak in secret, in a land of darkness; I did not say to the offspring of Jacob, 'Seek me in vain.' I the LORD speak the truth; I declare what is right."

Three verses after the confession that God hides himself comes the denial that he has ever been secretive. Both stand. What is hidden is the timing and the method; what has been published is his character, his intention, and his invitation.

Hold the middle clause through a dry season: he has never told anyone to seek him for nothing. Whatever else is uncertain, the search itself has not been set up to fail.

"They have no knowledge who carry about their wooden idols, and keep on praying to a god that cannot save... Who told this long ago? Who declared it of old? Was it not I, the LORD?"

The picture of verse 20 is a procession of refugees carrying their gods on their backs — which is precisely where chapter 46 will open. The contrast is set up here and paid off there: gods that must be carried, and a God who carries.

verseByVerse.quote: "Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other. By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.' "Only in the LORD, it shall be said of me, are righteousness and strength; to him shall come and be ashamed all who were incensed against him. In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am God, and there is no other."

Everything narrows to one imperative, and the imperative is the smallest possible action. The Hebrew word is about facing: turn round, look this way. Nothing is required in the hand, nothing in the record, no qualification, no journey. A man on the far rim of the world is told to change the direction he is facing.

The scope of the invitation is deliberate. This is the chapter that began with an uncircumcised Persian being called God's anointed, and it ends by throwing the door open to every ends-of-the-earth outsider who will look.

"By myself I have sworn; from my mouth has gone out in righteousness a word that shall not return: 'To me every knee shall bow, every tongue shall swear allegiance.'"

God swears, and there is no higher name to swear by, so he swears by himself. What he guarantees is universal: not that everyone will be saved, but that everyone will bow. The knee bends either in worship or in surrender, and both are covered by the oath.

Paul quotes this verse twice, and the second time he does something that should stop the reader cold. Isaiah has God insisting there is no other and swearing that every knee will bow to him alone. Paul writes that at the name of Jesus every knee will bow and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord (Phil. 2:10-11), and he does not pause to justify the move. He did not think he was transferring the honour of God to somebody else.

"In the LORD all the offspring of Israel shall be justified and shall glory."

The last word of the chapter is the word Paul will build a letter on. Justified: declared in the right, by a verdict rather than by an achievement. The oath was sworn by God on his own name, and the name he chose to make it good by was the name of his Son.

45.theology:
An anointed who does not know him. Cyrus is given the title mashiach — messiah — and in the same breath told twice that he does not know the God who names him (vv. 4-5). Two things follow. First, God is not limited to willing instruments: the release of his people is arranged through a man with no interest in him, which is the logic Peter later applies to Herod and Pilate (Acts 4:27-28). Second, the title is a warning against reading too much into a role. Cyrus holds the office and never knows the Lord of it. Standing in a useful place in God’s plan is not the same thing as knowing God.

Light and darkness, well-being and calamity. Verse 7 is the chapter’s hardest sentence and its plainest. It does not make God the author of moral evil — James is explicit that he tempts no one — and the word translated calamity is the ordinary word for disaster. What the verse denies is a universe under two managements, with a good power over the light and a rival over the dark. Amos asks whether disaster comes to a city unless the LORD has done it (Amos 3:6), and Job, sitting in ashes, asks whether we shall receive good from God and not evil (Job 2:10). The doctrine is severe and it is the only version in which a catastrophe can be timed, limited and redeemed.

A God who hides himself, who never spoke in secret. Verse 15 and verse 19 are four verses apart and both are true. He does not explain his timing or his method on demand; he has never left the world without a word it could act on, and he has never told anyone to seek him in vain. Hiddenness is not vagueness. A vague God has no edges; a hidden God has edges that cannot be seen round, and the frustration of not seeing round them is the ordinary experience of dealing with somebody real.

The oath, and the knee. God swears by himself, because there is no higher name available, that every knee shall bow and every tongue swear allegiance to him (v. 23). Paul quotes it twice: once of the judgment seat of God (Rom. 14:11), and once of the name given to Jesus after the cross (Phil. 2:10-11). Isaiah’s whole argument is that this honour cannot be shared with anyone — I am God, and there is no other — and Paul, who knew that argument better than anyone, applies it to the crucified Christ without a word of explanation.

46.subtitle: Bel Bows Down
46.intro: Overview. Chapter 46 is one of the sharpest contrast-passages in Isaiah: the gods of Babylon are carried on the backs of weary animals, unable to save their worshipers; the God of Israel carries his people from birth to old age. The chapter also contains a pointed challenge to the stubbornly resistant: “remember this and stand firm.”

keyVerse.quote: “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.”
keyVerse.note: The contrast with Bel and Nebo is precise: they were carried to exile; God carries his people to salvation. The idol is the god you must transport; the LORD is the God who transports you. The whole life — from womb to gray hair — is held in arms that have never grown tired.

46.reflection: At what stage of life do you most easily forget that you are being carried? Youth tends to feel self-sufficient; success amplifies it; weariness in old age sometimes makes the carrying visible again. What would it mean, today, to let yourself be carried rather than carrying the weight yourself?
46.text: <sup>1</sup>Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts.<sup>2</sup>They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity.<sup>3</sup>"Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb;<sup>4</sup>even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.<sup>5</sup>"To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike?<sup>6</sup>Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship!<sup>7</sup>They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place.
