If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble.<sup>8</sup>"Remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors,<sup>9</sup>remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me,<sup>10</sup>declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,'<sup>11</sup>calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it.<sup>12</sup>"Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness:<sup>13</sup>I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Gods That Have to Be Carried
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Babylon's two great gods are named and shown being evacuated: Bel bows down, Nebo stoops, and the images are roped onto pack animals that are already tired (vv. 1-2). They cannot save the cart they are riding on. Against that picture God sets his own record with this people — carried from before birth, carried to grey hairs, four verbs of bearing in a single verse (vv. 3-4). Then the challenge, to whom will you liken me (v. 5), and the economics of idolatry: gold weighed out, a goldsmith hired, the finished god hoisted onto shoulders and set down in its place, where it stands and cannot move and does not answer (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: The whole chapter turns on one preposition and one direction of travel. Every other religion in the ancient world required its god to be transported. Israel's God does the transporting, and the difference is not a matter of degree.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 runs the promise the full length of a human life. Most comfort is offered for a crisis; this is offered for the slow decline — the years when a person is not in danger so much as diminishing, and needs to be told that the arms underneath have not been changed.

verseByVerse.quote: Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts. They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Bel bows down; Nebo stoops; their idols are on beasts and livestock; these things you carry are borne as burdens on weary beasts. They stoop; they bow down together; they cannot save the burden, but themselves go into captivity."

Bel and Nebo are not obscure. Bel is Marduk, the chief god of Babylon; Nebo is his son, the god of wisdom and writing. Their names are in the names of the men who ran the empire — Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar — the way a Christian family once named children after saints.

Once a year those two images were carried through the city in the great procession, gold in the sun, the whole population in the streets. Isaiah shows the same statues on the move again, and the second procession is nothing like the first. They are lashed to the backs of pack animals in a refugee column, and the animals are described as weary.

Read the verbs. Bows down, stoops, and then both again in verse 2. These are worship words. The gods are made to do to the invader exactly what their worshippers used to do to them.

Then the sentence that finishes them: they cannot save the burden. The god cannot rescue the cart it is tied to. Whatever else is uncertain about Babylon's future, the freight manifest has settled the theological question.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me, O house of Jacob, all the remnant of the house of Israel, who have been borne by me from before your birth, carried from the womb; even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save."

The pivot is immediate and the picture is exactly reversed. Babylon's gods are freight; Israel's God is the carrier. Nobody has ever had to lift him onto anything.

Look at how far back the carrying is dated: from before your birth. Not from the day of decision, not from the exodus, but from before there was anyone there to be grateful. And notice how far forward it runs. Most promises in Scripture are addressed to people in danger. This one is addressed to people getting old.

That is a rarer comfort and a more searching one. There is a stage of life where nothing dramatic is happening and something is quietly being lost each year — the strength, the names, the driving licence, the friends. It is not a crisis. It is a slow subtraction, and it is the point at which a person is most likely to feel that he has become a burden.

To that specific fear God says: I have carried you since before you could walk, and I will carry you when you cannot. Four verbs, one after another — made, bear, carry, save — and every one of them has God as the subject and the grey-haired man as the object.

The Lord Jesus told a story about a shepherd who finds a lost sheep and does not drive it home. He puts it on his shoulders and walks the whole way back rejoicing (Luke 15:5). The same shoulders later carried something heavier out of the city, and the sins of many were borne in his own body up a hill (1 Pet. 2:24). From the womb to the grey hairs, and from Bethlehem to Calvary, it is the same load-bearing God, and he has never once set his people down.

verseByVerse.quote: "To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike? Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship! They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"To whom will you liken me and make me equal, and compare me, that we may be alike? Those who lavish gold from the purse, and weigh out silver in the scales, hire a goldsmith, and he makes it into a god; then they fall down and worship!"

The question is answered with an invoice. Gold is poured out of the purse, silver is weighed on the scales, a craftsman is engaged at an agreed rate. Isaiah lets the reader watch a god being commissioned like a piece of furniture, and then, without a break in the sentence, watch the customers kneel down in front of what they have paid for.

"They lift it to their shoulders, they carry it, they set it in its place, and it stands there; it cannot move from its place. If one cries to it, it does not answer or save him from his trouble."

Every verb belongs to the worshippers until the last two. They lift, they carry, they set it down. All the god does is stand where it was put, and the reason it never moves is not patience.

Then the moment that matters, which is not the buying or the carving but the crying out. Somebody in real trouble is on his knees in front of it, and the verse records the response: it does not answer.

Here is the useful test, since nobody reading this owns a statue. Take whatever you would turn to first if the worst news came this afternoon. Ask which way the carrying runs. Do you maintain it, fund it, defend it, keep it upright and in its place — or does it carry you?

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The tone hardens into summons: remember, stand firm, recall it to mind, transgressors (v. 8). What they are to remember is a definition — I am God and there is no other, declaring the end from the beginning, saying my counsel shall stand (vv. 9-10). The proof is a bird of prey called from the east, a man summoned from a far country for a purpose he did not choose (v. 11). The chapter closes by addressing the stubborn of heart who are far from righteousness (v. 12) and telling them that the righteousness is being brought to them, and will not be late (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 10 gives as clear a definition of God as the Old Testament offers, and it is a definition by tense: the one who declares the end at the beginning. Prediction is not a party trick in these chapters. It is the difference between a God who governs history and a god who is carried through it.
verseByVerse.examples: The last two verses do not tell the far-off to come nearer. They announce that the righteousness is coming near instead — the same direction of travel as the carrying in verse 4, and the same direction as the whole gospel.

verseByVerse.quote: "Remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors, remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me, declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Remember this and stand firm, recall it to mind, you transgressors, remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other; I am God, and there is none like me."

Three imperatives about memory in one verse, addressed to transgressors. The problem is not that these people have never been told. The problem is that they have forgotten, and Isaiah treats forgetting as a moral condition rather than a mental lapse.

"...declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose.'"

This is as close to a definition of God as the Old Testament comes, and it is a definition in terms of tense. He declares the end at the beginning. Everything the last six chapters have been arguing sits inside that clause: a god you have to carry cannot tell you about tomorrow, and a God who tells you about tomorrow before it arrives is not the sort of thing you carry.

The counsel is said to stand, not to be attempted. There is no clause anywhere in these chapters about God's purposes being frustrated and rescheduled.

"...calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it."

Cyrus is a hunting bird here rather than a shepherd, which is the other side of the same truth: swift, sudden, and coming for something. He is called the man of God's counsel, and he has never been consulted about it.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me, you stubborn of heart, you who are far from righteousness: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off, and my salvation will not delay; I will put salvation in Zion, for Israel my glory."

Look carefully at what does not happen in these two verses. God addresses people who are described, in his own words, as stubborn and a long way from being right with him. The obvious next line is a command to close the distance.

It does not come. Instead God moves. I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off. The gap between the stubborn heart and the righteousness it lacks is closed from the far side, exactly as the carrying in verse 4 was done from the far side, and as everything in this chapter that actually works is done from the far side.

Paul is reading this kind of sentence when he insists that the righteousness of faith does not say who will ascend into heaven to fetch it down; the word is near you (Rom. 10:6-8). Nobody is being asked to climb.

The promise ends with a schedule attached: my salvation will not delay. Not that it will arrive eventually, but that it is not late now. Every year the exiles spent waiting was inside the timetable rather than outside it.

Righteousness came near in the end, and it came near in a body. The gods of Babylon had to be lifted onto shoulders and set in their places, and they never once crossed the room to anybody. The God of Israel crossed everything there is to cross, was carried in a womb, walked out to the far country himself, and brought his righteousness to the stubborn of heart in his own two hands.

46.theology:
Which way the carrying runs. The chapter is built on one reversal, stated in pictures rather than propositions. Bel and Nebo are roped to exhausted animals and cannot save the cart they are on (vv. 1-2); a god bought by the ounce is hoisted onto shoulders, set in its place, and stands there because it cannot do anything else (vv. 6-7). Israel’s God has been carrying this people since before they were born and undertakes to carry them to grey hairs (vv. 3-4). That is the practical difference between an idol and God, and it is a test anyone can run without owning a statue: the thing you fund, defend, maintain and keep upright is the thing you are carrying.

A promise for the slow years. Most of Scripture’s comfort is addressed to people in danger. Verse 4 is addressed to people in decline — the stage where nothing dramatic is happening and something is being subtracted every year, and where the deepest fear is not death but of having become a burden. God answers that fear with four verbs in a row, every one of them with himself as the subject: I have made, and I will bear; I will carry and will save. The shepherd of Luke 15 does not drive the found sheep home; he puts it on his shoulders (Luke 15:5), and the same shoulders bore our sins in his body on the tree (1 Pet. 2:24).

The end declared from the beginning. Verse 10 is as near a definition of God as these chapters give, and it defines him by tense: the one who announces the outcome before the events begin, whose counsel shall stand. This is why prophecy carries so much weight from chapter 41 onwards. A god that has to be carried cannot tell anybody about tomorrow; the God who tells you about tomorrow is by definition not being carried by you.

Righteousness brought near. The people addressed at the end are stubborn of heart and far from righteousness, and they are not told to close the distance (vv. 12-13). God closes it: I bring near my righteousness; it is not far off. Paul hears that note exactly when he says the righteousness of faith does not require anyone to ascend into heaven and fetch it down, because the word is near (Rom. 10:6-8). The gods of Babylon never crossed a room. This one crossed everything.

47.subtitle: The Fall of Babylon
47.intro: Overview. Chapter 47 is a taunt song against Babylon — the personified city addressed as a proud queen brought low. It is one of Isaiah’s most sustained pieces of rhetorical art: every claim Babylon made about herself is systematically dismantled. The proud city said “I shall be mistress forever” and “I am, and there is no one besides me.” These are divine prerogatives stolen by a creature. The judgment follows inevitably from the theft.

keyVerse.quote: “I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children.”
keyVerse.note: Babylon takes for herself the language of divine uniqueness — the exact words God uses of himself. The claim is both audacious and suicidal: to speak what belongs only to God is to put yourself in the place where only God can stand. The widow-and-loss of the next verse is the precise reversal of the claim: both things you said would never happen will happen in a single day.

47.reflection: The chapter shows what happens when a system — political, economic, cultural — begins to claim divine attributes: self-sufficiency, uniqueness, the guarantee of its own continuation. Where do you see that dynamic in the world today? And where might it be present, more subtly, in your own heart?
47.text: <sup>1</sup>Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate.<sup>2</sup>Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers.<sup>3</sup>Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one.<sup>4</sup>Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name— is the Holy One of Israel.<sup>5</sup>Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms.<sup>6</sup>I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy.<sup>7</sup>You said, "I shall be mistress forever," so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end.<sup>8</sup>Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children":<sup>9</sup>These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments.<sup>10</sup>You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, "No one sees me"; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me."<sup>11</sup>But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing.<sup>12</sup>Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror.<sup>13</sup>You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you.<sup>14</sup>Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!<sup>15</sup>Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Come Down and Sit in the Dust
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A funeral song is sung over a city still standing. Babylon is addressed as a queen and told to come down, sit on the ground, take the millstones and grind (vv. 1-2) — the work of the lowest slave in the house. Verse 4 interrupts everything with a sentence about the Redeemer that has nothing to do with Babylon at all. Then the charge is laid: God did hand his people over, and Babylon showed them no mercy and loaded the aged with a heavy yoke (v. 6). She said I shall be mistress forever and never thought about how it ends (v. 7), and she said I am, and there is no one besides me (v. 8) — which is God's own sentence in a creature's mouth. Widowhood and childlessness arrive together in a single day (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The crux of the chapter is in verse 6. Babylon was genuinely the instrument of God's anger and is genuinely guilty, and both halves are stated in one breath. Being used by God is no defence, because the cruelty was hers: no mercy was in the commission.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 is the theft that the whole judgment answers. I am, and there is no one besides me is what God says of himself four times in chapter 45. John hears it again on the lips of the last Babylon, still saying she will never be a widow (Rev. 18:7), which suggests the sentence outlives every particular empire that says it.

verseByVerse.quote: Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers. Your nakedness shall be uncovered, and your disgrace shall be seen. I will take vengeance, and I will spare no one. Our Redeemer—the LORD of hosts is his name— is the Holy One of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Come down and sit in the dust, O virgin daughter of Babylon; sit on the ground without a throne, O daughter of the Chaldeans! For you shall no more be called tender and delicate. Take the millstones and grind flour, put off your veil, strip off your robe, uncover your legs, pass through the rivers."

Babylon is called a virgin because no army had ever taken her. She is called tender and delicate because she had never had to do anything hard. Both titles are read out at the beginning of the sentence, the way a court reads out a defendant's full style before it is taken away.

Then the instructions, and each one strips off a layer of status. Come off the throne. Sit on the floor. Take the millstones — the hand-quern was the work of the lowest slave woman in a household, hours of it, every day. Put off the veil that marked a lady, hitch the robe, ford the river on foot with the rest of the deportation column.

This is deliberately hard to read, and it is meant to be. It is exactly what Babylon's own columns of prisoners had looked like for a century, and Isaiah is describing the queen walking in them.

"Our Redeemer — the LORD of hosts is his name — is the Holy One of Israel."

Then verse 4, which does not belong to the taunt at all. In the middle of a song about a falling city, another voice cuts in and says something about God, and it is not he is strong or he is just but our Redeemer — the family word, the kinsman who buys back what his relatives have lost.

Empires rise and are taken down and Isaiah gives them a verse or two apiece. The one line in the chapter that is not about Babylon is about the Holy One of Israel, and it is spoken in the plural by people who have nothing left except a relative who owns everything.

verseByVerse.quote: Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms. I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy. You said, "I shall be mistress forever," so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Sit in silence, and go into darkness, O daughter of the Chaldeans; for you shall no more be called the mistress of kingdoms."

Silence and darkness are what is left when a great city stops being a great city. No court, no delegations, no lamps in the palace windows. Isaiah does not describe the ruins; he describes the quiet.

"I was angry with my people; I profaned my heritage; I gave them into your hand; you showed them no mercy; on the aged you made your yoke exceedingly heavy."

Here is the hinge of the chapter, and it holds two things at once. God says plainly that the deportation was his doing: I gave them into your hand. Babylon was the instrument. And in the same sentence Babylon is condemned for how she handled what she was handed.

The commission did not include cruelty. You showed them no mercy is the charge, and then the detail that makes it specific — the aged. Of all the prisoners, the ones who could carry least were loaded heaviest.

Read that beside the chapter immediately before it. There God says he carries his people to their grey hairs and will not set them down (46:4). Here an empire takes the same grey-haired people and puts an extra weight on them. Two ways of dealing with the old, one chapter apart, and only one of them survives to the end of the book.

"You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end."

The sin named in verse 7 is not brutality but the assumption underneath it. Believing that you will always be in the position you now hold is what makes cruelty feel safe. Nobody who has thought seriously about how his own power ends treats the weak the way Babylon did.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children": These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure, in spite of your many sorceries and the great power of your enchantments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Now therefore hear this, you lover of pleasures, who sit securely, who say in your heart, 'I am, and there is no one besides me; I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children'."

Four words in the middle of that boast should stop a reader of Isaiah dead. I am, and there is no one besides me is not Babylonian court flattery. It is God's own self description, used four times in chapter 45 alone, now recited by a city about herself.

That is what the chapter means by pride, and it is more than arrogance. It is a counterfeit: a system taking the vocabulary of deity and applying it to itself — self-existent, unique, answerable to no one.

The second half of the boast names her two unthinkable losses. To sit as a widow and to lose her children were the ancient world's two pictures of a woman with no future and no protector. Babylon says neither will ever happen to her.

"These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day; the loss of children and widowhood shall come upon you in full measure."

Both arrive, together, inside twenty-four hours. God does not argue with the boast; he simply dates it.

The same sentence is still being said. John, writing about the last Babylon of all, hears a city say in her heart that she sits as a queen and is no widow and will never see mourning (Rev. 18:7). Empires change; the sentence does not.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–15 — Let Your Astrologers Stand Up and Save You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second half turns to the machinery of Babylonian security. She felt safe in her wickedness and said no one sees me (v. 10); against that come three things she cannot handle — an evil she cannot charm away, a disaster she cannot atone for, a ruin she will not see coming (v. 11). Her enchanters are invited to try (v. 12), and then the astrologers by name: the men who divide the heavens and read the new moons (v. 13). The answer is a bonfire in which they are the fuel and nobody gets warm (v. 14), and the last line of the chapter is five words long: there is no one to save you (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 11 puts the finger on the one commodity Babylon never stocked. She could charm, predict and negotiate; she could not atone. An empire can insure against almost everything except guilt.

verseByVerse.quote: You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, "No one sees me"; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray, and you said in your heart, "I am, and there is no one besides me." But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You felt secure in your wickedness; you said, 'No one sees me'; your wisdom and your knowledge led you astray."

The security came from two things. The first is the belief that nobody was watching — which is what makes wickedness feel safe rather than merely profitable. The second is stranger: her wisdom and knowledge are named as the things that led her astray. Babylon was the most learned city on earth, and Isaiah says the learning was the road out.

"But evil shall come upon you, which you will not know how to charm away; disaster shall fall upon you, for which you will not be able to atone; and ruin shall come upon you suddenly, of which you know nothing."

Three troubles are named and each is matched to a Babylonian speciality that fails. She had charms, and this cannot be charmed. She had rituals of appeasement, and this cannot be atoned for. She had astronomers, and this one is not on the charts.

The middle clause is the deepest of the three. Disaster... for which you will not be able to atone. Babylon could buy grain, armies, allies and information; the one thing not for sale anywhere in the empire was the covering of guilt.

That is the gap the whole Bible is written across. The word Isaiah uses here for atonement is the temple word, the one attached to blood and a mercy seat, and five chapters later it will be attached to a man who was wounded for transgressions that were not his. What Babylon could not purchase at any price was given away.

verseByVerse.quote: Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror. You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you. Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before! Such to you are those with whom you have labored, who have done business with you from your youth; they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Stand fast in your enchantments and your many sorceries, with which you have labored from your youth; perhaps you may be able to succeed; perhaps you may inspire terror."

The tone here is not rage but something colder. God tells her to go ahead and use everything she has. Perhaps, he says, twice. It is the voice of a man watching somebody try a key that will not turn.

"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you, those who divide the heavens, who gaze at the stars, who at the new moons make known what shall come upon you."

The astrologers are described precisely and not unfairly. Babylonian sky-watching was serious work: the heavens divided into sections, records kept for centuries, forecasts issued at each new moon. This was the best predictive science in the world, and the whole of chapters 41 to 48 has been asking one question of it — did anyone tell you Cyrus was coming?

She is also wearied by her counsellors. Managing the machinery of security had become exhausting in itself.

"Behold, they are like stubble; the fire consumes them; they cannot deliver themselves from the power of the flame. No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"

The image turns savage and then oddly domestic. The wise men go up like dry straw, and Isaiah adds a line that is almost an aside: you could not even warm your hands at this. In chapter 44 the idolater at least got a hot meal out of half his log. Here the fire consumes and gives nothing back.

"...they wander about, each in his own direction; there is no one to save you."

The last sentence of the chapter is flat and final: there is no one to save you. Which is true of Babylon, and is not a statement about the universe. Four chapters earlier the same voice said that besides him there is no savior (43:11), and the whole point of the trial in these chapters is that a Savior exists, has said so out loud in advance, and is at that moment arranging a homecoming for prisoners who had nothing to bring him.

47.theology:
An instrument can still be guilty. Verse 6 says both things without flinching: I gave them into your hand, and you showed them no mercy. God’s sovereignty over an event does not transfer the moral responsibility for it to him, and being used by God is not a defence at the bar. The specific charge is the treatment of the aged — the prisoners least able to carry were loaded most heavily — which lands with particular force one chapter after God promised to carry his own people to their grey hairs (46:4).

The sentence that empires say. I am, and there is no one besides me (vv. 8, 10) is not a Babylonian phrase. It is God’s, repeated four times in chapter 45, and here a city says it about herself. That is what idolatry looks like at civic scale: not carved wood but a system claiming the attributes of deity — self-existence, uniqueness, and a guaranteed future. John hears the last Babylon saying it still, insisting she will never be a widow (Rev. 18:7). The specific empire always falls; the sentence keeps being spoken by the next one.

The one thing not for sale. Three disasters are named in verse 11 and each defeats a Babylonian speciality: an evil that cannot be charmed away, a ruin the astronomers did not forecast, and, in the middle, a disaster for which you will not be able to atone. Atonement is the temple word, the one attached to blood and a mercy seat. The richest city on earth could buy grain, armies, allies and intelligence, and could not buy the covering of guilt. Five chapters later that covering is provided, without charge, by a man wounded for transgressions that were not his own (53:5).

How the chapter ends, and why it is not the last word. There is no one to save you (v. 15) is a verdict on Babylon, not a description of the world. Four chapters earlier the same voice said besides me there is no savior (43:11), and the trial running through chapters 41–48 exists to prove that a Savior is present, announced in advance, and already arranging a homecoming. The tragedy of Babylon is not that no rescuer existed. It is that she had said aloud that she needed none.

48.subtitle: Refined in the Furnace of Affliction
48.intro: Overview. Chapter 48 closes the first movement of Isaiah 40–55 with a complex word to Israel — a mixture of rebuke and promise. Israel calls itself by the name of the LORD but not in truth; it has been obstinate and stubborn. God has refined them in the furnace of affliction for his own name’s sake. And then the call: go out from Babylon with singing — and the lament that if only they had listened, their peace would have been like a river.

keyVerse.quote: “Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea.”
keyVerse.note: The “oh that” is a divine wish — God grieving over the peace his people did not take hold of. River-peace suggests both depth and continuity: not a burst of feeling but a sustained, flowing shalom. It was always available; obedience was always the channel. The lament is an invitation dressed as regret.

48.reflection: God says he refined Israel “for my own sake” — not primarily for their growth but for his name’s vindication. How does it feel to know that God’s purposes in your suffering may have more to do with his name than your comfort? And what does the promise of river-peace say to you about the connection between obedience and the peace you most want?
48.text: <sup>1</sup>Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right.<sup>2</sup>For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name.<sup>3</sup>"The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass.<sup>4</sup>Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass,<sup>5</sup>I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.'<sup>6</sup>"You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known.<sup>7</sup>They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.'<sup>8</sup>You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel.<sup>9</sup>"For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off.<sup>10</sup>Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction.<sup>11</sup>For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another.<sup>12</sup>"Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last.<sup>13</sup>My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together.<sup>14</sup>"Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans.<sup>15</sup>I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way.<sup>16</sup>Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit.<sup>17</sup>Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go.<sup>18</sup>Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea;<sup>19</sup>your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me."<sup>20</sup>Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, "The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!"<sup>21</sup>They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out.<sup>22</sup>"There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The last chapter of the trial opens by describing a very religious people and then adding four words: but not in truth or right (v. 1). They swear by the name and lean on the God of Israel (v. 2), and God says their necks are iron and their foreheads brass (v. 4). He explains why he announced the former things so far in advance — to close off the excuse that an idol did them (v. 5) — and why he now announces new things nobody has heard, to close off the excuse that they knew already (vv. 6-7). Then the reason they still exist: for his name's sake he defers his anger (v. 9), the furnace of affliction has refined them but not as silver (v. 10), and the motive is stated twice over in verse 11 — for my own sake.
verseByVerse.theology: God's reason for keeping this people is given plainly and it is not their improvement. Twice in one verse: for my own sake. That is the most secure ground available, because a commitment God has made to his own name cannot be cancelled by anything in the people it protects.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 4 is a physical picture. An iron sinew in the neck is a neck that will not turn to look; a brass forehead is a face that cannot be made to blush. Stubbornness is described as a posture and a complexion rather than an opinion.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel, and who came from the waters of Judah, who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right. For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name. "The former things I declared of old; they went out from my mouth, and I announced them; then suddenly I did them, and they came to pass. Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them, my carved image and my metal image commanded them.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Hear this, O house of Jacob, who are called by the name of Israel... who swear by the name of the LORD and confess the God of Israel, but not in truth or right. For they call themselves after the holy city, and stay themselves on the God of Israel; the LORD of hosts is his name."

Read the first two verses without the qualifying clause and they describe model believers. They carry the covenant name, they swear by the LORD, they confess the God of Israel, they identify themselves with the holy city, they lean on him. Every box is ticked.

Then the four words that undo it: but not in truth or right. Isaiah is not describing pagans. He is describing the religious, and the charge is that the vocabulary is entirely correct and the reality behind it is not there.

"Because I know that you are obstinate, and your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead brass, I declared them to you from of old, before they came to pass I announced them to you, lest you should say, 'My idol did them.'"

The diagnosis is given as anatomy. An iron sinew in the neck is a neck that will not turn when someone calls; a brass forehead is a face that has lost the ability to colour. Stubbornness is not treated as a view a person holds but as something that has happened to his body.

What God does about it is remarkable. He does not remove the stubbornness first. He works around it: the prophecies were issued centuries early specifically so that this iron-necked people could not credit the outcome to a carved image. God anticipated the excuse and closed the door before anyone reached it.

verseByVerse.quote: "You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known. They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.' You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You have heard; now see all this; and will you not declare it? From this time forth I announce to you new things, hidden things that you have not known. They are created now, not long ago; before today you have never heard of them, lest you should say, 'Behold, I knew them.'"

The second excuse is closed the same way as the first. Old prophecies stopped them crediting the idols; brand-new ones stop them claiming they had worked it out themselves. God knows both faces of the human heart here — the one that gives the credit elsewhere, and the one that takes it.

There is something almost humorous in it, and something serious. God is arranging his revelation so that no available form of self-congratulation will fit.

"You have never heard, you have never known, from of old your ear has not been opened. For I knew that you would surely deal treacherously, and that from before birth you were called a rebel."

The last clause goes further than anything else in the chapter. Not that they became rebels under pressure, or that exile spoiled them, but that the name applied before they were born. This is what the church later called original sin, said in five words and without any of the technical vocabulary.

Consider what it does to the chapter. If the rebellion is that old, then nothing in the following verses is a reward for a promising start. And notice the phrase in the middle: your ear has not been opened. Two chapters further on, a servant will stand up in this same book and say that the Lord GOD has opened his ear, and that he was not rebellious (50:5).

verseByVerse.quote: "For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off. Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction. For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For my name's sake I defer my anger; for the sake of my praise I restrain it for you, that I may not cut you off."

The verse states why the nation still exists, and the answer has nothing to do with the nation. Anger is deferred and restrained — both words imply something real being held back rather than something that was never felt.

"Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have tried you in the furnace of affliction."

The qualification in the middle is honest and slightly bleak. Silver refining is taken to completion: the heat goes up until the dross is off and the metal is pure. God says the exile was not that. Either the fire was restrained, because refining this people to that standard would have consumed them, or the yield was disappointing — the ore did not produce much silver. The Hebrew allows both and the chapter's argument fits either. What it does not allow is the sentimental reading in which suffering automatically improves people.

The furnace is still God's furnace. Nothing enters it that he did not permit and nothing leaves it before his purpose is served, which is exactly how Peter puts it when he tells scattered Christians that their tested faith is more precious than gold refined by fire (1 Pet. 1:7).

"For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? My glory I will not give to another."

He says it twice, as though he expected to be misheard. Not for your sake. For mine.

That can sound cold until it is examined, and then it turns out to be the one ground solid enough to hold a person who knows his own record. A rescue undertaken because the rescued were worth it can be reconsidered when they prove they were not. A rescue undertaken for the sake of God's own name can only fail if he stops caring what his name is worth. He has staked his reputation on keeping people who have given him no reason to keep them, and the staking is the security.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–19 — If Only You Had Paid Attention
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls for attention and rehearses who is speaking: the first and the last, whose hand laid the earth's foundation and whose right hand spread the heavens, so that when he calls them they stand to attention together (vv. 12-13). Cyrus is referred to once more as the man God loves and called and will prosper (vv. 14-15), and verse 16 ends with a sentence nobody expects: And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. Then the tone changes entirely. The Redeemer who teaches his people to profit says Oh that you had paid attention (v. 18), and describes the peace like a river and the descendants like sand that they did not have (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 18 is a lament rather than a threat. God is not warning them what they will lose; he is grieving what they did not take. Jesus weeps over a city in exactly the same construction, saying would that you knew the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41-42).
verseByVerse.examples: The end of verse 16 is one of the Old Testament's genuine puzzles. The speaker has been God throughout, and suddenly says he has been sent by the Lord GOD along with his Spirit. Isaiah does not resolve it and should not be forced to; the New Testament does, and reading it back here is legitimate as long as the order is kept.

verseByVerse.quote: "Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together. "Assemble, all of you, and listen! Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon, and his arm shall be against the Chaldeans. I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way. Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me, O Jacob, and Israel, whom I called! I am he; I am the first, and I am the last. My hand laid the foundation of the earth, and my right hand spread out the heavens; when I call to them, they stand forth together."

Two hands are at work: one setting the footings of the earth, the other stretching the sky like a tent. Then a picture that has no equal in the chapter — he calls, and heaven and earth stand forth together, the way a room of soldiers comes to attention when the officer speaks. The universe is not merely made; it is on parade.

"Who among them has declared these things? The LORD loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon... I, even I, have spoken and called him; I have brought him, and he will prosper in his way."

Cyrus is described one last time, and with a word that has not been used of him before: loved. A Persian who does not know God is spoken of with affection, which is a further enlargement of everything chapters 44 and 45 have been saying about who God may use.

"Draw near to me, hear this: from the beginning I have not spoken in secret, from the time it came to be I have been there." And now the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit.

The last sentence of verse 16 is one of the strangest in the Old Testament. Through the whole passage the speaker has been God — the first and the last, the maker of heaven and earth. Then, without warning, the same speaker says that the Lord GOD has sent him, together with his Spirit.

Whatever else it is, it will not flatten into one voice. Somebody who has been talking as God is also sent by God and accompanied by God's Spirit. Isaiah does not explain it, and it would be dishonest to pretend that his first readers had a doctrine of the Trinity to file it under.

What can be said is that when the sent one finally stood up in a synagogue in Nazareth, he read from this same book, from a passage that begins the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me (61:1), and told the room it had just come true. The seam in verse 16 is small. It runs in the same direction.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: "I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go. Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains; their name would never be cut off or destroyed from before me."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, your Redeemer, the Holy One of Israel: 'I am the LORD your God, who teaches you to profit, who leads you in the way you should go.'"

Two verbs describe what God has been doing all along: teaching and leading. The first is about content, the second about direction, and both are ordinary. This is not the language of thunder on a mountain. It is the language of a parent walking a child to school.

"Oh that you had paid attention to my commandments! Then your peace would have been like a river, and your righteousness like the waves of the sea; your offspring would have been like the sand, and your descendants like its grains."

Here God grieves out loud. It is not a threat about what will happen and not a rebuke about what did; it is a lament over something that was available and was not taken.

The two images repay slow reading. A river is not a cloudburst. It is unspectacular, continuous, and it is there in August as well as in March — the picture of a peace that runs rather than arrives. And waves of the sea are the one thing on earth that has never once failed to come in: righteousness with the reliability of a tide.

They were promised sand-grain descendants once before, to Abraham, and the chapter says that promise was standing here in the reach of people who did not pick it up.

The sound of this verse is heard again on a hillside overlooking Jerusalem, where a man who knew this book better than anyone looked at the city and wept, saying: would that you, even you, had known on this day the things that make for peace (Luke 19:41-42). The construction is the same, and so is the grief.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The command everything has been building towards is finally given, and it is a marching order: go out, flee, and do it with a shout that reaches the end of the earth (v. 20). The song they are to sing is one line long — the LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob. Verse 21 supplies the precedent, the split rock in the desert where the water gushed out, which is the first exodus offered as the guarantee of the second. And then verse 22, which stops the celebration cold: there is no peace, says the LORD, for the wicked.
verseByVerse.theology: The last verse is not tacked on. It marks a boundary at the edge of the invitation: the gate out of Babylon is open, and walking through it is the whole of what is required, and those who prefer to stay are not covered by a promise made to those who leave.

verseByVerse.quote: Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, "The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!" They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out. "There is no peace," says the LORD, "for the wicked."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Go out from Babylon, flee from Chaldea, declare this with a shout of joy, proclaim it, send it out to the end of the earth; say, 'The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob!'"

After eight chapters of argument, a marching order. Five imperatives come in a row — go, flee, declare, proclaim, send — and only the first two are about leaving. The rest are about telling everyone.

Feel the instruction in the body. These people had been in Babylon long enough to own houses in it. Going out means leaving a settled life for a ruined city eight hundred miles away, on the strength of a sentence. Some of them, in the event, did not go.

"They did not thirst when he led them through the deserts; he made water flow for them from the rock; he split the rock and the water gushed out."

The evidence offered for the second journey is the first one. Isaiah does not argue that the desert will be survivable; he reminds them that it already was, once, when a rock was split open and a nation drank. Paul, writing to Corinth, says of that rock a sentence no one saw coming: the Rock was Christ (1 Cor. 10:4). Struck, opened, and pouring out what a dying people needed, in a place where there was no other source.

"'There is no peace,' says the LORD, 'for the wicked.'"

The chapter ends on a hard line, and it is placed where it is on purpose. A door has just been opened and a road home described; verse 22 says the road is the only one there is. Peace is not a mood available in Babylon to those who would rather stay.

The trial that began in chapter 41 closes here. Every witness has been called, every idol has been asked to speak and has not, and the verdict is a set of prison gates standing open with light coming through them. The LORD has redeemed his servant Jacob, and the redemption was announced, dated, financed and carried out by the one who had been saying from the beginning that there was no other.

48.theology:
For my own sake, twice. The chapter gives the reason this people survive, and it is not their repentance, their usefulness, or their promise. For my own sake, for my own sake, I do it, for how should my name be profaned? (v. 11). Stated coldly it sounds like divine self-interest. Examined, it is the only foundation strong enough for someone who knows his own record: a rescue undertaken because the rescued were worth it can be reconsidered when they prove they were not, and a rescue undertaken for the sake of God’s own name can fail only if he ceases to care what his name is worth.

Refined, but not as silver. Verse 10 refuses the comfortable doctrine that suffering automatically improves people. Silver refining runs to completion, and God says the exile was not that — either the heat was held back because full refining would have destroyed them, or the yield was poor. Both readings are honest to the Hebrew and both are honest to the chapter, which has just called this people iron-necked and brass-faced. What remains true either way is whose furnace it is: nothing enters it unpermitted and nothing leaves before its purpose is served (1 Pet. 1:7).

A rebel from before birth. Verse 8 says the name applied before they were born. This is the doctrine of original sin without the technical vocabulary, and it settles what the rest of the chapter can mean: nothing that follows is a reward for a promising start. The same verse says your ear has not been opened — and two chapters later a servant stands in this book and says that the Lord GOD opened his ear and he was not rebellious (50:5). What Israel could not do, the servant does in her place.

Sent, with his Spirit. The speaker in verses 12-16 is God: the first and the last, whose hands laid the earth and spread the heavens. The last clause of verse 16 then says the Lord GOD has sent me, and his Spirit. The sentence will not flatten into a single voice, and Isaiah leaves it standing. It would be wrong to claim his first hearers held a doctrine of the Trinity; it would be equally wrong to pretend the seam is not there. When the sent one read aloud in Nazareth from this same scroll — the Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me — and said the words had been fulfilled that day, the seam had a face.

49.subtitle: The Second Servant Song
49.intro:
Overview. The second Servant Song (vv. 1-6) has the servant speak for himself, and he addresses the coastlands rather than Israel. He was called before he was born and prepared in concealment — a sword hidden in the shadow of God’s hand, an arrow hidden in a quiver. He is given Israel’s own name and sent to bring Israel back, which is the puzzle the song exists to pose. And then, extraordinarily, he says his work has come to nothing: I have labored in vain. God’s answer is not reassurance but a larger commission — restoring Israel is too light a thing, and the salvation is to reach the end of the earth.

The rest of the chapter answers Zion, who interrupts the singing of heaven and earth to say that the LORD has forsaken and forgotten her. God does not rebuke the complaint. He measures his commitment against a nursing mother’s, concedes that hers can fail, and puts his own past it — and then holds out his hands, with her name cut into the palms. The chapter closes with builders outstripping destroyers, a bereaved woman bewildered by the number of her children, and God contending in person with those who contend with his people.

keyVerse.quote: “Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you. Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands.”
keyVerse.note: The argument moves from the most reliable human attachment — mother to nursing infant — to something more reliable still. God does not merely match maternal love; he exceeds it. The engraving-on-palms image anticipates the wounds in the hands of Christ — the permanent bodily record of what it cost to keep the promise.

49.reflection: The Servant confessed that he had labored in vain — and God immediately expanded his commission. The experience of apparent futility preceded the revelation of greater purpose. Where in your life have you been most tempted to conclude that your faithfulness has been wasted? And what would it mean to respond with the Servant’s posture: “yet my right is with the LORD”?
49.text: <sup>1</sup>Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name.<sup>2</sup>He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.<sup>3</sup>And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."<sup>4</sup>But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."<sup>5</sup>And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength—<sup>6</sup>he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."<sup>7</sup>Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."<sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages,<sup>9</sup>saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;<sup>10</sup>they shall not hunger or thirst, neither scorching wind nor sun shall strike them, for he who has pity on them will lead them, and by springs of water will guide them.<sup>11</sup>And I will make all my mountains a road, and my highways shall be raised up.<sup>12</sup>Behold, these shall come from afar, and behold, these from the north and from the west, and these from the land of Syene."<sup>13</sup>Sing for joy, O heavens, and exult, O earth; break forth, O mountains, into singing! For the LORD has comforted his people and will have compassion on his afflicted.<sup>14</sup>But Zion said, "The LORD has forsaken me; my Lord has forgotten me."<sup>15</sup>"Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should have no compassion on the son of her womb? Even these may forget, yet I will not forget you.<sup>16</sup>Behold, I have engraved you on the palms of my hands; your walls are continually before me.<sup>17</sup>Your builders make haste; your destroyers and those who laid you waste go out from you.<sup>18</sup>Lift up your eyes around and see; they all gather, they come to you. As I live, declares the LORD, you shall put them all on as an ornament; you shall bind them on as a bride does.<sup>19</sup>"Surely your waste and your desolate places and your devastated land— surely now you will be too narrow for your inhabitants, and those who swallowed you up will be far away.<sup>20</sup>The children of your bereavement will yet say in your ears: 'The place is too narrow for me; make room for me to dwell in.'<sup>21</sup>Then you will say in your heart: 'Who has borne me these? I was bereaved and barren, exiled and put away, but who has brought up these? Behold, I was left alone; from where have these come?'"<sup>22</sup>Thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, I will lift up my hand to the nations, and raise my signal to the peoples; and they shall bring your sons in their arms, and your daughters shall be carried on their shoulders.<sup>23</sup>Kings shall be your foster fathers, and their queens your nursing mothers. With their faces to the ground they shall bow down to you, and lick the dust of your feet. Then you will know that I am the LORD; those who wait for me shall not be put to shame."<sup>24</sup>Can the prey be taken from the mighty, or the captives of a tyrant be rescued?<sup>25</sup>For thus says the LORD: "Even the captives of the mighty shall be taken, and the prey of the tyrant be rescued, for I will contend with those who contend with you, and I will save your children.<sup>26</sup>I will make your oppressors eat their own flesh, and they shall be drunk with their own blood as with wine. Then all flesh shall know that I am the LORD your Savior, and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — Called from the Womb, and Sent Further Than He Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The servant speaks for himself, and he addresses the coastlands rather than Israel. Verses 1 and 2 describe a calling that predates his birth and a preparation spent entirely in concealment — a sword hidden in the shadow of God's hand, an arrow hidden in a quiver. Verse 3 names him Israel. Verse 4 is his own confession that the work has come to nothing. Verses 5 and 6 are God's answer, which enlarges the commission instead of consoling him: restoring Israel is too small a thing, and the salvation is to reach the end of the earth. Verse 7 promises that the despised one will be stood up before kings.
verseByVerse.theology: The song makes the identification of the servant unavoidable. He is called Israel in verse 3 and sent to bring Jacob back in verse 5 — so he is Israel and he is not Israel, which means he is the true Israel doing what the nation could not do for itself. Verse 4 adds something the first song did not: this servant experiences the work as failure from the inside, and holds on by entrusting the verdict to God rather than by seeing results.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul and Barnabas, turned out of a synagogue, quote verse 6 as their own marching orders — I have made you a light for the Gentiles (Acts 13:47) — which is a striking use of a verse about the servant. What was said to Christ is applied to the church sent out in his name. And verse 4 has kept more discouraged ministers, parents and missionaries at their posts than almost any other sentence in the prophets.

verseByVerse.quote: Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar. The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name. He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Listen to me, O coastlands, and give attention, you peoples from afar."

The servant speaks for himself for the first time, and notice who he is speaking to. Not Jerusalem. The coastlands and distant peoples — the far edge of the map, the places that had never heard of the covenant. The second song is addressed outward from its opening word, before it has said anything at all about what the servant is for.

"The LORD called me from the womb, from the body of my mother he named my name."

His vocation is older than he is. Jeremiah was told the same (Jer. 1:5), and Paul said it of himself (Gal. 1:15), and both of them were echoing a pattern that belongs most exactly to one man — the only one whose name was announced by an angel to his mother before he was conceived (Luke 1:31).

"He made my mouth like a sharp sword; in the shadow of his hand he hid me; he made me a polished arrow; in his quiver he hid me away."

Two weapons, and both of them are the mouth. The word is the sword and the word is the arrow; nothing here is metal. The New Testament keeps the image exactly — the word of God living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword (Heb. 4:12), and a risen Christ with a sharp two-edged sword coming out of his mouth (Rev. 1:16).

But the striking thing is that both weapons are described as hidden. A sword in the shadow of a hand, an arrow shut in a quiver. Isaiah spends half the verse on concealment, and the concealment is not failure — it is what you do with a weapon you intend to use. A polished arrow is polished in the dark, and then it is kept in the dark until the moment it is wanted.

Which is the honest description of nearly every life God is preparing for something. Thirty years in a carpenter's shop is the shadow of the hand. Nobody watching would have called it preparation; from the inside it does not feel like being sharpened, it feels like being shelved. It was neither.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to me, "You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And he said to me, 'You are my servant, Israel, in whom I will be glorified.'"

God names the servant, and the name he gives him is the name of the nation.

Hold that beside verse 5, two sentences later, where the same servant is formed in the womb "to bring Jacob back to him, and that Israel might be gathered to him." He is called Israel, and he is sent to Israel. He cannot simply be the nation, because he has a mission to the nation. And he cannot simply be a private individual either, because God has given him the nation's own name.

The resolution is the one the whole book has been moving toward. Israel was called to be God's son, God's servant, God's light; Israel failed at all three, as chapter 42 said with painful directness. So one comes who is everything Israel was supposed to be — carrying the name, doing the work, succeeding at the calling — and then does for Israel what Israel could not do for itself.

Everything the New Testament says about being in Christ stands on this verse. A believer is not saved by becoming a better Israelite. He is saved by being joined to the one who wears the name and kept the covenant, so that what is true of him becomes true of those attached to him. Isaiah 49:3 is where the grammar of that begins.

"In whom I will be glorified." The purpose is not first the rescue. It is the glory of God displayed in a person, and the rescue is how the display happens.

verseByVerse.quote: But I said, "I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity; yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But I said, 'I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for nothing and vanity.'"

This is the servant speaking, and it is one of the most unexpected sentences in the Old Testament. Not the nation complaining, not the prophet despairing — the chosen servant, in the middle of his own song, saying that the work has come to nothing.

Read what he actually claims. Not that the work was hard. Not that it took longer than he hoped. In vain. For nothing. Vanity — the word is the one Ecclesiastes uses for vapour, breath, the thing that will not stay in your hand. He has spent his strength, all of it, and there is nothing to show.

Anyone who has taught the same child the same thing for eleven years, or prayed for a marriage that got worse, or preached faithfully in a place that emptied, knows the temperature of that sentence. What it is not is unbelief. It is the honest report of a faithful worker's eyes.

"Yet surely my right is with the LORD, and my recompense with my God."

And there is the turn, and it is the whole art of persevering. He does not talk himself out of the assessment. He does not find a hidden fruitfulness to console himself with. He moves the verdict to a different court. My right — my case, my vindication — is with the LORD: it is not lying about unresolved, it is lodged somewhere, held by somebody, and it will be given.

Which is what makes the next two verses so extraordinary. A man says his life's work has failed, and God's answer is not to reassure him that it has not.

verseByVerse.quote: And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him; and that Israel might be gathered to him— for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength— he says: "It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"And now the LORD says, he who formed me from the womb to be his servant, to bring Jacob back to him, and that Israel might be gathered to him — for I am honored in the eyes of the LORD, and my God has become my strength."

Before the commission is enlarged, the servant is told what he already is. I am honoured in the eyes of the LORD. The man who has just said he laboured for nothing is told that in the only eyes that assess anything he is honoured — which is not a contradiction of his experience but a correction of the court he had been reporting to.

"He says: 'It is too light a thing that you should be my servant to raise up the tribes of Jacob and to bring back the preserved of Israel; I will make you as a light for the nations, that my salvation may reach to the end of the earth.'"

Consider what God does not say. He does not say the labour was fruitful after all. He does not explain the apparent failure or offer evidence that it went better than it looked. He says the job is too small.

Restoring an entire nation from exile — the thing the servant has been pouring his strength into and believes he has failed at — is described as too light a thing, a load not worth the strength of the man carrying it. So it is doubled. Not Israel: the nations. Not the return: salvation to the end of the earth.

That is God's characteristic answer to the sense of futility, and it should be remembered by anyone who is ready to give something up. He rarely responds by shrinking the assignment to fit our discouragement. Paul and Barnabas, thrown out of the synagogue at Antioch, took this verse as theirs and turned to the Gentiles with it in their mouths (Acts 13:47) — which is what a rejection looked like when God got hold of it.

And the reach of the promise is total. Not many nations. Not most. The end of the earth, which in a book written for a small people pinned between empires is the most implausible sentence available, and which has since been fulfilled in front of everybody for two thousand years.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers: "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD, the Redeemer of Israel and his Holy One, to one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation, the servant of rulers."

Three descriptions, and each is worse than the last. Deeply despised — the Hebrew is a despising of the whole soul, contempt without qualification. Abhorred by the nation — not by foreigners but by his own people. The servant of rulers — a man with no standing, at the disposal of whoever holds power.

Every one of the three landed. He came to his own and his own people did not receive him. He was handed between a Sanhedrin, a governor and a tetrarch in the space of one morning, each of them free to do as they liked with him.

"Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves."

And there is the reversal, in the same sentence as the contempt. The men before whom he stood as a prisoner will stand up when he comes into the room, and then go down on their faces. Note the sequence: they see, and then they rise. Nothing has to be argued to them. What overturns their judgment is the sight of him.

"Because of the LORD, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you." The grounds of the reversal are stated and they are not in the servant. It is not that he earns his way back up, or that public opinion eventually comes round. It is that God is faithful and God chose him, and those two facts will finish what they started regardless of how the middle of the story looks.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — The Day of Salvation and the Road Home
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the servant with a timetable and a task. Verse 8 sets a time of favour and a day of salvation, and makes the servant a covenant to the people. Verses 9 to 11 have him saying two words to prisoners — come out — and then shepherding them home along roads made out of mountains, with no hunger, no thirst, and nothing scorching them on the way. Verse 12 gathers them from every direction of the compass. Verse 13 calls on the heavens and the earth and the mountains to sing about it.
verseByVerse.theology: The comfort here is covenantal rather than circumstantial: it rests on an appointed day that God has fixed, not on an improvement in conditions. Paul takes verse 8 and applies it to the present moment of gospel opportunity — behold, now is the favourable time, now is the day of salvation (2 Cor. 6:2) — reading the servant's appointed day as having arrived.
verseByVerse.examples: The promises of verses 9 and 10 turn up almost word for word at the end of the Bible, said of a multitude nobody could number: they shall hunger no more, neither thirst any more, the sun shall not strike them, and the Lamb will be their shepherd and guide them to springs of living water (Rev. 7:16-17). The road home in Isaiah 49 and the arrival in Revelation 7 are the same journey.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you; I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages, saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.' They shall feed along the ways; on all bare heights shall be their pasture;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Thus says the LORD: 'In a time of favor I have answered you; in a day of salvation I have helped you.'"

The servant said his right was with the LORD and left it there. Here is the answer, and it comes with a time attached — a set moment, chosen by God, when the case is taken up. Not if, and not eventually. In a time of favour I have answered you, spoken in the past tense over something not yet visible.

Paul takes this verse and does something remarkable with it. Quoting it to the Corinthians, he adds: "Behold, now is the favorable time; behold, now is the day of salvation" (2 Cor. 6:2). The appointed day the servant was told to wait for has, in Paul's reading, arrived — and the window it opened is the one his readers are standing in while he writes.

"I will keep you and give you as a covenant to the people, to establish the land, to apportion the desolate heritages."

The title from the first song comes back: he does not deliver the covenant, he is it (42:6). And the work attached to it is oddly practical — establishing land, parcelling out ruined inheritances, the business of a surveyor after a war. Salvation in Isaiah is never purely interior. It ends with people back on their own ground.

"Saying to the prisoners, 'Come out,' to those who are in darkness, 'Appear.'"

Two words to each group, and no procedure attached to either. No ransom named at the door, no conditions read out, no interview. The prison is opened by an imperative.
