And here is why it is safe to believe. The restoration is not grounded in God's softness. It is grounded in his justice: he loves justice and hates robbery, and his people have been robbed. A God who merely felt sorry for them might change his mind. A God whose own character is offended by what was taken from them will not rest until it has been returned.

That is the sentence to hold on to in a wrong that was never put right. The case is not being carried by anybody's sympathy, and it has not been dropped. It is being carried by what God is.

"Their offspring shall be known among the nations, and their descendants in the midst of the peoples; all who see them shall acknowledge them, that they are an offspring the LORD has blessed."

And the blessing becomes visible, in the next generation, without being announced. Outsiders looking at these families draw the conclusion themselves — all who see them shall acknowledge. Nothing is preached in that verse. Something is simply noticed, by people who were not looking for it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–11 — The Garments, and the Garden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in song. Verse 10 has the speaker exulting in God for two garments he did not make: the clothes of salvation and the robe of righteousness, put on him the way a bridegroom puts on his headdress and a bride her jewels. Verse 11 closes with a garden — as surely as sown ground sends up shoots, God will cause righteousness and praise to sprout up in front of all the nations.
verseByVerse.theology: Both verbs in verse 10 are passive and that is the doctrine: he has clothed me, he has covered me. The righteousness worn here is received rather than achieved, which is the same logic as the servant of chapter 53 bearing iniquities so that many are accounted righteous. And the headdress of verse 10 is the same word as the headdress given to mourners in verse 3 — what was handed to the ashes-covered at the start of the chapter is what the bridegroom is wearing at the end of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 11 answers the question of whether any of this will actually happen with an agricultural certainty rather than an argument. Nobody stands over a sown garden wondering whether it will come up. Righteousness among the nations is not manufactured and it is not campaigned into existence; it is grown, and the gardener is God.

verseByVerse.quote: I will greatly rejoice in the LORD; my soul shall exult in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself like a priest with a beautiful headdress, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will greatly rejoice in the LORD; my soul shall exult in my God, for he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decks himself like a priest with a beautiful headdress, and as a bride adorns herself with her jewels."

The song at last, and everything in it is passive. He has clothed me. He has covered me. The singer is not describing an achievement. He is describing what he is wearing, and somebody else dressed him.

Two garments. The garments of salvation — rescue worn rather than merely received, so that it is the first thing anyone sees. And the robe of righteousness, which is the phrase that matters most: a covering that makes a person fit to be seen, laid over him from outside. This is the Old Testament's own picture of what the New Testament calls being counted righteous — not a quality generated inside a man, but a garment fitted over one who did not have it and could not make it.

Then two pictures of how it looks to wear them, and both are wedding pictures. A bridegroom putting on his headdress with the care of a priest robing for the sanctuary; a bride putting on her jewels. Nobody in either image is dressed for duty. They are dressed for joy, and they have taken trouble over it.

And look closely at the headdress. It is pe'er — the same word as verse 3, where it was handed to people sitting in ashes. What was given to the mourners at the beginning of the chapter turns out to be what the bridegroom is wearing at the end of it. The finery of the wedding and the gift to the grieving are the same article of clothing.

He was anointed to give a headdress instead of ashes, and he wears one. The garments are his to give because they are his to begin with, and the robe that covers a sinner was woven by the one who needed no covering at all.

verseByVerse.quote: For as the earth brings forth its sprouts, and as a garden causes what is sown in it to sprout up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to sprout up before all the nations.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For as the earth brings forth its sprouts, and as a garden causes what is sown in it to sprout up, so the Lord GOD will cause righteousness and praise to sprout up before all the nations."

The chapter ends by answering the question that has been sitting under all of it — will any of this actually happen? — and the answer is not an argument. It is a garden.

Nobody stands over sown ground wondering whether it will come up. There is a delay, and during the delay nothing whatever can be seen, and the delay is not evidence. Seed does what seed does, and the gardener is not anxious.

Two things are described as growing, and the pairing matters. Righteousness and praise — right living and glad worship, coming up out of the same soil, in front of all the nations. Isaiah does not treat them as separate projects. A world put right and a world at worship are one harvest.

And the gardener is named. The Lord GOD will cause it to sprout. Righteousness among the nations is not campaigned into existence and not manufactured by the church's strategy; it is grown, on a timetable belonging to somebody else, out of seed that was sown long before anybody now living was watching.

So the chapter that opened with a man claiming the Spirit was on him closes with a harvest he plants. The poor have been given news, the brokenhearted bandaged, the prisoners brought blinking into the light, the ashes swapped for a headdress and the mourners turned into oaks — and the last picture is of the whole earth quietly coming up green in front of the nations, because the Lord GOD said it would.

62.subtitle: A New Name
62.intro: Overview. Chapter 62 is one of sustained, urgent intercession — both from the prophet and from God himself, who will not be silent until Zion’s righteousness goes forth as brightness and her salvation as a burning torch. A new name will be given; the land will be called “married.” The chapter ends with a call to the watchmen and the whole people: prepare the highway, lift up an ensign, proclaim to the nations — your salvation is coming.

sections.title: Silence Broken
sections.commentary:
For Zion’s sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not be quiet. The speaker is either the prophet or God himself — the ambiguity is deliberate. The righteousness must come out, the salvation must shine, the nations must see the vindication. Then a new name: no longer Forsaken or Desolate but Hephzibah — “My Delight Is in Her” — and Beulah — “Married.”

v. 5 — “As a young man marries a young woman, so shall your sons marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.” The image of God as rejoicing bridegroom is one of the most intimate in Scripture. Zephaniah 3:17 echoes it (“he will rejoice over you with gladness”) and Revelation 19:7 fulfills it in the marriage supper of the Lamb. The joy is God’s, directed toward his people: they are not merely rescued but cherished.

Reminders of the LORD are commissioned: you who put the LORD in remembrance, take no rest, and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth. This is the grammar of persistent intercession: authorized, urgent, aimed at God’s own promise.

sections.title: The Highway and the Coming Salvation
sections.commentary: Go through the gates; go through the gates; prepare the way for the people; build up, build up the highway; clear it of stones; lift up a signal over the peoples. Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth: say to the daughter of Zion, behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him. And they shall be called the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD; and you shall be called Sought Out, a City Not Forsaken. The names at the end of the chapter answer the names at the beginning: Forsaken becomes Not Forsaken; Desolate becomes Sought Out.

keyVerse.quote: “As a young man marries a young woman… so shall your God rejoice over you.”
keyVerse.note: The comparison reaches for the most intense and uncomplicated joy in human experience — a young bridegroom — and applies it to God’s delight in his people. This is not metaphor as literary decoration; it is the closest the human vocabulary can come to describing an actual divine reality. God is not merely committed to his people; he delights in them.

62.reflection: The prophet says he will not keep silent until Zion’s righteousness goes forth as brightness. This is a model of persistent, authorized intercession — not badgering God but reminding him of his own promise. Is there a situation, a person, a community for which you have been called to refuse silence until the answer comes? What would sustained intercession — giving God no rest — look like in that situation?
62.text: <sup>1</sup>For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not be quiet, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness, and her salvation as a burning torch.<sup>2</sup>The nations shall see your righteousness, and all the kings your glory, and you shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give.<sup>3</sup>You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God.<sup>4</sup>You shall no more be termed Forsaken, and your land shall no more be termed Desolate, but you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married; for the LORD delights in you, and your land shall be married.<sup>5</sup>For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your sons marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you.<sup>6</sup>On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all the day and all the night they shall never be silent. You who put the LORD in remembrance, take no rest,<sup>7</sup>and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth.<sup>8</sup>The LORD has sworn by his right hand and by his mighty arm: "I will not again give your grain to be food for your enemies, and foreigners shall not drink your wine for which you have labored;<sup>9</sup>but those who garner it shall eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather it shall drink it in the courts of my sanctuary."<sup>10</sup>Go through, go through the gates; prepare the way for the people; build up, build up the highway; clear it of stones; lift up a signal over the peoples.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth: Say to the daughter of Zion, "Behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him."<sup>12</sup>And they shall be called The Holy People, The Redeemed of the LORD; and you shall be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: For Zion's sake God will not keep silent until her righteousness goes forth as brightness. She will receive a new name — no longer Forsaken or Desolate but Hephzibah (my delight is in her) and Beulah (married). Watchmen are set on Jerusalem's walls to give God no rest until he establishes Jerusalem. The highway is prepared; the banner lifted for the peoples. The redeemed are called: Sought Out, a City Not Forsaken.
verseByVerse.theology: New names and new identity: the renaming of Zion (Forsaken → Hephzibah; Desolate → Beulah) is the prophetic sign of transformed identity. In Scripture, new names mark new realities — Abram to Abraham, Jacob to Israel, Simon to Peter. The city that bore the name of its condition (forsaken, desolate) now bears the name of God's delight and covenant commitment. The new name is the new identity, and both are gifts.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer notes that the repetition of prayer language in vv.6-7 — watchmen who give God no rest, who remind him of his promise — is one of the strongest biblical encouragements to persistent, importunate intercession. The very boldness of reminding God of his promises is itself an act of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: For Zion's sake I will not keep silent, and for Jerusalem's sake I will not be quiet, until her righteousness goes forth as brightness, and her salvation as a burning torch. The nations shall see your righteousness, and all the kings your glory, and you shall be called by a new name that the mouth of the LORD will give. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God himself is the watchman who will not be silent — contrasting with the sleeping dogs of 56:10. His speech continues until righteousness blazes and salvation burns visibly before all nations. The new name given by the LORD himself is the highest possible honor — as with Abraham and Jacob, it signals a new identity established by divine act. Oswalt: God's refusal to be silent about Zion is the ultimate encouragement for prayer — if God himself intercedes for his city, we need not fear that our intercession is futile.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall be a crown of beauty in the hand of the LORD, and a royal diadem in the hand of your God. You shall no more be termed Forsaken, and your land shall no more be termed Desolate, but you shall be called My Delight Is in Her, and your land Married, for the LORD delights in you, and your land shall be married. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Jerusalem as a crown in God's hand — the ultimate image of valued possession, carefully held. The old names (Forsaken, Desolate) are retired; the new names (Hephzibah — my delight is in her; Beulah — married) express God's active delight and covenant commitment. Motyer: the marriage metaphor (Beulah) picks up the husband-imagery of 54:5 — God as husband restoring the forsaken wife. The new name does not merely describe a new state; it enacts it. When God names Zion my delight, she becomes his delight.

verseByVerse.quote: For as a young man marries a young woman, so shall your sons marry you, and as the bridegroom rejoices over the bride, so shall your God rejoice over you. On your walls, O Jerusalem, I have set watchmen; all the day and all the night they shall never be silent. You who put the LORD in remembrance, take no rest, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The bridegroom's rejoicing over the bride — the most intense human joy — is the image of God's delight over restored Zion. The watchmen on the walls pray continuously, night and day. Put the LORD in remembrance — the language of bold intercession, reminding God of his own promises (not because he forgets, but as an expression of faith). Young: the watchman-prayers of vv.6-7 are the church's calling in every age — to persist in prayer for the full realization of God's promises, giving him no rest until he fulfills what he has spoken.

verseByVerse.quote: and give him no rest until he establishes Jerusalem and makes it a praise in the earth. The LORD has sworn by his right hand and by his mighty arm: I will not again give your grain to be food for your enemies, and foreigners shall not drink your wine for which you have labored; (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Give him no rest — the holy impertinence of persistent prayer. God swears by his own right hand and mighty arm (the arm that brought salvation in 59:16) that the enemies will no longer plunder Israel's harvest. The exile is over; what Israel labors for, Israel will keep. The oath grounds the community's prayer and their confidence: God has sworn, and what he swears by his own arm cannot fail. Childs: the divine oath transforms the watchman's prayer from a petition into a reminder — you have sworn; we are holding you to your word.

verseByVerse.quote: but those who garner it shall eat it and praise the LORD, and those who gather it shall drink it in the courts of my sanctuary. Go through, go through the gates; prepare the way for the people; build up, build up the highway; clear it of stones; lift up a signal over the peoples. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The harvest is eaten with praise in the sanctuary courts — every meal becomes worship when judgment is over. Then the command to prepare the highway (echoing 40:3 and 57:14) — but now the preparation is for the peoples, not just for Israel. The signal (banner) lifted over the nations is the same sign of 11:10 — the root of Jesse as a rallying point for all peoples. Motyer: the highway prepared for the return is now presented as a highway for all nations, showing that the restoration of Zion is simultaneously the opening of access for the whole world.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the LORD has proclaimed to the end of the earth: Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your salvation comes; behold, his reward is with him, and his recompense before him.' And they shall be called The Holy People, The Redeemed of the LORD; and you shall be called Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The proclamation of Zion's salvation goes to the ends of the earth — global gospel announcement. The reward and recompense coming with the LORD echo 40:10 (his reward is with him) — the divine warrior returning with the fruits of victory. The final names for the community: The Holy People, The Redeemed of the LORD, Sought Out, A City Not Forsaken — four names that reverse every aspect of the exile's shame. Forsaken was the deepest wound; not forsaken is the deepest healing. Young: the city that named itself by its abandonment now names itself by its election — the names we carry from God define us more truly than the names our circumstances impose.

63.subtitle: Who Is This Coming from Edom?
63.intro: Overview. Chapter 63 opens with one of the most dramatic and disturbing visions in Isaiah: a warrior coming from Edom, garments soaked in blood, treading the winepress of God’s wrath alone. It is followed by a sustained act of communal remembrance and lament (63:7–64:12) — recalling God’s mercies, confessing failure, pleading for his return. The two halves belong together: the vision of the divine warrior grounds the hope of the intercession.

sections.title: The Winepress of Wrath
sections.commentary:
Who is this coming from Edom, in crimsoned garments, marching in his great might? It is God himself, speaking: I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save. Why is your apparel red, your garments like his who treads in the winepress? I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me. I trod them in my anger; their lifeblood spattered on my garments. For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come.

v. 3 — “I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me.” Revelation 19:13–15 applies this vision directly to Christ at his return: “He is clothed in a robe dipped in blood… He will tread the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty.” The warrior who acts alone is the one who also bore the iniquity alone (53:6). The same solitary figure appears in both chapters.

sections.title: Remembrance, Lament, and Prayer
sections.commentary:
I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD, the praises of the LORD, according to all that the LORD has granted us — the great goodness to the house of Israel. In all their affliction he was afflicted; the angel of his presence saved them. But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; he turned and became their enemy and fought against them. The lament is historical and honest: Israel brought the judgment on herself, and God was right to give her enemies into their hands.

Yet now you are our Father; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name. Return, for the sake of your servants. Your holy people held your sanctuary for a little while; our adversaries have trampled it down. The prayer holds together honest confession and bold appeal to the Father-name. It refuses both cheap grace (no confession) and cheap despair (no appeal).

keyVerse.quote: “In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old.”
keyVerse.note: This verse identifies God’s solidarity with his people’s suffering as the ground of their redemption. He was not a distant manager of the exodus but present within it, afflicted in their affliction. Hebrews 4:15 extends this to Jesus: a high priest who has been “tempted in every way as we are.” The God who enters our suffering is not a new idea in the New Testament; it is the character of God revealed in the Old.

63.reflection: The prayer in this chapter holds together honest memory of God’s goodness in the past and equally honest confession of failure in the present. This is the hardest kind of prayer to pray — the kind that doesn’t resolve the tension. Where in your life do you need to hold both at once: gratitude for what God has done and grief over where you are now?
63.text: <sup>1</sup>Who is this who comes from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah, he who is splendid in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength? "It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save."<sup>2</sup>Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress?<sup>3</sup>"I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me; I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath; their lifeblood spattered on my garments, and stained all my apparel.<sup>4</sup>For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come.<sup>5</sup>I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled, but there was no one to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation, and my wrath upheld me.<sup>6</sup>I trampled down the peoples in my anger; I made them drunk in my wrath, and I poured out their lifeblood on the earth."<sup>7</sup>I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD, the praises of the LORD, according to all that the LORD has granted us, and the great goodness to the house of Israel that he has granted them according to his compassion, according to the abundance of his steadfast love.<sup>8</sup>For he said, "Surely they are my people, children who will not deal falsely." And he became their Savior.<sup>9</sup>In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old.<sup>10</sup>But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; therefore he turned to be their enemy, and himself fought against them.<sup>11</sup>Then he remembered the days of old, of Moses and his people. Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit,<sup>12</sup>who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses, who divided the waters before them to make for himself an everlasting name,<sup>13</sup>who led them through the depths? Like a horse in the desert, they did not stumble.<sup>14</sup>Like livestock that go down into the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name.<sup>15</sup>Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation. Where are your zeal and your might? The stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back from me.<sup>16</sup>For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us, and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name.<sup>17</sup>O LORD, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart, so that we fear you not? Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your heritage.<sup>18</sup>Your holy people held possession for a little while; our adversaries have trampled down your sanctuary.<sup>19</sup>We have become like those over whom you have never ruled, like those who are not called by your name.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–19 — The Divine Warrior and the Prayer of the Remnant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A dramatic dialogue: the prophet sees a figure coming from Edom in garments stained red, who has trodden the winepress of divine judgment alone. Then follows a prayer of the remnant — the most sustained communal lament in Isaiah — recalling God's past mercies (the exodus), confessing present rebellion, and crying out for God to act again. 'You, O LORD, are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter.'
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment and intercession: the divine warrior who treads the winepress alone (vv.1-6) is applied to Christ in Revelation 19:13-15 (garment dipped in blood, treading the winepress). The prayer of vv.7-19 is the prayer of a community that has lost everything except the memory of God's past mercies and the knowledge of God's fatherhood. It teaches that lament which grounds itself in historical theology and divine character is never far from hope.
verseByVerse.examples: Motyer calls the prayer of 63:7-64:12 one of the greatest prayers of communal lament in Scripture, comparable to Psalm 44. Its structure — praise of past mercies, confession of present failure, plea for future intervention — is the model for intercession in every age of the church's difficulty.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is this who comes from Edom, in crimsoned garments from Bozrah, he who is splendid in his apparel, marching in the greatness of his strength? It is I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save. Why is your apparel red, and your garments like his who treads in the winepress? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The dialogue opens with a sentry's challenge: who is this coming from Edom (Israel's ancient enemy) with crimson-stained robes? The answer comes in first person — the divine warrior identifying himself: I, speaking in righteousness, mighty to save. Revelation 19:13 applies this to the returning Christ, whose robe is dipped in blood. Motyer: the figure coming from Edom represents God's judgment on all who have opposed his people, with Edom standing for the prototype of hostility. The stained garments are not his own blood but the blood of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: I have trodden the winepress alone, and from the peoples no one was with me; I trod them in my anger and trampled them in my wrath; their lifeblood spattered on my garments, and stained all my apparel. For the day of vengeance was in my heart, and my year of redemption had come. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Alone — the divine warrior acted without human assistance, just as no human intercessor could be found in 59:16. The day of vengeance and the year of redemption are two sides of the same event: when God acts finally against evil, he simultaneously vindicates his people. Childs: the winepress of judgment (also Joel 3:13; Rev 14:19-20) is the image of thorough, complete judgment — the wrath of God poured out on evil exhaustively. The one who treads it alone bears the full weight of executing justice.

verseByVerse.quote: I looked, but there was no one to help; I was appalled, but there was no one to uphold; so my own arm brought me salvation, and my wrath upheld me. I trampled down the peoples in my anger; I made them drunk in my wrath, and I poured out their lifeblood on the earth. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine warrior's self-sufficiency in judgment mirrors his self-sufficiency in salvation (59:16 — his own arm brought him salvation). The arm that saves and the arm that judges are the same. The peoples made drunk with wrath is the cup imagery again — the cup that Jerusalem drank (51:17) is now administered to her oppressors. Young: the judgment oracle of vv.1-6 is not vindictive but vindicatory — God acts in judgment to establish justice where no human justice could reach. The community's prayer in vv.7-19 flows from confidence that this God has acted and will act again.

verseByVerse.quote: I will recount the steadfast love of the LORD, the praises of the LORD, according to all that the LORD has granted us, and the great goodness to the house of Israel that he has granted them according to his compassion, according to the abundance of his steadfast love. For he said, 'Surely they are my people, children who will not deal falsely.' And he became their Savior. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer begins with remembered praise — the recounting of hesed (steadfast love). The community grounds its prayer in what God has already done: past grace is the basis for present petition. He said, Surely they are my people — the covenant declaration, the choosing. Motyer: the prayer of lament that begins with praise is theologically healthy. To remember God's past mercies before listing present griefs keeps the prayer anchored in the character of the God being addressed, rather than in the severity of the problem.

verseByVerse.quote: In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them up and carried them all the days of old. But they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit; therefore he turned to be their enemy; he himself fought against them. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: In all their affliction he was afflicted — divine solidarity with Israel's suffering. God does not observe pain from a distance; he is moved by his people's distress. The angel of his presence (the divine messenger of the exodus) saved them. Then the turn: they rebelled and grieved his Holy Spirit. The grieving of the Spirit (see Eph 4:30 — Paul picks up this language) is the covenant tragedy — the people who had experienced the most intimate divine compassion turned against the compassionate God. Young: the rebellion that grieves the Spirit is not ignorance but deliberate ingratitude.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he remembered the days of old, of Moses and his people. Where is he who brought them up out of the sea with the shepherds of his flock? Where is he who put in the midst of them his Holy Spirit, who caused his glorious arm to go at the right hand of Moses, who divided the waters before them to make for himself an everlasting name, (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: God remembers — or the people remember God remembering — the exodus. The cascade of questions (where is he?) is not doubt but appeal: the God who did all of this, where is he now? The Spirit given in the exodus (the pillar of cloud and fire as divine presence), the glorious arm, the divided waters — all marshaled as evidence that God can and has acted magnificently. The purpose of past acts: to make himself an everlasting name. Childs: the appeal to God's past glorious acts is the most powerful form of intercession — asking God to be consistent with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: who led them through the depths? Like a horse in the desert, they did not stumble. Like livestock that go down into the valley, the Spirit of the LORD gave them rest. So you led your people, to make for yourself a glorious name. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The exodus generation led through the deep sea like horses on solid ground — the miracle of stability in impossible terrain. The Spirit of the LORD as rest-giver anticipates the promised rest of Hebrews 4. The purpose of all divine leading: to make for yourself a glorious name. God's great acts in history serve his own glorification. This is not divine ego but the deepest truth about reality — God's glory is the highest good, and his people's flourishing flows from it. Motyer: when we pray for God to act for his name's sake, we are praying for the most motivated possible prayer — God's own character is engaged.

verseByVerse.quote: Look down from heaven and see, from your holy and beautiful habitation. Where are your zeal and your might? The stirring of your inner parts and your compassion are held back from me. For you are our Father, though Abraham does not know us and Israel does not acknowledge us; you, O LORD, are our Father, our Redeemer from of old is your name. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: Look down from heaven — the posture of lament. God seems to have withdrawn to heaven while his people suffer on earth. The appeal to his zeal, might, and compassion is an appeal to his character: these things are in you; show them to us. Then the profound claim: you are our Father — even if Abraham and Israel (the patriarchal heroes) could not recognize the exiles as their true heirs, God is still Father. Oswalt: the fatherhood of God is the final court of appeal when all human lineage seems severed. Even covenant failure cannot erase the Father-child relationship that God established by grace.

verseByVerse.quote: O LORD, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our heart, so that we fear you not? Return for the sake of your servants, the tribes of your heritage. Your holy people held possession for a little while; our adversaries have trampled down your sanctuary. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The most anguished question of the prayer: why do you make us wander? — holding God responsible for the hardening. This is not blaming God for their sin but the cry of a community bewildered by its own spiritual condition. The trampled sanctuary (the Jerusalem temple destroyed by Babylon) is the physical sign of what feels like divine abandonment. Young: the prayer does not let God off the hook — it presses him with the full reality of the situation. This holy impertinence is not sinful but faithful; the God who commands prayer invites this kind of honest engagement.

verseByVerse.quote: We have become like those over whom you have never ruled, like those who are not called by your name. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The final lament: the exiled community feels as if they were never God's people — as nameless and ruleless as the pagans who never knew the covenant. The contrast with the opening of ch62 (you shall be called by a new name) is stark — the community knows what they should be called but experiences the opposite. Motyer: this lament creates the urgency for what follows in ch64. The gap between God's declared purposes and the community's experienced reality is the space where prayer must cry most urgently. The lament does not end the prayer; it intensifies it.

64.subtitle: Oh That You Would Rend the Heavens
64.intro: Overview. Chapter 64 is the climax of the communal lament begun in 63:7. It opens with a cry for divine intervention — “Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down!” — and moves through honest confession to a final question left hanging before God: “Will you keep silent and afflict us so severely?” The prayer does not end with an answer; it ends with an open appeal to the one who is Potter and Father.

sections.title: Rend the Heavens
sections.commentary:
Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. Paul quotes verse 4 in 1 Cor. 2:9 as the description of what God has revealed through the Spirit: “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, God has prepared for those who love him.” The prayer for God to come down anticipates the incarnation — God rending the heavens in the most literal way.

We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away. There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you. The confession moves from polished garment imagery to leaf-fading decay. The community has no ground to stand on but the character of the one they are addressing.

v. 6 — “We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.” The Hebrew behind “polluted garment” is among the strongest expressions of uncleanness in the Torah. The confession is not measured; it is total. All righteous deeds — not just the obvious failures but the best attempts at righteousness — fall short of the holiness they are measured against.

sections.title: The Potter and His Clay
sections.commentary: But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand. Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people. The prayer closes with five questions that leave the community in suspense before God: will you restrain yourself? Will you keep silent and afflict us so severely? The prayer does not manufacture its own resolution. It ends where many of our prayers need to end — with the appeal delivered, the outcome held in God’s hands, and the people still on their knees.

keyVerse.quote: “But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.”
keyVerse.note: The potter-clay image has appeared throughout Isaiah as a warning against human presumption (29:16; 45:9). Here it becomes a resource for prayer: the very creatureliness that makes us answerable to God is also the ground of our appeal to him. We have no independent standing — but we are his clay, his work, and the potter does not discard what his hands have made.

64.reflection: The prayer in chapter 64 ends without an answer — the community is still in suspense before God. This is not a model of weak faith but of honest prayer: not every prayer resolves before you close it. Is there a prayer you have been trying to resolve yourself rather than letting it end openly before God? What would it look like to lay it down as the community does here — completely, and without manufacturing your own answer?
64.text: <sup>1</sup>Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence—<sup>2</sup>as when fire kindles brushwood and the fire causes water to boil— to make your name known to your adversaries, and that the nations might tremble at your presence!<sup>3</sup>When you did awesome things that we did not look for, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence.<sup>4</sup>From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him.<sup>5</sup>You meet him who joyfully works righteousness, those who remember you in your ways. Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved?<sup>6</sup>We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.<sup>7</sup>There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities.<sup>8</sup>But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand.<sup>9</sup>Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people.<sup>10</sup>Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation.<sup>11</sup>Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant places have become ruins.<sup>12</sup>Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly?

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–12 — Oh That You Would Rend the Heavens
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The communal prayer of ch63 continues. The community cries for God to tear open the heavens and come down — to make his name known to the nations. God has acted for those who wait for him. But we are all like an unclean thing, our righteous deeds like a polluted garment. You are our Father; we are the clay. Now your cities are a wilderness and your holy house is burned. Will you restrain yourself?
verseByVerse.theology: Total depravity and grace: vv.6-7 contain one of Scripture's most comprehensive statements of human moral inability — 'all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment.' Not our sins but our righteous deeds. Even our best efforts at obedience, separated from the Spirit's work, are unclean. Yet the prayer immediately turns to the potter-clay image — we are the clay; you are the potter. The solution to total depravity is not human improvement but divine formation.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul alludes to vv.4 in 1 Cor 2:9 ('what no eye has seen, nor ear heard') as describing what God has prepared for those who love him, revealed now through the Spirit. The prayer of ch64 is the darkest in the book, and it is answered by the new heavens and new earth of ch65.

verseByVerse.quote: Oh that you would rend the heavens and come down, that the mountains might quake at your presence — as when fire kindles brushwood and the fire causes water to boil — to make your name known to your adversaries, and that the nations might tremble at your presence! (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The prayer for theophany — God tearing the sky and coming down in fire as at Sinai. The shaking of mountains, the boiling of waters, the trembling of nations — all the physical responses to God's personal presence. The motive is again his name: to make your name known. Motyer: every great prayer in Scripture is oriented toward God's fame, not our comfort. When we pray for God to rend the heavens and come down, the theological purpose is that the watching world will know who he is.

verseByVerse.quote: When you did awesome things that we did not expect, you came down, the mountains quaked at your presence. From of old no one has heard or perceived by the ear, no eye has seen a God besides you, who acts for those who wait for him. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The historical warrant for the prayer: God has done unexpected awesome things before. The Sinai theophany, the Red Sea crossing — events beyond human anticipation. Then the theological claim: no ear has heard, no eye has seen a God besides the LORD who acts for those who wait for him. Paul quotes v.4 in 1 Cor 2:9 but adds: these things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. The waiting community receives what no natural perception can achieve. Young: the God who acts for those who wait makes waiting itself an act of faith, not passivity.

verseByVerse.quote: You meet him who joyfully works righteousness, those who remember you in your ways. Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; in our sins we have been a long time, and shall we be saved? We have all become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment. We all fade like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: All our righteous deeds are like a polluted garment — the Hebrew is beged iddim, literally a menstrual cloth — the strongest possible image of ritual uncleanness. Even our best acts, in the condition of sin, are defiled. This is total depravity applied to human virtue: not just our obvious failures but our celebrated successes are tainted. We fade like leaves; sin drives us away like wind. Paul's use of similar language in Romans 3 confirms that this describes the universal human condition, not merely Israel's exile. Childs: the confession does not spare even the righteous deeds from indictment — this is total, not partial, humility before God.

verseByVerse.quote: There is no one who calls upon your name, who rouses himself to take hold of you; for you have hidden your face from us, and have made us melt in the hand of our iniquities. But now, O LORD, you are our Father; we are the clay, and you are our potter; we are all the work of your hand. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: No one prays, no one reaches out — the community's spiritual paralysis is complete. God has hidden his face. Yet the prayer itself is happening — the very act of praying disproves the despair. Then the pivot: but now, O LORD, you are our Father — holding the fatherhood of God against the experience of abandonment. We are the clay, you are the potter (Jer 18; Rom 9:20-21) — total dependence on the divine Former rather than human self-improvement. Young: the potter-clay image is not fatalistic but trustful — the clay is in good hands, the most capable hands possible.

verseByVerse.quote: Be not so terribly angry, O LORD, and remember not iniquity forever. Behold, please look, we are all your people. Your holy cities have become a wilderness; Zion has become a wilderness, Jerusalem a desolation. (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The pleading intensifies: be not so terribly angry… remember not iniquity forever… we are all your people. The appeal to ownership — we are yours — is the final card. Then the evidence of disaster: holy cities a wilderness, Zion and Jerusalem desolate. The external rubble mirrors the internal ruin confessed in vv.6-7. Motyer: the prayer moves through the full arc of honest intercession — praise (63:7-14), lament (63:15-19), confession (64:1-7), and petition (64:8-12). Every element is present, none is skipped. This is the shape of mature prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, has been burned by fire, and all our pleasant places have become ruins. Will you restrain yourself at these things, O LORD? Will you keep silent, and afflict us so terribly? (ESV)
verseByVerse.commentary: The temple burned — the holiest and most beautiful place where fathers praised God, now ash and ruins. The prayer ends with two questions that are also accusations of the gentlest kind: will you restrain yourself? will you keep silent? The very boldness of addressing God with these questions is itself an act of faith — you can only address a God you believe is present and attentive. Childs: the prayer that ends in questions is not a prayer that has lost faith but one that has maintained enough faith to keep engaging God even in the silence.

65.subtitle: Behold, I Create New Heavens and a New Earth
65.intro:
Overview. Chapter 65 is God’s answer to the anguished prayer of chapters 63 and 64, and it answers far past what was asked. It opens with God calling Here I am, here I am — the words Isaiah himself said in chapter 6 — to a nation that never called on his name, and with his hands held out all day to people walking the other way. What follows is a catalogue of their religion (garden shrines, brick altars, nights in tombs) ending on the most startling line in the passage: keep to yourself, I am too holy for you.

Then the chapter divides, and the line runs inside the covenant community rather than round it. A picker holds up a ruined bunch of grapes and says do not destroy it, there is a blessing in it — and that is why the whole nation is not lost. The rest is the fullest description of the new creation in the Old Testament: new heavens and a new earth, a Jerusalem created to be a joy, the sound of weeping never heard again, houses lived in by the people who built them, prayers answered before they are spoken, and the wolf and the lamb at the same grass. Revelation 21 takes verse 17 almost word for word.

keyVerse.quote: “For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.”
keyVerse.note: Revelation 21:1 quotes this verse almost exactly: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away.” The new creation is not the destruction of creation but its transformation — the same creation, purged of everything that corrupted it. “Former things shall not be remembered” is not amnesia but healing: what will make the former things forgettable is not that they are erased but that they are overwhelmed by joy.

65.theology:
Grace precedes the search. Paul splits the first two verses between the Gentiles who found God without looking for him and the Israel to whom he held out his hands all day long (Rom. 10:20-21). Nobody in this chapter starts the search; the hands were already out. The corresponding sobriety is verse 12 — when I called you did not answer — which makes the dividing line in the covenant community response rather than descent.

New creation, and why it is physical. Verses 17-25 are the Old Testament’s fullest account of where redemptive history is going, and everything in it is material: houses, vineyards, work, children, animals, soil. The hope is not escape from the world but its repair, which is why Christian faith has always held to a bodily resurrection and a renewed earth rather than a released soul. The former things shall not be remembered promises eclipse rather than amnesia — not that the losses did not matter, but that they will not come into mind, because of what is standing in front of them.

The one curse left standing. Verse 25 undoes the predation of a fallen order — the lion is not restrained from the ox, it eats straw — and in the same sentence leaves dust as the serpent’s food, which is the sentence of Genesis 3:14 and the only part of that chapter not reversed here. In the world to come the evil that began all of it will not have been rehabilitated. It will be defeated, permanently, in a world where everything else has been healed.
65.reflection: God says the former things will not be remembered — not because they are denied but because joy will overwhelm them. What “former things” are you carrying right now that feel permanent? What would it mean to let the new creation vision recalibrate your sense of what is permanent and what is temporary? And what is the most specific thing you are most looking forward to about the world this chapter describes?
65.text: <sup>1</sup>I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, "Here I am, here I am," to a nation that was not called by my name.<sup>2</sup>I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices;<sup>3</sup>a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks;<sup>4</sup>who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels;<sup>5</sup>who say, "Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you." These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day.<sup>6</sup>Behold, it is written before me: "I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap<sup>7</sup>both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds."<sup>8</sup>Thus says the LORD: "As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all.<sup>9</sup>I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there.<sup>10</sup>Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me.<sup>11</sup>But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny,<sup>12</sup>I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."<sup>13</sup>Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame;<sup>14</sup>behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit.<sup>15</sup>You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name,<sup>16</sup>so that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes.<sup>17</sup>"For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind.<sup>18</sup>But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness.<sup>19</sup>I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.<sup>20</sup>No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed.<sup>21</sup>They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit.<sup>22</sup>They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands.<sup>23</sup>They shall not labor in vain or bear children for calamity, for they shall be the offspring of the blessed of the LORD, and their descendants with them.<sup>24</sup>Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.<sup>25</sup>The wolf and the lamb shall graze together; the lion shall eat straw like the ox, and dust shall be the serpent's food. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain," says the LORD.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Hands Spread Out All Day
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers the prayer of chapters 63 and 64, and begins by describing himself as available to people who were not looking for him. Verse 1 has him saying 'Here I am, here I am' to a nation that never called on his name; verse 2 has his hands spread out all day to a people walking their own way. Verses 3 to 5 catalogue what they were doing instead — sacrificing in gardens, offering on bricks, sitting in tombs, eating what the law forbade — and end on the most startling line in the passage: keep your distance, I am too holy for you. Verses 6 and 7 answer that there is a written record, and it will be paid.
verseByVerse.theology: Paul quotes both of the first two verses in a single breath, applying verse 1 to Gentiles who found God without seeking him and verse 2 to an Israel to whom God held out his hands all day long (Rom. 10:20-21). The doctrine underneath is that God's initiative precedes every human search: nobody in this chapter starts looking before God starts calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 5 describes a spiritual condition more dangerous than open rebellion — religious superiority worn by people whose actual practice is listed in the two verses above it. The claim to holiness is being used to keep others at a distance, which is the exact inversion of what holiness does in this book, where it drives a man to confess unclean lips.

verseByVerse.quote: I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, "Here I am, here I am," to a nation that was not called by my name. I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices;
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me; I was ready to be found by those who did not seek me. I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name."

Two chapters of desperate prayer have just ended with God apparently silent. This is his answer, and it does not begin where anyone expects. It begins with God describing himself as findable — and findable by people who were not even looking.

Then listen to what he says twice over: Here I am, here I am.

Those are the words a servant says when his master calls. They are what Isaiah himself said in chapter 6, when he heard the voice asking whom to send and answered Here I am, send me. Now it is God saying them, and he is saying them first, and he is saying them to a nation that has not called his name at all. The master is answering a summons nobody issued.

"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people, who walk in a way that is not good, following their own devices."

The posture in verse 2 is the posture of appeal — arms open, held out, the gesture of someone asking another to come. And the phrase that carries the weight is all the day. Not once. Not at the crisis. For the whole length of the day, held out, to people who were walking the other way while he did it.

Paul takes these two verses and splits them. Verse 1, he says, is about the Gentiles — "I have been found by those who did not seek me; I have shown myself to those who did not ask for me." Verse 2 is about Israel — "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people" (Rom. 10:20-21). One verse describes people who never looked and found him; the next describes people who were looked for and would not come. The difference between them is not effort.

Which settles something about how anyone comes to God. Nobody in this chapter starts the search. The hands were already out, all day, before the first person turned round — and they were still out at the end of the day, after nobody had.

verseByVerse.quote: a people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels; who say, "Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you." These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"A people who provoke me to my face continually, sacrificing in gardens and making offerings on bricks; who sit in tombs, and spend the night in secret places; who eat pig's flesh, and broth of tainted meat is in their vessels."

The catalogue is specific, and every item is a religious act. That is what makes it damning. These are not people who had abandoned worship; these are people worshipping energetically in every direction at once.

Sacrificing in gardens — the Canaanite grove shrines, with their fertility rites. Making offerings on bricks — an altar of the wrong construction, when the law was explicit about how an altar was to be made. Sitting in tombs and spending the night in secret places — consulting the dead, seeking information from the one place God had forbidden anyone to look for it (8:19). Eating pig's flesh and tainted broth — the food laws broken deliberately, as part of a rite.

Then verse 5, which is the sentence to stop at.

"Who say, 'Keep to yourself, do not come near me, for I am too holy for you.'"

These same people — the tomb-sitters, the garden-worshippers — say this. To others. It is a claim to superior sanctity, used as a reason to keep other people at a distance, and it is made by the most religiously compromised individuals in the book.

Notice what holiness does everywhere else in Isaiah. When it came near a man in chapter 6 he said Woe is me, I am lost, I am a man of unclean lips. Real proximity to God produces a confession. What we have in verse 5 is the exact opposite — holiness as a boundary marker, a way of establishing that one is not like the others, and the entirely reliable sign that a person has not been anywhere near it.

"These are a smoke in my nostrils, a fire that burns all the day." The image is not anger so much as irritation that will not clear — smoke in the face, all day, from a fire somebody else lit. The same phrase as verse 2: all the day. He held out his hands all day, and all day this is what came back.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, it is written before me: "I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together, says the LORD; because they made offerings on the mountains and insulted me on the hills, I will measure into their lap payment for their former deeds."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, it is written before me: 'I will not keep silent, but I will repay; I will indeed repay into their lap.'"

Something has been written down, and it is lying in front of God. The picture is a ledger — an account kept, entry by entry, over years — and the reason it is mentioned is that the people in question had concluded from the silence that nothing was being recorded.

That is the ordinary inference and it is always wrong. Silence gets read as absence, or as indifference, or as tacit permission. God's answer here is that the silence was not the absence of a response; it was the postponement of one, and meanwhile the writing was going on.

Into their lap. The lap is the fold of a robe gathered up at the waist, which is what a man in that world used as a pocket — you carried grain in it, or coins, or whatever a merchant had just measured out for you. The image is deliberately commercial: this is a quantity measured and poured into the fold of the buyer's own garment. Nothing arbitrary, nothing approximate. He gets exactly what he came away with.

"Both your iniquities and your fathers' iniquities together." That is a hard clause and it should not be softened into unfairness. Isaiah is not saying children are punished for what parents did; he is describing a generation that continued its fathers' practices and so joined itself to the account. The offerings on the mountains had gone on for centuries.

The chapter has, so far, an outstretched hand in verse 2 and an open ledger in verse 6, and both belong to the same God. Neither one cancels the other, and anyone who has to choose between them has not read to verse 8.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–16 — Two Kinds of People, and a Blessing in the Cluster
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter divides. Verse 8 gives the reason it does not end in wholesale destruction: as a picker holds up a poor bunch of grapes and says do not throw it away, there is juice in it, so God will not destroy them all. Verses 9 and 10 give the servants a landscape, including a valley named after the nation's worst disgrace. Verses 11 and 12 address those who set tables for the gods of luck. Verses 13 and 14 set the two futures side by side four times over — eat and hunger, drink and thirst, rejoice and be ashamed, sing and wail. Verses 15 and 16 give the servants a new name and declare the former troubles forgotten.
verseByVerse.theology: The division running through these verses is not between Israel and the nations but inside the covenant community itself, and it is drawn by response rather than descent. Verse 12 states the ground plainly: when I called you did not answer, when I spoke you did not listen. And verse 16 twice calls God the God of truth — in Hebrew, the God of Amen, the only place in the Old Testament where that title appears.
verseByVerse.examples: The cluster in verse 8 is the remnant doctrine in a picture anyone can hold. What spares the bunch is not that it is a good bunch; it is that there is something in it worth keeping, and the picker can see it. And Achor in verse 10 is the valley where Achan was stoned (Josh. 7) — the place named Trouble becomes a field where cattle lie down, which is what Hosea meant by a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: Thus says the LORD: "As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all. I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"As the new wine is found in the cluster, and they say, 'Do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it,' so I will do for my servants' sake, and not destroy them all."

Here is the reason the chapter does not end at verse 7, and it is a scene from a vineyard at harvest.

A picker lifts a bunch that is mostly ruined — shrivelled, spoilt, not worth the basket space — and is about to throw it on the ground. Then he sees juice in it. And he says the sentence that saves it: do not destroy it, for there is a blessing in it. Something in this bunch will make wine.

That is the doctrine of the remnant in a picture anybody can hold. What spares the cluster is not that it is a good cluster. It plainly is not. It is that there is something in it worth having, and the man holding it can see what nobody standing further off could see.

"I will bring forth offspring from Jacob, and from Judah possessors of my mountains; my chosen shall possess it, and my servants shall dwell there. Sharon shall become a pasture for flocks, and the Valley of Achor a place for herds to lie down, for my people who have sought me."

Two place names, and the second one is doing real work. Sharon is the fertile coastal plain, and there is no surprise in cattle there. Achor is different. Achor means trouble, and it is the valley where Achan was taken out and stoned after he stole from the spoil at Jericho — the site of the nation's first and most humiliating covenant failure in the land (Josh. 7:24-26). It was named after the disaster and it kept the name.

God says herds will lie down there. Not that the valley will be avoided, or renamed, or quietly forgotten, but that the place called Trouble will become the place where animals lie down in the afternoon because there is nothing to be afraid of. Hosea says the same thing in three words: the Valley of Achor as a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

verseByVerse.quote: But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny, I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter, because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen, but you did what was evil in my eyes and chose what I did not delight in."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"But you who forsake the LORD, who forget my holy mountain, who set a table for Fortune and fill cups of mixed wine for Destiny."

Two more gods appear, and in the Hebrew they have names: Gad and Meni, Fortune and Destiny. They were deities of luck, and the worship described is a meal — a table laid, cups filled with spiced wine, an offering set out to persuade fate to be favourable.

It is the most understandable idolatry in the chapter. Nobody sets a table for Fortune out of conviction; they do it because the future is unknown and terrifying and they want some purchase on it. Every generation has its own version of the meal, and most of them are respectable.

"I will destine you to the sword, and all of you shall bow down to the slaughter."

And there is a pun in the Hebrew that the English cannot carry. The word for I will destine is maniti — the same root as Meni, the god of destiny they have been feeding. They set a table for Destiny; God says, very well, I will destine you.

The point is not wordplay for its own sake. It is that fate was never a free-standing force to be negotiated with. There is one God who appoints outcomes, and the people laying a table for a rival have not escaped his appointment; they have simply chosen a worse one.

"Because, when I called, you did not answer; when I spoke, you did not listen." The charge is not idolatry as such. It is the failure to answer — and it lands with particular weight in a chapter that opened with God himself calling out Here I am, here I am. He answered before he was asked. They would not answer when they were.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore thus says the Lord GOD: "Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"Behold, my servants shall eat, but you shall be hungry; behold, my servants shall drink, but you shall be thirsty; behold, my servants shall rejoice, but you shall be put to shame; behold, my servants shall sing for gladness of heart, but you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit."

Four times behold, and four contrasts, and the effect of the hammering is that nobody can pretend the two outcomes have been blurred. Eat and hunger. Drink and thirst. Rejoice and be shamed. Sing and wail.

These are the blessings and curses of Deuteronomy 28 arriving at their final form, and the shape is deliberately covenantal — the same table, the same land, the same God, and two entirely different futures for people who have been living side by side.

The division here is not between Israel and the nations. Both groups in these verses are inside the covenant community. They share ancestry, worship in the same city and read the same law, and the line runs straight between them, drawn by what they did when God called. That has always been the more uncomfortable division and it is the one this book keeps insisting on.

And the terms are physical rather than abstract. Not my servants shall be blessed but my servants shall eat. The vocabulary is bread, water, singing, the noise a person makes when their heart breaks. Isaiah does not deal in general conditions; he deals in what will actually be happening at a table.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name, so that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth; because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"You shall leave your name to my chosen for a curse, and the Lord GOD will put you to death, but his servants he will call by another name."

One group leaves a name behind as a byword, an example used when people want to say how badly a thing can go. The other group is given a new name altogether — which in Scripture is never a relabelling but a re-founding. Abram became Abraham; Jacob became Israel; and to the one who conquers, Revelation says, God will give a white stone with a new name written on it that no one knows except the one who receives it (Rev. 2:17).

"So that he who blesses himself in the land shall bless himself by the God of truth, and he who takes an oath in the land shall swear by the God of truth."

Twice in one verse God is called the God of truth, and the Hebrew is more striking than the English. It is elohei amen — the God of Amen. It is the only place in the Old Testament where God is given that title, and amen is the word a congregation says when it wants to put its weight on something: let it be so, this is reliable, I stake myself on it.

So God is here named after the word people use to agree with him. He is the God who is the Amen — the one in whom what is said and what is true have never once come apart. And at the other end of the Bible a letter opens with a greeting from "the Amen, the faithful and true witness" (Rev. 3:14), which is a title being worn by a person.

"Because the former troubles are forgotten and are hidden from my eyes." The last clause is the extraordinary one. Not merely forgiven, and not merely put behind the people. Hidden from God's eyes — the wound no longer visible to the one who healed it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — New Heavens and a New Earth
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The fullest description of the new creation in the Old Testament. Verses 17 and 18 announce new heavens and a new earth and a Jerusalem created to be a joy. Verse 19 removes the sound of weeping. Verse 20 removes infant death and premature age. Verses 21 to 23 reverse the covenant curses one by one — they will build and live in what they build, plant and eat what they plant, and not labour for nothing or bear children into calamity. Verse 24 closes the distance between prayer and answer to nothing. Verse 25 puts the wolf and the lamb at the same grass.
verseByVerse.theology: This is the goal of redemptive history, and it is emphatically physical: houses, vineyards, work, children, animals, soil. The hope held out is not escape from the material world but its repair, which is why Christian faith has always insisted on a bodily resurrection rather than a released soul. Revelation 21:1 takes verse 17 almost word for word, and Revelation 21:4 takes verse 19.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 is the direct answer to chapter 64, which ended with a community shouting questions at a silent sky. In the world this chapter describes, the answer arrives before the sentence is finished. And verse 25 is careful about what it does not reverse: dust is still the serpent's food, which is the one sentence of Genesis 3 left standing when everything else has been undone.

verseByVerse.quote: "For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind. But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"For behold, I create new heavens and a new earth, and the former things shall not be remembered or come into mind."

The verb is bara, the word used in the first sentence of the Bible and used in Hebrew only of God. Nothing else in the language does this. And what he makes is not a tidier version of the present arrangement but new heavens and a new earth — the whole frame of things, top and bottom, sky and ground.

John saw it and reported it in almost these words: "Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and the first earth had passed away" (Rev. 21:1). Peter uses the same phrase and adds what will be living there: new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells (2 Pet. 3:13).

"The former things shall not be remembered or come into mind." That clause troubles people, and it should be read carefully. It does not promise amnesia, and it is not saying that what happened to you did not happen or did not matter — the God speaking is the one who keeps a ledger in verse 6 and counts every tear elsewhere in Scripture. What it promises is eclipse. The former things will not come into mind because there will be something in front of them large enough that the mind does not go back.

"But be glad and rejoice forever in that which I create; for behold, I create Jerusalem to be a joy, and her people to be a gladness."

And then a sentence that repays a second look: God creates joy. Gladness is not described here as a mood the redeemed will manage to work up once the conditions are right. It is listed among the things he makes, with the same verb as the heavens and the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people; no more shall be heard in it the sound of weeping and the cry of distress."

The first half of the verse is easy to read past and should not be. I will rejoice in Jerusalem and be glad in my people. God is the one enjoying himself here. The gladness of the new creation begins with his, and ours is downstream of it.

Then the second half, and Isaiah does something very precise. He does not say there will be no more sorrow, in the abstract. He says a sound will no longer be heard.

Anybody who has been in a hospital at night, or a house after a death, or a corridor outside a room where bad news is being given, knows that sound. It is the most recognisable noise human beings make, and it is entirely distinct from any other kind of crying. Isaiah promises a city in which it is never heard again — not because people have learned to bear it quietly, but because there is nothing left to make it.

John reaches for the same picture and makes it more intimate still: he will wipe away every tear from their eyes, and death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying nor pain anymore (Rev. 21:4). The tears are not merely stopped. They are wiped off a face, by a hand, one person at a time.

verseByVerse.quote: No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"No more shall there be in it an infant who lives but a few days, or an old man who does not fill out his days, for the young man shall die a hundred years old, and the sinner a hundred years old shall be accursed."

This is the hardest verse in the chapter, and honesty requires saying why. Everything around it describes a world without weeping — and this verse still has people dying in it.

Godly readers take it two ways and neither should be dismissed. Some understand the chapter as describing a long intermediate age before the final state, in which death is drastically reduced but not abolished. Others read the whole passage as poetry that describes an unimaginable condition in the strongest terms an ancient reader had available — for whom the most extravagant possible picture of flourishing was a world where nobody buries a baby and the old die full of years. On that reading the numbers are not a ceiling but a way of saying that the ceiling is gone. The New Testament finally says it without figures: death shall be no more.

Stay with what the verse names, whichever way it is read, because the two griefs it removes are the ones that break people. An infant who lives but a few days. An old man who does not fill out his days — the life cut off with things unfinished, the plans that never got made.

Isaiah does not comfort the exiles by telling them these losses are small. He tells them the losses are going to stop. For anyone who has stood at the wrong kind of graveside that is the promise being made here, and it is made in the specific terms of the loss rather than in general assurances about eternity.

verseByVerse.quote: They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat; for like the days of a tree shall the days of my people be, and my chosen shall long enjoy the work of their hands.
verseByVerse.commentary:
"They shall build houses and inhabit them; they shall plant vineyards and eat their fruit. They shall not build and another inhabit; they shall not plant and another eat."

Read those two verses against Deuteronomy 28, and they turn out to be a curse being undone clause by clause.
